body:
When the support moves
“With more samples, we can detect smaller changes.” But how much smaller? Suppose an instrument produces independent measurements uniformly between zero and an endpoint θ. Another setting moves that endpoint slightly. Most readings could have come from either setting; one reading beyond the old endpoint could not. That sharp edge gives another sample an opportunity unlike the one it has in a smooth shift of an average.
We can calculate what the opportunity is worth. Let the original law be uniform on [0, θ], with θ positive, and compare it with a uniform law on a slightly longer interval. The endpoint changes which observations are possible. Following that change through a two-hypothesis test gives a detection scale that sample count alone would not tell us.
A single observation can rule out one hypothesis
Call the original endpoint \theta and the alternative endpoint \theta+\delta, with \delta>0. If any observation exceeds \theta, it is impossible under the original law. If every observation lies below \theta, both laws remain possible.
Under the alternative, one observation lies below \theta with probability \theta/(\theta+\delta). For n independent observations, the probability that all remain below it is

q_n=\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\delta}\right)^n.

The support boundary is doing the work. Yibi Huang's parameter-estimation lecture uses the uniform-endpoint family to show why a sample maximum constrains which endpoints have nonzero likelihood. Here we use that same boundary for a two-hypothesis test rather than estimate an unrestricted endpoint.
The optimal balanced test has an exact error
Give the two hypotheses equal prior probability and charge the same loss for either wrong answer. On the common region, the original law has the greater joint density: \theta^{-n} rather than (\theta+\delta)^{-n}. Outside it, only the alternative can occur.
The optimal decision is therefore original when all observations are at most \theta, alternative otherwise. It never mistakes the original law for the alternative. Under the alternative, it is wrong with probability q_n. Averaging over the equal priors gives total error q_n/2.
This is a complete calculation for the declared test. It is not an empirical error estimate or a guarantee for an unknown population. Different priors or unequal losses would change the decision threshold.
An inverse-sample change remains detectable
Now let the alternative depend on sample count: set \delta=h/n, for fixed h>0. Then

q_n=\left(1+\frac{h}{n\theta}\right)^{-n}\longrightarrow e^{-h/\theta},
\qquad \text{balanced error}\longrightarrow\frac12e^{-h/\theta}.

The limit lies strictly between zero and one half. Thus an endpoint difference on the 1/n scale retains nontrivial discrimination in this model.
For an arithmetic illustration, choose θ and h both equal to ten. With one hundred observations, the alternative endpoint is 10.1 and the error is about 0.185. As n grows, the error approaches e⁻¹/2, about 0.184, while the endpoint difference shrinks. These are model calculations, not measurements from an experiment.
At a larger difference h/\sqrt n, the same test's error instead tends to zero. The square-root scale is therefore not the smallest scale that retains discrimination here. That does not disprove square-root conclusions in models whose assumptions justify them. It disproves their unrestricted use across different experiments.
Keep local and fixed alternatives separate
If δ is fixed while n grows, q_n decays exponentially. If δ changes with n, a different limiting problem is being asked. A theorem for fixed alternatives cannot be silently transferred to the second comparison.
Exact test error tends to zero for a fixed endpoint gap and for a gap of 10 divided by square root n, but approaches about 0.184 for a gap of 10 divided by n.
All three curves use \theta=10 and the exact error q_n/2. The alternatives differ: a fixed gap of 0.1, a local gap of 10/n, and a gap of 10/\sqrt n. At n=100 the first two compare the same endpoints and meet. Beyond that point, only one keeps moving the alternative closer.
Dependence, measurement noise, a different distribution family or a different decision can change the information in each observation. A noisy instrument may erase the sharp boundary that makes this calculation possible.
MONAD's formal testing work includes this moving-support counterexample. Its particular resource consequence comes from the sharp boundary: each sample has an opportunity to enter a region the original hypothesis cannot produce. Changing that opportunity changes what another sample is worth. Sample count becomes informative through the observation model, and the model's support is part of the detection claim rather than a detail to omit from its reported rate.

Dependence, measurement noise, a different distribution family or a different decision can change the information in each observation. A noisy instrument may erase the sharp boundary that makes this calculation possible.
MONAD's formal testing work includes this moving-support counterexample. Its particular resource consequence comes from the sharp boundary: each sample has an opportunity to enter a region the original hypothesis cannot produce. Changing that opportunity changes what another sample is worth. Sample count becomes informative through the observation model, and the model's support is part of the detection claim rather than a detail to omit from its reported rate.
indexed.notes:
Testing two uniform endpoints
Let P be uniform on [0,\theta] and Q uniform on [0,\theta+\delta], with \theta,\delta>0. Observe n independent samples. On the common region A=[0,\theta]^n, their joint densities are
f_P=\theta^{-n},\qquad f_Q=(\theta+\delta)^{-n}.
Outside A, only Q has positive density. The probability of A under Q is
q_n=\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\delta}\right)^n.
With equal priors and unit loss for either mistake, selecting P on A and Q outside it minimises error pointwise. The resulting risk is q_n/2: the rule never errs under P, and errs under Q exactly on A.
The same overlap calculation gives the normalised total-variation distance
\operatorname{TV}(P^{\otimes n},Q^{\otimes n})=1-q_n.
Indeed, the overlap integral \int\min(f_P,f_Q) equals q_n, since the smaller density on A is the constant Q density and there is no overlap outside A.
Unequal priors change the decision
Let the priors be a for P and b for Q, with a+b=1. On A, compare af_P with bf_Q; outside it, choose Q. The optimal risk is
R_n=\int\min(af_P,bf_Q)=\min(a,bq_n).
If a<bq_n, even a sample entirely within the smaller interval does not outweigh the prior preference for Q, and always selecting Q attains risk a. Otherwise the support-boundary rule attains risk bq_n.
For a local alternative \delta=h/n with h>0 fixed,
q_n=\left(1+\frac{h}{n\theta}\right)^{-n}\longrightarrow e^{-h/\theta},\qquad R_n\longrightarrow\min(a,be^{-h/\theta}).
These are exact comparisons for known endpoints and independent uniform samples. They show why this experiment retains discrimination at an inverse-sample scale. Adding measurement noise, estimating the original endpoint or changing the distribution family produces another testing problem rather than an automatic extension of this calculation.

body:
This collection is about systems whose description itself changes.
A description offers a particular view of a thing. It may preserve every answer we currently need while collapsing states that a later question would separate. The difficulty appears when those states must become distinguishable again: is the answer merely hidden, was it discarded, or does the present language have no way to express it? Even when nothing is lost, different coordinates can leave us disagreeing about which quantities the description has recovered.
There is a bargain behind any useful description. We discard detail so that a problem becomes tractable, while expecting enough of it to survive for the next judgment. Storage, access, the language of the question and the permitted error all participate in that bargain. Its failure can demand another measurement, another representation or a narrower promise. Understanding which change is needed matters more than making the old account confidently answer again.

node.description: An ordered path from a lost answer through affordable questions to the full cost of an accessible repair.

body:
A summary can omit a distinction while an accessible source preserves the means to recover it. That possibility changes what a useful record needs to keep, but only after we understand what was lost and what another read can supply.
The order of this inquiry follows that dependency. First establish which answer the summary can no longer give. Then ask whether the remaining resources let an observer reach it. Only then can a sequence of queries be priced as a repair: a cheap first question may leave an expensive branch, or no feasible branch at all. Storage and access together determine the promise. Losing the source changes what the same retained bytes can support.

body:
What can you distinguish with one more move?
What does looking again add? An object may reveal nothing new from the same position, but one allowed move can bring another feature into view. Two states indistinguishable at a glance can separate during a short investigation. The observer's resources now belong inside the description of what it can know: the next view costs something, and paying for it changes which views remain possible.
Consider three bits (a,b,c). The observer can read only the first position. It can also rotate the state to (b,c,a), paying one unit per rotation. Reading is free in this toy model, and doing nothing is allowed.
With each affordable rotation, another coordinate becomes observable:
Successive reads reveal a, then b, then c, dividing the same eight states into two, four and eight classes; each question mark denotes an unread coordinate.
Read the tree from left to right. The first column uses no rotation and reveals a; one rotation reveals b, and a second reveals c. The edge label is the newly read bit. The resulting two, four and eight classes divide the same eight states.
The state space did not grow. The accessible question family grew. At budget one, states 000 and 001 remain indistinguishable even though their third bits differ. After one rotation, the third bit sits one more paid move away.
Spending the budget changes what remains possible
Suppose two states agree on every observation reachable with budget two. After one rotation they must still agree on every observation reachable with the remaining budget one. Any such observation can be prefixed with the rotation to form a question already covered by the original budget.
Write x\sim_B y when all observations affordable with budget B agree. If an action u costs k\leq B, then the residual-budget law is

x\sim_B y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u(x)\sim_{B-k}u(y).

A separating continuation of cost at most B-k would, when prefixed by u, separate the original states within budget B. That contradicts the premise. Reusing the full original budget after the move would smuggle in an extra resource allocation.
The example assumes deterministic total actions, state-independent non-negative costs and a declared set of observations. If an action sometimes fails, costs depend on the state or measurements disturb it, those features have to enter the model.
Accessibility is different from retention
The observer might have access to the full three-bit state but currently lack the budget to inspect it. The bits are hidden from that observer's present protocol, not erased. Alternatively, a store might have retained only a and discarded b and c. Rotating that one-bit summary does not recreate the original state.
An archive or a fresh measurement could make the missing bits available. Its storage, access permission, transfer and latency are part of the repair. The distinction between “I have not looked” and “I no longer have it” is as important for a retrieval system as it is for this finite model.
More resources do not necessarily mean one scalar
Three-bit rotation uses one simple cost. Real investigations may be limited by memory, compute, bandwidth, trials and elapsed time. A procedure using less memory but more communication is not automatically cheaper. A larger allowance can bring another query within reach, but only if its source remains accessible.
A useful comparison first names which resources can substitute for one another, which are hard ceilings and which measurements actually require them. Otherwise a claim of greater distinguishability may merely have changed the accounting unit.
The broader MONAD question asks how descriptions remain adequate as their admissible questions change. This example makes one part tractable: future questions can be indexed by a finite cost, and spending that cost changes the remaining comparison. The observer's representation is now tied to a protocol with an allowance, rather than to a glance treated as the whole investigation. Choosing among those reads introduces repair cost: an affordable first question may leave an expensive distinction unresolved.

notes.body_html:
The missing distinctions inside a summary class

The essay's factorisation criterion identifies which answers survive a summary. For a family of questions, the relevant distinction is their joint answer signature, not necessarily the complete original state.

For a finite family of questions FF, collect their answers into one signature:

sF(x)=(f(x))f∈F.s_F(x)=(f(x))_{f\in F}.

The coarsest sufficient summary identifies exactly the states with the same signature. A summary sufficient for FF must distinguish different signatures, but it need not distinguish states on which every question in FF agrees. Enlarging FF can split these classes without changing XX.

One record, two possible exchanges

Imagine two requests, A and B, sent at times 0 and 1, followed by replies X and Y at times 2 and 3. The replies' contents do not identify their requests.

Retained event times History h1h_1 History h2h_2
A at 0; B at 1; X at 2; Y at 3 X answers A; Y answers B X answers B; Y answers A
Did X answer A? Yes No

The timestamp-only record is identical in both histories, while the answer to the relation question differs.

Write the retained record as q(h)q(h) and the answer to that question as f(h)f(h). Here

q(h1)=q(h2),f(h1)≠f(h2). q(h_1)=q(h_2),\qquad f(h_1)\ne f(h_2).

No function of the retained timestamps alone can recover the answer for both histories. Increasing timestamp precision does not supply the missing reply relation. Adding a trustworthy relation can distinguish the histories without changing the measured intervals. In the essay's terms, the reply relation does not factor through the timestamp summary.

Note

Drawing the dependency diagram cannot supply a fact omitted by the record. The relation must come from somewhere: a protocol's reply identifier, retained contents that resolve the association, or an explicitly uncertain interpretation. A clearer picture can reveal what we need to learn before it can represent the exchange correctly.

The size of a supplement

Suppose the old summary q:X→Yq:X\to Y is retained and an encoder, with access to xx, may also retain a supplement z(x)z(x) from a finite alphabet ZZ. To recover the complete original state, the pair (q(x),z(x))(q(x),z(x)) must be injective. Within any one fibre of qq, the set of states sharing a summary value (the essay's summary class), different states therefore need different supplement symbols. Consequently

∣Z∣≥max⁡y∈Y∣q−1(y)∣.|Z|\geq\max_{y\in Y}|q^{-1}(y)|.

For finite XX, that bound is attained: enumerate each fibre and reuse the same supplement labels across fibres. The retained value of qq identifies the fibre, so labels need only be unique within it. A fixed-length binary supplement needs kk bits where 2k2^k reaches the largest fibre size.

For example, suppose seven original states have been grouped into fibres of sizes two and five. Five supplement symbols suffice to recover the original state: the two-state fibre uses labels 0 and 1, and the five-state fibre uses labels 0 through 4. The summary says which fibre those labels describe. Fewer than five symbols force a collision in the larger fibre. A fixed-length binary supplement therefore needs three bits, even though no fibre has eight states.

Recovering the full state is a stronger demand than answering one additional question ff. For that narrower demand, states in the same fibre that give the same answer may share a supplement symbol. The minimum alphabet size becomes

max⁡y∈Y∣{f(x):q(x)=y}∣.\max_{y\in Y}|\{f(x):q(x)=y\}|.

If the new question is binary and both answers occur in each of those fibres, two symbols now suffice. Within a fibre, all states answering zero share one label and all states answering one share the other. For several new questions, replace ff by their joint signature. The maximum number of distinct signatures within a fibre determines the supplement alphabet. Adding each question's separate requirement can overcount, because their answers may be related.

Note

What the count measures. This is an exact finite alphabet count. It prices neither the acquisition of the original state nor a variable-length code under a probability law. If the encoder never had access to the distinction, allocating a larger alphabet cannot encode it.

body:
Compression is a promise about questions
Yesterday's summary answered every question we asked of it. Today we need one more answer, and the summary gives two different situations the same name. It has not necessarily become inaccurate. Its earlier success concealed a choice about which differences were worth keeping. Can we locate that choice precisely enough to know what the new question needs?
Take four states, represented by two bits. Suppose the only question is whether the first bit is one. The summary q(a,b)=a answers it perfectly:
Original state	Summary q	First-bit answer	Second-bit answer	
00	0	0	0	
01	0	0	1	
10	1	1	0	
11	1	1	1	
It keeps two classes, \{00,01\} and \{10,11\}, instead of four states. Nothing relevant to the first question has been lost. The final column shows exactly what the summary cannot recover.
Now ask whether the second bit is one. The old summary cannot answer. Both 00 and 01 became 0, but their answers differ. There is no function of that single retained bit which returns both answers correctly. More computation, a more persuasive explanation and a larger language model cannot repair this exact ambiguity from the same input alone.
The question family defines the summary
Write a question as a function f on the original states. It can be answered from a summary q when some function g satisfies

f=g\circ q.

For a surjective summary, this is equivalent to f being constant on every group of states that q merged. Necessity follows because equal summaries give g the same input. For sufficiency, choose any representative of a summary class and return its answer; constancy makes the choice irrelevant. This is the small proof behind the promise.
The second bit existed before anybody asked about it. Making it relevant changed the question family, not the state space. A richer language capable of representing previously unavailable objects would pose a further problem; the two-bit example isolates the simpler change so that its consequence can be calculated exactly.
An agent's notes have the same vulnerability. They can be excellent for the task that produced them and inadequate for a new task. Understanding which answers they preserve lets the agent recognise that inadequacy before it turns an ambiguous record into a confident response. The missing distinction points towards what another read or measurement would need to supply.
A publication gives this a practical form. A listing can keep an article's title, description and address while leaving out its argument. That is enough to choose something to read. It is not enough to check a proof: two revisions can keep the same listing while one changes the crucial step. Gazette keeps the authored article as the source and derives the listing from it, so the reader can follow the address to the reasoning. The short description serves discovery; the retained article makes a deeper question answerable. If only the listing survived, no amount of searching those three fields would recover the missing step.
Repair needs an information source
Several repairs are possible, and they have different costs. Retaining the original two bits preserves both answers directly; a supplement containing the second bit restores just the missing distinction. Measuring the original object again can supply that bit if the object still exists and the measurement is permitted. Without one of these sources, declining to answer preserves the boundary between an unresolved question and a guess presented as reconstruction.
In this example, preserving the ability to answer both coordinate questions requires distinguishing all four states. A binary supplement with two values suffices because each old summary class contains two states. This is finite alphabet accounting, not a coding theorem about an arbitrary stream, and it assumes the supplement's encoder had access to the original state.
The question sits near established mathematics of abstraction. Cousot and Cousot's abstract interpretation studies computation through abstractions; an exact correspondence would locate which existing constructions a changing-question account can reuse and where its additional obligations begin.
An exact supplement and a noisy observation make different promises. A report can be informative while leaving both original states possible. Repeated measurements may reduce a decision's error, but improving the chance of being right is not the same as restoring the answer in every state.
The future cannot be unrestricted for free
If every possible question separating every pair of states must remain answerable, a sufficient summary cannot merge any two states. Perfect future safety then removes nontrivial compression. A useful system must choose a restricted family, tolerate an explicit approximation, retain a repair source or accept that some later questions will remain unanswered.
The two-bit construction gives the changing-description problem a small but useful starting point: a summary's failure can be identified as a particular unanswered question, and a repair can be specified by the distinction it must restore. With budgeted continuations, the future family also depends on what the observer can afford to do next. The summary and the remaining access together determine which promise can still be kept.

body:
The price of another question
A summary can tell us that an answer is missing without supplying the answer. Repair becomes possible only when an available source can still distinguish the states that need different answers. Unlike a distinction erased without a supplement, the original source here remains available, and an observer can ask exact questions of it without changing it. The question is how much access that distinction costs. The available, nondestructive source is essential to the calculation: an experiment whose measurement alters its subject would need another model.
A cheap first question is not the whole cost
Suppose the hidden state is one of A, B or C. The retained summary is identical in all three cases, so identifying the state requires another read. Three source queries are available: asking “Is it A?” costs one unit, asking “Is it B?” costs two, and reading the complete identity costs four. These costs are stipulated for a toy model, not observed retrieval prices.
Ask the first question. If its answer is yes, stop. Otherwise ask the second:
The query tree identifies A for one unit and either B or C for three units.
Each leaf carries the total paid along its path. Removing the second query leaves the cheap-first strategy with a cost-five branch, while a direct complete read still costs four.
The tree's worst-case cost is three, even though one branch finishes after a single read.
No tree can guarantee the answer within two. The first query leaves B and C unresolved, and the second alone leaves A and C unresolved. Distinguishing either remaining pair requires paying for another question. The direct identity read costs four. Three is consequently the minimum worst-case cost for this query set.
Now remove the second query. A cheap-first strategy costs five in its unresolved branch: one for the first question, then four for the full read. Reading the full identity immediately costs four. The cheaper individual query has become the worse first choice.
Optimise over the questions that actually remain
Let S be the states still compatible with what is known. If the required answer is constant on S, set V(S)=0: no further query is needed. Otherwise choose an available question, pay its cost, and continue inside the subset compatible with its answer.
For finite states, queries and outcomes, the minimum worst-case value has the recurrence

V(S)=\min_{j\,\text{productive on }S}\left[c_j+\max_{o:S_{j,o}\ne\varnothing}V(S_{j,o})\right],
\qquad S_{j,o}=\{x\in S:q_j(x)=o\},

where the minimum considers productive queries: those that actually split S. A query that gives the same answer throughout S can be removed from an exact nondestructive tree without losing information. Each productive branch contains fewer compatible states, providing a finite recursion even when a useful query is free.
This is the Bellman principle in the declared query problem. Finding the best tree can still be computationally expensive for a large finite problem.
Unavailable information cannot be purchased with more reasoning
If two compatible states give the same answer to every available query but require different final answers, adaptation cannot help. They follow the same branch after every query and reach the same leaf. No correct tree exists for both.
Conversely, zero repair cost need not mean the answer was stored. A free measurement of an accessible original bit can recover that bit from a constant summary. The result is free only within the declared access model; storage, latency, permission and real instrumentation have not vanished because the mathematical query cost is zero.
Worst-case and expected cost serve different promises
Our tree costs one for A and three for B or C. With equal probabilities,

\mathbb E[\text{cost}]=\frac{1+3+3}{3}=\frac73,
\qquad\max_x\text{cost}(x)=3.

Changing the probabilities changes the expectation without changing that guarantee. A hard deadline may need a worst-case allowance, while a repeated operation may also care about expected expenditure. A method can be cheaper under one promise without being cheaper under the other.
MONAD's formal repair branch establishes feasibility and minimum-cost results within exact, available-source query models. The calculation changes what it means to preserve a useful record. A summary may deliberately omit a distinction if an admitted source can recover it at an acceptable cost. That promise belongs to the summary and the access path together. When the source or query set changes, the same retained bytes can support a different answer, a more expensive one, or none at all.

body:
An observation can leave uncertainty and still support a useful decision. The promise then depends on the error we permit, the source of another observation and the transformations the evidence undergoes. Exact recovery, a bounded decision risk and closeness to a previous description are different successes.
The distinction matters over a sequence of changes. Repeating a measurement can supply new evidence; processing one report cannot do the same job. A simulator can preserve a decision well enough without reproducing the original experiment. A locally acceptable replacement can also carry a chain beyond its first tolerance. These are related questions about what a description preserves, but answering one does not settle the others.

node.title: How tolerances accumulate
node.description: Each replacement stays close to its predecessor. How far can the chain travel from the original?

body:
How tolerances accumulate
Each replacement is close enough to the component it replaces. After several replacements, the result is no longer close enough to the component we started with. Nothing had to fail a local check. What travelled through the chain was permission to vary, not a guarantee that the whole chain stayed within the first allowance.
Choose a positive tolerance \varepsilon. Let three values be 0, 0.75\varepsilon and 1.5\varepsilon. The first two are within tolerance; so are the last two. The endpoints are not. If “close enough” is treated as an equivalence relation, grouping through the middle value merges a pair the original rule meant to distinguish. The calculation is small, but it changes what a sequence of individually acceptable edits can promise.
For Bernoulli laws, total-variation distance is the absolute difference between success probabilities. With tolerance 0.1, the same construction becomes:
The rolling comparison accepts both changes of 0.075, while the fixed-reference comparison rejects the final drift of 0.15 against tolerance 0.1.
The rolling comparison passes both replacements. The fixed comparison passes the first and rejects the second. At step zero there has been no replacement; both distances start at zero.
This is the ordinary difference between a distance threshold and a transitive relation, now expressed for observable probability laws rather than positions on a line.
Local acceptance does not settle accumulated drift
Imagine replacing one component repeatedly. Each candidate is accepted because it differs from its immediate predecessor by less than a tolerance. After enough replacements, the final component can be far from the initial reference. Comparing every candidate to that fixed reference would answer a different question, as would allocating a cumulative error budget and charging each change against it. Deliberately establishing a new reference is another legitimate policy, but it changes the comparison being promised. The error is to run the predecessor-only policy while claiming the guarantee of the fixed-reference policy.
If a distance obeys the triangle inequality and two steps have bounds \delta_1 and \delta_2, then

d(P_0,P_2)\leq d(P_0,P_1)+d(P_1,P_2)\leq\delta_1+\delta_2.

The generic bound is the sum, not the larger allowance. Additional structure may improve it, but it has to be shown.
The loss the distance controls
A representation can be close in one sense and poor in another. Two probability laws can be close under a declared measure while a chosen rare-event decision remains sensitive. Two models can agree on average accuracy while disagreeing on a protected task. A small reconstruction error need not mean low decision regret, and neither is a measurement of repair cost.
For a concrete total-variation statement, take a loss \ell with 0\leq\ell\leq1. Then

\left|\mathbb E_P[\ell]-\mathbb E_Q[\ell]\right|\leq\operatorname{TV}(P,Q).

This controls the change in expected loss across the declared observation laws. The loss range matters: multiplying the loss by a thousand multiplies the possible difference too.
A common simulator lets one experiment supply observations for a decision rule designed for another. Its uniform error buys a bounded-loss transfer guarantee. That is another use of total variation, with its own condition: the simulator must work without knowing the hidden answer.
Exact classes and approximate neighbourhoods serve different jobs
An exact quotient groups states on which every question the description must answer agrees. That gives genuine classes, and each such answer is a function of the class. Approximate neighbourhoods instead carry tolerances and comparison procedures. Their overlap is not a licence to merge them into exact classes.
MONAD keeps these branches separate. Its research question needs approximation, but adding approximation does not merely decorate the exact definitions with a small epsilon. It changes what can compose and what a downstream caller may conclude.
A tolerance lets a system accept variation instead of demanding an exact copy. Its usefulness depends on carrying the comparison through subsequent changes: the reference, observation family and cumulative allowance determine what remains promised. Approximation gains that flexibility by keeping the error visible, rather than by turning overlapping neighbourhoods into identities.

node.title: When one experiment can stand in for another
node.description: A common simulator transfers a decision rule between observation laws. Its error controls the change in bounded loss.

body:
When one experiment can stand in for another
A decision rule expects observations from one experiment, but we can run another. To reuse the rule, we need a way to turn the available observations into the kind it expects. Matching an average output is too weak: the transformation has to work across the unknown conditions the decision is meant to distinguish.
One transformation across the unknown conditions
Comparing observations from two experiments introduces another promise. Let E_\theta and F_\theta be their observation laws under an unknown condition \theta. A simulator K processes an observation from E to resemble one from F. It must be the same Markov kernel for every condition: a simulator given the hidden answer could manufacture precisely the evidence a decision needs.
Suppose its uniform error is

\sup_\theta\operatorname{TV}(KE_\theta,F_\theta)\leq\delta.

Any decision rule D designed for F can then run after K on E. With a loss in [0,1], its expected loss changes by at most \delta in each condition. The reason is concrete: the decision and its loss together are another bounded test of the simulated law. The guarantee concerns using that rule through that simulator, not a claim that the two experiments are identical.
Take two stipulated binary sensors for a condition \theta\in\{0,1\}. The first reports the correct bit with probability 0.9; the second with probability 0.8. Flip the first report independently with probability 1/8. Its probability of remaining correct becomes

0.9(1-1/8)+0.1(1/8)=0.8.

This one kernel simulates the second sensor exactly in both conditions. A decision rule expecting the second sensor therefore has exactly its old risk after the simulation. If the target instead reports correctly with probability 0.82, the same simulated output is within total variation 0.02 of it in either condition. Guessing the reported bit has risk 0.2 after simulation and 0.18 under the target: a difference of 0.02, meeting the bound. The numbers describe a constructed comparison, not a sensor experiment.
The smallest attainable error raises a further mathematical question. Simulation deficiency is the infimum of the uniform errors over common kernels. It follows the deficiency Lucien Le Cam introduced for comparing statistical experiments. An infimum need not have a minimising kernel, so the general transfer uses a kernel within a positive tolerance of it rather than assuming an exact best simulator exists. MONAD formalises that forward guarantee. It does not turn a small decision difference into a converse construction of an affordable simulator; feasibility and resource cost need their own account.
Composing simulators also spends an error allowance
Suppose K simulates F from E within uniform total variation \delta_1, and L simulates G from F within \delta_2. Their composition obeys

\operatorname{TV}(LKE_\theta,G_\theta)
\leq \operatorname{TV}(LKE_\theta,LF_\theta)+\operatorname{TV}(LF_\theta,G_\theta)
\leq\delta_1+\delta_2.

The second inequality uses contraction of total variation under the same Markov kernel L. It does not let the two tolerances collapse into one. Accumulated drift asks why overlapping neighbourhoods fail to give exact classes; simulation asks whether a single admissible transformation can carry evidence into another decision problem. Keeping both the transformation and its error explicit makes the forward promise useful.

Information and error in the same report

Fix a retained-summary class in which the missing bit BB is fair, and let YY be its report through an independent flip with probability p=0.1p=0.1. All probabilities here are conditional on that retained summary. The joint masses are 0.450.45 for each matching pair and 0.050.05 for each mismatching pair. Both marginals are fair. Using natural logarithms, their mutual information is

I(B;Y)=∑b,yP(b,y)log⁡P(b,y)P(b)P(y)=0.9log⁡(1.8)+0.1log⁡(0.2)≈0.3681 nats. I(B;Y)=\sum_{b,y}P(b,y)\log\frac{P(b,y)}{P(b)P(y)} =0.9\log(1.8)+0.1\log(0.2) \approx0.3681\text{ nats}.

Dividing by log⁡2\log2 gives approximately 0.53100.5310 bits. This is the information in one use under the declared fair input law, not a count of exact answers recovered or a repeated-use coding result. The alphabet still has two symbols.

The minimum binary error can be computed from the overlap of the prior-weighted report laws. Write P0(y)P_0(y) and P1(y)P_1(y) for the conditional masses given the two original bits. For a fair prior,

R∗=∑ymin⁡{12P0(y),12P1(y)}=0.05+0.05=0.1. R^*=\sum_y\min\{\tfrac12P_0(y),\tfrac12P_1(y)\} =0.05+0.05=0.1.

At either report, choosing the more probable original bit attains that value. Randomising between answers cannot lower it. The positive information and positive minimum error describe the same channel without contradicting one another.

For three independent uses conditional on the original bit, majority error is the probability of two or three flips, 3p2(1−p)+p3=0.0283p^2(1-p)+p^3=0.028. The repeated evidence changes the observation law. Processing one fixed report, by contrast, cannot increase its information about the bit or beat the best decision already available from it. With 0<p<10<p<1, every finite report sequence has positive probability under both original bits, so exact recovery in every case remains impossible. A zero-error supplement uses a different delivery assumption, not a different name for the same risk.

node.title: A noisy answer is not an exact repair
node.description: A one-bit report can be useful without restoring the missing bit. Repetition changes risk only when it supplies new evidence.

body:
A noisy answer is not an exact repair
A summary may preserve one part of a state and discard another. If a new question needs the discarded bit, a fresh report can help without making the answer certain. That difference is easy to miss when the report and an exact supplement both occupy one binary symbol.
One report, two possible original states
Suppose that within each retained-summary class the missing bit is equally likely to be zero or one, and a source reports it incorrectly with probability 0.1 in either case. Reading the report supplies useful evidence. It cannot supply an exact supplement that recovers the bit in every state: either received value remains possible under either original bit.
For this symmetric source and equal prior, using the reported bit is the best decision, with error probability 0.1. Three reads with conditionally independent errors let a majority vote reduce that error to

3(0.1)^2(0.9)+(0.1)^3=0.028.

The improvement comes from new source observations, not further processing of the first report. Copying that report three times leaves the error at 0.1. Even genuinely independent repetition cannot give a perfect finite guarantee here: every finite sequence of reports has positive probability under either original bit.
Alphabet size, channel information and acquisition cost now answer different questions. Two supplement symbols can represent the exact missing answer when the encoder knows it and delivery preserves it. A noisy report carries information while leaving a chance of the wrong answer. Asking again spends access or measurement resources to change that chance. A repair can trade those costs against an acceptable error, but it has changed the promise from answering every state correctly to controlling a declared risk. The smallest exact repair tree and the best statistical test consequently solve different problems.
MONAD studies the distinction between exact preservation and comparison under uncertainty. An exact summary is sufficient for a family of questions. A statistical observation instead gives a decision some attainable risk under a declared law. Both accounts can be precise, but their hypotheses determine what the word ‘repair’ can mean.

body:
When the description must change
Suppose a model estimates every quantity available to it perfectly. We still cannot decide what to do. The missing answer concerns a relation its language never represented, so a better estimate has nowhere to put it. That failure asks more than another inaccurate prediction does: how can a system recognise that it needs another kind of description, rather than another value inside this one?
That is the larger question behind MONAD. Compression is one entry into it, because a summary makes an explicit choice about which distinctions survive. The programme asks how to follow that choice through changes in questions, allowed continuations and the description itself. It begins with sets and functions rather than assuming that every needed distinction is a coordinate in a vector space.
A correct answer to the smaller question
Consider a small inventory system with two bits: a says whether a replacement part is available; b says whether it is compatible with a particular machine. A dashboard preserves only a. If the question is “is anything in stock?”, that is sufficient. A perfect predictor of a cannot answer “can this machine be repaired?” when repair requires both a and b. States 10 and 11 have the same dashboard answer and different repair answers.
There are several materially different ways this problem can arise. The compatibility information might still be in an accessible original record, so the dashboard hid it. The original might have been discarded, making repair impossible from the retained material. Compatibility might have existed in the old carrier, the things the description represents, but never been an admitted question, one the summary was asked to keep answerable. Or the carrier might represent only stock counts, with no objects for machines, interfaces or compatibility relations at all. Asking for a new column in that last case actually asks for a different description of the situation. These failures should not all be called information loss.
The mathematical test is elementary and useful. Let q:X\to S be the summary and f:X\to Y a required question. The summary answers it exactly when there is a function g:S\to Y such that

f=g\circ q.

If f distinguishes two states that q identifies, no such g exists. That is the fixed-context promise of compression. Failure to factor establishes what this summary cannot answer; it does not yet tell us whether the remedy is another query, a refined summary or a richer carrier.
Relevance belongs to a path
Two machines can have the same current stock and compatibility status but different maintenance histories. Suppose an overheating event leaves a required inspection before a replacement may be used. An inspection flag i now matters:
Description	What it can decide	What is still absent	
Stock bit a	A part is available	Compatibility and inspection history	
Pair (a,b)	A compatible part is available	Whether an inspection is still required	
Triple (a,b,i)	Repair is allowed under this inspection rule	Which other historical consequences matter	
Machine–part compatibility relation	Compatibility across several machines and parts	The rule for extending this relation as interfaces change	
The last row is not just another flag on the original dashboard. It introduces objects and a relation that a stock-only carrier did not express. Choosing which historical consequences deserve flags is also a modelling question, not an automatic consequence of adding storage.
Permitted continuations matter as well. A distinction irrelevant to a routine inspection may become decisive after an admitted upgrade. If a future question can separate states that the present summary merges, preservation must account for that possibility or state the limitation. “Future” here means the continuations considered in the problem, not tomorrow transmitting information into today. Restricting those continuations, allowing revision, retaining a recovery source or accepting a tolerance makes compression useful. Requiring exact answers to every separating future question would force an injective summary and leave no nontrivial collapse.
This joins four ambitions: admitting distinctions when the language is too small, compressing relative to meaningful continuations, accounting for preservation and recoverability, and following relevance along a trajectory. They constrain one another. A path cannot make a distinction relevant and then permit the account of preservation to ignore that the current representation cannot express it. The response may be refinement, a larger context or an explicit unresolved question; silently improving the score inside the old frame is not a response to that failure.
Carrying an old answer into a new description
A change of carrier needs a way to compare the two descriptions. Let e:X\to X' transport an old state into a new carrier, and let f':X'\to Y be a new question. On transported old states, the question is f'\circ e. An old summary q:X\to S preserves that answer precisely when some g:S\to Y satisfies

f'\circ e=g\circ q.

The obstruction is still concrete: find x,y with q(x)=q(y) but f'(e(x))\ne f'(e(y)). This detects where the old summary fails to carry the new question, relative to the chosen transport. It neither constructs e nor justifies why those are the right states to compare.
For the two-bit inventory carrier, adding an inspection flag gives X'=X\times\{0,1\}. If a recorded history supplies the flag through h:X\to\{0,1\}, then e(x)=(x,h(x)) is a particular transport. But if the old state contains no history from which to determine inspection, h is missing information, not a function we can recover by notation. Two extended states (x,0) and (x,1) have the same old projection and can give different repair answers. The added coordinate needs a source.
Introducing machines, parts and their compatibility relation goes further. A stock count does not specify which machine an item fits. There may be several richer descriptions above the same old count, with no preferred one. Here a relation between descriptions may be more appropriate than a single chosen map; answers and permitted continuations also need their own transport. Agreement after relabelling an answer is different from discovering a new distinction. The fixed-map criterion makes one comparison exact while leaving that larger choice of carriers, relations and changing question families open.
When the rules of change become objects
A system can change a state, change the language describing that state, or change which transformations its descriptions permit. The third step makes the rules of change part of what the theory must describe. MONAD’s longer-term recursive goal lets transformations at one level become objects at another. The same problem then recurs: what does this higher-level description preserve, what can it no longer distinguish, and what would justify changing it?
That is more than adding another variable to an inventory record. It asks how a system can revise its representational possibilities while earlier judgments remain checkable or are explicitly marked as no longer portable. The theory does not become its own unrestricted judge. Each level still needs a stated comparison and a warrant for what it admits.
Who supplied the questions?
A preservation theorem is relative to its contract. It may establish that every admitted question survives and still leave out the question a person needed. This is why the origin and justification of the contract are part of the programme, alongside the mathematics of keeping it. A change to a description can propose a new question; it cannot establish the question's relevance simply by making itself answer it. The earlier search for a vocabulary began with that attraction to another way of seeing. The formal question gives the attraction a particular demand: which distinction became expressible, and what can we now do with it?
There is a further ambiguity even when a representation reconstructs every observation: which factors did it recover? Different latent coordinates can explain the same observed distribution. A preservation contract needs a reason to call one coordinate compatibility, inspection or something else; reconstruction by itself cannot provide that meaning.
Abstract interpretation supplies established ways to reason about sound approximation and completeness relative to properties of a system. MONAD's inquiry is not a replacement name for that machinery. The question is how such precisely understood fixed-context constructions behave when the carrier, question family and permitted changes themselves become objects of change. Where an existing construction answers the question, the useful outcome is an exact correspondence, not a claim of a new theory.
The challenge is to make inadequacy visible before it becomes a confident answer. A residual can prompt the question, but surprise alone cannot distinguish noise from a missing variable or a language that has become too small. A calculus of changing descriptions would have to say what changed, where the new information came from, what earlier judgments still mean and which questions now demand another representation.

body:
Which factors did we recover?
A model reconstructs the observations perfectly, and its learned coordinates are independent. We would like to call those coordinates the underlying factors. The difficulty is not necessarily that the fit is poor. Another set of coordinates may satisfy the same observational tests while mixing the quantities we intended to separate.
The observed distribution leaves a choice
Even an unlimited collection of the same kind of observation may leave the intended factors unidentified. Locatello and colleagues' 2019 result concerns latent generative models with more than one factor and a factorised prior admitting a density. They construct invertible, entangling changes of latent coordinates which, with the corresponding change of decoder, preserve the observed distribution. A representation separating the original factors can mix the transformed ones. Identifying the intended factors therefore needs information beyond that observed distribution, such as explicit model and data biases or supervision. This is not an impossibility theorem for every representation-learning problem or for MONAD.
A finite illustration makes the ambiguity visible without reproducing that continuous construction. Let two independent fair bits be U and V. Describe the same four states either by (U,V) or by (A,B)=(U\mathbin{\oplus}V,V), where \oplus is exclusive-or:
Original coordinates (U,V)	Changed coordinates (A,B)	Probability	
(0,0)	(0,0)	1/4	
(0,1)	(1,1)	1/4	
(1,0)	(1,0)	1/4	
(1,1)	(0,1)	1/4	
Both coordinate pairs are uniform and independent. The inverse U=A\oplus B, V=B lets a decoder reconstruct exactly the same observations. Independence and reconstruction therefore cannot tell us whether the first coordinate means U or parity. Yet changing V while holding U fixed changes both A and B. An observed, controlled change to the named factor supplies a comparison absent from the four observational frequencies.
For a modelling contract, that extra information has a concrete job. A label can associate a coordinate with a named quantity; a restricted model family can encode an assumption about how the quantities combine; an intervention witness can show what changes when one of them is altered. Each may exclude alternatives, under its own conditions. A useful test keeps an observation-preserving alternative beside the preferred account and asks which supplied evidence actually separates them. Choosing the questions after seeing the representation could otherwise make the representation pass a contract whose meaning it helped invent.
Meaning has to enter somewhere
The inventory example behind a change of description names stock, compatibility and inspection because the problem already tells us what those quantities mean. A representation learner does not inherit that interpretation merely by finding three coordinates. The source of the names and relevant interventions is part of the modelling problem.
This is a narrower question than whether a description needs another carrier. It can arise with two invertibly related descriptions of exactly the same states. Their observational adequacy agrees, while their response to a named intervention differs. A test of factor recovery therefore has to say what information fixes the intended factors, and whether that information actually excludes the alternative representation.

body:
This collection is about how a computation's organisation, which parts interact and what they keep, can be learned rather than declared.
A reasoning architecture can contain more than a set of capable parts. Which parts interact, what experience they retain and how their roles change can themselves become learned computation. The attraction is an organisation shaped by the task: local specialisation, useful memory and information reaching the place where it changes an answer.
MUON investigates the adaptive local unit; HENA investigates the collective. Their ambition reaches beyond placing stock models in a fixed workflow. A hierarchy could arise through local interaction and evolve with what the system is trying to do. An early cue reaching a later request is one concrete demand on that organisation, not its whole purpose.
Q-MUON and Q-HENA ask the same two questions on a quantum substrate, so two essays here compare a quantum unit with its classical counterpart and ask what recovering a saved swarm can preserve once its resources have changed.
Messages still consume capacity, memory choices lose things and local improvements can conflict. Following the interaction into its consequences reveals whether the learned organisation helped: what relation survived, which route carried it, what the group could answer and what the full computation cost.

body:
Change the rule without moving the finish line
Imagine a search discovering a routing rule with a better score. Looking closer, the improvement came from no longer counting missed deadlines. The rule has changed the answer to an easier question, while the original jobs still wait. What kind of variation would let a system improve its way of working without losing the problem it was meant to solve?
Consider a toy search for a rule that routes jobs between two workers. One worker is faster for short jobs; the other handles long jobs more reliably. The objective combines completed work with a penalty for missed deadlines. A candidate which changes the routing threshold is a legitimate variation. One which drops missed jobs from the denominator changes the meaning of success. Both edits might increase the visible score, but only one addresses the declared problem. Protecting the denominator and the measurement procedure from anything the candidate may edit keeps that difference observable.
A fixed workload passes through an editable routing candidate to a protected evaluator, with run feedback updating only permitted state.
The routing rule can change; the workload and the way success is measured stay outside the candidate's control.
The threshold may change which worker receives a job. Queue estimates may change within the state budget, and messages within the communication ceiling. The generator cannot supply easier jobs to a favoured candidate, and the evaluator continues counting every missed deadline. These boundaries make the candidate's extra expressiveness testable.
A local rule has a collective expression
One way to make the search concrete is to let a candidate specify a local update rule: how a unit responds to its inputs, which messages it sends and which bounded internal state it retains. The candidate is the rule; the pattern produced by many units interacting is its collective expression. Changing the rule may change traffic concentration, specialisation or recovery after a unit disappears, even when every unit runs the same code. A topology drawn in advance and a topology shaped by those interactions therefore answer different questions.
For the two-worker example, a richer candidate could use a small local state for recent queue pressure and send a bounded message when its own deadline risk rises. The behaviour emerges over a workload rather than existing entirely in the threshold's source text. It could reduce missed deadlines, oscillate between workers or turn communication into the bottleneck. Evaluating only the local rule on isolated jobs would miss those effects; evaluating its collective behaviour under one workload would miss its sensitivity to another.
One illustrative rule keeps an exponentially smoothed queue estimate q_i at worker i:

q_i(t+1)=(1-\alpha)q_i(t)+\alpha n_i(t),\qquad 0\leq\alpha\leq1,

where n_i is its current queue length. The worker sends a pressure alert when q_i crosses a threshold \kappa. A short job normally goes to the faster worker, but a pressure difference exceeding \tau sends it to the other one, subject to that worker's availability. The research proposal limits what a candidate may edit. Improving one niche and selecting across niches are different operations
Local improvement asks whether a small edit improves a particular rule under its existing conditions. Population selection asks which rules deserve further attention across different conditions. A diverse archive can preserve a rule that is excellent for long jobs even if another dominates the common short-job workload, but keeping specialists also changes what a leaderboard can mean. Incomparable niche scales make global ranking arbitrary; a single global score can instead erase the specialists the archive was meant to preserve. Local improvement and population selection therefore need different comparisons.
Causality proposes separating validation-gated edits inside a niche from selection across a population. The experiment would start with frozen mutation and evaluation machinery, candidates held within fixed limits and recorded ancestry, making it possible to compare local improvement with the population’s ability to keep useful specialists.
This mechanism has a place in the architectural programme. MUON supplies the unit boundary against which a local rule is defined; HENA would execute the rules and population dynamics. The aim is to discover useful organisation, including specialisation and routes that a designer did not prescribe for every case. What the search edits is the local rule inside a fixed experiment, not a live model’s architecture.
There is a nearby practical comparison in changing an agent's procedure while keeping its model fixed. SkillOpt uses trajectory feedback and validation to search in that text space. Its target helps locate the difference here: the proposed routing experiment varies a collective update rule, not just a procedure executed by one agent. A validation-gated search can supply a useful pattern without transferring its results to the new candidate or workload.
The safety control is also a research variable
A frozen evaluator and an editable one create different experiments. In the routing example, allowing a candidate to drop missed jobs from its score exposes the temptation to improve the mark without improving the work. An independent count of completed jobs and missed deadlines can then reveal the exploit. That count must stay out of the candidate's reach, or the comparison loses the means to distinguish improvement from tampering.
Local selection adds another question. It can preserve useful specialists that a global average would discard, but a niche can also develop a locally convenient deception. The relation between locality and reward hacking is therefore an experimental variable, not a safety property conferred by distributing the population.
What a rejected change contributes
A candidate's ancestry explains how it arrived, including revisions that made performance worse. A rejected routing rule can make a later search less wasteful when its workload, evaluator and failure remain identifiable. Its value is the specific contrast: this routing rule, under this evaluator and workload, performed worse. Remembering only that it lost says little about the next candidate, while an explanation of why it failed remains another hypothesis. Retaining both the result and that distinction lets a later search reuse the evidence without turning one failed proposal into a universal prohibition.
An ancestry record would distinguish a child that lowers \tau from one that changes the alert policy, and keep the parent, edit, niche and comparison attached to each. If the first child improves short-job throughput but worsens long-job deadlines, it may be rejected in one niche and worth testing in another. If a later child also changes \alpha, the earlier result cannot be attributed to that new pair of edits. Rejected siblings are consequently part of the search history, not missing rungs on a straight ladder of winners. Search cost includes their trials too.
Search and use have different boundaries
A sandbox can let candidates vary aggressively without allowing each variation to replace a live component. The protected evaluator and its separate evaluation coordinates give those variations something stable to answer to. A live change also needs the operator's decision; generating it is a different operation from using it.
The routing example makes the boundary concrete. A better completion rate can come from allocating work more effectively or from dropping missed jobs out of the denominator. Only the first improves the work. Letting the rule evolve is useful precisely because the independent count can still tell those outcomes apart.

body:
How much of a collective answer belongs to its parts, and how much to their arrangement? We need a usable component boundary before that question can be tested. Even then, individually adequate units can lose a joint fact or compete for the same capacity.

node.title: What would count as emergent hierarchy?
node.description: An early cue and a later request reach different units. Can their learned organisation carry the relation into an answer?

body:
What would count as emergent hierarchy?
An early cue reaches one unit; a much later request reaches another. Neither sees the whole stream. Somewhere between them, the cue has to survive, find a route and become part of the answer. Can the units learn an organisation that makes that happen, rather than relying on a designer to place the right connection in advance?
That is the constructive question in HENA. Sparse communication, limited memory and local rules give the units a way to interact; useful hierarchy would have to emerge through what those interactions contribute. A nested arrangement is easy to draw. The harder problem is discovering an arrangement whose changes help the task, and understanding why it helps more than a simpler one.
From an explicit organisation to a learned one
Pale makes an organisation explicit enough to operate: responsibilities, capabilities, context and coordination are described and compiled. HENA’s architectural direction goes further. Could more of that organisation arise and evolve from intent through interactions among local units? The intended result is a collective model whose learned organisation carries part of its intelligence, rather than a fixed workflow arranging otherwise unchanged models.
This is why hierarchy matters beyond an attractive arrangement of nodes. Specialisation, memory and routes would have to become useful responses to what the collective is trying to do. A future HENA could stand alone; a surrounding harness could retain its responsibilities for external effects and resources while less of the internal coordination needed to be specified by hand. The cue example gives one small demand on that larger architecture.
The work happens between units
A concrete candidate gives each unit a local slice of input \tilde x_i, state h_i, neighbour messages m_i and reads r_i from a limited record store:

h_i(t+1)=f_\theta\bigl(h_i(t),\tilde x_i(t),m_i(t),r_i(t)\bigr),
\qquad
m_i(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i(t)}a_{ij}(t)g_\theta\bigl(h_j(t)\bigr).

The neighbourhood \mathcal N_i(t) and weights a_{ij}(t) are subject to a routing policy. These are candidate update rules, not a trained HENA model. Their interest is that each unit's access is local while the task may require a relation distributed across several units.
Imagine a long stream containing a machine's maintenance cue near its beginning and a repair request much later. One unit processes the cue; another receives the request. The first has to preserve an interpretable record, the second has to reach it, and the answer has to use the relation between them. Sending every input to every unit avoids part of the problem by abandoning locality. Having a powerful central unit read the full stream can solve it by abandoning the many-unit explanation. A useful sparse composition would have to carry the relevant distinction through its actual messages and memory operations.
Each round can read records, exchange messages, update local state and write selected records before a subset produces an answer. The proposed objective combines task loss with communication and latency costs, and a declared term controlling routing entropy. The direction of that last term matters: discouraging uncertainty can collapse traffic onto one route, while encouraging dispersion can send irrelevant messages everywhere. A sparse graph is not a substitute for specifying what routing is meant to learn.
Consider an illustrative three-unit trace with only two retained-record slots. Unit A receives “machine 7 requires inspection” and writes a record carrying the machine identity and requirement. Intervening events compete for the second slot; retaining them must not silently evict the first. When B later receives a request to repair machine 7, it needs more than a generic “maintenance happened” message. A route through C can carry the key needed to find A's record, after which B can combine that record with the current request. Sending a key, reading its record and applying the inspection rule are three separate operations, each observable in the trace.
This trace suggests distinct ablations. Erase the machine identity while retaining the same-sized record and the matching relation disappears. Keep the record but disable the learned route, and the information survives without reaching B. Deliver the record but remove its influence on the answer, and retrieval succeeds while the task fails. These are constructed failure modes, not HENA results. They give a collective experiment something more precise to explain than an attractive cluster diagram.
There is an established constructive precedent for local learned rules. In Growing Neural Cellular Automata, cells perceive a local neighbourhood and share a learned state-update rule; training shapes the resulting pattern, and different training regimes affect persistence and regeneration. That experiment shows how a local update can participate in a global process. HENA asks a different task question about reasoning, adaptive communication and limited records. The analogy suggests mechanisms to study, not a transfer of the cellular automaton's result.
Sparse edges do not make the whole computation cheap
Suppose N units each send at most k messages per round and interact for R rounds. Then the send count obeys

M\leq NkR.

For 64 units, four outgoing messages and eight rounds, the ceiling is 2,048 sends. All-to-all communication without self-messages over the same eight rounds would make 64\times63\times8=32{,}256 sends. The comparison holds the round count fixed; it does not silently compare eight sparse rounds with one dense round. Nor is a send count a runtime measurement: payload size, routing, memory access and inference remain part of the cost. If the rounds grow with N, an apparent scaling benefit can disappear.
The intended experiment must measure the whole answer, not only the sparsity of one adjacency matrix. A system can save communication while spending more compute searching for routes. It can save memory by forgetting the very relation the task requires. Joint facts are a simple way to make that failure visible.
A per-unit store with K vectors of width d has Kd scalar positions; across N units the raw vector state has NKd, before keys, provenance and indexing. Sparse selected edges do not make edge selection sparse: a router that scores all N destinations per unit still performs a dense search before sending its few messages. Record lookup can have the same hidden cost. Measuring destination candidates examined, payload bytes, reads, writes and rounds alongside inference exposes where a proposed saving actually occurs.
Organisation has to change the answer
An imposed hierarchy gives the adaptive organisation something concrete to improve on. At the same task and budgets, the designer's best fixed hierarchy may already carry the needed relation efficiently; a flat organisation or a single unit may do so with less coordination. Those comparisons can reveal a contribution that a changing graph alone leaves invisible: the organisation has learnt a useful route, rather than merely learnt to redraw itself.
One possible question is whether units specialise into stable roles and route information to the right place under a changing workload. A topology can look orderly while contributing nothing to the answer. Removing its learned routing while preserving compute supplies a sharper contrast: if performance remains unchanged, the apparent organisation may be incidental. If performance falls, the task, routing decisions and communication cost reveal what the organisation contributed. Removing a useful unit asks a different question about how that contribution survives disruption.
The criterion cannot be invented after seeing the prettiest run. Nor should every successful cluster count as a new level of description. A nested coarse-graining simply forgets distinctions at successive levels unless a separate argument establishes what new question became expressible.
When the swarm becomes a costly single model
Suppose most requests eventually reach one strong unit. The other units might be useful filters, or they might merely add delay before the same model answers. The distinction appears when the strong unit runs alone at the same total budget. Similarly, a sparse swarm that needs many rounds can spend its communication saving on repeated inference, while shared memory can circulate a mistaken premise until the whole group agrees with it. Each case changes the account of where the computation happens: filtering may help the answer, repeated inference may consume its saving, and shared agreement may preserve an error rather than useful knowledge.
HENA's proposed first stock-model swarm would make those comparisons possible as an orchestration experiment. MUON's shared slot would allow its units to vary while the task and resource boundary stayed fixed. A later differentiable architecture would ask how the units can learn routing and organisation together, with the stock-model comparison supplying a baseline. Useful specialisation, information that reaches the right place, and the cost of making that happen are the contributions that would give the learned organisation its meaning.

node.description: A replacement model returns a valid reply but fails the caller's task; the shared boundary gives three different things to investigate.

body:
Three tests for a reasoning unit
Replace the model behind an interface and the caller still receives a valid reply. On a harder task, the answer fails; under load, the successful answer arrives too late. What did the shared interface let us preserve? It made the replacement possible, but a valid reply is only part of what the caller needs. The new model also has to do the task within the available time and resources.
MUON starts with a unit slot: inference, declared state, ordered records, resource behaviour and lifecycle operations. Behind that boundary, its longer-term micro-transformer design asks how temporal processing, routed computation and distributed records could form a small reasoning unit. The interface lets those internals change without making their differences disappear.
The native unit is intended to be a local building block of an intelligence, not only a wrapper around a larger model. Its smallness makes organisation among units necessary: useful computation, experience and specialisation must combine through HENA rather than be assumed to exist inside every part. The contract is meant to let units work together while each unit's architecture develops.
The state a unit carries from earlier inputs can contribute in two quite different ways. It can choose which of the unit's routed computations, its experts, runs, or it can carry information into the prediction itself. When a cue arrives well before the request that needs it, those two paths need separate tests: knowing which computation to select is not the same as preserving the cue that computation needs. A direct path from that state to the output, compared with a control in which the state only routes, would expose the distinction; MUON's guide follows that comparison through a road notice. Whether several dependent transformations share one routing choice is another design decision, separate from the question of whether the final unit fits its caller.
One request through MUON's unit slot
The proposed slot makes a request inspectable before the model runs. The caller declares its requirements: input shape, streaming, deadline, state and replay needs. A capability report identifies the exact model, tokenizer and backend and describes what the filler supports. Its estimate of this request's demand is then compared with fixed capacity and current availability. Those are five different things: a requirement is not a capability, an estimated demand is not capacity, and reported availability is not a reservation.
Only an atomic reservation gives the request a live allocation. Two callers may both see enough free capacity; admitting both on that observation alone would overspend it. A lease binds the allocation and its lifetime. Expiry or a failed reservation leads to a typed refusal, rather than an inference that silently consumes another caller's budget.
After admission, inference produces an output and may change the declared state. Ordered records connect input, output and resource events within an episode, step and sequence. A checkpoint captures the state according to its opaque, summary or typed descriptor; restoration must honour that descriptor's promise. Shutdown also belongs to the lifecycle and leaves a final record. This is the proposed dataflow that a stock filler would have to implement before its benchmark result could be interpreted as a MUON-slot result.
The MUON slot compares caller requirements and filler capabilities, estimates demand, reserves a lease or refuses, then records inference and lifecycle events in a host-owned store.
Requirements, capabilities, estimated demand, capacity and availability remain distinct; the reservation is the step that allocates resources. Checkpoint, restore and shutdown contribute records alongside inference.
The record protocol and the store are separate again. A host can retain its own unit records using shared semantics without calling a research evaluator. That permits different local memory designs to be compared through a common record boundary, rather than requiring every unit to surrender its history to one central service.
Three claims, three questions
Conformance asks whether the component honours the contract. Does it really stream when it says it does? Does its checkpoint restore the declared state? Does it refuse work it cannot reserve resources for, rather than silently truncating it?
Task adequacy asks whether it meets a floor for a particular workload. Correct message shape does not answer that question. Nor does an accurate model identifier.
Substitution asks whether one component can replace another in a named context, under specified observations, tasks and tolerances. Two units might both exceed an accuracy floor but differ so much in latency or error distribution that only one fits a caller's needs. Opacity hides internals; it does not hide capability or erase differences.
Count the work around the model
Consider a hypothetical workload with a total compute allowance of 100 units. Ten small agents use six units each. Their router uses fifteen, memory and verification use ten, and failed attempts consume another fifteen. That uses the full hundred. Reporting only the sixty units spent inside agents makes the swarm look cheaper by excluding forty units of its own work. The same accounting has to apply to the single stronger model, which also needs orchestration and verification. Count rejected proposals in both systems.
Work in the hypothetical composition	Compute units	
Ten units, six each	60	
Routing	15	
Memory and verification	10	
Failed attempts	15	
Whole answer	100	
The intended experiment has four arms: many identical units, one stronger unit, a mixture of units and a no-swarm control. Compare them on the same tasks, with the same capability floor and resource ceilings. Compute, latency, energy and communication may still move in different directions; keeping those costs visible would show what one arrangement saves and what it spends in exchange.
A losing thesis can leave a useful architecture
If the many-small-unit arm loses after coordination is charged, the strongest admissible filler can still serve the slot. The interface remains useful even if the swarm thesis fails, because its contract lets the experiment change implementations without rewriting success criteria to protect a preferred result. Stock models would provide the first working controls; a proposed micro-transformer unit would have to earn its place later. Conversely, a swarm victory on one task would establish a reason to use that composition there, not a universal replacement for larger models.
The same discipline applies to a quantum counterpart. Preserving the outer contract establishes a common comparison boundary, not equal behaviour or quantum advantage. An interface is the beginning of a fair test, not its conclusion.
