node.title: Every pair can agree while the whole differs
node.description: Matching pairs can leave incompatible wholes possible; parity and simultaneous reservations reveal different missing relations.

body:
Every pair can agree while the whole differs
Every pair of reports agrees. Taken together, the reports still leave two incompatible worlds possible. How much of the whole did those pairwise agreements actually preserve? A tiny distribution gives the question an exact answer; a shared pool of resources reveals a different way locally satisfactory reports can fail to describe a working arrangement.
The statistic that every pair loses
Two laws on three bits differ only in which parity they admit:
The even law puts probability one quarter on 000, 011, 101 and 110, and the odd law on 001, 010, 100 and 111, yet every two-bit marginal is uniform under both.
The upper panel shows disjoint joint supports; every omitted probability is zero. The lower panel shows what survives projection: each two-bit outcome has probability one quarter under both laws.
Look only at the first two positions. In either law, 00, 01, 10 and 11 each occur with probability 1/4. For example, the first law's 00 pair comes from 000; the second law's comes from 001. Dropping the third coordinate removes their difference. The same happens for either other pair. Every pairwise marginal agrees; the joint parity always differs.
Reconstructing the joint distribution from these marginals has no unique answer. In the relational version, joining the three pair projections admits all eight tuples, including the four the original relation excluded. The projections lost a constraint.
This is not the stronger claim that no global model exists. Both distributions are valid global models. Nor is it true that all labelled pairs of one concrete tuple lose that tuple: knowing its coordinate pairs determines its coordinates. Projecting a distribution or relation is a different operation from redundantly encoding one occurrence.
The request that every pair permits
Three jobs each require four units from a pool of ten. Any pair requires eight and fits. All three require twelve and do not. A matrix of successful pair tests cannot authorise the aggregate allocation.
Here the missing object is not a higher-order probability law. It is a simultaneous reservation. Reading the same availability snapshot three times and approving each request separately does not create twelve units. The allocator must account for accepted reservations together.
The two examples have a shared lesson but different mechanisms. Statistical projection loses a joint constraint; separate capacity decisions fail to account for a shared resource. Treating both as generic “emergence” conceals what needs fixing.
A binary graph can still represent a many-way fact
The issue is not a competition between graph and hypergraph names. A graph can introduce an occurrence node and link it to its participants through typed roles. Its identity keeps the participants attached to one event instead of allowing arbitrary recombination. The W3C's n-ary relation patterns describe this established approach.
The encoding must preserve the constraint its user needs. Adding a node is not automatically sufficient: if its roles, time or occurrence identity disappear in an export, the export may again permit combinations the original excluded.
What this asks of a swarm
In HENA, a useful unit is not evidence of a useful composition. Units can make correlated errors, interpret messages differently, contend for memory or jointly exceed a budget. A task may depend on a joint relation none of their isolated summaries retained.
These two failures give a proposed HENA experiment concrete tasks: concurrent requests that contend for shared capacity, and an answer that depends on a joint fact its messages must retain. Comparing the swarm with simpler alternatives at matched resources would reveal whether its organisation helps preserve those relations. A learned hierarchy would matter if its routing and memory carried those joint relations more effectively, rather than merely arranging units into nested groups.

body:
Comparing a quantum unit with its classical counterpart
Suppose the central step of a computation becomes dramatically shorter. Preparing its input and obtaining a sufficiently precise answer take longer than before. Has the computation become cheaper? A quantum candidate makes that familiar boundary question especially consequential: the circuit is part of a workload whose preparation, measurement and repetition may decide whether the change helps.
Q-MUON proposes a quantum unit behind MUON's unit contract; Q-HENA proposes a corresponding swarm adaptation. A common outer boundary would make the change of substrate easier to examine: what task can the candidate perform, at which tolerated error, and for what complete cost?
The same interface supplies a question, not an answer
If both units accept a common task and return a common result shape, they can be compared. That establishes a boundary for observations; it does not establish equal accuracy, equal state or interchangeable checkpoints. The three tests for a reasoning unit separate these questions: conformance establishes whether each unit honours the contract, task adequacy tests whether it meets the workload's floor, and substitution concerns replacing one with the other in a specified context. Those answers give an advantage claim a meaningful object.
Preparation, measurement and repetition
There are constructive questions worth putting inside that boundary. A quantum feature map could transform classical input before a kernel comparison; a parameterised circuit could learn a measurement-based response; a composite design could ask what correlations its units can establish and use. Each proposes a different place where the substrate might matter. None becomes a Q-MUON result merely by being a recognised research direction.
Candidate mechanism	Question it makes concrete	Work the comparison must include	
Quantum feature map and kernel	Does this representation separate the chosen examples usefully?	Encoding, kernel estimation, sample needs and classical kernel alternatives	
Parameterised circuit	Can its parameters learn the task response?	Optimisation, repeated measurements and classical simulation where applicable	
Composition of quantum units	Does their interaction contribute to the collective answer?	Communication, usable correlations, unit preparation and collective evaluation	
Choosing a task would narrow one of these into an experiment. Keeping them distinct prevents “quantum reasoning” from standing in for an unspecified mechanism.
Suppose a candidate circuit uses few internal operations but requires expensive data preparation and repeated shots to estimate its answer. Counting only the circuit's central step would compare different workloads. The classical system's preprocessing and verification must also be charged at the same boundary.
The task size and tolerated error decide how much repetition is needed before the circuit produces a usable answer. A simulation can expose how that cost behaves in the chosen model; device noise and calibration introduce another experiment. Wall-clock time also includes access arrangements, queues and classical work around the circuit. A shorter run through one provider cannot, by itself, isolate a substrate-level advantage.
Trainability is itself a question
The barren-plateau result of McClean and colleagues identifies exponentially vanishing gradients for an important class of randomly initialised parameterised circuits. It is a reason to examine a proposed ansatz, not a theorem that every quantum learning design fails. Escaping that obstacle would make a construction easier to train, but would not establish an advantage over classical methods: the same construction may admit an effective classical simulation. The relevant comparison therefore includes appropriate classical methods, rather than a deliberately weak baseline or a convenient library default.
Whether many quantum units can form a useful collective
MUON and Q-MUON investigate the local building block; HENA and Q-HENA investigate how many units can form a useful intelligence. Q-HENA's target is a distributed quantum compute substrate with quantum communication, entanglement-mediated memory and hierarchy from quantum local rules. That is an architectural aspiration, not just a test harness around an isolated circuit. The comparisons locate what would make it worthwhile, while the exact unit and collective mechanisms remain research.
Keeping the classical and quantum paths apart makes a negative result usable
Keeping classical and quantum paths distinct avoids forcing every result into a succession story. A quantum component may lose on the intended task. It may win only within a narrow scale or error regime. It may remain inconclusive because the total comparison is too costly. Those are informative outcomes if the claim was fixed beforehand.
Compatibility makes such findings portable only to the extent actually shown. Repeating a probability distribution, restoring a declared internal representation and recovering a live swarm are different promises. A component might preserve one while requiring the next run to start afresh. The useful comparison identifies which task benefit survives that change, and which preparation or recovery cost must be paid again.

Wall-clock time also includes access arrangements, queues and classical work around the circuit. A shorter run through one provider cannot, by itself, isolate a substrate-level advantage.
Trainability is itself a question
The barren-plateau result of McClean and colleagues identifies exponentially vanishing gradients for an important class of randomly initialised parameterised circuits. It is a reason to examine a proposed ansatz, not a theorem that every quantum learning design fails. Escaping that obstacle would make a construction easier to train, but would not establish an advantage over classical methods: the same construction may admit an effective classical simulation. The relevant comparison therefore includes appropriate classical methods, rather than a deliberately weak baseline or a convenient library default.
Whether many quantum units can form a useful collective
MUON and Q-MUON investigate the local building block; HENA and Q-HENA investigate how many units can form a useful intelligence. Q-HENA's target is a distributed quantum compute substrate with quantum communication, entanglement-mediated memory and hierarchy from quantum local rules. That is an architectural aspiration, not just a test harness around an isolated circuit. The comparisons locate what would make it worthwhile, while the exact unit and collective mechanisms remain research.
Keeping the classical and quantum paths apart makes a negative result usable
Keeping classical and quantum paths distinct avoids forcing every result into a succession story. A quantum component may lose on the intended task. It may win only within a narrow scale or error regime. It may remain inconclusive because the total comparison is too costly. Those are informative outcomes if the claim was fixed beforehand.
Compatibility makes such findings portable only to the extent actually shown. Repeating a probability distribution, restoring a declared internal representation and recovering a live swarm are different promises. A component might preserve one while requiring the next run to start afresh. The useful comparison identifies which task benefit survives that change, and which preparation or recovery cost must be paid again.

node.title: Recovery across a changing world
node.description: A saved swarm returns to a world whose leases and components have changed; what can its recovery actually preserve?

body:
Recovery across a changing world
A saved process can remember what it believed. It cannot ensure that its resources, device or permissions still exist. Recovery has to reconcile the saved state with the current world, not simply deserialize the most convenient file.
Consider a hypothetical swarm that reserved eight units from a pool of ten and then crashed. Its checkpoint records the reservation. During the interruption the lease expires and those eight units are reassigned. Loading the file cannot revive the old lease: doing so would let two holders claim the same capacity. Resuming the work requires a new reservation from the current allocator. If none is available, the process cannot resume even though its saved state loaded correctly. The checkpoint preserves a belief about capacity, while the current allocator determines whether that capacity can be used.
Three restoration promises
A restore may aim at the same declared state, a state equivalent under specified observations, or merely a fresh start. These are different promises. Even exact restoration of one component does not establish exact recovery of the surrounding system.
For a quantum unit, compatibility also depends on the backend, circuit representation, topology, calibration or noise model and measurement procedure. A classical checkpoint does not acquire quantum meaning because the new unit preserves the old API. Q-MUON's proposed profile separates exact, semantic and restart-only modes so that each candidate would declare which state and observations its restoration preserves.
If a swarm contains one restart-only unit, its saved internal state is not restored. A semantic unit needs its equivalence criterion checked. Combining these with exact units cannot produce an unqualified claim of exact whole-swarm recovery.
Proposed mode	What carries across the interruption	What the task must tolerate	
Exact	The declared internal state	Changed external resources may still prevent resumption	
Semantic	A possibly different state with the declared observable behaviour	Differences outside the declared observations	
Restart only	No retained internal state	Repeating preparation and any lost work	
Semantic recovery needs declared observations
Suppose two restored components behave alike on three selected probes but differently on a fourth. Whether they are equivalent depends on whether that fourth probe belongs to the declared family. “Same enough” requires a named family and tolerance, for the same reason that a summary preserves answers to particular questions rather than every possible future question. A changed calibration or capability profile can invalidate the promised comparison even when the checkpoint bytes themselves remain unchanged.
For a finite illustration, compare restored states 000 and 001. Reading the first bit gives zero in both; reading the second does too. A profile that declares only those reads can treat the states as equivalent. Declaring the third read separates them completely. For probabilistic probes, one possible comparison is

\sup_{p\in\mathcal P}\operatorname{TV}\bigl(L_p(x),L_p(y)\bigr)\leq\varepsilon,

where L_p(x) is the output law of probe p on state x. This illustrative comparison makes equivalence depend on the probe family \mathcal P and a tolerance \varepsilon. A task using a probe outside \mathcal P would ask for a guarantee the comparison never made.
Recovery of the collective task
Q-HENA proposes adapting HENA's swarm responsibilities on top of quantum units. A recovery experiment would have to follow the restored units into the collective task, identifying the candidate, profiles, budgets, repetitions and coverage. That makes it possible to ask whether the differences each unit's restore mode allows change the result the swarm was meant to produce.
In the reservation example, the bytes can restore exactly while the work still cannot resume. In a mixed swarm, one unit may resume from its exact state, another from a state that agrees only on selected observations, and another from a fresh start. The collective result depends on which of those changes the task can tolerate, not on the number of files that loaded successfully.
A useful recovery report tells us what was restored, what was restarted, what changed and what was refused. That makes partial recovery a visible state rather than a silent weakening of the promise. It also keeps rollback honest: returning to older bytes is not permission to return to older authority.

node.title: What should a surprise change?
node.description: A traffic prediction fails. Should the unit remember the event, adjust a parameter or propose another account of the road?

body:
What should a surprise change?
A predictor expects a quiet road and observes heavy traffic. The mismatch deserves attention, but it does not tell us whether a sensor is broken, the model is poor, the distribution changed or an omitted event blocked the road. Surprise identifies a failure of expectation, not the mechanism behind it. That distinction matters when a system uses surprise to change itself: a signal that deserves a memory write does not automatically deserve a parameter update, and neither automatically warrants a new variable or a structural edit.
Keeping an event is not learning a rule
Three operations can follow the same residual: retaining an event for later inspection, adjusting a learned parameter using evidence across episodes, or proposing a change to the model's structure. Keeping the event preserves a particular observation; learning attempts to improve predictions beyond that observation; a structural proposal changes what the model can represent. Their risks and time scales differ because they alter different parts of the unit.
The Titans paper gives a technical example of learning a neural memory at test time using a memory-loss gradient as a surprise signal. Its mechanism connects surprise to a particular memory objective. A useful adaptation would need to specify what the unit can change, which evidence triggers that change and how the change affects subsequent tasks.
MUON proposes studying surprise-driven learning inside a reasoning unit. The candidate controller would need to use the unit's actual state, measurements and update operations. A retention rule and a parameter-learning rule can then be compared on their own terms, rather than treating every response to the same residual as one learning mechanism.
For a local construction, let h_t be temporal state and M_\phi a candidate adaptive memory. It predicts a target v_t from a key k_t, using a memory loss

L_t=\tfrac12\lVert M_\phi(k_t)-v_t\rVert^2.

The gradient \nabla_\phi L_t has a specific object to update. A candidate step \phi_{t+1}=\phi_t-\eta_t\nabla_\phi L_t attempts to improve that key-to-target association. It is not a gradient of a global causal graph, and its norm measures sensitivity of this loss, not the event's importance to every later task. This illustrates a mechanism to compare, rather than an implemented MUON memory.
A prediction head would have to consume h_t, a memory read, or both for the stored distinction to reach the output. If a closure cue changes only which of the unit's routed computations, its experts, is selected, the unit can still forget which road is closed. A matched routing-only control keeps that choice while removing the direct state contribution; a frozen-memory control keeps the architecture while removing adaptation. Their errors reveal different parts of what the candidate memory does.
Scale can masquerade as importance
Suppose one proposed signal has two components: gradient magnitude and distributional divergence. Adding their raw values is arbitrary. Multiplying the loss by a constant can enlarge the gradient term without supplying stronger evidence that anything important changed.
A bounded controller can instead calibrate each component against a fixed reference, transform it into a finite dimensionless value between zero and one, and combine those values using non-negative weights summing to one. If the transformed values are 0.8 and 0.2, equal weights give 0.5; weights 0.25 and 0.75 give 0.35. The weights express a policy, not a discovered truth about the event.
Calibration also needs an answer for inputs outside the reference distribution. Clipping limits numerical damage; it does not make an unfamiliar input understood. Rejecting non-finite values and bounding an update prevents one class of instability without proving the chosen update is useful.
Three responses to one signal
Suppose the calibrated aggregate is S=0.5. A candidate learning-rate rule is

\eta(S)=\operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\eta_{\mathrm{base}}[1+\alpha\tanh(\beta S)],\eta_{\min},\eta_{\max}\right).

With \eta_{\mathrm{base}}=0.01, \alpha=1, \beta=2 and allowed rates from 0.005 to 0.02, it gives approximately 0.0176. This is a larger step within a specified range. The parameter update still needs a loss, a gradient and a choice of parameters allowed to adapt. Saturation limits the rate; a sufficiently large or misdirected gradient can still make the update harmful.
A memory response answers another question. A clipped logit followed by a sigmoid can assign a bounded priority to the event using surprise, estimated usefulness and age. If the score passes a retention threshold, the owner of the record store may keep it. A road closure may be worth remembering for the next route even if one episode is insufficient evidence for changing a general traffic model. Forgetting the event and declining to learn a new rule are therefore different decisions.
A structural response is slower again. Persistent error might suggest a missing event variable, a different expert connection or a richer representation. Crossing a threshold nominates such a hypothesis for comparison; it does not make the edit true. These three time scales create a useful design: attention now, adaptation across observations, and structural search when the existing account keeps failing. They also give an experiment something to separate. Retention alone, bounded parameter adaptation and separately evaluated structural proposals can be tested against a fixed unit on the same changing stream.
Response	What changes	What later observations can test	
Retain the closure report	Which event remains available	Whether another route decision uses it	
Update traffic-model parameters	Predictions within the existing representation	Whether held-out traffic predictions improve	
Propose a closure variable	What the model can express	Whether the richer account explains cases the old one cannot	
The same road event can justify examining all three without making them interchangeable updates.
Different explanations predict different failures
A sensor fault should leave evidence in the consistency of the measurements, while a model fitted on newer data may respond differently to a changing traffic distribution. A residual that persists across matched conditions poses a different problem from one tied to a particular setting. An omitted event variable becomes a useful candidate when adding it improves the account on held-out cases, rather than merely explaining the surprising observation after the fact. These comparisons gather different evidence; the initial residual establishes none of their conclusions.
A structure-changing system therefore needs a proposal boundary. Crossing a surprise threshold may nominate a candidate edit. An independent comparison decides whether the edit improves the task without violating protected behaviour. The signal cannot both propose the explanation and certify it.
The sharper question is whether the failure arose inside an adequate representation or because the representation cannot answer the required question. Noise, model error, drift and lost information demand different repairs. Surprise keeps the inquiry open long enough to discover which one we have.

node.title: What does the measurement establish?
node.description: A record gets its chance to be useful through the policy that selects it. How can its contribution be estimated?

body:
This collection asks what a measurement establishes about a change, and why a candidate must not choose the test that admits it.
The decision to keep a record changes what an agent can later retrieve. Retrieval changes what it does, and what it does changes the outcomes available for scoring that record. Usefulness is entangled with the policy that gives a record its chance to be useful.
A faster request after a cache rollout raises a similar difficulty. The cache may have helped, or the traffic may have changed. A comparison that separates those explanations is more informative than the before-and-after number alone. In memory, the comparison becomes harder still: an early cue may matter only after many intervening decisions, and the record with the newest reward may not deserve the credit.
Estimating a contribution and deciding how much confidence to place in that estimate are different problems. Repeated runs can be stable while sharing one mistaken premise. Independent-looking reports can all descend from the same observation. Coverage can omit the very regime in which a rule fails. These distinctions affect the result itself, not only the presentation of an evaluation.
Small exact examples make some of the difficulty visible. An influence can cancel along a path, and a moving support can change a detection rate. Their assumptions differ, but both make a tempting shortcut answerable to a constructed case. The aim is a useful estimate whose interpretation survives closer examination, so that the next decision is informed by what was actually learned.

body:
A score cannot repair the attribution it was fed. Before estimating a memory record's usefulness, we need a comparison that gives its contribution a meaning. Before trusting the resulting estimate, we need to understand how it behaves and what the evaluation left unexamined.
That dependency supplies the order here: an intervention and its alternatives, an update from attributed experience, then scrutiny of the resulting comparison and the completed experiments that give it an outcome and a price. A smooth or reproducible score can still track the wrong contribution. Separating those stages lets a failure reach the stage capable of explaining it, instead of demanding a more confident number from the last one.

body:
Did the cache make it faster?
Suppose a cache rollout coincides with lower request latency. The graph establishes a change in the measured requests. It does not yet establish how much the cache caused, because traffic, request mix, upstream behaviour and other releases may also have changed. Crediting the wrong mechanism has a practical consequence: the next rollout may repeat the change and fail to repeat the result.
The comparison behind the metric
For an eligible population over a stated period, the question is what would change if requests used the cache rather than the previous path. The assignment unit and outcome give that comparison its meaning. Average latency, tail latency, error rate and resource cost answer different questions; an improvement in one can hide a loss in another.
For a request i, write Y_i(1) for latency with the cache and Y_i(0) for latency without it. The average treatment effect is

\tau=\mathbb E\bigl[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\bigr].

A negative value means lower average latency. We cannot serve the same request both ways in the same circumstances and observe both outcomes. The experiment therefore needs a defensible way to use different requests to estimate that missing comparison.
A before-and-after comparison leaves time and treatment tangled. Random assignment can make the comparison stronger, but only if assignment is followed, measurement is comparable and interference is understood. A shared cache can let one group's traffic change the other group's experience. Randomisation does not erase that mechanism.
Mechanism	What changes in the experiment	
Request mix changes	Compare eligible requests with comparable difficulty, not whichever traffic happens to arrive	
Cache warm-up crosses groups	Assignment to independent cache pools may be needed instead of request-level assignment	
A release changes both paths	Hold that release common across groups or model its separate effect	
The cache changes resource contention	Include the shared load in the treatment definition rather than treating it as unrelated noise	
With interference, latency is better written Y_i(z_i,s_i): it depends on the request's assignment z_i and the cache state s_i created by other traffic. A pool-level comparison then asks about the effect of a cache policy, not an isolated request switch.
An experiment with paired cache pools
One possible design uses paired, isolated cache pools and a common release. Within each time block, randomly assign one pool to the new cache policy and the other to the old path. Keep eligibility and traffic allocation fixed, and declare whether warm-up belongs inside the measurement window. Pool assignment prevents the same cache entries being warmed by both arms. Shared upstream capacity can still connect them; isolation has to concern the actual interference, not only two names in a configuration.
The causal picture explains why. Time and request difficulty can both affect latency; a rollout scheduled at a particular time can become associated with either. Assignment changes the cache policy, which changes cache state and upstream reads, which affect latency. Shared upstream load can also carry a path from one pool's policy into the other pool's result. Random assignment addresses the first association, while independent pools address one interference path. Neither automatically removes the shared-load path.
Suppose four paired blocks produce the following invented mean latencies. Each block has two newly prepared pools and the same stipulated eligible workload; these are arithmetic examples, not measurements of a deployment.
Paired block	New-policy pool, ms	Old-path pool, ms	Paired difference, ms	
1	90	100	-10	
2	104	110	-6	
3	85	95	-10	
4	114	120	-6	
The average paired difference is -8 ms. Averaging all requests without retaining their blocks would discard part of the assignment design. Treating every request as an independent randomised unit would also overstate how many independent treatment allocations occurred: the policy was assigned to pools. Reusing a warm pool in another block would introduce carryover that this stipulated construction excludes.
A report of this experiment would keep the block-level differences and allocations, request counts and difficulty mix, warm-up interval, upstream-read counts, errors, tail latency and resource cost together. Four blocks are a small comparison, not grounds for a precise production guarantee. If average latency improves while timeouts rise, the experiment has found a trade-off rather than an unqualified victory. If an uncached negative-control workload improves similarly, shared load becomes a concrete competing explanation to examine.
A useful explanation includes its strongest alternative
The proposed mechanism might be fewer upstream reads. A competing explanation might be lighter traffic. Their predictions differ: the cache hypothesis should relate improvement to the requests it can actually serve, while a general load reduction may affect uncached requests too. A negative control can expose an explanation that fits every movement too conveniently.
Repeated trials help distinguish a stable result from noise. They do not repair a biased assignment, a leaking comparison or a metric changed halfway through. Uncertainty belongs beside the effect and its assumptions, not in place of them.
Retaining a useful record is another question
Reckon studies which records an agent should keep under a budget. Removing a record and observing a performance drop is an informative contrast, but it still needs a design and assumptions before receiving a causal interpretation. A retention score can be useful without being causal proof.
Delayed contribution makes the memory problem harder. A record can matter well after its arrival, and other records may have intervened before the successful decision. An updated estimate has to absorb some account of that credit. The update can faithfully process the observations while their attribution still needs the same care as the cache rollout.

notes.body_text:
One record through seven observed updates
A calculator result in Reckon’s simulated conversation was retrieved and scored seven times. Its utility moved from 1.5 to 0.667221. Following the actual reads, rewards and score updates makes the clamp and equal-credit rule visible.
This is the first complete episode in context_controls.jsonl from run 045229537dbf, recorded on 15 November 2026 at source 2f74405. The file’s SHA-256 is f2bdee7009b1e7e7b40c108802489a3ef082f74431a1332d37af3f855c635d96. It contains both the transcript and event stream for the same record IDs. This notebook embeds their scoring fields; it does not rerun the conversation.
The episode used FIFO, 100 record slots, seed 42 and the simulated backend with no fallback. It finished eight steps with 13 records and no pruning. It demonstrates scoring under ample memory, not a benefit from selective retention. Notebook source cell 27 fixes that control; the separate inspection episode and policy-comparison transcripts are not used here.
The adapter writes tool results with utility 1.5. On observation, SIMPLE credit divides one equally among the retrieved records, and the kernel applies clip(0.9 * old + 0.1 * credit * reward, 0, 1). Rewards and retrieved IDs below are saved observations. Credit and the predicted next utility are calculated from the source rule.

# Scoring fields selected from one complete retained episode.
# All 17 score updates are retained, not only the record shown in the table.
turns = {0: {'retrieved_ids': [], 'reward': 0.5}, 1: {'retrieved_ids': ['68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.0}, 2: {'retrieved_ids': ['68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.0}, 3: {'retrieved_ids': ['68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.5}, 4: {'retrieved_ids': ['e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.5}, 5: {'retrieved_ids': ['bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.5}, 6: {'retrieved_ids': ['b2056658-f826-4fe5-af0d-1e446f22963e', 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.5}, 7: {'retrieved_ids': ['29b5edb9-5e24-4ec2-a7d6-3b560e5c7360', 'b2056658-f826-4fe5-af0d-1e446f22963e', 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 3.0}}
# Each update: event ID, step, sequence, record ID, old utility, new utility.
updates = [[5, 1, 2, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 1.5, 1], [8, 2, 2, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 1, 0.9], [12, 3, 3, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.9, 0.8600000000000001], [16, 4, 3, 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', 1, 0.925], [17, 4, 4, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.8600000000000001, 0.7990000000000002], [20, 5, 2, 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 1, 0.9166666666666667], [21, 5, 3, 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', 0.925, 0.8491666666666667], [22, 5, 4, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.7990000000000002, 0.7357666666666669], [26, 6, 2, 'b2056658-f826-4fe5-af0d-1e446f22963e', 1.5, 1], [27, 6, 3, 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 0.9166666666666667, 0.8375], [28, 6, 4, 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', 0.8491666666666667, 0.77675], [29, 6, 5, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.7357666666666669, 0.6746900000000002], [33, 7, 2, '29b5edb9-5e24-4ec2-a7d6-3b560e5c7360', 1.5, 1], [34, 7, 3, 'b2056658-f826-4fe5-af0d-1e446f22963e', 1, 0.9600000000000001], [35, 7, 4, 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 0.8375, 0.8137500000000001], [36, 7, 5, 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', 0.77675, 0.7590750000000002], [37, 7, 6, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.6746900000000002, 0.6672210000000003]]
selected_record = "68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7"
eta, lower, upper = 0.1, 0.0, 1.0

import math
rows = []
for event, step, sequence, record_id, old, observed in updates:
    turn = turns[step]
    assert record_id in turn["retrieved_ids"]
    count = len(turn["retrieved_ids"])
    assert count == len(set(turn["retrieved_ids"]))
    credit = 1 / count
    reward = turn["reward"]
    before_clamp = (1 - eta) * old + eta * credit * reward
    expected = min(upper, max(lower, before_clamp))
    assert math.isclose(expected, observed, rel_tol=0, abs_tol=1e-14)
    if record_id == selected_record:
        rows.append((step, count, reward, credit, old, observed, before_clamp))
assert len(updates) == 17 and len(rows) == 7
assert [r[0] for r in rows] == list(range(1, 8))
assert all(math.isclose(a[5], b[4], rel_tol=0, abs_tol=1e-14)
           for a, b in zip(rows, rows[1:]))
print("All 17 recorded score updates match the same episode’s reads and rewards.")
print("The selected record has seven consecutive updates.")

stdout
All 17 recorded score updates match the same episode’s reads and rewards.
The selected record has seven consecutive updates.

print("Step  Read  Reward  Credit    Old       New")
for step, count, reward, credit, old, new, before_clamp in rows:
    print(f"{step:>4}  {count:>4}  {reward:>6.1f}  {credit:>6.3f}  {old:>8.6f}  {new:>8.6f}")
print(f"First update before clamp: {rows[0][6]:.2f}; saved value: {rows[0][5]:.2f}.")
print(f"Last credited target: {rows[-1][2] * rows[-1][3]:.2f}.")

stdout
Step  Read  Reward  Credit    Old       New
   1     1     0.0   1.000  1.500000  1.000000
   2     1     0.0   1.000  1.000000  0.900000
   3     1     0.5   1.000  0.900000  0.860000
   4     2     0.5   0.500  0.860000  0.799000
   5     3     0.5   0.333  0.799000  0.735767
   6     4     0.5   0.250  0.735767  0.674690
   7     5     3.0   0.200  0.674690  0.667221
First update before clamp: 1.35; saved value: 1.00.
Last credited target: 0.60.

What changed the score?
At the first update, the saved reward is zero. Multiplying the old utility of 1.5 by 0.9 gives 1.35; the upper bound makes the saved result 1.0. The clamp is doing real work here.
Later, more records share the outcome. The final turn records a task reward of 3, shared among five retrieved records. This record’s target is therefore 0.6, below its previous utility of 0.67469, so its score falls again to 0.667221. A positive reward need not raise every retrieved record’s utility. The reward is the simulator’s task score, not a probability of success; the utility is not a measured causal effect.
The record being followed contains the calculator result 2835 from 81 × 35. It remains among the retrieved records while the conversation adds a length constraint, a tone constraint and search results. Equal credit is assigned by retrieval membership, not by a demonstration that the calculation helped satisfy a later constraint. That is precisely why a scorer trace and a causal evaluation answer different questions.
Source and reproduction
The memory-manager guide explains retrieval and observation; the notebook guide distinguishes controls and policy comparisons. At source 2f74405, notebook cell 27 runs the FIFO 100-slot context controls and cell 33 saves them as complete results. The adapter calls observe with that turn’s reward and retrieval context; its default credit policy is SIMPLE. The kernel constants fix the learning rate at 0.1 and output bounds at zero and one.
The original notebook 04_agentic_conversation_simulator.ipynb has SHA-256 5cdc3f1f4189f441f658ac7df05a7aed8c2052f2e23be951ab8f4737b435203f; its adapter conversation.py has SHA-256 fd21368189b1e907139a0ecde40e8801b03a4a5fdd9368883c7ec55872b00c97. Both match the saved source record. The saved rows allow the arithmetic to be checked without the laboratory or a model call. Agreement with those rows establishes this numerical reconstruction; it does not independently identify the binary loaded by the original process.

body:
EMA and Bayesian updates for online scoring
A cue arrives before it is useful. Many observations later, it helps an agent choose the right door. The memory budget was too small to keep everything in between, so a retention policy had to make its choice before that outcome arrived. How should experience change the score attached to the cue, and how quickly should an old score lose its hold?
Reckon's laboratory uses an exponential moving average in particular utility-update paths. One scalar absorbs each credited observation with little work or storage. Following that update into the delayed-cue problem lets us examine both its attraction and the decisions hidden inside the credit it receives.
An EMA decides how quickly the past fades
The implemented form is

u_{t+1}=(1-\eta)u_t+\eta c_t o_t,

where u is the stored utility estimate, \eta the learning rate, c the assigned credit and o the outcome. The implementation clamps the resulting utility to configured lower and upper bounds; the first arithmetic illustration below remains inside zero and one, so clipping does not change its arithmetic. For a fixed scalar, this update uses constant work and storage. The laboratory’s default is \eta=0.1, with utility clamped to [0,1]. For the first arithmetic illustration, deliberately choose u_0=0.4 and the faster rate \eta=0.25:
Credited observation co	Old score	New score	
1	0.4	0.75(0.4)+0.25=0.55	
0	0.55	0.75(0.55)=0.4125	
The arithmetic makes the estimate's response concrete, while leaving the origin of its credit unresolved: it does not show that the record caused the outcome.
Credit matters as much as decay. Giving a record credit in proportion to its existing score feeds the estimate back into itself. A smooth transformation may improve numerical behaviour without removing that circularity. The useful test is a matched comparison against alternatives, not the elegance of the recurrence.
Delayed usefulness makes credit difficult
Consider a constructed key-and-door task. An early observation says which of two doors will open later. Several irrelevant observations arrive between the cue and the door. The agent can retain only one record. Keeping the cue can improve the eventual choice even though nothing immediately rewards the write; retaining the latest vivid observation can destroy the only useful distinction. First-in-first-out and recency are informative controls precisely because delayed usefulness can disagree with both.
Credit assigned after success is still ambiguous. Suppose the agent retrieved both a key cue and a general navigation hint. Equal credit gives each half the outcome. Weighting credit in proportion to existing utility gives the already favoured record more evidence for being favoured. If utilities are 0.9 and 0.1, the successful episode reinforces a nine-to-one allocation before the episode has shown which record mattered. The current laboratory’s SHAPED rule instead normalises \log(1+e^{u_i/s}) across retrieved records, with default scale s=1 and utility 0.5 when a record’s utility is missing. For utilities 0.9 and 0.1, this gives shares of about 0.625 and 0.375, rather than nine to one. It softens the preference without establishing that either record caused the success. The credit and memory-manager guide explains the implemented rules and update path. Matched omission or substitution runs can supply a more informative contrast, provided they keep the task and alternative information access comparable.
The completed Tutor, Continual, Conversation and TextWorld comparisons put the current policies beside their controls and full probe price. They test retention outcomes; the softplus credit transformation still needs its own matched comparison against equal credit.
The task also separates storing, retrieving and using. A cue kept in memory but never reached cannot help the answer. A cue retrieved and quoted may still be ignored by the policy. A successful answer might come from guessing. Measuring those events separately lets the outcome challenge the score rather than merely reward activity around the record.
A calculator result keeps receiving credit
An actual simulated conversation makes the distinction visible. In a recorded Reckon episode, the agent calculates 81 \times 35 and stores the result, 2835. The conversation moves on to a length requirement, a tone requirement and searches for information. The calculator result remains among the retrieved records, so it continues to receive a share of each turn’s reward.
This episode used first-in-first-out retention with 100 slots and finished with thirteen records, without pruning. It lets us examine scoring under ample memory; it does not establish that a selective policy kept the right things. The saved notebook follows one record through all seven updates and checks the episode’s full set of seventeen score updates against the recorded reads and rewards.
Step	Records retrieved	Recorded reward	Equal credit	Old utility	New utility	
1	1	0	1	1.500000	1.000000	
2	1	0	1	1.000000	0.900000	
3	1	0.5	1	0.900000	0.860000	
4	2	0.5	1/2	0.860000	0.799000	
5	3	0.5	1/3	0.799000	0.735767	
6	4	0.5	1/4	0.735767	0.674690	
7	5	3	1/5	0.674690	0.667221	
The retrieved IDs, rewards and old and new utilities are saved observations. Equal credit is calculated from the source’s rule of dividing one among the retrieved records; the table rounds utilities to six decimal places. The notebook keeps the original precision and recomputes each update with \eta=0.1 and bounds [0,1].
The first row shows the clamp at work. This adapter writes tool results with an initial utility of 1.5. With a zero reward, the next value before clamping is 0.9(1.5)=1.35, which becomes 1 at the upper bound. The following rows carry that new value forward.
The final row is more surprising. The turn earns a reward of 3, but five retrieved records share it. This record’s target is therefore 3/5=0.6, below its previous utility of 0.67469. Its score falls to 0.667221 even after a positive reward. The simulator’s reward is a task score, not a probability of success.
The arithmetic is doing what the rule asks. What it has not established is whether the old calculation helped satisfy the later tone or length requirement. Retrieval membership gave it credit. A causal comparison would have to ask what changed when that record was unavailable, under a suitable alternative. The trace makes the scoring mechanism inspectable without resolving that harder question.
A posterior adds a model, not automatic certainty
A Bayesian alternative would specify what is being estimated, how observations arise and what prior assumptions apply, then update a posterior. A suitable model can carry uncertainty that a single moving average does not. A misspecified model can also produce confident answers about the wrong quantity.
For an elementary candidate, suppose p is the probability of success when a particular cue is available under a fixed task policy. A \operatorname{Beta}(1,1) prior and conditionally independent Bernoulli observations give

p\mid s,f\sim\operatorname{Beta}(s+1,f+1),
\qquad\mathbb E[p\mid s,f]=\frac{s+1}{s+f+2}.

Three successes and one failure give a posterior mean of 4/6, rather than the raw fraction 3/4.
Note
This Bayesian comparison model is not an implemented scorer. The model’s uncertainty concerns that availability-conditioned success probability, not the cue's causal contribution. Policy selection and an easier set of trials can bias the observations without violating the posterior arithmetic.
We can follow the same four binary observations through simple estimates. Let the sequence be 1,1,0,1, take u_0=0.5, \eta=0.25 and full credit c_t=1 for the EMA, and retain the uniform Beta prior. A running mean supplies a baseline that uses no decay or prior:
Observation	EMA	Running mean	Beta posterior mean	
1	0.625	1	2/3	
1	0.71875	1	3/4	
0	0.5390625	2/3	3/5	
1	0.654296875	3/4	4/6	
These methods are processing an availability-conditioned success trace here, not receiving causal credit. The comparison isolates their arithmetic before introducing a retention decision. Two records can have the same posterior mean and different numbers of observations, which changes posterior concentration; an EMA's current scalar does not supply that count. Conversely, a late zero immediately changes the EMA's weighting of all earlier observations. Neither behaviour establishes which estimate will keep the useful cue under a memory ceiling.
That simple model also treats the success probability as stationary. An EMA deliberately fades old observations; an undiscounted posterior accumulates them. When a hidden task mode changes, a score can remain confident in a cue that belonged to the old mode. A fair comparison must therefore declare whether adaptation comes from a fixed decay, a change model or another reset rule, and count the observations each needs to recognise the change.
The budget belongs inside the test
The value of a retention policy depends on what it keeps within the memory and compute budget, including the cost of probing a record's usefulness. First-in-first-out, least recently used, random retention and simple importance rules are meaningful baselines. A delayed cue tests whether a record survives until needed; an occasionally observed hidden mode tests detection lag; a bounded replay buffer tests forgetting across tasks. A small tutoring simulation can ask whether retaining a student's specific misconception helps a later hint more than retaining a generic summary. These are different uses of memory, not interchangeable points on one leaderboard.
Storage cost changes the decision too. Ranking utility per byte can favour a small cue over a large history record, but a ratio-based greedy rule is only a heuristic when useful records interact or costs are indivisible. Two fragments might matter only together. And a probe that consumes another trial or model call spends part of the same budget whose allocation it is supposed to improve. A better estimate earns its place only when the decisions it supports repay that expense.
A removal contrast depends on assignment, alternatives and measurement for its causal interpretation. If a run without the cue also changes the task or gives the agent another source of the answer, the contrast has changed more than the retained record. A responsive score cannot disentangle those changes on its own.
Reckon's completed retention comparisons now connect the implemented policies to measured outcomes and their probe price. Comparing shaped credit with equal credit, or a moving average with a separately specified posterior-based retention rule, remains another experiment. Those comparisons would ask whether a better account of a record's usefulness and uncertainty changes what the agent keeps enough to repay the work of estimating it.

EMA and Bayesian updates for online scoring
A cue arrives before it is useful. Many observations later, it helps an agent choose the right door. The memory budget was too small to keep everything in between, so a retention policy had to make its choice before that outcome arrived. How should experience change the score attached to the cue, and how quickly should an old score lose its hold?
Reckon's laboratory uses an exponential moving average in particular utility-update paths. One scalar absorbs each credited observation with little work or storage. Following that update into the delayed-cue problem lets us examine both its attraction and the decisions hidden inside the credit it receives.
An EMA decides how quickly the past fades
The implemented form is

u_{t+1}=(1-\eta)u_t+\eta c_t o_t,

where u is the stored utility estimate, \eta the learning rate, c the assigned credit and o the outcome. The implementation clamps the resulting utility to configured lower and upper bounds; the first arithmetic illustration below remains inside zero and one, so clipping does not change its arithmetic. For a fixed scalar, this update uses constant work and storage. The laboratory’s default is \eta=0.1, with utility clamped to [0,1]. For the first arithmetic illustration, deliberately choose u_0=0.4 and the faster rate \eta=0.25:
Credited observation co	Old score	New score	
1	0.4	0.75(0.4)+0.25=0.55	
0	0.55	0.75(0.55)=0.4125	
The arithmetic makes the estimate's response concrete, while leaving the origin of its credit unresolved: it does not show that the record caused the outcome.
Credit matters as much as decay. Giving a record credit in proportion to its existing score feeds the estimate back into itself. A smooth transformation may improve numerical behaviour without removing that circularity. The useful test is a matched comparison against alternatives, not the elegance of the recurrence.
Delayed usefulness makes credit difficult
Consider a constructed key-and-door task. An early observation says which of two doors will open later. Several irrelevant observations arrive between the cue and the door. The agent can retain only one record. Keeping the cue can improve the eventual choice even though nothing immediately rewards the write; retaining the latest vivid observation can destroy the only useful distinction. First-in-first-out and recency are informative controls precisely because delayed usefulness can disagree with both.

The credit and memory-manager guide explains the implemented rules and update path. Matched omission or substitution runs can supply a more informative contrast, provided they keep the task and alternative information access comparable.
The completed Tutor, Continual, Conversation and TextWorld comparisons put the current policies beside their controls and full probe price. They test retention outcomes; the softplus credit transformation still needs its own matched comparison against equal credit.
The task also separates storing, retrieving and using. A cue kept in memory but never reached cannot help the answer. A cue retrieved and quoted may still be ignored by the policy. A successful answer might come from guessing. Measuring those events separately lets the outcome challenge the score rather than merely reward activity around the record.

An actual simulated conversation makes the distinction visible. In a recorded Reckon episode, the agent calculates 81 \times 35 and stores the result, 2835. The conversation moves on to a length requirement, a tone requirement and searches for information. The calculator result remains among the retrieved records, so it continues to receive a share of each turn’s reward.
This episode used first-in-first-out retention with 100 slots and finished with thirteen records, without pruning. It lets us examine scoring under ample memory; it does not establish that a selective policy kept the right things. One record through seven observed updates
A calculator result in Reckon’s simulated conversation was retrieved and scored seven times. Its utility moved from 1.5 to 0.667221. Following the actual reads, rewards and score updates makes the clamp and equal-credit rule visible.
This is the first complete episode in context_controls.jsonl from run 045229537dbf, recorded on 15 November 2026 at source 2f74405. The file’s SHA-256 is f2bdee7009b1e7e7b40c108802489a3ef082f74431a1332d37af3f855c635d96. It contains both the transcript and event stream for the same record IDs. This notebook embeds their scoring fields; it does not rerun the conversation.
The episode used FIFO, 100 record slots, seed 42 and the simulated backend with no fallback. It finished eight steps with 13 records and no pruning. It demonstrates scoring under ample memory, not a benefit from selective retention. Notebook source cell 27 fixes that control; the separate inspection episode and policy-comparison transcripts are not used here.
The adapter writes tool results with utility 1.5. On observation, SIMPLE credit divides one equally among the retrieved records, and the kernel applies clip(0.9 * old + 0.1 * credit * reward, 0, 1). Rewards and retrieved IDs below are saved observations. Credit and the predicted next utility are calculated from the source rule.

# Scoring fields selected from one complete retained episode.
# All 17 score updates are retained, not only the record shown in the table.
turns = {0: {'retrieved_ids': [], 'reward': 0.5}, 1: {'retrieved_ids': ['68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.0}, 2: {'retrieved_ids': ['68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.0}, 3: {'retrieved_ids': ['68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.5}, 4: {'retrieved_ids': ['e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.5}, 5: {'retrieved_ids': ['bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.5}, 6: {'retrieved_ids': ['b2056658-f826-4fe5-af0d-1e446f22963e', 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 0.5}, 7: {'retrieved_ids': ['29b5edb9-5e24-4ec2-a7d6-3b560e5c7360', 'b2056658-f826-4fe5-af0d-1e446f22963e', 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7'], 'reward': 3.0}}
# Each update: event ID, step, sequence, record ID, old utility, new utility.
updates = [[5, 1, 2, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 1.5, 1], [8, 2, 2, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 1, 0.9], [12, 3, 3, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.9, 0.8600000000000001], [16, 4, 3, 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', 1, 0.925], [17, 4, 4, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.8600000000000001, 0.7990000000000002], [20, 5, 2, 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 1, 0.9166666666666667], [21, 5, 3, 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', 0.925, 0.8491666666666667], [22, 5, 4, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.7990000000000002, 0.7357666666666669], [26, 6, 2, 'b2056658-f826-4fe5-af0d-1e446f22963e', 1.5, 1], [27, 6, 3, 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 0.9166666666666667, 0.8375], [28, 6, 4, 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', 0.8491666666666667, 0.77675], [29, 6, 5, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.7357666666666669, 0.6746900000000002], [33, 7, 2, '29b5edb9-5e24-4ec2-a7d6-3b560e5c7360', 1.5, 1], [34, 7, 3, 'b2056658-f826-4fe5-af0d-1e446f22963e', 1, 0.9600000000000001], [35, 7, 4, 'bea89efd-645d-434d-bd55-a72b56322a37', 0.8375, 0.8137500000000001], [36, 7, 5, 'e8983037-0b93-4df0-bdee-0ce15b9646c1', 0.77675, 0.7590750000000002], [37, 7, 6, '68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7', 0.6746900000000002, 0.6672210000000003]]
selected_record = "68849b1d-8ecc-41c3-8578-ab1008812ea7"
eta, lower, upper = 0.1, 0.0, 1.0

import math
rows = []
for event, step, sequence, record_id, old, observed in updates:
    turn = turns[step]
    assert record_id in turn["retrieved_ids"]
    count = len(turn["retrieved_ids"])
    assert count == len(set(turn["retrieved_ids"]))
    credit = 1 / count
    reward = turn["reward"]
    before_clamp = (1 - eta) * old + eta * credit * reward
    expected = min(upper, max(lower, before_clamp))
    assert math.isclose(expected, observed, rel_tol=0, abs_tol=1e-14)
    if record_id == selected_record:
        rows.append((step, count, reward, credit, old, observed, before_clamp))
assert len(updates) == 17 and len(rows) == 7
assert [r[0] for r in rows] == list(range(1, 8))
assert all(math.isclose(a[5], b[4], rel_tol=0, abs_tol=1e-14)
           for a, b in zip(rows, rows[1:]))
print("All 17 recorded score updates match the same episode’s reads and rewards.")
print("The selected record has seven consecutive updates.")

stdout
All 17 recorded score updates match the same episode’s reads and rewards.
The selected record has seven consecutive updates.

print("Step  Read  Reward  Credit    Old       New")
for step, count, reward, credit, old, new, before_clamp in rows:
    print(f"{step:>4}  {count:>4}  {reward:>6.1f}  {credit:>6.3f}  {old:>8.6f}  {new:>8.6f}")
print(f"First update before clamp: {rows[0][6]:.2f}; saved value: {rows[0][5]:.2f}.")
print(f"Last credited target: {rows[-1][2] * rows[-1][3]:.2f}.")

stdout
Step  Read  Reward  Credit    Old       New
   1     1     0.0   1.000  1.500000  1.000000
   2     1     0.0   1.000  1.000000  0.900000
   3     1     0.5   1.000  0.900000  0.860000
   4     2     0.5   0.500  0.860000  0.799000
   5     3     0.5   0.333  0.799000  0.735767
   6     4     0.5   0.250  0.735767  0.674690
   7     5     3.0   0.200  0.674690  0.667221
First update before clamp: 1.35; saved value: 1.00.
Last credited target: 0.60.

What changed the score?
At the first update, the saved reward is zero. Multiplying the old utility of 1.5 by 0.9 gives 1.35; the upper bound makes the saved result 1.0. The clamp is doing real work here.
Later, more records share the outcome. The final turn records a task reward of 3, shared among five retrieved records. This record’s target is therefore 0.6, below its previous utility of 0.67469, so its score falls again to 0.667221. A positive reward need not raise every retrieved record’s utility. The reward is the simulator’s task score, not a probability of success; the utility is not a measured causal effect.
The record being followed contains the calculator result 2835 from 81 × 35. It remains among the retrieved records while the conversation adds a length constraint, a tone constraint and search results. Equal credit is assigned by retrieval membership, not by a demonstration that the calculation helped satisfy a later constraint. That is precisely why a scorer trace and a causal evaluation answer different questions.
Source and reproduction
The memory-manager guide explains retrieval and observation; the notebook guide distinguishes controls and policy comparisons. At source 2f74405, notebook cell 27 runs the FIFO 100-slot context controls and cell 33 saves them as complete results. The adapter calls observe with that turn’s reward and retrieval context; its default credit policy is SIMPLE. The kernel constants fix the learning rate at 0.1 and output bounds at zero and one.
The original notebook 04_agentic_conversation_simulator.ipynb has SHA-256 5cdc3f1f4189f441f658ac7df05a7aed8c2052f2e23be951ab8f4737b435203f; its adapter conversation.py has SHA-256 fd21368189b1e907139a0ecde40e8801b03a4a5fdd9368883c7ec55872b00c97. Both match the saved source record. The saved rows allow the arithmetic to be checked without the laboratory or a model call. Agreement with those rows establishes this numerical reconstruction; it does not independently identify the binary loaded by the original process.

body:
Four questions behind a benchmark result
Measured retention improved a classifier's accuracy by 2.448 percentage points over learned utility. It also lost 1.580 points against no memory. Measured retention is the policy that ranks a memory record partly by what happens when that record is removed; learned utility ranks it by a score updated from credited outcomes. Both comparisons came from the same completed Reckon experiment, and both declared intervals excluded zero. Calling the candidate “better” without naming its comparator would hide the more useful result: measurement improved one policy while a simpler control still did better.
Reckon separates four coordinates in its intended evaluation contract: repeatability, independence, grounding and coverage. They are not ingredients to average into a prettier score. Each asks a question the others cannot answer.
Can the result be repeated?
A single favourable run cannot show how an improvement varies. Reckon's Tutor confirmation fixed 256 fresh seeds before inspecting their outcomes, with each seed contributing a mean over five carried-memory episodes. Measured retention beat utility at two slots in fifty seeds, tied in 180 and lost in 26. Its average gain was 0.339 percentage points, with a declared 97.5% interval of 0.037–0.640 points. The average and paired trace carry different parts of the result.
Repetitions and their variability become informative alongside the changing seed, runtime, model and configuration. Replaying the same seed checks reproduction; fresh seeds test variation within the declared generator. Even deterministic reproduction answers only part of the question: a leaking test can reproduce its mistake perfectly. Repeatability characterises the measurement procedure without establishing the validity of its interpretation. The complete memory comparison gives the protocols, other controls, uncertainty and measurement cost.
Who made the answer and who judged it?
If the same model generated a candidate, produced its preferred rubric and judged its output, agreement may reflect shared assumptions. Separate code, data, models or human review can reduce particular dependencies, but the actual overlap determines which independence matters. A second evaluator sharing the training examples may not supply an independent test of generalisation; a separate model with the same source assumptions may repeat the same blind spot. Opening another chat changes the session without necessarily changing either dependency. Independence has to concern the particular failure the comparison is meant to expose.
The distinction also applies when an agent improves its own procedure. Feedback can help propose an edit, validation can select it, and a held-out comparison can examine the selected result. Reusing the last comparison as search feedback changes its role. Pale's procedure-and-model example develops that separation around SkillOpt and a four-arm comparison; the procedure that wins validation still has to face cases it did not help select.
What supports the interpretation?
Removing a memory record changes an outcome. That is an intervention contrast within the tested system. Calling it causal requires the treatment and control, experimental unit, estimand, identification assumptions and contamination checks to be specified. Ablation alone does not provide all of them.
A measured contrast and a proxy such as gradient magnitude contribute different information. The proxy can help choose what to examine; normalising it into the same numeric range does not make it evidence of the mechanism.
What was not tested?
A candidate may improve the declared workload while omitting refusal cases, long inputs, resource exhaustion or recovery after interruption. An omitted case supplies no result. Tests cut short by a budget limit are particularly revealing: the comparison's coverage has become entangled with the resources needed to complete it.
Many comparisons also change the statistical problem. At a nominal five-percent false-positive rate, one hundred independent tests under the null would produce five false positives in expectation. Declaring a multiple-testing policy is part of the experiment; choosing only the favourable pairs afterwards changes the meaning of the reported evidence.
A worked report for the memory comparison
The Tutor result makes the four coordinates concrete. It presents six questions about six initially misunderstood concepts, with two- and four-slot memory conditions. Each seed's five episodes carry memory forward; the independent analysis unit is the seed mean, not each of the 1,280 main episodes in a policy row and certainly not every probe.
Repeatability names the fixed generator, retention formula, source and runtime, all 256 seeds, and the complete paired differences. At four slots, measured retention gains 0.755 percentage points over utility, with a 97.5% interval of 0.421–1.089. Both slot comparisons use the declared two-test correction. Their intervals are positive but lie below the five-point effect used for sample planning. That planning assumption is not an acceptance threshold for a useful system.
Independence distinguishes the confirmation's fresh seeds from the exploratory cases used to develop the comparison. Starting students and response randomness are paired independently of action choices, so a changed hint decision does not silently give one policy a different random stream. The outcome is scored by the simulation's cleared misconceptions, rather than by a language model judging its own teaching. These choices address particular dependencies; they do not make a small simulation representative of every learner.
Grounding keeps the question narrow: does this implemented retention mixture improve the declared Tutor outcome over utility? Its record-removal probes copy memory into fresh FIFO-reference episodes. They do not continue the live student's state, and the policy-level gain does not establish the causal contribution of every record that received credit. The ranking uses utility and positive measured effects together, so the experiment also does not isolate which ingredient produced the gain.
Coverage includes all nine policies and both limited budgets, including null and adverse outcomes. It does not include arbitrary students, larger curricula, different continuation rules or a common total-compute allowance. The measured arms consume 5,790,720 extra probe episodes. At two slots, measured retention's inclusive time is about 2,087 seconds against utility's 0.772; at four, about 4,254 against 0.846. These are the recorded machine times, with probe time already inside the totals. An accuracy comparison that omits that price has left out part of what the candidate did.
Each coordinate points to a different next question. Fresh cases examine variation; a different reference intervention examines attribution; a changed curriculum examines transfer; a common compute allowance examines practical value. Combining the four into one quality score would make those distinctions harder to see.
What the difference supports
The laboratory's memory update is itself a subject for this kind of comparison. Its score may be cheap and responsive; whether that response helps retention is another question. Repeatability, independence, grounding and coverage describe different ways the answer can remain uncertain.
A small positive difference can survive this examination while its adoption case remains weak. A negative comparison can reveal a simpler way to do the task. An evaluation earns its value by keeping those answers visible, with the question and cost that give each one meaning.

How to read the complete comparison

Each table retains every policy and budget in that experiment. Means and sample standard deviations are fractions, so multiply by 100 for percentages. The independent unit is an outer seed: five-episode means for Tutor, three-episode means for Continual, and one episode per seed for Conversation and TextWorld. The no-memory and full-memory controls run once per seed, rather than once for each limited budget. A dash means the control has no two/four-slot label; it does not mean zero slots were measured after a transient write.

Inclusive time already contains probe or replay time. All times are seconds summed over that row's main episodes, observed on the experiment's machine. Artifact writing and verification lie outside the per-policy timers; TextWorld game preparation also lies outside these rows, and early TextWorld timings overlap other local work. Store peaks measure record accounting, not process RAM or the working memory of all probes.

The main article reports only the predeclared inferential comparisons. These full-policy tables are descriptive; ranking the means supplies no additional significance tests. The three confirmations use paired outer-seed t comparisons with two 97.5% intervals and Bonferroni-adjusted p-values per declared family. That relies on the stated independence and distributional approximation. TextWorld is a sixteen-game diagnostic with no inferential test. The five-percentage-point planning targets belong to sample design, not an adoption rule.

Each row has sixteen main episodes. Measured retention and FIFO have identical final score vectors, not necessarily identical command sequences or completion times. Five candidate pairs have positive effects, three negative and 5,328 zero. Full memory peaks at 7–65 slots; limited arms peak and finish at their two/four-slot allowance. There is no byte cap. A two-slot controller cannot normally retain the goal plus two earlier actions, while four slots can; descriptions and inventory still compete for that space. The full-memory failure and the seventeen-command fallback win remain in the result.
What the retained traces can and cannot answer
Tutor and Continual probe fresh tasks with copied memory. Conversation and TextWorld replay the live episode prefix and then use a FIFO continuation. Neither experiment turns a positive record estimate into a causal claim independent of its intervention and reference policy. The measured ranking grants a bonus to positive effects, keeping adverse estimates in the saved results without using their magnitudes as removal preferences.
KeyDoor and Bandit serve as memory-path controls in the separate diagnostic: every positive-slot policy keeps the new cue until use, while fresh-task probes fail to read copied historical records. Equal outcomes there do not establish equivalence or useful ranking. MiniGrid's useful-memory calibration arms reach the ceiling, which similarly limits their value for comparing retention rules. Earlier exploratory results keep their original source and limits; later repaired controllers do not rewrite them.
The benchmark manual and notebook guide connect the protocols, complete seed reports, configuration and source identities. The article's attached notebook uses the exact stored summary values underlying these rounded tables. Its arithmetic does not rerun the experiments or recompute the predeclared inferential analysis from raw seed outcomes.

Time includes all probe or replay work. The measured ratios describe the recorded machine runs; early TextWorld cases overlapped other local work. An absent slot label denotes a control, not a measured zero. Figures in percentage points subtract two fractions and multiply by one hundred.
