body:
What did selective memory buy?
A memory policy can spend more time discovering which record to keep than the task spends using it. That is what makes the first completed Reckon comparisons interesting. Measuring record removal sometimes improved the outcome over learned utility. In one classification workload it still lost to using no memory. In a text-game diagnostic it matched the simpler first-in-first-out policy's wins while paying for thousands of extra replays.
The research question is whether a limited memory can retain what measurably changes an answer, at a price worth paying. A positive difference answers only part of that question. The outcome, the comparator, the measurement process and its cost have to travel together.
What the policies were allowed to remember
These experiments compare nine policies. No memory discards each new admission before it can be retrieved; full memory has enough capacity to avoid pruning in the declared workload. The limited policies choose which record to discard by age (FIFO), last use (LRU), seeded randomness, an explicitly supplied importance score, learned utility, Diversity (which favours coverage across record types), or measured retention. Full capacity is a reference, not a claim that storing more always improves the answer.
Learned utility updates a record's score from credited outcomes. Measured retention mixes that utility with a bonus for a positive record-removal estimate, per byte. The experiments retain negative and zero estimates even though the ranking gives only positive estimates that bonus. A comparison between these policies therefore tests the implemented mixture; it does not isolate measurement from utility or establish that every useful record received the right score.
Tutor and Continual copy the current memory into fresh task episodes, then compare keeping it with removing a named record under a FIFO reference policy. Their probes do not continue the live student's or classifier's hidden state. Conversation and TextWorld instead reconstruct the actual episode prefix and earlier removals, compare FIFO at the pending write with removing a candidate first, then continue both under FIFO. The FIFO baseline may itself remove that candidate. These are different interventions, not interchangeable estimates of a record's universal value.
Small tutoring gains had a large price
The Tutor workload starts with six misunderstood concepts and asks six questions in a session. Each of 256 fresh outer seeds supplies five episodes with carried memory. The outcome is the fraction of those misconceptions cleared, averaged within the seed. At two slots, measured retention clears 33.320% on average, versus utility's 32.982%; at four, the figures are 36.823% and 36.068%.
The paired gains are 0.339 and 0.755 percentage points. Their declared 97.5% intervals are 0.037–0.640 and 0.421–1.089 points. Both exclude zero under the two-comparison correction, but lie wholly below the five-point effect used to plan the sample. That planning value was an analyst's detectability target, not an accepted threshold for adoption.
At two slots, fifty seeds improve, 180 tie and 26 worsen. At four, 74 improve, 157 tie and 25 worsen. The average preserves a small positive effect while the paired outcomes show how unevenly it occurs. Acquiring those measurements used 5,790,720 additional probe episodes across the two measured arms. A small gain can be statistically distinguishable and still leave its practical value unanswered. Four questions behind a benchmark result reads this Tutor confirmation for what can be repeated, who judged it, what supports its interpretation and what it left untested.
Classification improved against utility and lost against no memory
The Continual workload trains a small classifier across three tasks, with replay opportunities for retained examples. The confirmation uses 64 fresh seeds, each averaged over three carried episodes. At two slots, measured retention reaches 85.556% accuracy, utility 83.108%, and no memory 87.135%.
Measured retention gains 2.448 percentage points over utility, with a corrected interval of 1.739–3.156. Against no memory it loses 1.580 points, with interval −2.193 to −0.967. Both declared contrasts exclude zero, in opposite directions. Reporting only the first would turn an improvement over one weak comparator into a misleading account of the whole experiment.
All one-slot limited policies produce identical seed outcomes because a new admission leaves only one retained candidate to remove. The measured policy nevertheless pays for probing that sole candidate. At two slots it has a real choice, and its probes reach carried records, yet it takes about 1,408 times utility's inclusive elapsed time on this machine. The result points towards the representation, replay rule and comparison workload as objects to investigate, rather than making selective memory valuable by definition.
Literal recall shows a gain, but the other controls still matter
Conversation uses an eight-step scripted controller whose final answer is scored for literal constraint recall. Across 256 fresh outer seeds, measured retention improves over utility by 6.185 points at two slots and 4.883 at four. The corresponding corrected intervals are 4.045–8.325 and 3.016–6.749 points.
At two slots, however, LRU recalls 24.349% on average, compared with measured retention's 16.927%. At four, measured retention reaches 77.604%, utility 72.721%, and LRU 71.745%. Full memory recalls everything; no memory recalls nothing. The declared tests establish the two comparisons against utility. The other means describe the tested alternatives without supplying additional significance tests or a universal ranking.
The measured arms add 26,972 replay episodes and take about 74 and 117 times utility's inclusive time. The controller is scripted, and the endpoint is literal recall. A gain here does not measure the reasoning quality of an arbitrary language model.
A text-game diagnostic exposes another limit
The later TextWorld diagnostic uses sixteen fresh generated games and a repaired controller that follows visible instructions and retrieved action history. Full memory wins fifteen of sixteen. Measured retention wins one at two slots and three at four, matching FIFO's complete score vectors. Random retention wins four games at four slots; utility wins zero and two.
These are descriptive outcomes, with no confirmation test or confidence interval. The measured policy improves over utility by one seed at each budget, adds 10,672 replays, and takes about 266 and 469 times utility's recorded inclusive time. Early timings overlapped other local work, so those ratios are observations of that run rather than an isolated hardware benchmark.
Capacity and language both matter. The normal third instruction needs the goal and two earlier action records; two slots cannot hold all three. Four slots can, but repeated descriptions and inventory compete for that allowance. Two generated quests need only two actions despite the three-command generation setting. In this diagnostic, even full memory failed one case because the controller misread an insertion instruction. Another full-memory win took seventeen commands after an earlier instruction-grounding failure. The parser now separates the requested action from clauses describing completed prerequisites. Regression checks cover those two parsing repairs.
Of 5,336 candidate-removal pairs, five have positive signed effects, three negative and 5,328 zero. The negative cases retain an especially useful distinction: removing a candidate lets the FIFO continuation win, but the main ranking removes a different record. The recorded effects expose something the default scoring rule does not exploit. A zero final-score effect also need not mean that intermediate actions were unchanged or that the record is irrelevant under every continuation.
A subsequent four-game development used the repaired parser to compare that default rule with an optional rule that selects a removal when its measured continuation improves on FIFO. At four slots the optional rule won one game; default measured retention, FIFO and utility won none. Seeded random won the same game. Every limited policy scored zero at two slots, while full memory won all four games in three actions each. The two measured rules together added 5,408 replays. The optional rule's one improving selection kept the goal for the next action, then lost it before the third; its eventual win came through a six-action fallback. This development compares selection rules under the repaired controller. It does not isolate the benefit of repairing the parser, and four games with the same wins as random do not confirm a general retention gain.
Put measurement on the same bill
The counts below belong to the measured arms. Each row's elapsed time already includes its probes or replays. Adding the two time columns would charge that work twice.
Workload	Slots	Main episodes	Extra probe or replay episodes	Inclusive seconds	Probe or replay seconds	
Tutor	2	1,280	2,096,128	2,087.329	2,086.370	
Tutor	4	1,280	3,694,592	4,253.775	4,252.780	
Continual	1	192	113,792	301.467	301.022	
Continual	2	192	246,528	618.282	617.819	
Conversation	2	256	10,356	17.000	16.673	
Conversation	4	256	16,616	30.840	30.464	
TextWorld	2	16	3,912	1,028.318	1,024.377	
TextWorld	4	16	6,760	1,803.517	1,799.584	
Those are episode-execution timings. Saving and checking the result files adds work outside them; TextWorld's game preparation is also separate. Store byte and slot counts describe retained record payloads, not process memory or every probe's working storage. The full policy outcomes, seed spreads and costs are in the notes; the saved notebook recomputes the reported gain and cost comparisons from the retained summaries.
What a useful next comparison has to preserve
These findings give the laboratory a real answer to build on. Tutor and Conversation establish gains against their declared utility comparators. Continual establishes a gain against utility and a loss against no memory. TextWorld provides diagnostic cases where a simpler policy gets the same wins for far less work. Changing the workload, controller or retention rule can be worthwhile precisely because those differences now have identifiable causes to investigate.
A revised method needs a separately declared comparison on fresh cases, with the old adverse and null outcomes still visible. The three-seed FIFO replay-budget example asks a separate question about capacity; it is not a confirmation of these policy results. Nor do memory-path controls whose policies all retain the current cue establish useful ranking among those policies.
The stronger question is whether a policy improves the answer under a common total resource allowance, including the work spent deciding what to remember. Until that comparison is made useful, an expensive measurement is evidence to understand, not a reason to deploy its winner.

Reckon, Continual confirmation completed 16 November 2026, result 7e2728490cc1, source adad858. The benchmark manual preserves both primary contrasts, 64 seed means over three episodes, and full measurement cost.
Reckon, Conversation confirmation completed 16 November 2026, result df3d0053c39f, protocol source e60a4a2. The notebook guide distinguishes the 256-seed confirmation from calibration and earlier read-boundary ablations. Each candidate has one deterministic replay pair; inferential intervals concern outer-seed policy differences.
Reckon, TextWorld retention diagnostic completed 16 November 2026, result 6676e6a9ecd8, source dc90275. The notebook guide preserves the sixteen cases, controller limits and complete costs. These games use live environments and a scripted controller, with no model call or hidden solution.

Measuring record removal sometimes improved the outcome over learned utility. In one classification workload it still lost to using no memory. In a text-game diagnostic it matched the simpler first-in-first-out policy's wins while paying for thousands of extra replays.
The research question is whether a limited memory can retain what measurably changes an answer, at a price worth paying. A positive difference answers only part of that question. The outcome, the comparator, the measurement process and its cost have to travel together.
What the policies were allowed to remember
These experiments compare nine policies. No memory discards each new admission before it can be retrieved; full memory has enough capacity to avoid pruning in the declared workload. The limited policies choose which record to discard by age (FIFO), last use (LRU), seeded randomness, an explicitly supplied importance score, learned utility, Diversity (which favours coverage across record types), or measured retention. Full capacity is a reference, not a claim that storing more always improves the answer.
Learned utility updates a record's score from credited outcomes. Measured retention mixes that utility with a bonus for a positive record-removal estimate, per byte. The experiments retain negative and zero estimates even though the ranking gives only positive estimates that bonus. A comparison between these policies therefore tests the implemented mixture; it does not isolate measurement from utility or establish that every useful record received the right score.
Tutor and Continual copy the current memory into fresh task episodes, then compare keeping it with removing a named record under a FIFO reference policy. Their probes do not continue the live student's or classifier's hidden state. Conversation and TextWorld instead reconstruct the actual episode prefix and earlier removals, compare FIFO at the pending write with removing a candidate first, then continue both under FIFO. The FIFO baseline may itself remove that candidate. These are different interventions, not interchangeable estimates of a record's universal value.
Small tutoring gains had a large price
The Tutor workload starts with six misunderstood concepts and asks six questions in a session. Each of 256 fresh outer seeds supplies five episodes with carried memory. The outcome is the fraction of those misconceptions cleared, averaged within the seed. At two slots, measured retention clears 33.320% on average, versus utility's 32.982%; at four, the figures are 36.823% and 36.068%.
The paired gains are 0.339 and 0.755 percentage points. Their declared 97.5% intervals are 0.037–0.640 and 0.421–1.089 points. Both exclude zero under the two-comparison correction, but lie wholly below the five-point effect used to plan the sample. That planning value was an analyst's detectability target, not an accepted threshold for adoption.
At two slots, fifty seeds improve, 180 tie and 26 worsen. At four, 74 improve, 157 tie and 25 worsen. The average preserves a small positive effect while the paired outcomes show how unevenly it occurs. Acquiring those measurements used 5,790,720 additional probe episodes across the two measured arms. A small gain can be statistically distinguishable and still leave its practical value unanswered. Four questions behind a benchmark result reads this Tutor confirmation for what can be repeated, who judged it, what supports its interpretation and what it left untested.
Classification improved against utility and lost against no memory
The Continual workload trains a small classifier across three tasks, with replay opportunities for retained examples. The confirmation uses 64 fresh seeds, each averaged over three carried episodes. At two slots, measured retention reaches 85.556% accuracy, utility 83.108%, and no memory 87.135%.
Measured retention gains 2.448 percentage points over utility, with a corrected interval of 1.739–3.156. Against no memory it loses 1.580 points, with interval −2.193 to −0.967. Both declared contrasts exclude zero, in opposite directions. Reporting only the first would turn an improvement over one weak comparator into a misleading account of the whole experiment.
All one-slot limited policies produce identical seed outcomes because a new admission leaves only one retained candidate to remove. The measured policy nevertheless pays for probing that sole candidate. At two slots it has a real choice, and its probes reach carried records, yet it takes about 1,408 times utility's inclusive elapsed time on this machine. The result points towards the representation, replay rule and comparison workload as objects to investigate, rather than making selective memory valuable by definition.
Literal recall shows a gain, but the other controls still matter
Conversation uses an eight-step scripted controller whose final answer is scored for literal constraint recall. Across 256 fresh outer seeds, measured retention improves over utility by 6.185 points at two slots and 4.883 at four. The corresponding corrected intervals are 4.045–8.325 and 3.016–6.749 points.
At two slots, however, LRU recalls 24.349% on average, compared with measured retention's 16.927%. At four, measured retention reaches 77.604%, utility 72.721%, and LRU 71.745%. Full memory recalls everything; no memory recalls nothing. The declared tests establish the two comparisons against utility. The other means describe the tested alternatives without supplying additional significance tests or a universal ranking.
The measured arms add 26,972 replay episodes and take about 74 and 117 times utility's inclusive time. The controller is scripted, and the endpoint is literal recall. A gain here does not measure the reasoning quality of an arbitrary language model.
A text-game diagnostic exposes another limit
The later TextWorld diagnostic uses sixteen fresh generated games and a repaired controller that follows visible instructions and retrieved action history. Full memory wins fifteen of sixteen. Measured retention wins one at two slots and three at four, matching FIFO's complete score vectors. Random retention wins four games at four slots; utility wins zero and two.
These are descriptive outcomes, with no confirmation test or confidence interval. The measured policy improves over utility by one seed at each budget, adds 10,672 replays, and takes about 266 and 469 times utility's recorded inclusive time. Early timings overlapped other local work, so those ratios are observations of that run rather than an isolated hardware benchmark.
Capacity and language both matter. The normal third instruction needs the goal and two earlier action records; two slots cannot hold all three. Four slots can, but repeated descriptions and inventory compete for that allowance. Two generated quests need only two actions despite the three-command generation setting. In this diagnostic, even full memory failed one case because the controller misread an insertion instruction. Another full-memory win took seventeen commands after an earlier instruction-grounding failure. The parser now separates the requested action from clauses describing completed prerequisites. Regression checks cover those two parsing repairs.
Of 5,336 candidate-removal pairs, five have positive signed effects, three negative and 5,328 zero. The negative cases retain an especially useful distinction: removing a candidate lets the FIFO continuation win, but the main ranking removes a different record. The recorded effects expose something the default scoring rule does not exploit. A zero final-score effect also need not mean that intermediate actions were unchanged or that the record is irrelevant under every continuation.
A subsequent four-game development used the repaired parser to compare that default rule with an optional rule that selects a removal when its measured continuation improves on FIFO. At four slots the optional rule won one game; default measured retention, FIFO and utility won none. Seeded random won the same game. Every limited policy scored zero at two slots, while full memory won all four games in three actions each. The two measured rules together added 5,408 replays. The optional rule's one improving selection kept the goal for the next action, then lost it before the third; its eventual win came through a six-action fallback. This development compares selection rules under the repaired controller. It does not isolate the benefit of repairing the parser, and four games with the same wins as random do not confirm a general retention gain.
Put measurement on the same bill
The counts below belong to the measured arms. Each row's elapsed time already includes its probes or replays. Adding the two time columns would charge that work twice.

Store byte and slot counts describe retained record payloads, not process memory or every probe's working storage. The full policy outcomes, seed spreads and costs are in the notes; the saved notebook recomputes the reported gain and cost comparisons from the retained summaries.
What a useful next comparison has to preserve
These findings give the laboratory a real answer to build on. Tutor and Conversation establish gains against their declared utility comparators. Continual establishes a gain against utility and a loss against no memory. TextWorld provides diagnostic cases where a simpler policy gets the same wins for far less work. Changing the workload, controller or retention rule can be worthwhile precisely because those differences now have identifiable causes to investigate.
A revised method needs a separately declared comparison on fresh cases, with the old adverse and null outcomes still visible. The three-seed FIFO replay-budget example asks a separate question about capacity; it is not a confirmation of these policy results. Nor do memory-path controls whose policies all retain the current cue establish useful ranking among those policies.
The stronger question is whether a policy improves the answer under a common total resource allowance, including the work spent deciding what to remember. Until that comparison is made useful, an expensive measurement is evidence to understand, not a reason to deploy its winner.

How to read the complete comparison
Each table retains every policy and budget in that experiment. Means and sample standard deviations are fractions, so multiply by 100 for percentages. The independent unit is an outer seed: five-episode means for Tutor, three-episode means for Continual, and one episode per seed for Conversation and TextWorld. The no-memory and full-memory controls run once per seed, rather than once for each limited budget. A dash means the control has no two/four-slot label; it does not mean zero slots were measured after a transient write.
Inclusive time already contains probe or replay time. All times are seconds summed over that row's main episodes, observed on the experiment's machine. Artifact writing and verification lie outside the per-policy timers; TextWorld game preparation also lies outside these rows, and early TextWorld timings overlap other local work. Store peaks measure record accounting, not process RAM or the working memory of all probes.
The main article reports only the predeclared inferential comparisons. These full-policy tables are descriptive; ranking the means supplies no additional significance tests. The three confirmations use paired outer-seed t comparisons with two 97.5% intervals and Bonferroni-adjusted p-values per declared family. That relies on the stated independence and distributional approximation. TextWorld is a sixteen-game diagnostic with no inferential test. The five-percentage-point planning targets belong to sample design, not an adoption rule.

questions.question: Would HENA replace Pale?
questions.answer_html: HENA is Pale’s research successor in one limited sense: its learned organisation could take over some of the coordination Pale describes explicitly. Pale sits around the tools people already use; should HENA prove itself, Pale would stand to it as a harness stands to the model it runs, more guardrail than organiser, still governing permissions and resources and observing its work. In Harsh’s account HENA is an evolving swarm of MUONs that reasons about what could have happened, the third rung of the ACI framework in Beyond the Mirage; today’s products come first because they let agents see what a change would affect before they make it. body:
HENA
Can a warning read by one small unit reach another unit’s later decision? HENA asks whether a collective can learn which messages to send, what experience to keep and how to organise around a task.
Follow a connector warning through the design. One unit reads that a replacement part has a different connector. Another gets the repair request much later. The experiment asks whether that warning survives the gap and changes the repair decision, through learned communication and memory rather than a route declared for every case.
From arranging a system to learning its arrangement
Pale coordinates work through declared responsibilities and capabilities, while HENA asks how a division of work and a hierarchy could arise as units learn to solve tasks together, as Causality’s About page sets out.
A whole answer from local views
A long input can exceed what any one unit holds. In HENA’s design, each sees part of the input. Messages and memory carry a useful detail beyond the unit that first saw it. The design has to work within limits on compute, communication and memory.
Give each unit a local view
The input is streamed or encoded in parts. One unit receives the maintenance note while another sees the later repair request. Each begins with its own state and a partial view of the task.
Connect what the task needs
Over several rounds, the units send messages, read from fixed-size memory and update their own state. The connector warning has to reach the right unit before it answers.
Form the collective answer
A subset of units or the shared memory supplies the answer. Training judges its quality and counts the messages and time it took to produce it. The question is whether useful routes and a hierarchy emerge under those conditions.
Questions about a learned organisation
Broadcasting the connector warning to every unit might get the right answer while spending the communication HENA hopes to save. Keeping it in memory helps only if the repair unit retrieves it in time and uses it correctly. The experiment needs to follow the warning all the way into the decision.
Compare the learned arrangement with a flat collective, a central coordinator, an imposed hierarchy and a single stronger unit under matched resources. A useful hierarchy should improve the complete task after communication and memory costs are counted. What would count as emergent hierarchy? develops that comparison, including the possibility that the organisation adds no benefit.
Questions about HENA
What makes HENA different from orchestrating agents?
Orchestration scripts who does what; HENA tests whether the units can learn that organisation themselves, deciding whom to message, sharing limited memory and forming a hierarchy that helps them solve a task. The first swarm coordinates existing open-weight models as its baseline.
Would HENA replace Pale?
HENA is Pale’s research successor in one limited sense: its learned organisation could take over some of the coordination Pale describes explicitly. Pale sits around the tools people already use; should HENA prove itself, Pale would stand to it as a harness stands to the model it runs, more guardrail than organiser, still governing permissions and resources and observing its work. In Harsh’s account HENA is an evolving swarm of MUONs that reasons about what could have happened, the third rung of the ACI framework in Beyond the Mirage; today’s products come first because they let agents see what a change would affect before they make it. HENA is a hypothesis under study, and how that would work remains open. HENA also stands on its own. Causality’s wider question explains that direction.
Could it serve as a model behind a coding harness?
A coding harness such as Claude Code or Codex could use a HENA-backed model as its model provider. The harness still decides which actions to allow and carries them out.

body:
Why communication and memory are computation
One unit reads about a changed connector. Another later gets a request to repair the machine. HENA would give each unit part of the input, messages from a few neighbours and reads from limited memory. The proposed swarm would have to get the warning to the unit that answers.
A local view can miss a joint fact
Each unit's information can be accurate and still be insufficient. The relation between the part, the machine and the repair must reach the unit that forms the answer.
Broadcasting everything might solve the information gap, but spends the communication HENA seeks to save. Sending every question through a central unit creates a different bottleneck. The research asks whether learned routes can deliver the relevant contribution without every unit reconstructing the complete problem.
Messages change who can contribute
In each round, the proposed incoming message combines contributions from a set of neighbouring units:
m_i^t=\sum_{j\in N_i^t}a_{ij}^t\,g(h_j^t).
N_i^t determines which units can contribute in that round. The weights a_{ij}^t determine how their messages combine; g(h_j^t) produces a message from a neighbour's state. Changing those routes or weights changes what the next update can use, even with the same external input.
More rounds can carry the cue further, but add latency and communication. A denser route may preserve the connector relation or bury it among redundant messages. The useful route must help the task within compute, communication and memory limits together.
Memory limits make time part of the choice
The early note must survive until the repair question arrives. In a fixed-size store, keeping it can displace something else. Retrieval must then put it where it can affect the answer. A saved note or a retrieval hit alone does not show that the answer used it correctly.
A text store could support the first stock-model swarm. The longer-term trainable memory target would let task errors guide memory access itself. HENA would keep this store and its history; Reckon's proposed record interface would let an evaluator examine them. The developer manual in the HENA repository explains these store responsibilities.
Learned hierarchy needs a useful collective effect
Repeated complementary routes could produce specialisation and larger structures. Test whether those structures improve what the collective can answer, what it remembers and the complete cost of its work. Compare a single stronger unit, a flat collective, an imposed hierarchy and a central coordinator.
The result might show that a route helps, that communication costs consume the gain or that the apparent hierarchy adds nothing beyond stronger units. The emergence inquiry follows those comparisons through an example.
How units form a collective connects these choices to local unit learning, evolution and HENA's broader aim.

body:
How units form a collective
Imagine a maintenance note warning that a replacement part has a different connector. Much later, a repair request arrives. One small reasoning unit reads the warning; another gets the request. Can the first unit's experience change the second unit's answer?
HENA is a proposed architecture for learning that coordination. Instead of one large model attending to the whole input, many small units would each see part of it, exchange a few messages and share limited memory.
Memory and communication are the architecture
The connector warning has to survive the intervening input, stay associated with the right machine and reach the unit choosing the repair. Saving the note is only the beginning. A retrieved note might concern another machine; a correct message might arrive too late. The answer needs to account for the connector when deciding which work can proceed.
This gives us a path to investigate: where the cue enters, what keeps it available, how it reaches the later question and whether it changes the answer. Fixed-size memory means that keeping one item can displace another. Sparse communication means that every unit cannot receive every update. Learning what to keep and where to send it together could produce specialisation: some units perform particular computations, and recurring routes connect complementary work.
How a unit updates from its view, messages and memory
Each unit would combine its local input with its current state, incoming messages and reads from memory. A candidate update is
h_i^{t+1}=f_\theta(h_i^t,\tilde x_i^t,m_i^t,r_i^t).
Here h_i^t is the unit's current state, \tilde x_i^t its local input, m_i^t the messages it receives and r_i^t what it reads from memory. The learned update f_\theta produces its next state. The repair unit could therefore respond to the connector warning in a message or memory read even if the repair request itself says nothing about it.
Repeated rounds carry information beyond the first local view. A subset of units or the collective memory then supplies the answer. MUON studies the individual unit; HENA studies how those units work together.
The target is to handle long sequences at less than quadratic cost while keeping or improving accuracy, context retention, compositional reasoning and adaptability. Compute, communication and memory each have a limit. Linear or near-linear processing and memory that does not grow with the whole input are targets to test.

If the answer misses the connector warning, training should be able to improve how that relation survives and reaches the later decision. The programme also asks whether changing local rules can produce better collective behaviour. Here a candidate is a set of local rules, kept as a rule document, edited and tested in separate trials. Ancestry records retain the rejected candidates too.
Mutation and evaluation operators start fixed. That lets an experiment change a candidate without changing how it is judged at the same time. Changing the rule develops this distinction.
What would establish useful hierarchy?
The connector example needs a correct answer, delivered at an acceptable cost. A diagram of nested groups cannot tell us whether those groups learned to organise or whether they helped. HENA would keep its own swarm store and run history. Reckon would provide ways to inspect and evaluate records from that store.
The swarm might make correlated errors, lose a joint fact, route everything through one bottleneck, fill memory with noise, communicate too much or fail to train reliably. The first planned swarm would coordinate stock open-weight models through MUON's unit interface. A unit built for MUON could later replace one of those models through the same interface. The longer-term design would train the units, routes and memory together and test whether a useful hierarchy emerges. Q-HENA explores the corresponding quantum architecture.

Pale describes an organisation's responsibilities and coordination explicitly, and HENA asks how more of that organisation could be learned through local interactions; Causality's About page sets out how the two relate. Inspect the source
With source access, developers can check the kernel crate in the HENA repository, which re-exports the MONAD, MUON and Reckon kernels because swarm coordination is not implemented. They can also inspect what the kernel exposes; its developer manual covers the resource and recovery decisions an implementation would need to make.

How units form a collective

MONAD: Minimal Ontological Notions for Axiomatic Distinction

body:
MONAD
An inventory says a part is in stock. Can it tell you whether the part fits the machine? MONAD studies which answers survive a change of description and what you need to recover a missing answer. It asks what would let a fixed frame become something a system can change without losing account of its meaning.
When a better answer needs a different language
Work through the stock-and-fit example to see which questions an inventory can answer. A Lean library and paper develop the mathematics. A small Rust kernel supplies types and numerical operations for research code.
Follow what a description can answer
Start with the answer you need. Try to reconstruct it from the shorter description, then work out which information a new observation could supply.
State the questions
Decide which questions you need to answer now and after any changes you plan to make. An inventory for ordering parts and one for repairing a machine can need different information.
Examine the transformation
Compare cases that the summary treats alike. In the example below, the stock summary gives the same answer for both parts even though only one fits.
Repair or enrich the account
Recover the missing distinction from an available source, or enrich a description whose objects, questions or rules cannot express what is needed. The longer-term calculus also asks how the rules of change can themselves become objects of change.
Questions a description must answer
The stock summary cannot tell the two parts apart, but a compatibility record might supply the missing answer. Finding that record repairs an omission. If the description has no way to represent machines or their compatibility with parts, it needs a richer language before it can even ask the question. Descriptions and repair follows that distinction from an available observation to a change in what the description can express.
Questions about MONAD
What does MONAD let researchers do?
State which distinctions a representation must preserve, examine a transformation or compression, and reason about the information and cost needed to repair an inadequate account. The Lean library makes parts of that mathematics exact, and the Rust kernel brings its types and numerical operations into research code.
Is MONAD only about AI?
MONAD is a pure mathematical programme, and AI is one source of its examples. Adaptive models, changing scientific descriptions and other systems supply examples and tests; they do not define its axioms.
How does the stock-and-fit example relate to the larger aim?
It shows a summary preserving availability while losing the distinction needed for repair. Moving from that fixed example to descriptions whose objects, questions and rules can change is the broader research task.
Do I need software to follow MONAD?
You can read the worked example without software. Descriptions and repair then follows the same question into the Lean library and the Rust kernel.

body:
Descriptions and repair
Two parts are in stock. One fits the machine you need to repair; the other does not. An inventory can be perfectly accurate about availability and still leave you unable to choose between them.
MONAD starts from this difficulty: which answers does a description keep, and what happens when a later question needs a distinction it left out?
A small exact example
Write the state of a part as (a,b). The first value says whether it is available; the second says whether it fits. Repair requires both. A summary that keeps only a=1 gives the same answer for (1,0) and (1,1), although only the second part permits repair. No amount of calculation on that summary can tell you which part fits.
Write the answer you need as f:X\to Y and the summary as q:X\to S. The answer survives if there is a rule g:S\to Y such that
f=g\circ q.
In other words, you can get the required answer from the summary alone. When two states share a summary but need different answers, no such rule exists. What a summary preserves works through all four states and shows how choosing a different question changes which summary is sufficient.
The representation can become the problem
Perhaps a compatibility record can supply the missing answer. Then the problem is finding and reading that record, at whatever cost the observation requires. But suppose the description has no way to represent machines or the relation between a machine and a part. It needs more than another value: it needs a way to express compatibility.
Summary and repair follows the first problem, recovering an answer from information we can reach. Changing the description follows the second. MONAD asks how to reason about both, including which earlier answers a richer description should preserve.
That is the ambition behind a calculus of endogenous distinguishability: the descriptions, the questions they can express and the rules for changing them can themselves change. The eventual calculus must account for those changes without allowing a rule to justify its own replacement.
What a description can distinguish
The four part states form the carrier, the things this description represents. Asking whether a part is available is a probe. A description also declares continuations, the changes it permits. Two states may give the same answer now, yet become distinguishable after one of those changes.
To call two states indistinguishable now, every present probe must agree on them. To say they remain indistinguishable, every probe after every permitted continuation must agree too. The choice of questions and continuations therefore matters as much as the current values.
Changing availability from 0 to 1 leaves the four-state description intact. Adding the compatibility question separates states the availability question grouped together. Adding kinds of objects the carrier could not represent goes further still. These are different changes, with different information to account for.
What the calculus needs to explain
Four working requirements follow from that question. They guide the research; they are not a finished set of axioms.
Generative openness asks how a description can express a distinction it could not previously support. Finding the old compatibility bit is different from introducing machines and compatibility into a language that had neither. Both can change the answers we can give, but they do not change the description in the same way.
Anticipatory compression asks what a summary must retain for the future changes we choose to allow. Keeping today's answers is not enough when tomorrow's question separates states the summary merged. The permitted changes, approximation and cost must be stated.
Invariant accounting asks what each transformation preserves, hides, loses or makes newly expressible. Information that can be recovered from an accessible record is in a different position from information no available source can supply.
Trajectory-sensitive relevance asks how the path taken, and the futures still possible, change which distinctions matter. Two descriptions can agree now without making the same information relevant along every later path.
Three principles for an honest comparison
Looking the same through today's questions does not make two states identical under every later question. A system can also be optimal within an inadequate description: the best stock count still cannot decide whether a part fits.
A persistent error deserves the same care. It might be measurement noise or a poor fit inside the current model; it might also point to a missing distinction. MONAD has to investigate those possibilities, rather than assume every mismatch calls for a new language. Preserving answers, choosing an adequate description and explaining a residual are separate questions.
What the Lean library already makes exact
The Lean library makes parts of this question exact. It proves results about grouping states that give the same answers, limits on future-safe compression, residual budgets, repair from available sources and the size of a supplement. It also treats probabilistic comparison and gives counterexamples to treating detectable influence as an order. The wider calculus of changing carriers and transformation rules remains open.
The example above requires every declared answer to survive exactly. Preservation under uncertainty asks what can be said when the descriptions instead produce probability laws. Under a stated simulation error, it bounds how much a decision loss can change. A small numerical distance alone does not establish that two descriptions are equivalent or that recovering an answer is affordable.
Take the example into the Lean library
Try the four-state example on paper first. In the MONAD repository, you can then read the same example in Lean and inspect the hypotheses behind the theorem. Its formal guide leads through the rest of the proof library.
For Rust integration, the repository's kernel guide compares two finite probability distributions.
Note
The kernel's scope. The kernel provides types and a few numerical operations for a fixed-context observer model. It does not implement the changing-description calculus or solve repair problems automatically.
Where MONAD sits beside Pale, MUON and HENA
Pale works within an explicit world model. MUON and HENA investigate how adaptive units and their collective organisation might change. Their practical questions can test MONAD's usefulness, while its mathematical definitions remain independent of those applications. Economic transitions pose a related question: when is a changed parameter enough, and when do the actors or relations themselves need to change?
Working with the source
The Lean library and paper require source access. The existing proofs hold under their stated assumptions. A downstream adaptive system still needs tests of its own behaviour.

It also treats probabilistic comparison and gives counterexamples to treating detectable influence as an order. The wider calculus of changing carriers and transformation rules remains open.
The example above requires every declared answer to survive exactly. Preservation under uncertainty asks what can be said when the descriptions instead produce probability laws. Under a stated simulation error, it bounds how much a decision loss can change. A small numerical distance alone does not establish that two descriptions are equivalent or that recovering an answer is affordable.
Take the example into the Lean library
Try the four-state example on paper first. In the MONAD repository, you can then read the same example in Lean and inspect the hypotheses behind the theorem. Its formal guide leads through the rest of the proof library.
For Rust integration, the repository's kernel guide compares two finite probability distributions.
Note
The kernel's scope. The kernel provides types and a few numerical operations for a fixed-context observer model. It does not implement the changing-description calculus or solve repair problems automatically.
Where MONAD sits beside Pale, MUON and HENA
Pale works within an explicit world model. MUON and HENA investigate how adaptive units and their collective organisation might change. Their practical questions can test MONAD's usefulness, while its mathematical definitions remain independent of those applications. Economic transitions pose a related question: when is a changed parameter enough, and when do the actors or relations themselves need to change?
Working with the source
The Lean library and paper require source access. The existing proofs hold under their stated assumptions. A downstream adaptive system still needs tests of its own behaviour.

body:
What a summary preserves
A summary can discard details while keeping the answers you need. This four-state example shows how to check that claim, choose a sufficient summary, and identify the information a failed summary would need. No software is required.
Fix the question before judging the summary
Let a state be (a,b), where a says whether a part is available and b whether it fits the machine. Both take values 0 or 1. The repair question is whether both conditions hold, so its answer is f(a,b)=a\land b.
Suppose the summary keeps only availability, so q(a,b)=a. Try to answer the repair question using only the middle column before checking the last one.
State	Availability summary	Repair possible?	
(0,0)	0	No	
(0,1)	0	No	
(1,0)	1	No	
(1,1)	1	Yes	
The first two states can share a summary for this question because their answers agree. The last two cannot: the same summary, 1, would need to yield both No and Yes. No rule using only that summary can answer correctly for every state.
In general, an answer f:X\to Y survives a summary q:X\to S when there is a rule g:S\to Y with f=g\circ q. This says what has to remain possible after compression; it does not require retaining every detail of the original state.
Keep the answer rather than every original detail
For the repair question alone, a sufficient summary is the repair answer itself: r(a,b)=a\land b. It has two possible values. Three states share the answer No, and only (1,1) has the answer Yes:
\{(0,0),(0,1),(1,0)\},\qquad \{(1,1)\}.
These groups are the observational equivalence classes for this one question: states belong together exactly when the required answer agrees. The quotient is the set of those classes. Reading the class tells us the answer, so compression to these two classes is sufficient. Any sufficient summary must keep (1,1) apart from the other three states, though it may retain additional distinctions.
Notice that r cannot tell whether a part is available when repair is impossible. That was not part of its contract. If both availability and repair must remain answerable, the coarsest sufficient grouping has three classes:
\{(0,0),(0,1)\},\qquad \{(1,0)\},\qquad \{(1,1)\}.
The pair of answers (a,a\land b) identifies these three classes. It still merges the two unavailable-part states because neither required question separates them. This is semantic minimality: the fewest distinctions needed for the declared answers. It does not yet minimise storage, computation or the cost of obtaining those answers.
A different question changes the judgement
If the only question were whether a part is available, the original summary q=a would be sufficient. Its inadequacy appears when the repair question needs compatibility. A description can therefore be sufficient for one purpose and insufficient for another without either claim being contradictory.
That is why preserving every currently asked question is not the same as preserving every question a later language or task might admit. The broader programme asks what happens as those descriptions, questions and change rules themselves grow.
Now admit the compatibility question b independently of availability. The two coordinate questions a and b together separate all four states. Any summary preserving both must keep all four states apart. A different encoding is possible; a merger is not. The formal obstruction generalises this argument: if a family of questions separates every distinct pair and a compression preserves every question in that family exactly, the compression must be injective, meaning different states never share an output.
The assumptions matter. A restricted question family allowed the two- and three-class summaries above. Allowing error, limiting continuations, paying for later observations or revising the summary changes the problem. MONAD studies how to state and account for those choices, rather than treating perfect preservation under unrestricted future questions as a useful compression rule.
Recover information or enrich the description
If an accessible compatibility record exists, a permitted observation can supply what the summary omitted. Whether that repair is possible depends on the actual source and access, not only on the fact that another bit would be helpful.
Starting from q=a, no further observation is needed when a=0: the repair answer is already No. When a=1, asking for b determines the answer. If that query is permitted and costs one unit, the strategy costs zero on the unavailable-part branch and one on the available-part branch. An average cost would also need a distribution over states. If no source of b is accessible, noticing the collision between (1,0) and (1,1) cannot recover the missing value.
Keeping b before discarding the original state would be a different operation. A supplement encoder with access to (a,b) can save the missing information; a later procedure with access only to a cannot manufacture it. Revealing this old coordinate also adds nothing to the original four-state carrier. It is not evidence that a new dimension has emerged.
A description with no objects for machines, parts or compatibility has a different problem. Another value in the old vocabulary cannot express the missing relation. The account needs a richer description before it can ask the repair question properly.
Summary and repair develops the information-and-access problem, while changing the description follows the need for a different representational frame. The wider calculus remains a research programme.
The formal guide in the MONAD repository translates this example into Lean's existing definitions and results. The kernel's finite-distribution example addresses a separate, narrower task: computing a numerical distance between supplied probability laws. It does not implement the quotient or the repair strategy above.

body:
MUON
A road closes just before a route request arrives. Can a small reasoning unit carry the notice into its answer? MUON studies how a unit uses earlier information and learns from experience. Follow the route example.
A building block that can keep learning
A common interface lets the caller try an existing model first and test a unit that learns through the same calls. HENA studies how several units work together.
Experience that changes the next computation
The road notice can change the next route, help with a later request or reveal a recurring mistake. Follow what the unit does with each kind of experience.
Temporal state that reaches the answer
The unit combines the current question, earlier state and messages. The route it suggests should change when the road closes.
Experience worth retaining
A unit marks the notice as useful. The store decides whether to keep it within its memory budget so a later request can use it.
Learning across episodes
Repeated mistakes change how the unit weighs notices in future tasks. Surprise adjusts the rate of learning within a stated limit.
Proposals for a richer structure
If the same kind of error persists, researchers can try a change to how the unit routes computation. A separate comparison shows whether the change helps.
Questions about MUON
What exists today?
Today the repository holds the slot contract as a draft and a kernel that builds on MONAD. A conformance suite, then adapters for open-weight models, are in front, and no unit runs yet.
Is MUON an adapter around an existing model?
MUON starts with adapters for existing open-weight models. A smaller model designed for MUON later uses the same interface for inference, state, records, resources and lifecycle.
How does MUON relate to Counsel and Pale?
MUON studies a learning unit for the scale of work where Counsel supplies local judgments within Pale’s explicit organisation, and HENA studies how such units learn to organise collectively; Causality’s About page sets out how those directions connect.
Does the design require many small units to win?
No. The comparison includes many identical units, one stronger unit, a mixture and no swarm, with the full resource cost counted. A negative result can leave a useful unit interface and a stronger baseline.
Where should I start?
Start with the road notice. Computation, state and learning follows it into the next route answer and lays out the comparison between different reasoning units. Three tests for a reasoning unit then explains why meeting an interface, being adequate for a task and replacing another model are separate claims.

body:
Computation, state and learning
A unit learns that a road has closed. The next question asks for a route. Does the closure change the answer? MUON uses questions like this to design how one unit could carry information forward and how a caller could compare two models doing the same work.
One unit and a collective ask different questions
MUON asks what one unit needs to compute, remember and learn. If another unit received the notice, the question becomes how it would reach the unit making the decision. HENA studies that kind of coordination. Test the unit’s answer and the way units work together separately.
Local computation with useful temporal state
The long-term design is a micro-transformer unit: small enough to run in numbers, working from its own inputs and state. Units would exchange sparse messages rather than send everything through a central hub. Memory would be spread across units and their hosts’ stores, using a shared record protocol; each store would decide what to keep.
The road notice must have a path into the later answer. One candidate ingredient, selective state-space processing, updates a compact state as inputs arrive. Another, routed expert computation, chooses which expert computations to run. Combining them leaves a question: does the earlier state only choose an expert, or can it also change what that expert predicts?
Compare two designs that combine those ingredients. In the first, the state carrying the road notice affects only expert selection. In the second, it also has a direct path to the prediction. Give both the same notice, route question and available routes. If selecting a different expert still sends the traveller down the closed road, test whether the direct path changes that answer. This is a proposed comparison of the path information takes, not a choice between memory and routing.
Routing also needs a comparison of its own. Several learned transformations may depend on each other. Shared routing chooses experts for that group together; independent routing makes each choice separately. The design tests both rather than assuming that separately chosen parts will cooperate.
Surprise can change different things
An unexpected observation could change the state used for the next answer, deserve storage for later retrieval, or contribute to learning across episodes. Repeated failures might also suggest a different structure. How experience can change a unit follows those possibilities through the road-closure example.
A surprising route answer tells you where to look. It could come from an old notice, a missed message or a model error. MUON would put its candidate surprise signals on a common finite scale before using them to adjust a learning rate or score an observation for storage. A proposed structural change would need its own comparison. The surprise inquiry works through how to test the cause.
One interface, so a better unit can replace a stock model
The caller should be able to compare a new unit on the route task without rebuilding the application around that model. Stock open-weight models would fill the role first, through adapters for MLX, GGUF/llama.cpp, Ollama and Hugging Face. The later micro-transformer would answer through the same interface.
A common inference call is only part of what the caller needs:
What the caller needs to do	What the unit would expose	
Ask the route question and receive an answer as it is produced	Inference, including streaming	
Inspect the state being carried forward or recover a snapshot	Declared state and snapshots	
Follow the notice, answer and resource use through the run	Ordered records	
Check whether the work fits and obtain capacity for it	Resource estimates, reservations and refusal when capacity is unavailable	
Start the unit, advance it, recover or stop it	Lifecycle operations and checkpoints	
The caller also needs to know which model revision, tokenizer, quantisation and backend produced the answer, and which behaviours that version supports. The developer manual in the MUON repository explains how an adapter would report those choices and expose the interface.
Estimating the resources a request needs does not reserve them. An allocation example in that manual follows two requests that each fit a shared budget but cannot both spend it. Stock models would remain available as controls and fallbacks when another unit is tested.
Why many small units are worth testing
The hope is that useful organisation can accomplish work otherwise done by a larger model. The comparison includes many identical units, one stronger unit, a mixture and no swarm, using the same tasks and resource ceilings. Model inference, routing, memory, verification, failed proposals and communication all count toward cost. A cheaper answer cannot win by missing the task’s minimum performance.
If the many-unit design loses, the system can keep the strongest single or mixed alternative behind the same interface. Three tests for a reasoning unit explains why meeting an interface, being adequate for a task and replacing another model are separate claims. Q-MUON takes the one-unit question to a quantum substrate.
A possible place in a working system
Counsel is designed for local judgment within Pale’s compiled organisation, and a future MUON unit might serve a judgment role if it improves that work; Causality’s About page sets out the architecture MUON and HENA explore at those two scales.
Inspect the source
With the source checkouts, developers can compile the kernel crate in the MUON repository. It re-exports MONAD’s kernel, since the unit itself is not implemented yet.

A unit learns that a road has closed. The next question asks for a route. Does the closure change the answer? MUON uses questions like this to design how one unit could carry information forward and how a caller could compare two models doing the same work.
One unit and a collective ask different questions

body:
How experience can change a unit
At noon a road notice should change the next route. At four the road might reopen. A useful unit would need to use the first notice when it matters and stop relying on it once conditions change. MUON studies four ways a proposed unit might respond, from updating its current state to trying a different structure.
Remembering a closure is different from learning a rule
Ask for the same route with and without the noon notice. If the route changes when it should, the earlier observation has affected this answer. Sending the question to a different expert helps only if that expert’s computation can use the notice.
Storing the observation solves another part of the problem: making it available later. It still needs to be retrieved at the right time and used well. Keeping a closure after the road reopens could make the answer worse. The useful question is what retaining it contributes to later work, including the cost of keeping and retrieving it.
Learning across episodes changes how the unit behaves on future tasks. Repeated errors might motivate an update to its parameters so it handles similar notices differently later. If the unit’s structure cannot connect a notice to the affected route, changing parameters may be insufficient. A different structure becomes a candidate to test.
Change	What changes	How to tell whether it helps	
Temporal update	The state used for the current computation	Check whether an earlier cue changes the later answer appropriately	
Retention choice	Which observations remain available	Compare later performance and storage or retrieval cost	
Parameter learning	Learned behaviour across episodes	Check lasting improvement and effects on existing capabilities	
Structural hypothesis	The unit’s proposed sparse organisation	Compare the candidate with the existing structure on the failure it should address	
Use a separate comparison for each change. Saving the noon notice can help an afternoon request even if the model’s parameters stay the same. To test learning, try new cases after the update and check whether the unit still handles the ones it already got right.
Surprise can direct attention without explaining the cause
An observation that differs from a prediction may deserve attention. The disagreement could come from noise, changed conditions, too few resources or a poor representation. Its size alone cannot distinguish those causes.
MUON gives surprise three possible jobs: adjust a learning rate, contribute to a retention score, or trigger a structural hypothesis for separate evaluation. Learning rates and scores would have finite limits. The store would choose what to retain, and a proposed structure would not replace the current one until it had been tested.
The signals need interpretation before they can do any of this. A gradient describes how an error score changes when a component’s representation changes; its magnitude is one possible measure of sensitivity. A distributional divergence measures a difference between probability distributions, such as predicted activity with and without earlier context. The two measures answer different questions and can have very different numerical scales. Adding their raw values could let the larger-numbered one dominate for no useful reason.
The design therefore calls for calibrating each signal to a finite value on a common scale between zero and one. The calibration must specify its reference data, weights and limits, including what happens outside the conditions used to set it. Otherwise changing numerical representation could look like changing importance.
The surprise inquiry develops these mechanisms and their limits. Computation, state and learning places them within the broader unit design; the developer manual in the MUON repository explains the interface that would let a surrounding system use such a unit.

body:
Privacy notice
RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited (RTEPL) is responsible for deciding how personal data is used on rawthoughts.in, causality.in, sleepwalker.in and post-agi-economics.org, and on their subdomains, including the documentation at docs.rawthoughts.in and docs.causality.in. RTEPL publishes and operates these websites. This notice explains the information handled when you read these websites or use their contact and reading tools.
Visiting the website
GitHub Pages hosts these publications. Serving a page involves connection information, including your IP address and the page requested. GitHub logs visitors’ IP addresses for security, including when a visitor is not signed in. GitHub handles that information under its privacy statement and may process it outside India.
Mintlify hosts the documentation at docs.rawthoughts.in and docs.causality.in. Serving those pages involves the same connection information, which Mintlify handles under its privacy policy and may process outside India. Mintlify's own visitor telemetry is turned off for these sites. Mintlify also provides those two sites' search, page tools and display settings, under the same privacy policy; the in-browser search, assistant tools, display settings and passage links described below belong to the other websites.
On the other websites, search runs in your browser against each website's own index, so what you type is not sent to a search service. Your search is kept in the search page's address, so like any address it can reach GitHub with a page request, appear in your browser history and go with the address if you share it.
If your browser has an assistant that supports it, each page offers that assistant two read-only tools: the text of the page you are reading and the same in-browser search. They work on what the page already shows and send nothing to us; what the assistant does with what it reads follows its provider's terms.
Contacting us
A contact link opens a new message in your own email application. The website does not receive or store the message as a form submission. If you choose to send it, your email service and the recipient's mail service handle the correspondence. Any professional work that follows has its own correspondence and agreement.
For privacy questions, a grievance or a request concerning your personal data, write to info@rtepl.co.in. Include enough information to identify the request, but do not send passwords or unnecessary identity documents. We respond within 30 days and may ask for proportionate verification before disclosing or changing personal data.
Reading preferences
The display settings remember your colour and motion choices in your browser on this device. You can change them in Settings or clear the website's stored data through your browser. These preferences are used to display the page; they stay in your browser and are not sent to us.
After a page loads, your browser may request a few linked pages from the same site and keep copies on this device. These are ordinary page requests to the site's host. The browser can discard the copies, and clearing the site's stored data removes them.
Asking about a passage
When you select text and choose a reading assistant, the link opens that provider with the selected passage, nearby context, the section and article titles, the publication's name, and the article and publication addresses. The passage is limited to 4,096 characters and the nearby context to 1,024. Selecting text alone prepares the link in your browser; choosing the provider sends it there.
The assistant is an external service. The request is included in its link, so it can also appear in your browser history. The provider's own terms, privacy policy and your account settings govern what it does with the request and any conversation that follows. Reading the article does not require using an assistant.
How long information is kept
We keep no record of visits on our own systems; GitHub and Mintlify keep their connection logs for the periods their policies set. Correspondence you send is kept for as long as the matter it concerns needs it and as the law requires.
Security and incidents
These websites hold no accounts and receive no form submissions. If a personal-data breach affects you, we inform you and the authorities as applicable law requires.
Your choices
Following another external link takes you to that service under its own data practices.
You may ask us about your data, request correction or deletion, withdraw consent or raise a concern using the contact above. Requests are handled under applicable law; information needed to comply with a legal obligation or resolve a dispute may need to be kept. Withdrawing consent does not undo processing that has already occurred lawfully.
Changes to the website's data practices will be reflected in this notice. A new optional use that requires consent will ask for that consent rather than treating continued reading as agreement.
Last reviewed on 22 November 2026 by RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited.

arguments.label: Local quantum work, collective interaction and an answer

questions.question: How do Q-MUON and Q-HENA differ?
questions.answer_html: Q-MUON’s design concerns one quantum unit. Q-HENA’s design concerns how a group routes work, communicates, remembers and organises itself.

questions.question: Why retain both HENA and Q-HENA?
questions.answer_html: They investigate collective intelligence on different substrates. HENA remains the classical architecture; Q-HENA explores what quantum channels, state and memory change without discarding the classical work. Q-HENA has not demonstrated a quantum advantage.

questions.question: Why does recovery matter to the architecture?
questions.answer_html: Units may restore an exact state, return to behaviour equivalent under declared observations, or restart. A collective has to preserve the relationships its task needs across those differences, including preparation and work that must be repeated.

questions.question: Where should I start?
questions.answer_html: Quantum collective computation follows a joint operation between two units and what changes when one must restart. Developers can check the Rust crate in the Q-HENA repository, which re-exports its dependencies because quantum swarm coordination is not implemented yet.

body:
Q-HENA
What happens to a shared computation when one quantum unit has to start again? Q-HENA investigates how quantum units communicate, share memory and organise their work. Follow two units through recovery.
Quantum units learning to work as a whole
Q-MUON studies what one quantum unit can do. Q-HENA asks how several of those units route contributions, share memory through entanglement and learn how to divide a task. It carries forward HENA’s work on classical coordination and recovery while exploring different ways for units to interact.
Quantum interaction carrying a collective task
Imagine a task that needs one joint operation from two units. The design has to account for what each unit prepares, when both can act and which measurements help answer the task.
Prepare local contributions
Each Q-MUON unit prepares its local input and state. A joint operation also needs enough capacity for both units at the same time.
Connect the quantum units
The collective chooses a route and specifies how the units interact. If one unit has to restart, the collective needs to determine which preparation or interaction to repeat.
Read the collective result
The measurements have to contribute to the answer. A comparison counts preparation, communication, measurement and repeated work alongside local computation.
Questions about a quantum collective
An improved answer could come from the quantum computation, from a better division of work, or from both. The comparison needs to distinguish them:
Question	Keep the same	Compare	
What does quantum computation contribute?	Task and organisation	Relevant classical and quantum units	
What does the organisation contribute?	Task and substrate	Learned routes, an imposed hierarchy and simpler arrangements	
Follow each contribution through the units, channels and memory, counting preparation, measurement and repeated work. The collective-computation guide explains these comparisons alongside recovery. The classical architecture remains part of the programme.
Questions about Q-HENA
How do Q-MUON and Q-HENA differ?
Q-MUON’s design concerns one quantum unit. Q-HENA’s design concerns how a group routes work, communicates, remembers and organises itself.
Why retain both HENA and Q-HENA?
They investigate collective intelligence on different substrates. HENA remains the classical architecture; Q-HENA explores what quantum channels, state and memory change without discarding the classical work. Q-HENA has not demonstrated a quantum advantage.
Why does recovery matter to the architecture?
Units may restore an exact state, return to behaviour equivalent under declared observations, or restart. A collective has to preserve the relationships its task needs across those differences, including preparation and work that must be repeated.
Where should I start?
Quantum collective computation follows a joint operation between two units and what changes when one must restart. Developers can check the Rust crate in the Q-HENA repository, which re-exports its dependencies because quantum swarm coordination is not implemented yet.

body:
Quantum collective computation
Suppose two Q-MUON units need to perform one joint operation. Both would need capacity at the same time. If one unit had to start again, the collective would have to determine what work to repeat and which earlier observations it could still use. This design case illustrates Q-HENA, the proposal to explore HENA’s swarm question with quantum units.
Q-HENA asks about the group, not one quantum unit
Q-MUON concerns one unit’s computation. Q-HENA concerns which contributions reach each other, what the group remembers and how it organises a response. The joint operation illustrates why the group needs its own way to allocate resources and recover work.
Pale declares an organisation’s coordination explicitly where HENA asks how more of it could arise from intent, and Q-HENA asks what changes when that interaction involves quantum state, correlations and measurement; Causality’s About page sets out the comparison.
Quantum communication and collective memory
Q-HENA proposes quantum routing and communication, with memory mediated by entanglement. To turn that proposal into a mechanism, it must specify how state is prepared, which interaction occurs, what another unit can receive or measure and how the result contributes to an answer. Entanglement alone does not specify communication or storage.
The swarm would also keep operational records through Reckon’s record protocol. Those records would describe work and observations. They would not be copies of quantum state or proof that the state could be restored.
Two contributions to examine
A comparison must separate the contribution of quantum computation from the contribution of organisation:
Question	Hold fixed	Vary	
What does the substrate contribute?	Task and organisation	Relevant classical and quantum unit candidates	
What does the organisation contribute?	Task and substrate	Learned routing, an imposed hierarchy and simpler arrangements	
Count preparation, communication, measurement, memory, repeated interaction and failed attempts alongside local computation. Adding units is useful only if their interaction helps the task after those costs are counted. No quantum advantage has been demonstrated. The emergence inquiry develops that question.
Recovery is collective too
In the joint operation, suppose A can resume from a checkpoint and B must start again. Recovering A’s local state would still leave an open question about the relationship between A and B. They might need to repeat their joint preparation or interaction. A change in the hardware’s calibration could also make earlier measurements unsuitable for the resumed run.
Q-MUON’s proposed recovery modes distinguish restoring the declared state and results within stated tolerances, recovering equivalent behaviour under stated observations, and starting again. Their exact meanings and schema are still to be published. Q-HENA would need to establish which combinations can continue a collective task, and repeat preparation or interaction where necessary. Expired resource allocations must be obtained again.
The developer manual in the Q-HENA repository follows this problem through a proposed two-unit interaction. Recovery across a changing world explores why saved state alone is insufficient.
Q-HENA stays alongside HENA
Q-HENA would receive HENA’s classical progress and adapt it alongside Q-MUON. Both paths remain part of the programme. A quantum mechanism might help a particular task, lose its benefit once its full cost is counted, or leave the comparison inconclusive. Each result would inform the architecture without replacing the classical question.
Inspect the source
The repository contains a Rust crate that re-exports the MONAD, Q-MUON and Reckon kernels, and a draft paper; quantum swarm coordination is not implemented yet. Developers with the required source checkouts can check the crate in the Q-HENA repository.
