body:
Q-MUON
What could a quantum state let one reasoning unit do differently? Q-MUON investigates gates, entanglement and communication behind the same external interface as MUON, so preparation, computation and measurement can be compared as one complete task.
The same architectural question on another substrate
The state-overlap example follows two sensor readings from encoding to a similarity score. It shows which costs a comparison with a classical unit has to count. Q-HENA asks how units of this kind work together.
From quantum state to a useful response
A unit has to prepare an input, apply a circuit and measure an answer. All three steps count toward the cost of answering a task.
Prepare the input
The candidate encodes a task input as a quantum state. The encoding determines which differences between inputs the unit can use.
Transform the quantum state
A circuit applies quantum gates using the chosen parameters. A comparison tests which gates or interactions improve the result.
Return an observable answer
The unit measures the circuit and returns the result through MUON’s interface. If an answer requires repeated preparations and measurements, each repetition adds to its cost.
Questions about Q-MUON
What exists today?
The repository holds the fork of MUON, a kernel that builds on MONAD and a paper with an abstract. It has no quantum code; a classical candidate to mirror is the first problem in front.
Is Q-MUON meant to replace MUON?
Both paths are permanent. MUON develops the classical unit and owns the interface. Q-MUON carries that work into the fork and adapts what runs behind it.
Where could quantum structure enter?
Candidate directions include a quantum feature map used by a kernel, a parameterised circuit that learns an output law, and quantum communication between units.
Does one interface imply one kind of state?
No. Quantum state, measurement and recovery depend on the backend and calibration. Each unit declares what can be restored or repeated rather than inheriting a classical checkpoint promise.
How can I explore the design?
The guide follows a similarity calculation through the quantum unit and shows what a comparison with a classical unit has to measure. The substrate comparison develops those alternatives.

body:
The quantum local unit
Give a reasoning unit two sensor readings and ask how similar they are. Q-MUON asks whether a quantum processor could do a task like this behind the same interface as a classical MUON unit. Q-HENA would connect multiple units into a quantum swarm.
A local unit on a quantum substrate
For the sensor task, a quantum feature map could encode each reading as a state. A circuit could estimate the overlap between those states through repeated measurements, giving a classical learner a similarity score. A fair comparison counts preparing both states, running the circuit and repeating the measurements.
That example uses a kernel method. Other tasks could use a circuit with adjustable gates. Training would tune those gates against an objective measured from the circuit’s outputs. Quantum communication could let units exchange quantum states. Each is a candidate for research.
Why a quantum unit keeps MUON's interface
MUON’s draft interface covers inference, state, ordered records, resources and lifecycle operations. Keeping that interface would let a caller use a quantum unit without managing its gates. The developer manual in the MUON repository explains the five responsibilities.
A caller could receive the same kind of similarity score from either unit. It still needs to know whether that score helps on the task and whether it can swap in the new unit without disrupting its work. Conformance, adequacy and substitution explains those checks.
What would make a quantum unit worth using?
Compare a quantum candidate with a relevant classical alternative on the same task and at the same error tolerance. Count preparation, training, repeated measurement, noise, communication and recovery. A faster circuit can still produce a slower or more expensive answer.
For the sensor example, test whether the measured similarity helps the learner answer its task. If the candidate instead uses adjustable gates, first establish whether it can learn from the task objective. Then compare results and costs with a classical implementation. The substrate comparison develops those alternatives.
State and recovery need their own meaning
Suppose the sensor comparison stops halfway through. What would restarting the unit let you recover: its state, equivalent behaviour on the questions you can test, or only a new attempt? The proposed modes name those possibilities exact, semantic and restart_only.
A saved state format cannot answer that question alone. The backend and device topology matter, as do its calibration or noise model. So do the way the circuit was compiled and measured, the seed, the number of repeated measurements (shots) and the kind of replay being promised. A unit’s compatibility profile would identify these choices and the recovery mode it supports.
Note
The recovery modes’ precise guarantees, schema and tests remain undefined. A classical checkpoint cannot become a quantum checkpoint because its API has the same shape. A calibration change or new backend can also invalidate a recovery promise.
Q-HENA would need to respect each unit’s mode when recovering the swarm. Recovery across a changing world explains that collective problem.
MUON and Q-MUON stay side by side
MUON remains the classical path and owns the shared interface. Q-MUON would start from the corresponding MUON work before adapting it to a quantum backend. The programme keeps both paths for comparison.
Inspect the source
With source access, a developer can check the Rust crate, which re-exports MONAD because the quantum unit is not implemented yet. The developer manual in the Q-MUON repository explains the check and the proposed interface.

Suppose the sensor comparison stops halfway through. What would restarting the unit let you recover: its state, equivalent behaviour on the questions you can test, or only a new attempt? The proposed modes name those possibilities exact, semantic and restart_only.
A saved state format cannot answer that question alone. The backend and device topology matter, as do its calibration or noise model. So do the way the circuit was compiled and measured, the seed, the number of repeated measurements (shots) and the kind of replay being promised. A unit’s compatibility profile would identify these choices and the recovery mode it supports.
Note
The recovery modes’ precise guarantees, schema and tests remain undefined. A classical checkpoint cannot become a quantum checkpoint because its API has the same shape. A calibration change or new backend can also invalidate a recovery promise.
Q-HENA would need to respect each unit’s mode when recovering the swarm. Recovery across a changing world explains that collective problem.
MUON and Q-MUON stay side by side
MUON remains the classical path and owns the shared interface. Q-MUON would start from the corresponding MUON work before adapting it to a quantum backend. The programme keeps both paths for comparison.
Inspect the source
With source access, a developer can check the Rust crate, which re-exports MONAD because the quantum unit is not implemented yet. The developer manual in the Q-MUON repository explains the check and the proposed interface.

body:
Reckon
What should an agent keep when it has room for only a few records? Reckon measures what changes outcomes for what it costs, with the uncertainty shown. The laboratory runs locally for Causality’s research. The problem in front is serving RawThoughts’ agent tools with the same comparison, so a proposed improvement can be compared before anyone decides to use it. The cases for that comparison come from Pale's genealogy, its history of what each agent was given, what it did and what followed; the laboratory here runs without it.
Use the local laboratory to compare two replay budgets or inspect a saved run.
Keep useful experience. Understand what it changed.
An early clue can matter several steps later. Run the same task with different memory rules or limits, then follow the surviving records into the outcome.
To find out whether one record helped, compare runs with that instance present and absent. Report the cost of finding out alongside the outcome difference. The comparison tests one change under stated conditions; a causal claim also needs the assumptions that support that interpretation.
Follow what a memory changes
Give the same classifier room for 2 examples or 16. Compare its accuracy on earlier tasks, then investigate which memory choices made a difference.
Follow the record
Follow a record from when it was written to when it was read, scored or removed. Use the saved result to see how the task performed.
Change the memory
Change the space available, the retention rule or the presence of one record. Keep the other conditions fixed so the comparison answers the question you chose.
Compare the useful result
Compare accuracy or reward for each pair. When you test a policy or a record, report the uncertainty and what it cost to measure the difference, as well as the task's memory use.
Questions about Reckon
How do Reckon’s wider roles relate to the laboratory?
A correction can become a case for testing a better method. Reckon connects the case, comparison and owner's decision while keeping ordinary evaluation useful on its own. Cases, evaluations and decisions follows that wider use.
What does the laboratory show?
It is for finding which retained records mattered and what keeping them cost: the saved result gives accuracy or reward, and the log shows which memory operations wrote, read or dropped records. The laboratory guide explains how to follow those records and test a particular contribution.
Is every contribution score causal?
A causal claim needs a test that changes the record as intended, states the assumptions and keeps the other conditions fixed. Use a score to help choose what to keep, and use an outcome comparison to test what a record did. The cache example works through that reasoning.
Does Reckon own HENA’s or Scope’s memory?
HENA keeps its own swarm store and decides what to keep; Scope keeps only context derived from what Pale and Weave hold. Reckon runs a separate lab. Its wider services concern experiment inputs, results and decisions.
How do I run the laboratory?
The lab runs on your own machine. Start with the laboratory guide, then compare two replay budgets.

body:
Cases, evaluations and decisions
Imagine two teams testing whether a memory rule helps an agent remember an early clue. They need the same task inputs, results they can compare and a record of who decided whether to use the rule. The laboratory runs the comparison today; the repository holds no service yet for sharing cases, evaluations or decisions between teams, and Reckon's design gives each of those jobs its own service. For a worked comparison, compare two replay budgets in the lab.
Reuse the same case
In the design, the two teams name one version of the clue sequence and its expected outcomes. The curator keeps where it came from and how it may be used. A correction gets a new version, leaving the earlier one available to explain past results. HENA keeps its own live records and decides how to use them; Scope's context stays derived from what Pale and Weave hold, and a curated case changes none of it.
Evaluate a specified comparison
The experiment owner asks which memory rule works better on the delayed-cue task, with the task, inputs and budget specified. The evaluator reports what changed, the uncertainty, the cost and what another team needs to repeat the comparison.
Use that result to judge the tested rule in that task. If the reward changes during a bandit task, test the rule on that task separately. If the evaluator changes between runs, account for that before comparing the numbers. The experiment owner decides whether to use the candidate.
Preserve a decision
If the owner accepts, rejects or defers the candidate, the record identifies the version they decided on, confirms who decided and preserves the results they used. The artifact's owner still controls release, and the system running it still decides whether to activate it.
An ordinary evaluation can stand on its own. Promoting a learned change needs the case, comparison and owner's decision together, followed by the artifact owner's release checks and the caller's choice to use it. Applying a correction to today's work does not have to wait for that learning process.
A correction from everyday work can supply a case: what information was available, what the agent did, what the person changed and what happened later. Permission to reuse those sources matters. The correction tells us what someone wanted; the later outcome helps test whether it worked. The same cases can inform comparisons of tools, skills, policies or a successor to Counsel's local judge.
The developer manual covers the implemented lab.

body:
Compare two replay budgets
Does a classifier remember earlier tasks better when it can keep 16 examples for replay instead of 2? Run both allowances on the same starting data for each of three seeds. The script prints an accuracy difference for each pair and saves the results and memory activity from all six runs.
Important
Prepare the local environment. Use the reckon checkout and a Python environment with the Rust extension installed. If you need one, follow Set up the environment. You can run the comparison without a model service, notebook runner or daemon.
Set up the comparison
The classifier learns three two-dimensional problems in sequence. The line that divides the classes rotates from task to task. The classifier stores examples it gets wrong and sometimes uses a stored example for an extra update as training continues.
Setting	Value	
Training and test data	60 training and 60 test samples per task	
Learner	Two features; learning rate 0.1; replay probability 0.2	
Memory	2 or 16 slots, both with 50,000 bytes	
Seeds	41, 42 and 43, paired across allowances	
Run length	One episode per saved run	
Retention	Explicit FIFO in both runs of each pair	
The task generates training and test data before learning starts. That makes the data match within each seed. Later replay can differ because the buffers hold different examples. FIFO removes the oldest retained examples when either allowance is exceeded. Keep that policy and the byte limit fixed to compare slot allowances.
One episode here means one complete sequence of three classification tasks. Reckon can carry records, scores and retained events into later episodes; this small example uses one sequence so each accuracy matrix describes the same three problems. The larger memory-policy comparison also varies the retention rule and reports the cost of measuring record effects.
Save and run the script
With the Python environment active, save this as compare_replay_budgets.py in a folder for your results. Run it from that folder. If replay-budget-comparison already exists there, use a new folder or change the output name in the script.
import csv
from dataclasses import asdict
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path
from time import perf_counter

from reckon import CausalMemoryManager, MemoryBudget
from reckon.memory.policies import FIFOPolicy
from reckon.tasks.task_c_continual import ContinualConfig, ContinualTask

output = Path("replay-budget-comparison")
output.mkdir()
task_config = ContinualConfig(
    num_tasks=3,
    samples_per_task=60,
    test_samples_per_task=60,
    feature_dim=2,
    replay_fraction=0.2,
    learning_rate=0.1,
)
rows = []

for seed in (41, 42, 43):
    accuracy_by_slots = {}
    for slots in (2, 16):
        run = output / f"replay-s{slots}-seed{seed}"
        (run / "logs").mkdir(parents=True)
        budget = MemoryBudget(max_slots=slots, max_bytes=50_000)
        memory = CausalMemoryManager(budget, retention_policy=FIFOPolicy())
        config = {
            "task_name": "continual",
            "task": asdict(task_config),
            "budget": asdict(budget),
            "policy_name": type(memory.retention_policy).__name__,
            "seed": seed,
            "num_episodes": 1,
            "reset_memory": False,
            "learn_utility": True,
        }
        config_text = json.dumps(config, sort_keys=True, indent=2)
        (run / "config.json").write_text(config_text + "\n")
        started_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        started = perf_counter()
        result = ContinualTask(task_config).run(
            memory, num_episodes=1, seed=seed,
            reset_memory=False, learn_utility=True,
        )
        wall_time_ms = (perf_counter() - started) * 1000
        result_data = result.to_dict()
        (run / "result.json").write_text(json.dumps(result_data, indent=2) + "\n")
        (run / "logs" / "events.jsonl").write_text(memory.get_event_log_jsonl())
        episode = result_data["raw_data"]["episodes"][0]
        metrics = {
            "mean_accuracy": result_data["performance"]["mean_accuracy"],
            "forgetting": result_data["performance"]["forgetting"],
            "total_writes": episode["total_writes"],
            "total_reads": episode["total_reads"],
        }
        summary = {
            "config_id": hashlib.sha256(config_text.encode()).hexdigest(),
            "notebook_name": "replay-budget-comparison",
            "task_name": "continual",
            "started_at_ms": int(started_at.timestamp() * 1000),
            "policy_name": config["policy_name"],
            "num_episodes": 1,
            "budget_slots": slots,
            "config": config,
            "metrics": metrics,
            "wall_time_ms": wall_time_ms,
        }
        (run / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")
        rows.append({"seed": seed, "slots": slots, **metrics})
        accuracy_by_slots[slots] = metrics["mean_accuracy"]
        print(run)
    difference = accuracy_by_slots[16] - accuracy_by_slots[2]
    print(f"Seed {seed}: 16 minus 2 slots = {100 * difference:+.2f} percentage points")

with (output / "comparison.csv").open("w", newline="") as handle:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(handle, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(rows)

Run the script:
python compare_replay_budgets.py

Look for six run directories, three paired differences and comparison.csv, which has one row per run. Open any run to find:
File	Contents	
config.json	Task settings, budget, policy and seed	
result.json	Accuracy matrix and task results	
logs/events.jsonl	Recorded memory operations	
summary.json	Metadata used by the debugger importer	
If the script stops early, treat the comparison as incomplete and start again in a fresh folder. A missing row does not count as zero accuracy.
To repeat a run later, record the Reckon revision, dependency lockfiles, local edits, Python packages, Rust toolchain and extension build with the results. Seeds tell you which data to generate; they do not identify the implementation that uses it. The reproducibility guide covers the rest. wall_time_ms measures the task call, excluding setup, imports and file writes.
Read the accuracy matrix
Start with the paired differences. A positive number means 16 slots had higher final mean accuracy for that seed. Running this example on 15 November 2026 with Reckon revision 3d3aea6 gave:
Seed	2 slots	16 slots	Difference in percentage points	
41	81.11%	82.78%	+1.67	
42	82.22%	80.00%	−2.22	
43	81.11%	83.89%	+2.78	
The current runner uses separate random streams for task data and replay, and gives each training position a replay opportunity. Your results may therefore differ from these saved numbers. Read each pair in your comparison.csv before combining them. In the saved comparison, the larger buffer improved two seeds and worsened one. Three seeds describe this example; they do not establish which allowance generally performs better.
Open result.json. In raw_data.episodes[0].accuracy_matrix[i][j], the row tells you which training task just finished and the column tells you which task was tested:
A diagonal entry shows accuracy just after learning that task.
The final row shows accuracy after learning all three tasks.
Zeros above the diagonal mean “not evaluated yet.”
mean_accuracy averages the final row. Compare the final rows from your two runs to see which tasks gained or lost accuracy. In the saved seed 42 run above, most of the drop came from the first task.
forgetting compares each earlier task's first score on the diagonal with its score in the final row. Count drops only, treating gains as zero, and leave out the last task. An intermediate score higher than the diagonal score does not enter this calculation.
Two fields in the saved example have older names. In those original runs, causal_precision is one minus forgetting and reward_per_slot is final mean accuracy divided by counted writes, with a denominator of at least one. Current runs name these diagnostics.one_minus_mean_forgetting and diagnostics.mean_episode_accuracy_per_write; the latter averages each episode’s accuracy divided by its write count, with the same minimum denominator. This example runs one episode per configuration, so that average has one term. See the metrics reference for definitions. The three seeds give an exploratory comparison of this task and learner. To measure one record's contribution, run a separate comparison that changes whether that record is available.
Follow the memory activity
Open a run's logs/events.jsonl beside its result. Find op_type to see what happened. Copy a record ID from a write and look for it in a later read's details or in a pruning entry. For a write, bytes_after shows how many stored bytes counted toward the budget after that write. Use the result matrix for accuracy and the log for when those operations happened.
The log lacks full record payloads, classifier state and accuracy at each step.
Caution
A full log buffer discards earlier events. Its buffer holds at most 10,000 events. Carried episodes keep the retained events; an explicit memory reset starts a new buffer. For a longer study, consume the manager's event subscription while it runs so a full buffer does not discard the beginning. Those diagnostic copies consume memory outside the task's allowance.
Open a saved run in the debugger
You can read the results without a debugger. To view the activity there, follow Inspect an exported run to start the two servers. Run these commands from the folder that contains replay-budget-comparison:
reckon viz import "replay-budget-comparison/replay-s2-seed41"
reckon viz import "replay-budget-comparison/replay-s16-seed41"

The importer checks that the events can be projected for display before saving the run. The timeline preserves numeric event identities and their sequence, so operations at the same logical step remain distinct. Use it to compare writes, reads and removals; the raw log cannot supply full record snapshots or reconstruct the classifier.
Note
Success unavailable is not zero accuracy. The run list's success_rate is a separate field that this task does not supply. Current imports keep it unavailable (null), and the debugger shows “Success unavailable.” Read mean_accuracy from result.json for this classification task.
If import is refused, keep the original files and correct the reported format or identity problem; a missing display does not change the measured result. Stop both servers when you finish.

Compare two replay budgets
Does a classifier remember earlier tasks better when it can keep 16 examples for replay instead of 2? Run both allowances on the same starting data for each of three seeds. The script prints an accuracy difference for each pair and saves the results and memory activity from all six runs.
Important
Prepare the local environment. Use the reckon checkout and a Python environment with the Rust extension installed. If you need one, follow Set up the environment. You can run the comparison without a model service, notebook runner or daemon.
Set up the comparison
The classifier learns three two-dimensional problems in sequence. The line that divides the classes rotates from task to task. The classifier stores examples it gets wrong and sometimes uses a stored example for an extra update as training continues.
Setting	Value	
Training and test data	60 training and 60 test samples per task	
Learner	Two features; learning rate 0.1; replay probability 0.2	
Memory	2 or 16 slots, both with 50,000 bytes	
Seeds	41, 42 and 43, paired across allowances	
Run length	One episode per saved run	
Retention	Explicit FIFO in both runs of each pair	
The task generates training and test data before learning starts. That makes the data match within each seed. Later replay can differ because the buffers hold different examples. FIFO removes the oldest retained examples when either allowance is exceeded. Keep that policy and the byte limit fixed to compare slot allowances.
One episode here means one complete sequence of three classification tasks. Reckon can carry records, scores and retained events into later episodes; this small example uses one sequence so each accuracy matrix describes the same three problems. The larger memory-policy comparison also varies the retention rule and reports the cost of measuring record effects.
Save and run the script
With the Python environment active, save this as compare_replay_budgets.py in a folder for your results. Run it from that folder. If replay-budget-comparison already exists there, use a new folder or change the output name in the script.
import csv
from dataclasses import asdict
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path
from time import perf_counter

from reckon import CausalMemoryManager, MemoryBudget
from reckon.memory.policies import FIFOPolicy
from reckon.tasks.task_c_continual import ContinualConfig, ContinualTask

output = Path("replay-budget-comparison")
output.mkdir()
task_config = ContinualConfig(
    num_tasks=3,
    samples_per_task=60,
    test_samples_per_task=60,
    feature_dim=2,
    replay_fraction=0.2,
    learning_rate=0.1,
)
rows = []

for seed in (41, 42, 43):
    accuracy_by_slots = {}
    for slots in (2, 16):
        run = output / f"replay-s{slots}-seed{seed}"
        (run / "logs").mkdir(parents=True)
        budget = MemoryBudget(max_slots=slots, max_bytes=50_000)
        memory = CausalMemoryManager(budget, retention_policy=FIFOPolicy())
        config = {
            "task_name": "continual",
            "task": asdict(task_config),
            "budget": asdict(budget),
            "policy_name": type(memory.retention_policy).__name__,
            "seed": seed,
            "num_episodes": 1,
            "reset_memory": False,
            "learn_utility": True,
        }
        config_text = json.dumps(config, sort_keys=True, indent=2)
        (run / "config.json").write_text(config_text + "\n")
        started_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        started = perf_counter()
        result = ContinualTask(task_config).run(
            memory, num_episodes=1, seed=seed,
            reset_memory=False, learn_utility=True,
        )
        wall_time_ms = (perf_counter() - started) * 1000
        result_data = result.to_dict()
        (run / "result.json").write_text(json.dumps(result_data, indent=2) + "\n")
        (run / "logs" / "events.jsonl").write_text(memory.get_event_log_jsonl())
        episode = result_data["raw_data"]["episodes"][0]
        metrics = {
            "mean_accuracy": result_data["performance"]["mean_accuracy"],
            "forgetting": result_data["performance"]["forgetting"],
            "total_writes": episode["total_writes"],
            "total_reads": episode["total_reads"],
        }
        summary = {
            "config_id": hashlib.sha256(config_text.encode()).hexdigest(),
            "notebook_name": "replay-budget-comparison",
            "task_name": "continual",
            "started_at_ms": int(started_at.timestamp() * 1000),
            "policy_name": config["policy_name"],
            "num_episodes": 1,
            "budget_slots": slots,
            "config": config,
            "metrics": metrics,
            "wall_time_ms": wall_time_ms,
        }
        (run / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")
        rows.append({"seed": seed, "slots": slots, **metrics})
        accuracy_by_slots[slots] = metrics["mean_accuracy"]
        print(run)
    difference = accuracy_by_slots[16] - accuracy_by_slots[2]
    print(f"Seed {seed}: 16 minus 2 slots = {100 * difference:+.2f} percentage points")

with (output / "comparison.csv").open("w", newline="") as handle:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(handle, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(rows)

Run the script:
python compare_replay_budgets.py

Look for six run directories, three paired differences and comparison.csv, which has one row per run. Open any run to find:
File	Contents	
config.json	Task settings, budget, policy and seed	
result.json	Accuracy matrix and task results	
logs/events.jsonl	Recorded memory operations	
summary.json	Metadata used by the debugger importer	
If the script stops early, treat the comparison as incomplete and start again in a fresh folder. A missing row does not count as zero accuracy.
To repeat a run later, record the Reckon revision, dependency lockfiles, local edits, Python packages, Rust toolchain and extension build with the results. Seeds tell you which data to generate; they do not identify the implementation that uses it. The reproducibility guide covers the rest. wall_time_ms measures the task call, excluding setup, imports and file writes.
Read the accuracy matrix
Start with the paired differences. A positive number means 16 slots had higher final mean accuracy for that seed. Running this example on 15 November 2026 with Reckon revision 3d3aea6 gave:
Seed	2 slots	16 slots	Difference in percentage points	
41	81.11%	82.78%	+1.67	
42	82.22%	80.00%	−2.22	
43	81.11%	83.89%	+2.78	
The current runner uses separate random streams for task data and replay, and gives each training position a replay opportunity. Your results may therefore differ from these saved numbers. Read each pair in your comparison.csv before combining them. In the saved comparison, the larger buffer improved two seeds and worsened one. Three seeds describe this example; they do not establish which allowance generally performs better.
Open result.json. In raw_data.episodes[0].accuracy_matrix[i][j], the row tells you which training task just finished and the column tells you which task was tested:
A diagonal entry shows accuracy just after learning that task.
The final row shows accuracy after learning all three tasks.
Zeros above the diagonal mean “not evaluated yet.”
mean_accuracy averages the final row. Compare the final rows from your two runs to see which tasks gained or lost accuracy. In the saved seed 42 run above, most of the drop came from the first task.
forgetting compares each earlier task's first score on the diagonal with its score in the final row. Count drops only, treating gains as zero, and leave out the last task. An intermediate score higher than the diagonal score does not enter this calculation.
Two fields in the saved example have older names. In those original runs, causal_precision is one minus forgetting and reward_per_slot is final mean accuracy divided by counted writes, with a denominator of at least one. Current runs name these diagnostics.one_minus_mean_forgetting and diagnostics.mean_episode_accuracy_per_write; the latter averages each episode’s accuracy divided by its write count, with the same minimum denominator. This example runs one episode per configuration, so that average has one term. See the metrics reference for definitions. The three seeds give an exploratory comparison of this task and learner. To measure one record's contribution, run a separate comparison that changes whether that record is available.
Follow the memory activity
Open a run's logs/events.jsonl beside its result. Find op_type to see what happened. Copy a record ID from a write and look for it in a later read's details or in a pruning entry. For a write, bytes_after shows how many stored bytes counted toward the budget after that write. Use the result matrix for accuracy and the log for when those operations happened.
The log lacks full record payloads, classifier state and accuracy at each step.
Caution
A full log buffer discards earlier events. Its buffer holds at most 10,000 events. Carried episodes keep the retained events; an explicit memory reset starts a new buffer. For a longer study, consume the manager's event subscription while it runs so a full buffer does not discard the beginning. Those diagnostic copies consume memory outside the task's allowance.
Open a saved run in the debugger
You can read the results without a debugger. To view the activity there, follow Inspect an exported run to start the two servers. Run these commands from the folder that contains replay-budget-comparison:
reckon viz import "replay-budget-comparison/replay-s2-seed41"
reckon viz import "replay-budget-comparison/replay-s16-seed41"

The importer checks that the events can be projected for display before saving the run. The timeline preserves numeric event identities and their sequence, so operations at the same logical step remain distinct. Use it to compare writes, reads and removals; the raw log cannot supply full record snapshots or reconstruct the classifier.
Note
Success unavailable is not zero accuracy. The run list's success_rate is a separate field that this task does not supply. Current imports keep it unavailable (null), and the debugger shows “Success unavailable.” Read mean_accuracy from result.json for this classification task.
If import is refused, keep the original files and correct the reported format or identity problem; a missing display does not change the measured result. Stop both servers when you finish.

body:
Inspect an exported run
Pick one record in a saved run and see where it was written, read or removed. You can do this from the saved files without running the task again. The debugger can show more when the export contains full record snapshots.
Choose a run
Find the run folder that contains logs/events.jsonl. Notebook runs normally live under notebooks/runs/. If you followed Compare two replay budgets, use replay-s2-seed41 from your results. The importer needs the event file, even if you already have figures and scores. It copies the run into the debugger's local storage. Keep the original files for checking what the debugger shows.
Follow a record
In the replay example, pick one stored example. Open logs/events.jsonl in a text editor, find a write and copy its record_id. Search below it for that ID in a later read's details, a score update or a removal.
Use richer exports to see what a record contained and how it relates to other records. A read tells you that a record was returned. Showing that it helped requires a separate outcome comparison. For a measured connection between two records, supply the probe result for that pair. The debugger displays the result after you run the probe elsewhere.
The key-and-door example
The built-in key-and-door task gives a small example to follow. Its grid has a start (S), a place to see the key colour (K), two doors (L and R) and a goal (G). The # cells are walls:
S . . . .
. . K . .
. . . . .
# L # R #
. . G . .

At K, the controller writes the observed colour as a cue record. Before choosing a door, it asks for that episode's record by ID.
The saved example in notebooks/runs/2026-11-16/keydoor_export_demo/95585cb0799e/ ran three episodes on 16 November 2026 with seed 42, FIFO, one slot and 50,000 bytes. It kept memory between episodes and enabled utility learning. Its result.json records a green-cue failure followed by two blue-cue successes. Each episode wrote and retrieved its cue once. The log contains 11 events: three writes, three reads, three utility updates and two removals.
Follow the first blue cue, in keydoor_ep1, by searching for record b4b5c6bb-df57-4f6f-ac60-da08406783e8:
Event ID	Logical step	What the log records	
4	24	The cue is written	
5	26	A read returns its ID in details	
6	29	Utility changes from 0 to 0.1 after the successful episode	
7	33	FIFO removes it when the next episode writes its cue	
These steps are logical positions, not elapsed times. Read the cue colour and outcome from result.json: the raw log contains neither payloads nor a grid trajectory.
The controller chooses right for a retrieved blue cue and otherwise guesses left, without trying a second door. Red opens the left door, so it can succeed without retrieval. Green opens a seeded random door: in this run the right door was open, but remembering green still led to the left-hand guess. A stored and retrieved cue therefore need not produce success; success alone does not show that a cue helped.
This task writes one cue and reads it before the next write. With enough bytes for that cue, one slot is sufficient for this controller's memory path. It does not create competing records before the choice, so it cannot by itself show which retention ranking handles that competition better. The task contract explains those limits; the replay comparison exercises a different workload.
Start the debugger
This step is optional. Importing the replay example exposes its recorded writes, reads, removals and score updates on the timeline. Numeric event IDs remain distinct, including operations at the same logical step. A raw log supplies activity rather than full record snapshots; the timeline reference explains what each export can show.
Use the reckon checkout, a working Python environment with the Rust extension, Node.js 18 or later and pnpm 9. With that environment active, run this from the reckon root to add the Python debugger dependencies:
python -m pip install ".[viz]"

Start both servers from the reckon checkout. Keep the project Python environment active in the first and third terminals.
In the first terminal, start the backend:
python -m reckon.viz.server

In a second terminal, install the interface dependencies, build the shared components and start the interface. If the dependencies and build are already current, run just pnpm dev from viz-ui:
cd viz-ui
pnpm install
pnpm build:components
pnpm dev

In a third terminal, import the run using its full path. Use the results folder you actually chose, even if it is outside the checkout:
reckon viz import "/absolute/path/to/your-run"

Open http://localhost:5173 in your browser and select the imported run. The interface on port 5173 uses the backend on port 8000. If no runs appear, check that both terminals are still running.
To follow the key-and-door example in the interface, import its saved directory instead and select that run. The heading shows 3 episodes | 67% success. Start at event 0 and use Next event to reach the blue cue’s four events above; operations sharing a logical step remain separately selectable. Open Source operation to compare each complete log entry with logs/events.jsonl.
A successful import prints Imported run: and an event count. If it fails:
Message or situation	What to check	
Path not found	Check the full path and folder name. If you used a relative path, check the terminal's working directory too	
No events.jsonl found	The producer actually saved an event log	
Run identity already exists	Inspect the existing import, or choose a new identity	
Cannot display run	Read the reported format or identity error and correct the export; keep its original bytes for diagnosis	
The default run ID is the last part of the directory path. To keep another copy, give it a new ID:
reckon viz import "/absolute/path/to/your-run" --run-id inspected-copy

Compare outcomes, not just activity
Note
Activity is not accuracy. The debugger's default performance axis divides writes by writes plus removals and labels that as an operation proxy. It describes memory activity, not task success. Open the saved task result for accuracy or reward. Missing measurements remain unavailable; the event log alone cannot supply probe cost or accuracy.
When measured points are supplied, the frontier retains a point unless another uses no more cost and achieves at least as much performance, with one strict improvement. Exact duplicates remain visible, and overruns expand the budget axis beyond 100%. The plot does not choose a policy or calculate uncertainty across repeated trials. For adding measured points and declaring their units, see the frontier reference.
The laboratory guide explains what you can infer from a write, a read or an outcome difference.
Stop the debugger
Press Ctrl+C in each server terminal when finished. Closing the browser tab does not stop either process. Your saved export and imported copy remain available.

body:
Understand the memory laboratory
A classifier can learn a new task and get worse at an earlier one. Keeping examples to practise again may help, but memory has a cost. How many examples should it keep, and which ones should it give up when it runs out of room?
Reckon lets you compare those choices. Compare two replay budgets starts with one classifier, the same training data and room for either 2 or 16 examples. It takes you from running the comparison to reading the saved accuracy matrices. If you already have a run, follow a record through its event log instead.
Important
Local setup. These guides use the local reckon source checkout and its Python environment. Follow Set up the environment if you need that prerequisite, then return to the comparison. The laboratory works locally.
Choose what memory has to do
Remembering an early clue and practising an old skill put different demands on memory. Choose a task that presents the difficulty you want to study:
Task	Memory challenge	
Key and door	Remember an early cue until it becomes useful	
Hidden-mode bandit	Respond when the reward-generating mode changes	
Continual classification	Replay earlier examples while learning a new task	
Tutoring simulation	Retain information about a simulated learner's misconceptions	
You can change how much memory the task receives, or change the rule that chooses what survives. Keep the other choice fixed when you want to understand its effect. In the replay example, both buffers discard the oldest retained example first, so the comparison asks about room for examples rather than which removal rule is better.
The completed retention-policy comparison instead tests several rules on Tutor, Continual, scripted Conversation and TextWorld. It reports the controls and the cost of the extra experiments used to estimate record effects. Read those results when choosing a workload or deciding whether a more expensive rule is worth testing.
Follow a record
The task decides what to remember. In the key-and-door task, it sees a colour near the start and writes that colour as a cue. At the door, it asks for the cue again. Reckon keeps the record's content and ID, its resource cost, where it came from and the scores a retention rule can use.
The saved log lets you follow the write and the later read. It can also show score updates and the removal that eventually makes room for another record. Inspect an exported run follows a real blue cue through those four events. The raw log does not contain everything about the record; richer exports can supply record details and relationships for the debugger.
Getting a record back is only part of the story. The task still has to use it to make a useful choice. To find out whether the record helped, compare the outcome with and without it. A write establishes that something was stored, a read that it was returned, and an outcome comparison tests what difference its availability made.
Why a good result can lower a score
After using retrieved records, the task reports an outcome through observe(). Reckon shares credit among those records and blends each share of the outcome into the record's previous utility. With the default update rate, the calculation is:
new utility = 0.9 × old utility + 0.1 × credit × outcome
The result stays within the configured bounds. Suppose a record's utility was 0.5, its credit is 0.33 and the outcome is 1. Its new utility is 0.483. The episode went well, but the record's assigned share was below its old estimate, so its score fell.
Python's observe() shares credit equally by default. Shaped credit instead turns the current utilities into positive weights and normalises them. Daemon callers choose their credit policy explicitly. These rules assign a share; they do not measure each record's individual effect. The memory-manager guide explains the alternatives and their inputs.
An early record may matter long after its last use, while a recent one contributes nothing. A score matters for survival only if the retention rule uses it. FIFO removes the oldest record and LRU the least recently accessed one. Importance uses a score supplied by the caller; learned utility ranks records by updated utility per byte. That remains a per-byte ranking even when a slot limit forces the removal.
The replay tutorial uses FIFO. It still updates utilities, but those updates do not change which examples FIFO removes. Its one episode ends after the utility update. When a run carries memory into later episodes, surviving records can be retrieved and scored again. To compare the removal rules themselves, use the policy comparison with matched tasks, limits and seeds.
Test what made the difference
Start with the task's outcome: accuracy for the replay comparison, or reward for a task that reports reward. Keep the settings, results and activity log together. The log helps explain what happened during the run, but counting writes and removals does not tell you how well the task performed. The debugger's default frontier uses writes divided by writes plus removals and labels it as an operation proxy; read task accuracy from the saved result.
To find out whether remembering a cue helped the task, compare its outcome with and without that record. Reckon's evaluator waits until the first read that could return the chosen instance. It checks that both runs reached the same memory state and read boundary, then verifies that the record was actually removed in one of them. The task may later write the same fact again, so the comparison tests losing that instance rather than permanently forbidding the information. The evaluation guide explains how to set up the comparison and handle a target it cannot test.
Choosing what to discard raises another question: is it worth running extra trials to estimate which records matter? The measured retention policy copies the retained memory into fresh task episodes and compares outcomes with and without a candidate under a declared reference policy. Positive removal estimates contribute to the utility ranking; the report keeps the signed estimates, including zero and negative ones. Judge the resulting task performance alongside the extra trials and time needed to make those choices.
Those fresh episodes do not tell you what a different removal would do at the current write. For that comparison, the Conversation, MiniGrid and TextWorld notebooks can reconstruct the actual episode prefix and earlier removals, then compare removing a candidate with removing FIFO's choice. Both continuations use FIFO afterwards. The notebook guide explains this path and the separate record-removal experiments, including how the controller and continuation rule limit the result.
Whichever comparison you choose, report the outcome difference, its uncertainty and the measurement cost. To call the difference causal, explain what changed, what stayed fixed and which assumptions make the comparison informative. The cache example works through that reasoning.
Cases, evaluations and decisions beyond the laboratory
Reckon's wider design for cases, evaluations and decisions is the work in front: it preserves an experiment's inputs, compares a proposed change and keeps the decision its owner makes from the result, and none of it is built yet.
How Reckon relates to Scope and HENA
Scope asks which permitted context helps a task. A passage being retrieved or quoted does not answer that question. Reckon tests a related one under a memory budget: what changes when a record or retention rule changes? A result on one workload can help Scope design a comparison for its own tasks; Scope still has to test what works there.
HENA keeps its own swarm store and decides what to keep. It may keep it behind Reckon's record-store interface, designed and not yet published, so that Reckon can inspect and evaluate its records without HENA calling Reckon. Scope keeps only context derived from what Pale and Weave hold, and in the design requests evaluations through Pale.
Working with the code
The developer manual covers building the Python/Rust library and extending the laboratory. The comparison and event-log guides do not need the daemon.
Caution
The daemon has no caller authentication. If you use it separately, keep it on a trusted local machine. It listens only on loopback and uses plaintext.
The daemon's ExportRun returns the latest record snapshots observed by a named run. For an event history in the debugger, use the logs saved by Python or a notebook: ExportRun does not include events, metrics or a complete evaluation bundle.

content.description: The calculus, local units, collective architectures and measurement tools behind Causality’s research programme.

questions.question: How do these projects fit together?
questions.answer_html: Causality asks how a system can change its description and learn its own organisation, and these projects take the question in parts. MONAD asks what a change in description preserves. MUON studies one reasoning unit, HENA studies how units work together, and Reckon tests what memory contributes to a task. Q-MUON and Q-HENA ask related questions about a quantum unit and a quantum collective. Each page says what exists today.

questions.question: Where should I begin?
questions.answer_html: For a small mathematical example, follow a part from stock count to repair: knowing it is available does not tell you whether it fits. To try an experiment, give a classifier two different replay budgets and compare how well it remembers its earlier tasks.

body:
A dense constellation of points and fine connecting lines.
MONAD
Ask which distinctions survive when you compress or change a description. MONAD develops the mathematics in Lean, with a paper and a small Rust kernel.
A dense constellation of points and fine connecting lines.
MUON
Design a common interface for one reasoning unit, so a stock model and a unit that learns from experience can be compared on the same work.
A dense constellation of points and fine connecting lines.
Reckon
Run the same task at two memory budgets and see what changes. The local lab saves outcomes and shows which records were written, read or dropped.
A dense constellation of points and fine connecting lines.
HENA
Ask whether small reasoning units can organise around a task when they can send only a few messages and keep only some of their past work.
A dense constellation of points and fine connecting lines.
Q-MUON
Explore what a quantum implementation could change inside one reasoning unit while keeping MUON’s external interface.
A dense constellation of points and fine connecting lines.
Q-HENA
Explore how quantum units might communicate, route work and share memory through entanglement. The design carries over HENA’s collective interfaces.
Further questions
Intelligence in a working system
Reasoning has to meet the work around it. RawThoughts’ products make one system of that work, with people deciding. Pale is the meta harness through which they act, a harness over the tools people already use; it carries a goal forward through people, agents and applications, with useful context and the decisions that need a person kept in view.
Explore the systems
What cheaper intelligence changes
As cognitive work gets cheaper, constraints can move to energy, ownership and the institutions around production. Post-AGI Economics follows those consequences for firms, households and the models used to understand them.
Explore the economic inquiry
The questions behind the models
Small examples can reveal what a description loses, what a collective can learn and what an evaluation actually establishes. Follow these questions through the programme’s connected writing.
Explore the thoughts
Questions about the programme
How do these projects fit together?
Causality asks how a system can change its description and learn its own organisation, and these projects take the question in parts. MONAD asks what a change in description preserves. MUON studies one reasoning unit, HENA studies how units work together, and Reckon tests what memory contributes to a task. Q-MUON and Q-HENA ask related questions about a quantum unit and a quantum collective. Each page says what exists today.
Where should I begin?
For a small mathematical example, follow a part from stock count to repair: knowing it is available does not tell you whether it fits. To try an experiment, give a classifier two different replay budgets and compare how well it remembers its earlier tasks.

body:
Building
With source access, check that the HENA crate compiles or build the draft paper. The kernel needs Reckon as well as MONAD and MUON. The paper carries copies of those definitions in paper/shared/, so it builds alone.
Check the kernel
Fetch the pinned dependencies
The kernel manifest pins MONAD, MUON and reckon to one commit each of their GitHub repositories. Cargo fetches them on the first check and reuses its copies afterwards, so the first check needs network access. Reckon's repository name is lowercase reckon.
HENA uses Reckon's default Rust API. Its optional Python binding stays disabled, so this check needs no Python environment, Reckon wheel, debugger or notebook packages.
Provide the build tools
Use Rust and Cargo. Reckon's build supplies a pinned Protocol Buffers compiler through Cargo, so a separate protoc installation is optional. Set PROTOC to an executable path when selecting a compiler explicitly; PROTOC_INCLUDE can select its include directory. Offline builds need the packaged compiler dependencies in Cargo's cache too.
Compile the dependency graph
From HENA's repository root, run:
cargo check --manifest-path kernel/Cargo.toml

A successful command compiles hena-kernel and its three dependency re-exports. If it fails in a dependency crate, resolve that dependency's error before retrying HENA.
Important

The current crate contains no scheduler, message routing or swarm store. This check does not run units or demonstrate collective behaviour.
Build the paper
Install Make, Bash and a TeX distribution with pdflatex and bibtex. Use pdftotext to inspect the rendered text as well as opening the PDF.
From HENA's repository root:
cd paper
make all

The output is paper/HENA.pdf. The main source imports the MONAD, MUON and HENA definitions in paper/shared/, so the paper builds without the other repositories.
The problem statement presents the proposed differentiable collective, its equations, resource targets and comparison requirements. Read the generated PDF and review the build warnings; successful typesetting establishes neither the proposal’s performance nor its feasibility.
Return to the overview.

HENA uses Reckon's default Rust API. Its optional Python binding stays disabled, so this check needs no Python environment, Reckon wheel, debugger or notebook packages.
Provide the build tools
Use Rust and Cargo. Reckon's build supplies a pinned Protocol Buffers compiler through Cargo, so a separate protoc installation is optional. Set PROTOC to an executable path when selecting a compiler explicitly; PROTOC_INCLUDE can select its include directory. Offline builds need the packaged compiler dependencies in Cargo's cache too.
Compile the dependency graph
From HENA's repository root, run:
cargo check --manifest-path kernel/Cargo.toml

A successful command compiles hena-kernel and its three dependency re-exports. If it fails in a dependency crate, resolve that dependency's error before retrying HENA.
Important

The current crate contains no scheduler, message routing or swarm store. This check does not run units or demonstrate collective behaviour.
Build the paper
Install Make, Bash and a TeX distribution with pdflatex and bibtex. Use pdftotext to inspect the rendered text as well as opening the PDF.
From HENA's repository root:
cd paper
make all

The output is paper/HENA.pdf. The main source imports the MONAD, MUON and HENA definitions in paper/shared/, so the paper builds without the other repositories.
The problem statement presents the proposed differentiable collective, its equations, resource targets and comparison requirements. Read the generated PDF and review the build warnings; successful typesetting establishes neither the proposal’s performance nor its feasibility.
Return to the overview.

body:
HENA
HENA asks whether useful collective reasoning and hierarchy can emerge from local rules: many units learning sparse communication and using bounded, differentiable memory. This manual explains the proposed swarm coordination and how to compare it with simpler systems. The first stock-model swarm would provide a working baseline; it would not establish the learned routing and memory sought within a model.
The Rust crate re-exports MONAD, MUON and Reckon. Its build checks their dependency wiring; the research comparisons below would test the collective behaviour.
Build the current crate
Check the dependency wiring with MONAD, MUON and Reckon.
Understand the research
Follow one piece of information through the proposed collective.
What the current crate exposes
hena-kernel re-exports monad_kernel, muon_kernel and reckon_kernel. Each is a direct Cargo git dependency pinned to one commit of its repository. HENA can therefore use MONAD's types directly as well as through the other kernels.
There is no HENA scheduler, routing policy or store API. Its Protocol Buffers files declare packages and imports. They contain no messages. A successful kernel check confirms the dependencies compile together.
simulator/ is the planned home for the first single-machine experiment: run many stock units through MUON's slot, route messages sparsely and keep memory within a fixed capacity. Sequence modelling, key-value retrieval and simple reasoning would test the collective against a transformer at matched compute. The simulator has no implementation yet. Scaling the number of units and moving to distributed hardware follow a working local comparison.
Compose a unit without depending on its internals
MUON defines the intended interface for checking whether a unit can perform a task, invoking it and receiving a result. HENA would call that interface without inspecting a model's state. Adapters around existing open-weight models would provide the first units. A unit built for MUON could take one model's place through the same interface.
This keeps changes inside a unit separate from changes to the swarm. A stronger model might improve the answer even if the routing remains poor. An experiment needs to distinguish that gain from better coordination.
Routing decides which information meets
Each unit would receive part of the input, messages from a few neighbours and reads from memory. Over several rounds, details such as the connector warning could reach the units or memory that supply the answer.
Broadcasting every view spends communication on every recipient. Routing everything through a central unit moves the bottleneck. HENA instead aims to learn sparse routes within compute, communication and memory limits, so queries reach selected units and memory rather than attending to every key. Learned routing is intended to replace full attention; stock-model orchestration would provide the baseline for testing that aim.
The communication example follows a connector warning from a maintenance note to a later repair decision. It asks whether the route delivered information that changed the answer.
Shared resources need a swarm-level decision
Suppose two units each need the one free execution slot. Both could agree to run when asked separately. HENA's proposed allocator would reserve shared capacity once, bind the reservation to the scheduler's current generation and release it after the attempt.
Define the allocator and its records when the first swarm shares a resource pool. The unit contract distinguishes eligibility from reserved capacity; the allocator protocol is developed with the swarm coordination that uses the pool. The fields and failure cases below preserve the proposed design for that implementation.
Availability and reservations belong to the allocator
MUON's admission specification owns the caller's requirements, estimated demand, fixed capacity and eligibility decision. HENA would own the two records that change as work uses the shared pool. A standalone unit coordinator sharing capacity between callers has the same allocator responsibilities.
ResourceAvailabilitySnapshotV1 identifies the allocator and pool, the fixed capacity profile, generation, currently unreserved quantities, observation and expiry times, and previous snapshot.
ResourceReservationV1 binds one live generation to a holder and work identity, the requirement, demand and admission records, reserved quantities, lease generation, issue and expiry times, and recorded monotone transitions among active, consumed, released and expired states. These are lifecycle outcomes; a reservation need not pass through all four in sequence.
A positive admission decision does not reserve capacity. The allocator would issue a matching reservation atomically, so two decisions against one snapshot cannot spend the same capacity. Reserve, renew, consume and release use compare-and-swap transitions. Replaying the exact request returns its original result; changing a reused request conflicts.
Expiry or a new allocator generation releases capacity through a recorded successor, rather than an inferred timeout. A crashed holder cannot continue past its lease, and a stale reservation cannot consume a newer allocation. Tests must cover stale release, renewal and consumption for the exact generation, holder and attempt; concurrent reservations; crash and restart; and double consumption. Every outcome must leave one allocator head and consistent capacity accounting.
Recover the swarm as well as its units
Restoring a unit does not revive an expired reservation or rewind the swarm's store. The proposed SwarmCheckpointV1 would bind the swarm and run identity, scheduler generation, routing and population revision, live reservations with their hashes and expiries, ordered child checkpoints and each one's restore class, store and replay positions, the disposition of any partial recovery, and the preceding checkpoint. Its schema and manifest are to be written with the first simulator that needs to recover shared work.
Resume requires the current scheduler generation, matching store and replay positions, current reservations and an admitted mix of unit restore classes. Readmission issues successor reservations. Q-HENA's quantum compatibility layer would build on these rules; it cannot strengthen a participating unit's recovery guarantee.
The swarm keeps its own history
HENA would keep the swarm's operational store, retention decisions and run history. Reckon's proposed record interface would let an evaluator inspect records for scoring or debugging. It would not give the evaluator control over pruning the swarm's store.
Local, swarm-wide and episode-specific memory tiers remain a proposal. Text retrieval could support initial orchestration. The trainable memory target would make memory differentiable, putting reads and writes in the learning process alongside routes and unit updates.
Population changes stay inside a run
The proposed evolution mechanism varies local rules and compares the collective behaviour they produce. It keeps useful alternatives in behaviour categories, or niches, and records how each candidate arose. Fixed mutation and evaluation operators let an experiment change candidates without changing how they are judged.
Candidate state would be versioned and checkpointed within its run. Replacing a unit implementation or using a learned organization in another application would be a separate change. The evolution explanation develops the research question.
Judge organization by the complete task
The paper’s problem statement sets the quantitative targets: processing at O(T\log T) or O(T) rather than quadratic attention cost, a fixed-capacity store of O(K) records rather than storage growing with input length T, and sparse communication rather than all-to-all N^2 interaction among N units. Here K\ll T, and the memory comparison holds record width fixed; unit states, routing buffers and messages still count towards total memory. These are proposed targets, not measured properties of the crate. A useful hierarchy must improve the answer or the cost of producing it against simpler alternatives: a stronger single unit, a flat collective, a central coordinator and an imposed hierarchy. Count compute, messages, memory and interaction steps together.
Continue with Building to work on the source, or return to How units form a collective for the research explanation.

body:
HENA: Hierarchically Evolving Neural Automata
One large model attends to everything at once. HENA investigates whether collective reasoning can come instead from many local units, sparse learned communication, bounded differentiable memory and emergent hierarchy: an evolving swarm of MUONs, which is why its name is plural. It is the swarm layer of Causality, the research programme of RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited (RTEPL), authored by Harsh Joshi. Its intended first swarm would orchestrate stock open-weight models through MUON's unit interface; later units could enter through that same interface.
Start with How units form a collective for the research idea and worked example. The developer manual explains the current crate and the swarm coordination decisions an implementation would need to make.
The swarm is a research proposal
The Rust crate re-exports the MONAD, MUON and Reckon kernels. Its protocol declarations expose no swarm API. Today the repository holds that crate and the paper; routing, shared memory and scheduling are the work in front of it, and emergent hierarchy is the hypothesis they test. The paper’s problem statement sets out the proposed differentiable collective, its three budgets, quantitative targets, matched comparisons, failure conditions and open questions. It reports no swarm implementation or experimental result.
The first experiment would use simulator/ for a single-machine swarm of stock units, sparse routing and bounded memory, tested on sequence modelling, key-value retrieval and simple reasoning. Distributed execution follows a working local comparison.
The kernel builds on its three dependencies
The kernel depends on MONAD, MUON and Reckon at pinned commits of their repositories. Follow Building for the Rust and Protocol Buffers prerequisites, kernel check and separate paper build.
HENA composes MONAD, MUON and Reckon
Repository	Relationship	
MONAD	The calculus; a direct dependency	
MUON	The single unit and its slot contract; a direct dependency	
Reckon	Reckon's kernel is a direct dependency; HENA's future store would use its proposed record-store interface	
Q-HENA	The quantum variant, which keeps HENA's contracts and is kept in step with HENA by merge at each stage	
HENA is licensed AGPL-3.0-or-later
HENA's kernel, protocol headers and paper use AGPL-3.0-or-later. Third-party material keeps its own terms and required notices.
Commercial use is permitted under the applicable licence. Alternative terms require a separate written agreement with RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited, which can grant them only for material it is entitled to relicense; this repository grants none. See NOTICE for ownership, CITATION.cff for citation and CONTRIBUTING.md for contribution requirements. Outside contributions remain closed pending review of the draft agreement and a way to record acceptance.
