content.title: Plan a training or evaluation run

body:
Plan a training or evaluation run
This is the required procedure for MUON's future training and evaluation harness. No training or evaluation run has been performed, and the harness is not implemented. The first stock implementation can start on today's kernel types independently of MONAD's paused mathematical research. Later training follows its stage's agreed scope and the requirements below.
The stock stage evaluates existing models without finetuning. Parameter-efficient finetuning begins in the hardened stage at the earliest, with each finetuned checkpoint labelled as a variant in the unit comparison. Later micro-transformer training uses the same data, comparison and release requirements.
Offline finetuning adjusts the weights of models served through adapters. It does not implement online surprise-driven learning inside a unit. The unit interface keeps unit architecture separate from coordination across units and from a record store's retention policy. Its admission and conformance specification defines the interface checks that each candidate must satisfy.
Identify the data and permitted uses
Represent every training and evaluation dataset by a versioned manifest. Name its source, preprocessing hash, splits and separate grants to run, retain as context, evaluate, train, derive, generalise and publish. A repository licence does not establish these grants. Normalise data into one internal schema before producing backend-specific exports; each export refers back to the manifest.
Do not accept anonymous data folders. Include dataset manifest versions in the finetuned model's identity, so every checkpoint has a reproducible account of the data that produced it.
Fix the comparison before running it
Freeze a versioned evaluation manifest before training or benchmarking. Name the decision and its owner, the candidate, the retained baseline and the change being tested. Pair before-and-after finetune runs under matched conditions. Record:
Task definitions, permitted dataset and fixture hashes, splits and eligible cases.
Exact model, quantisation, backend, software and hardware versions.
Seeds, warm-up, repetitions and resource budget.
Primary measures, uncertainty method, tolerances and pass, fail and stop thresholds.
Keep results separate by model, quantisation and backend. Changing several components together cannot attribute an improvement to any one of them. Where that attribution matters, compare each change separately and together on matched cases.
Audit actual exposure to the held-out evidence before using it as an acceptance gate. Record which models, data, prompts and reviewers generation, reward scoring and evaluation share. A candidate or reward generator cannot be its own only promoting evaluator: require a separately tested check on protected evidence. Calling the same scorer again on its tuned cases supplies no independent check.
No optimised artifact deploys without passing its held-out gate. This applies to weights, configurations, skills and agent write-back. Missing mandatory evidence remains unresolved; an aggregate score cannot override a failed blocking requirement.
Separate conditions from measurements
For robustness comparisons, fix source cases, references, processing, measurement method and permitted operations. State where each condition enters, how its actual level is measured and which resource budget applies. Record the inputs actually consumed. A perturbation of an input and a change to the measurement are different interventions.
Compare conditions on paired cases while holding the route, reference and measurement fixed. Compare measurement methods while holding the input and condition fixed. If both change and their interaction matters, compare them separately and together. Version preprocessing, thresholds and record channels when they change what can be observed.
Report quality and resource coverage by tested condition and relevant subgroup, with the aggregation unit and denominator. Include unavailable and partial results. Exercise an unchanged baseline, a condition whose measured level contradicts its label, and substitution of an input or measurement method. A result supports robustness under the tested conditions; it does not establish a claim about a different observer, population or causal mechanism.
Keep checkpoints with their run records
Name checkpoints {base-model}+{method}-{dataset-manifest}-{run}. Each records its parent, dataset manifests and evaluation deltas against the base model. Store checkpoints with their training run records, outside this repository.
A candidate's record binds:
Base checkpoint, tokenizer, chat template and quantisation.
Datasets and every permitted-use grant, preprocessing and seeds.
Training code and toolchain, backend and hardware, and the finetuning artifact's identity.
Evaluation manifest and evidence on retained baselines, negative transfer, interference, privacy and memorisation.
Routing or merge behaviour, resource envelope and rollback target.
Keep generation scores, independent observations, unresolved criteria and the owner's decision distinct.
Release and activate in separate steps
Releasing a checkpoint, admitting it to a serving adapter, another consumer's admission, Harsh Joshi's activation, a canary and a rollback each need their own recorded decision or result. A rollback is never an unrecorded configuration edit. Retain the admitted baseline and identify the exact rollback target.
A MUON training result neither creates a consumer contract with Pale nor selects an occupant of its judgment seat. Each consumer must separately accept the exact candidate and its permitted use.
Return to the developer overview.

A rollback is never an unrecorded configuration edit. Retain the admitted baseline and identify the exact rollback target.
A MUON training result neither creates a consumer contract with Pale nor selects an occupant of its judgment seat. Each consumer must separately accept the exact candidate and its permitted use.
Return to the developer overview.

body:
Q-HENA
Q-HENA proposes a quantum swarm that composes Q-MUON units behind HENA’s contracts. The repository contains a Rust crate that re-exports MONAD, Q-MUON and Reckon, and a draft paper. You can check the crate against those pinned sources. HENA develops the classical swarm design, and Q-MUON studies one quantum unit.
Understand the research question
See what quantum collective computation would contribute and how to compare it with classical alternatives.
Check the kernel crate and the paper
Check the Rust dependencies or typeset the draft paper.
How computation becomes collective
Q-MUON would adapt a single unit behind MUON’s slot contract. Q-HENA would choose which units participate, which contributions reach each other and how their work produces the task response. Its quantum adaptation covers routing, channels and entanglement-mediated communication and memory. HENA supplies the classical coordination, population and recovery contracts. Keeping those responsibilities stable would help distinguish a substrate change from an organizational change.
An implementation must define actual preparations, interactions and measurements. Entanglement by itself specifies neither a message protocol nor a memory operation. Q-HENA would own a swarm-shaped operational store, while Reckon supplies the record protocol. Records of work, resources and observations remain distinct from quantum state and from a checkpoint’s recovery guarantee.
MONAD is another direct kernel dependency. Its re-export makes types available; a mathematical model of the swarm remains research work.
Follow a two-unit contribution
Consider a proposed joint operation between units A and B:
Schedule the interaction
The operation needs both units’ resources at once. An allocation that supports only one cannot execute that interaction by scheduling A and B successively unless a separate, equivalent arrangement has been established. Q-HENA would need to wait for capacity or use a supported alternative whose effect on the task is understood.
Recover after one unit restarts
The operation begins, but B must restart before the response is complete. A can recover its local state from a checkpoint. That checkpoint and a saved message record leave the state shared between the units unresolved. Recovery would need to determine which preparations or interactions to repeat and which measurements it could reuse. Count repeated preparation, measurement and failed attempts in the task cost.
This design case connects resource scheduling to what the collective would need to recover. The product explanation follows the same restart.
Bind recovery to the actual units
Q-MUON’s planned compatibility profile would identify the provider, backend, topology, calibration or noise model, circuit, measurement configuration and checkpoint representation. It names exact, semantic and restart_only restore modes. Their semantics and schema are unpublished, so those names are not a working serialization API.
Q-HENA would bind each unit reservation and swarm checkpoint to the exact profile and restore mode. Provider or calibration changes, partial recovery and mixed modes need their own supported outcomes. Exact recovery would require evidence for every unit and the composed swarm.
For the present one-person programme, a plain stage note identifies the candidate and resolved dependencies, profiles, comparisons, resource limits, results, uncertainty and missing coverage. The programme owner separately decides whether that evidence closes the stage. The linked specification keeps the later signed-record design, deferred until a second person or a release needs it.
Inspect the current source
The build guide owns the compiler prerequisites and online or offline kernel check. A passing check confirms that the kernel crate's dependency re-exports type-check.
Source	What a developer can inspect	
Kernel manifest and crate root	Dependencies on MONAD, Q-MUON and Reckon, and their re-exports. HENA is the fork’s classical upstream, not a current Cargo dependency.	
Paper and swarm notation	The proposed architecture’s notation and abstract.	
Message, routing and memory headers	Inherited protocol paths with no swarm messages implemented. The memory header reserves Q-HENA’s own store contract.	
For paper prerequisites and commands, use the build guide. The licensing section explains the selected policy and pending inherited-rights review; the rights review (docs/rights-review.md in the repository checkout, for maintainers) specifies the inventory and acceptance records required before release. Return to the classical-versus-quantum comparison when assessing what a future implementation would establish.

body:
Q-HENA: Quantum HENA
Two questions are open before a quantum swarm can claim anything: nothing yet shows a quantum advantage for a swarm, and HENA's classical swarm has still to show that it differs from neighbouring multi-agent systems. Q-HENA claims neither. Q-HENA is the quantum variant of HENA, developed within the Causality research programme by Harsh Joshi for RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited. It would compose Q-MUON units through quantum routing, communication and entanglement-mediated memory. Its own swarm store would use the record protocol of the Reckon laboratory.
The developer guide explains the proposed architecture and current source. For the research question and comparisons, read Quantum collective computation.
The repository contains a Rust crate that re-exports MONAD, Q-MUON and Reckon, and a paper with an abstract. The proposed quantum swarm must demonstrate its behaviour and any advantage against an adequate classical comparison.
Q-HENA takes HENA's classical work in by merge at each stage and reviews its quantum adaptation of that exact candidate; the classical kernel changes only where an integration point is needed.
Planned quantum work includes swarm orchestration and gate kernels in kernel/qpu/ for Qiskit and Cirq, Q-HENA’s own routing and communication protocols in protos/q-hena/, and Python wrappers for Qiskit, Cirq and PennyLane.
Building
The build guide gives the prerequisites, kernel check and paper validation commands, including offline checks and how to interpret warnings and skipped checks. These checks establish source integration and typesetting; they do not test quantum behaviour or advantage.
Licence
Q-HENA's kernel, protocol headers and paper use AGPL-3.0-or-later. Each inherited component keeps its existing grant and notices; this licence does not replace upstream terms or supply missing rights, and the rights review of the inherited material is still to be completed. The additions notice describes the draft paper and its definitions. Third-party material keeps its own terms and required notices.
Commercial use is permitted under the applicable licence. Alternative terms require a separate written agreement with RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited, which can grant them only for material it is entitled to relicense; this repository grants none. See NOTICE for ownership, CITATION.cff for citation and CONTRIBUTING.md for contribution requirements. Outside contributions remain closed pending review of the draft agreement and a way to record acceptance.

body:
Q-MUON
Q-MUON proposes a quantum implementation behind MUON’s reasoning-unit interface. A caller would request inference, inspect state and manage the unit’s lifecycle through that interface. Q-HENA would coordinate multiple units. The current Rust scaffold re-exports MONAD and has no callable unit API.
Read the state-overlap example
Follow two sensor readings through a proposed quantum similarity calculation.
Read the shared unit contract
See the responsibilities a quantum implementation would inherit.
Build the kernel crate and the paper
Check the kernel against its pinned MONAD dependency, or typeset the paper on its own.
Adapt the unit behind the shared contract
MUON’s draft interface gives every implementation five responsibilities:
Responsibility	What a quantum implementation would provide	
Inference	Prepare the input, run the chosen computation and return its measured response	
State	Declare what can be inspected or saved, and at what fidelity	
Ordered records	Identify inference, resource use, measurement procedure and shot count	
Resources	Estimate the complete operation and check permission and reserved capacity before running it	
Lifecycle	Initialize, step, checkpoint, restore and stop according to its compatibility profile	
The caller can work with a measurement summary without managing the backend. To resume an interrupted computation, it needs a separate promise about which state the unit can recover.
The fork would start from a fixed MUON revision before adding its quantum adaptation. A test of the interface checks whether callers can use the unit. A separate task comparison measures accuracy and resource use against a relevant classical unit at the same error tolerance. Preparing inputs, reading results and recovering interrupted work all contribute to that comparison.
A checkpoint needs a backend-specific promise
A compatibility profile would identify the classical contract and adaptation revisions, state and checkpoint formats, backend, topology, calibration or noise model, circuit compilation, measurement procedure, seed, shots and replay class. A restore must check those properties before using a saved checkpoint.
The proposed modes are exact, semantic and restart_only. They distinguish restoring state, recovering equivalent behavior under specified observations, and starting again. Their schema, tolerances and tests have not been defined.
Each admitted unit must declare exactly one mode in its proposed QuantumUnitCompatibilityProfileV1; recovery cannot promise more than that mode supports. Provider drift, expired calibration, changed topology, incompatible circuit or state representation, and an unverifiable checkpoint must all refuse recovery. A classical checkpoint is never presented as restorable by a quantum unit.
Q-HENA would bind each unit's reservation, swarm checkpoint and adaptation evidence to the exact profile digest and restore mode. Its collective recovery must respect every participating unit's guarantee, including any repeated preparation or measurement a restart requires.
Consider a future unit using backend A, topology T1, calibration C7 and 4,096 measurement shots. It can save its circuit parameters and classical configuration, and it declares restart_only. After interruption, those inputs would let it repeat the computation; they would not restore its interrupted quantum state. Q-HENA would have to budget for that restart.
If the backend now reports calibration C8, the old profile no longer matches. Reusing the circuit parameters would not establish that the recovery promise still holds. The replacement needs a compatible profile before the swarm can rely on it.
State and recovery in the product guide explains the consequence for the collective task.
Inspect the current source
Follow the build guide for the tools and online or offline kernel check. A successful check resolves the kernel manifest dependency on MONAD's kernel at its pinned commit and type-checks the crate root against it. The crate re-exports MONAD, and no quantum directories exist yet. A unit implementation and tests of inference, circuits and recovery are future work.
The paper imports inherited notation and Q-MUON’s definitions. It contains an abstract. The inherited protocol header declares no unit messages.
The build instructions cover the kernel and paper checks. For terms and notices, see Licence.

body:
Q-MUON: Quantum MUON
A quantum unit raises two separate questions: whether it learns anything useful, and whether it does so better than an adequate classical unit at the same total cost. Neither is shown for Q-MUON, and each capability has to be shown on its own before it is claimed. Q-MUON is the quantum variant of MUON, the single unit of Causality, a research programme of RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited with Harsh Joshi as its author. It would put quantum gates, entanglement and quantum communication inside a unit while keeping MUON's slot contract unchanged, and it is the unit that Q-HENA would compose into a quantum swarm. This repository is a fork of MUON: the planned workflow mirrors an exact frozen classical candidate before reviewing its quantum adaptation. The manual introduces Q-MUON.
Today the repository holds the fork of MUON, a kernel that re-exports MONAD, and a paper with an abstract; mirroring a fixed classical MUON candidate is the first problem in front of it. Small-scale quantum learning provides examples for investigating this proposed unit.
Planned quantum work includes gate kernels in kernel/qpu/ for Qiskit and Cirq, Q-MUON’s own communication protocols in protos/q-muon/, and Python wrappers for Qiskit, Cirq and PennyLane.
The proposed stack has parallel classical and quantum paths, sharing MONAD’s formal core:
Classical: MONAD → MUON  → HENA
Quantum:   MONAD → Q-MUON → Q-HENA

Reckon supplies the record protocol and measurement tools for comparisons along both paths. The diagram describes the design; Q-MUON’s current kernel still depends only on MONAD.
Building
The build guide gives the prerequisites, kernel check and paper validation commands, including offline checks and how to interpret warnings and skipped checks. These checks establish source integration and typesetting; they do not test quantum behaviour or advantage.

body:
Reckon Architecture
A laboratory for causal records under resource budgets
A Python memory manager over Rust storage, with separate experiment and debugger interfaces.
A task calls the Python manager to store or retrieve records and supplies the outcome. The manager chooses what to retain. The Rust extension stores and indexes records and buffers operation events; the manager retains native records with Python object adapters and separate fixed admission costs. To inspect a run, save an export and pass it to the debugger. These are separate places to look when a run fails to write, measure or display what you expected.
The complete retrieval/outcome example follows one stored cue through that Python boundary. The product comparison follows a task from paired inputs to saved results.
Build Pipeline
Run maturin build to assemble the Python API and Rust extension into the reckon wheel. Protocol Buffers generate Python wire dataclasses with betterproto2 and Rust structs with prost and serde. The Rust laboratory model generates the current record TypeScript and JSON Schema. The root Buf configuration generates historical wire TypeScript with protobuf-ts; the TypeScript SDK uses its own Protobuf-ES and Connect generators.
The debugger builds separately. Run pnpm build in viz-ui/ and copy dist/ into viz/static/ to ship the interface with the wheel. Follow the server guide for that bundle. When changing the interface, run the Python backend and Vite separately.
Component Responsibilities
Rust Core (kernel/)
Python requires the Rust extension. Verify its import before debugging the application.
The kernel's default Rust build has no Python dependency. Its python feature enables PyO3; maturin selects extension-module, which enables that binding and its extension linking mode. The daemon and other Rust consumers use the default Rust API.
Component	Responsibility	Data Structure	
RecordStore	Record storage, lookup, iteration	hashbrown::HashMap<String, Record>	
PriorityIndex	Record priority from utility and beneficial measured effects	BinaryHeap<RecordRef>	
RetentionPolicy	Rust-side retention policy implementations	Trait-based dispatch	
EventLogger	High-frequency event buffering and explicit export	Ring buffer	
Use these numbers as performance targets when profiling:
select_for_pruning(10K records): < 1ms
write(): < 100μs
read(): < 50μs
Python API (src/reckon/)
The Python CMM owns payload encoding for admission, budget-overflow calculation, policy selection and query filtering. kernel/src/record.rs owns the laboratory record shape and generates its TypeScript and JSON Schema. PyO3 adapters retain the caller’s opaque payload, mutable lists and metadata; memory/record.py supplies Python behavior and dataclass compatibility around those native fields. Resource configuration remains in core/resources.py. The generated betterproto2.Message classes describe the separate historical wire contracts. Validation still depends on each operation; a generated type alone does not validate an incoming value.
The CMM delegates storage/index accounting, access touches, retention ranking and budget-prefix selection to Rust. Python policy objects choose the kernel rule and supply ranking inputs from the full records; the random arm supplies its existing seeded permutation. Memory manager design explains the enforced byte, slot, token and operation-rate limits, and the retrieval controls still to build.
The kernel priority index and daemon capacity pruning use one store-priority function, with harmful measured effects contributing no bonus and ties ordered by record ID. This store ranking remains a distinct rule from the per-byte laboratory choices and raw-score Rust policies. Those policies share kernel selection machinery without treating their different formulas as equivalent.
For integration, the manager accepts a MemoryBudget, a Python retention policy and an episode identity. Call set_step() with the task’s logical step before memory operations. The retrieval/outcome example defines the observation, matching query, context, supplied outcome and expected utility update. The context groups returned IDs for credit assignment; it is not the store’s episode reset. Credit weights and bounded utility updates are implemented once in kernel/src/credit.rs; Python calls them through PyO3 and the daemon calls them directly. Python and the daemon validate all proposed updates before applying an observation.
TypeScript Debugger (viz-ui/)
pnpm monorepo with two packages:
Package	npm	Purpose	
packages/components	@rtepl/reckon-components	Stateless visualization components	
packages/debugger	@rtepl/reckon-debugger	Stateful app (Zustand + Tailwind)	
Components (stateless, reusable):
Component	Library	Purpose	
Timeline	Custom Canvas	Memory event timeline; 100K+ events is a design target	
CausalGraph	@xyflow/react	Directed graph of record inputs and supplied edge data	
ParetoFrontier	plotly.js	Budget/performance tradeoffs	
Debugger (stateful app):
Zustand store with RAF-batched WebSocket updates
Feature-sliced architecture (features/timeline, features/causal-graph, etc.)
Serves a separately built interface when its files have been copied into the Python package’s static directory; installing the Python extra alone does not compile that interface.
Protocol Buffers (protos/)
Edit the protocol declarations when changing a wire message. Check the explicit adapters to the Rust laboratory model and the debugger view for fields that need conversion. Preserve the fields their consumers rely on.
Source Files (authoritative - do not duplicate here):
protos/reckon/record.proto - MemoryRecord, PayloadType, RecordCost
protos/reckon/budget.proto - ResourceVector, MemoryBudget, RetentionPolicyType
protos/reckon/causality.proto - CausalRelation, DirectInfluenceRecords
protos/reckon/events.proto - MemoryEvent, DebuggerEvent
Data Flow
flowchart LR
    Task["Task"] --> Manager["Python manager"]
    Manager --> Store["Rust store and logger"]
    Store --> Export["Saved run export"]
    Export --> Debugger["Debugger"]

Write Path
Python admits the write through its operation-rate limit, refuses a record that exceeds its byte or token allowance, and calculates byte, slot and token overflow together. The configured policy supplies a removal set sufficient for all three. The manager validates that set before pruning: duplicate or absent IDs and insufficient freed capacity are errors. The memory manager's budget contract defines token counts and operation windows. Python computes a provenance hash when it constructs the record, but repeated writes still create records; deduplication remains design work.
Rust retains the native Python-facing record and a fixed admission projection for accounting and the priority index. The manager logs each removal with EventLogger.log_prune() and the write with EventLogger.log_write(), then returns the record ID.
The same selected policy controls byte, slot and token pressure; the manager does not substitute a utility ranking to finish the removal set. The Rust store’s separate priority index does not choose these Python-manager removals.
Read Path
Python admits the read through its independent operation-rate limit, then looks up the explicit IDs or filters the live native records. It ranks query results by utility, applies the limit, updates access statistics with RecordStore.touch_object(), logs the reads with EventLogger.log_read() and returns the records.
Query predicates are tags, payload_type and min_utility; similarity search and need-triggered retrieval remain part of the intended model. retrieve() uses this read path and adds credit-assignment tracking.
The record evaluator installs a scoped intervention after candidate selection and before access. It removes the chosen record, resolves the query again and checks matching paired state at that boundary. The returned records alone enter access logs and credit tracking.
Visualization Path
Save events.jsonl and run reckon viz import. The browser loads existing events with GET /v1/runs/{id}/events or streams them with /v1/stream?run_id=.... POST /v1/runs/{id}/events appends events and broadcasts them to subscribers.
The logger buffers events in memory. The caller must save them to produce a JSONL file. There is no automatic flush every 100ms. get_event_log() drains the buffer, while get_event_log_jsonl() returns its current rows as a string. The visualization module describes imported runs and the separately registered live-CMM path.
Configuration
Source Files (authoritative - do not duplicate here):
pyproject.toml - Python package configuration + Maturin build settings
kernel/Cargo.toml - Rust crate configuration
Testing Strategy
Layer	Framework	Focus	
Rust	cargo test	Store, logging and kernel behavior	
Python	pytest + Hypothesis	API tests, integration, property-based	
TypeScript	Vitest	Components and utility functions	
Key Invariants (Property Tests)
Storage budget invariant: successful writes remain within configured byte, slot and token limits. An oversized record is refused before existing records change.
Pruning invariant: the selected policy supplies sufficient distinct existing records before removal begins. Operation limits admit reads and writes separately, as described in the memory manager design.
Transitivity violations in the influence relation are detected and reported, never assumed away (influence is not transitive in general)
Keep logical steps in order when writing task code. With operation limits enabled, set_step() refuses a lower step; without those limits, it accepts one and does not correct the event order.
Local builds
Target: Local/laptop only (no cloud infrastructure)
# Development
pip install -e ".[dev,viz]"
maturin develop

# Build wheels in an explicit output directory
maturin build --release --out dist

Install the exact reckon-*.whl produced for your Python interpreter and platform with python -m pip install <wheel-path>. Use a new or empty output directory to keep an older wheel from being mistaken for the new build. A release-mode wheel is a build artifact, not a public release or a remotely deployable service.
Documentation Map
Python integration: connect a returned record to one supplied outcome and understand the context lifetime.
Memory manager: current records, policies, budget handling and mutable access.
Tasks: implement a benchmark through BaseTask and interpret its own result producer.
Metrics: distinguish usage helpers, actual intervention comparisons and cost accounting.
Visualization server: preserve an export, index its metadata and supply event bytes to the browser.
Debugger components: embed a timeline, evidence graph or plot with the required inputs.
Reproducibility: retain configuration, source, dependencies, results and event ordering for a repeatable comparison.
Future Considerations
The gRPC daemon owns a separate in-memory store. Its context store serializes retrieval admission and attribution updates, refuses new contexts when its independent count limit is full, and reclaims expired contexts on retrieval and on a server-lifetime timer. A live context keeps its original episode and expiry; observation takes an attribution snapshot before expiry. See the repository overview for its loopback-only bind and refused probes. Run export retains operation-bound snapshots separately from the live store and refuses unsupported attachments. Sharing Rust storage with the browser through WASM and adding distributed tracing remain possible extensions. Remote deployment would also require authentication, transport protection and state recovery.
Design choices and source map
Design Decisions
Decision	Choice	Rationale	
Schema Source	Rust laboratory model and separate historical protobuf contracts	Rust owns the current laboratory record and generates TypeScript and JSON Schema; protobuf declarations retain their historical wire meanings	
Performance Core	Rust (PyO3 + maturin)	Required storage/index extension; performance targets are listed below	
Python API	PyO3 record adapters and Python resource configuration	Mutable records follow the Rust laboratory model; generated betterproto2 dataclasses provide separate historical wire models	
Visualization	React + Vite + Canvas + React Flow	Interactive event timeline, record graph and budget comparisons	
Math Documentation	Markdown with fenced math blocks	Keep equations readable in the source manual	
Testing	Hypothesis + pytest	Property-based testing for invariants	
Repository	Monorepo	Single version control, atomic commits across languages	
Directory Structure
The implementation separates the things an experiment changes from the things that store or display its observations:
Location	Responsibility	
src/reckon/memory/	Full Python records, query filtering and retention-policy selection	
kernel/	Record storage, priority indexing and a fixed-capacity event logger, exposed through PyO3	
src/reckon/tasks/	Task data, agent or learner behavior, episode schedule and task-specific results	
src/reckon/metrics/	Optional analysis helpers, intervention runners and cost accounting	
protos/	Language-neutral wire declarations and their generation configuration	
src/reckon/viz/	Imported-run storage, REST retrieval and WebSocket delivery	
viz-ui/	Browser components and the stateful debugger application	
daemon/	A separate Rust gRPC service with its own in-memory store	
notebooks/	Exploratory notebooks and explicit artifact-saving helpers	
The laboratory model and conversions keep opaque Python objects in live native records and exchange explicitly encoded bytes in snapshots. New JSON snapshots preserve unknown token counts as null and int64 values as decimal strings. The historical scalar wire keeps its numeric meaning and refuses an unknown count on export. The daemon stores the generated core.v1.Record directly, preserving its typed tags and links through queries and named-run export; daemon record helpers initialize and score it without duplicating its fields. Those tags and links remain distinct from laboratory tags and origin. Losing a field or its absence during any translation changes which questions a later view can answer.

Reckon Examples
Start with Connect retrieval to an outcome to store one cue, retrieve it and update its utility from a supplied outcome. It includes complete code and expected output. For a task that actually trains a learner and saves its measurements, use Compare two replay budgets.
Available Examples
Example	Description	
basic_memory_manager.py	Write and query records under a five-slot budget, inspect pruning events, then try utility-based retention	
Prerequisites
Use the project environment from installation. It includes the Python package and required Rust extension; cargo build alone does not install that extension into Python.
Running Examples
From the repository root:
python src/examples/basic_memory_manager.py

Look for seven writes, five records still in memory and two prune events. The script prints the records with the important tag. After Remaining records with utility policy:, it prints the payloads and scores from the second manager. Record IDs vary between runs.
The event loop reads dictionaries returned by get_event_log(). Their op_type identifies the operation, timestamp is the logical step supplied to set_step(), and details is a JSON string that the example decodes to read the pruning reason. The call empties the buffer. Save the returned events if another tool needs them.
The first manager selects FIFOPolicy; the kernel uses that selected ranking to free bytes, slots and tokens together. Read Budget enforcement before interpreting those removals as a FIFO comparison. Use the task comparison linked above to measure outcomes under different memory allowances.
Integration Notes
Examples import from the reckon package:
from reckon import CausalMemoryManager
from reckon.core import MemoryBudget
from reckon.memory import PayloadType

body:
Build the API references
The Sphinx sources in this directory select the core and memory modules. Autodoc reads their actual signatures and docstrings, and Napoleon renders the existing argument and return descriptions. The authored laboratory manual keeps worked integrations, design reasoning and experiment limits; reference generation does not replace those explanations.
Use Python 3.11 or newer for Sphinx 8.2.3, with the selected Reckon checkout's dependencies and compiled extension available. Follow installation first, then install the pinned documentation dependency:
python -m pip install 'Sphinx==8.2.3'

The same dependency is declared by the docs extra. From the repository root, choose a new output directory and run:
python -m sphinx -W --keep-going -b json docs/reference build/reference-json

Use the selected environment's Python. Configuration puts this checkout's src/ first and imports its real native extension for the version; a missing extension is a build failure, not a reason to mock the API. -W treats documentation warnings as errors. Use a fresh output directory when retaining an earlier build: the JSON builder refuses overwriting its copied environment file under the strict warning policy.
The navigation source is index.rst, followed by core.rst and memory.rst. Assembly consumes the complete JSON-builder directory as sphinx-json, including its page contexts, global/search contexts, object inventory and static companions. Keep the generated directory under ignored build/; commit docstrings, this configuration and navigation instead. Inspect the assembled reference's signatures, examples and links as a separate step from a successful Sphinx build.
Kernel API documentation belongs in Rust library comments, built with cargo doc --manifest-path kernel/Cargo.toml --no-deps. Protocol and HTTP references
Install the proto and viz extras in the selected environment. The reference exporter compiles all .proto sources through the pinned grpcio-tools compiler and renders its descriptors as Markdown. body:
Run and extend the tests
 
Run the Python suite when changing the public API, retention behavior or Rust bindings. It checks core types, memory operations and their integration with the compiled extension.

Prepare the environment
Complete installation, including the extension import check. Install the dev extra before running the suite. If you followed the wheel setup, run this from the repository root with the same environment active:
pip install -e ".[dev]"

After Rust changes, rebuild using the kernel procedure. An old installed extension can hide a source/binding mismatch.
For the generated wire messages and RPC tests, use Python 3.10+ and install .[dev,proto]. The wire guide explains generation and the opt-in daemon check. The base suite stays usable on Python 3.9; missing optional protocol dependencies produce explicit skips.
    
Run the suite
From the repository root, choose the scope you need:
pytest src/tests/ -v

pytest src/tests/test_memory.py -v

pytest src/tests/test_properties.py -v

pytest src/tests/ --cov=reckon --cov-report=html

Pytest reports passing, failing and skipped cases. The coverage command also writes an HTML report. Inspect a failure against the source and extension revision actually loaded by that environment.
 
  
Find the relevant tests
File	What it exercises	
test_core.py	Resource values, memory budgets and influence-relation types	
test_memory.py	Records, manager operations and retention policies	
test_properties.py	Generated numeric and resource inputs	
test_transitivity.py	Diagnostics on supplied relation pairs	
The suite covers write/read/prune and logger integration. The relation tests diagnose supplied paths; they do not infer missing influence edges.

   
Add a regression case
Use test_<module>.py for a test file and test_<feature>_<scenario>() for a test function. Construct the task, budget and manager explicitly. The current core and memory tests create them in the test methods; there is no shared conftest.py supplying them.
For retention changes, include the incoming payload's cost and the expected records after the write. Test both byte and slot overflow when the change affects both. Verify that a record larger than max_bytes leaves existing records and logs unchanged. Token and operation-rate limits have separate cases; extend those cases when changing token admission, window expiry or episode resets. See budget enforcement.
For relation diagnostics, distinguish an untested endpoint pair from a measured value below its threshold. Both can appear as a missing link in the report.
Use Hypothesis when varied inputs help explore the behavior. State the property for the operation under test, including which budget it checks.

Related guides
Architecture: component boundaries and build dependencies.
Memory API: record lifecycle and current enforcement.
Hypothesis: strategies and property-based testing.

content.title: Export observations from a local run

body:
Export observations from a local run
The daemon keeps a shared in-memory record store and a separate, bounded account of each named run's observations. Supply run_id on Write and Retrieve from the first operation that belongs to a run. IDs contain 1–128 ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens. An empty ID keeps the operation unattributed; supplying a name later cannot recover its earlier history. A successful named retrieval can establish an empty run.
Reusing an episode context requires the same run ID, including whether it was omitted. Observe obtains its run from that context. A mismatched context is refused before retrieval, access counts or attribution change. Run identity distinguishes observations; it is not caller authentication. All clients of this trusted, loopback-only daemon share its authority and store.
Each successful named write or retrieval increments the run's revision and saves the records as that operation observed them. An observation with retrieved records increments it again and saves the resulting utilities for records still present. The latest observation of each record replaces that run's earlier snapshot; membership separately remembers whether the run wrote or retrieved it. A retrieval snapshot matches the returned record, before that retrieval increments its access count. Later writes, reads, credit updates or pruning outside that run do not alter its retained snapshots. This is an account of what the run last observed, not a current store snapshot or a complete event history.
Call ExportRun with the original ID and an explicit record_scope:
WRITTEN includes records that this run wrote.
RETRIEVED includes records returned to this run.
TOUCHED is their union, once per record.
NONE omits the record attachment. An empty selection in any other supported scope returns the JSON array [].
The daemon refuses ALL, UNSPECIFIED and unknown scopes. It filters membership before ordering by record ID and applying max_records; zero means all selected records, and a negative limit is invalid. The response preserves run_id and supplies source_revision. Pass that value as expected_revision to refuse an export after the run changes. Older revisions are not retained. Repeated exports of the same revision, scope and limit have identical snapshot bytes, including deterministic tag ordering.
records_snapshot_json is a UTF-8 array of the generated Rust Record serialization: camelCase field names, numeric enum values, byte arrays for payloads, and nullable optional fields. It is not protobuf JSON. The schema retains nested records, costs, utility and score fields; the generated TagValue serialization nests its oneof under value. Written string and list tags and ordered links, including their metadata bytes, survive storage, retrieval, credit updates and export.
No task, configuration, finish time, metric or performance result is invented: summary is absent. Events, metric CSV and archive flags each return UNIMPLEMENTED; unrequested attachments remain absent or empty according to their protobuf presence. Probe also remains unimplemented until a runner measures both comparison arms. This record-only export is not yet a complete debugger run bundle.
--max-runs defaults to 1,000 and --max-run-bytes to 67,108,864. Both must be positive. The byte limit counts each retained run ID, record ID, encoded JSON snapshot and two membership flags; it is a retained-data budget, not a bound on allocator overhead, temporary copies or process memory. A full budget refuses the operation before changing records or attribution. The daemon does not evict another run to make room. Snapshots survive record pruning but last only until the process exits; there is no persistence, automatic expiry or run deletion API. Save the export before ending the daemon.
Records and queries
The generated reckon.core.v1.Record is the daemon's stored record and response type. Its fields come from types.proto; record.rs supplies initialization and scoring helpers without another field definition. This model keeps typed tags and explicit links separate from the laboratory model's tag list and origin.
Write retains the declared payload bytes and kind, typed tag map, ordered links and initial utility. The daemon assigns identity, episode, timestamp and costs; compression, encoding, metadata and creation sequence keep their existing defaults because WriteRequest does not accept those fields. Link metadata bytes are retained without parsing or rewriting their JSON.
Tag queries require every requested key and its exact typed value. A string differs from a list containing that string; list order and repeated entries matter. Empty strings, empty lists and a present tag with no selected value stay distinct from one another and from a missing key. A list predicate is never discarded to broaden a query. ID and utility queries return the same complete record representation, with the existing retrieval and context behavior.
The repository guide covers startup and record/context limits. The Python wire guide and TypeScript client provide the generated request and response types.

body:
Debugger data and views
Choose a debugger view by what your export contains. The application has a run selector, an event inspector and three views. Each needs different inputs.
For ordinary startup and import, use Inspect an exported run. This chapter explains the data an integration supplies, how the views interpret it and which parts of the broader debugger design remain unimplemented.

Integrate the current views
What you want to inspect	What to supply	
When memory operations happened	Native kernel operations or debugger-shaped events with episode, step and sequence	
How records are related	Record snapshots and any additional edges. Supply a probe tied to the pair for a measured edge.	
How outcome varies with cost	Measured outcome and cost points. The application’s default frontier uses an operation-count ratio.	
The server maps native Rust operations into memory events and retains the complete source operation for inspection. It preserves event identity and sequence. Raw logs do not include full record snapshots, wall-clock times, task outcomes or paired probe evidence; those inputs remain absent. Keep the original event log and task result together.
Timeline
(A) Timeline View (per episode)
Use (episodeId, step, sequence) to order debugger events when all three fields are present. Convert the producer’s snake-case fields without changing their meaning. See Reproducibility.
If both events lack sequence, the comparator uses episode, step, wall time and then ID. Fully sequenced events use the sequence before the ID and leave wall time out. The server preserves sequence and converts all identities to strings, including zero and integers beyond JavaScript’s exact range. Decimal ID ties compare numerically. Kernel timestamps are logical steps; the timeline labels them as steps and the inspector says wall time was not recorded. Previous/next controls make operations at a shared step individually selectable.
A debugger-shaped event stream can supply a horizontal timeline with annotations for:
store / read / prune events
reward occurrences
uncertainty spikes / TD-error spikes
mode switches (if available)
The inspector can show the following when the selected event actually supplies them:
record payload
cost
retention reason
retrieval hits
downstream usage
The shared server projection handles write, read, prune, score-update, compress and budget-check operations. It exposes retrieved IDs, prune reasons and score changes when supplied, and keeps the original operation under kernelEvent. It leaves snapshots empty. Logged slot/byte fields are retained in that source record rather than promoted to a complete usage measurement: the Python logger does not supply full usage for every operation. The graph and frontier need their own recorded inputs. Unsupported root fields and malformed input cause an explicit import error with a line number.
Relationship graph

(B) Relationship graph
The graph draws directed provenance links between records present in its snapshots. The projection also accepts cycles in provenance or additional edges. Read a cycle as a description of the supplied relationships. Measuring mutual influence would require evidence for the corresponding pairs.
Edge Types:
Type	Source	Visual	Description	
MEASURED	Supplied probe evidence bound to the edge ID, source and target	Solid green	A direct probe assessed the pair. Read its result in the drawer.	
INFERRED	Supplied by the caller	Dashed orange	Candidate reachability under a closure assumption, pending direct evidence	
PROXY	Target record's influence_proxy, or zero if absent	Dotted blue	Provenance link with a heuristic display weight	
UI Controls:
Control	Purpose	Default	
EdgeDisplayControl	Choose measured pairs, all supplied edges or measured pairs with probe-queue details	MEASURED_ONLY (direct probe evidence only)	
TruthModeSwitch	Change the debugger's presentation	PRODUCT	
EdgeLegend	Explains edge visual encoding	Shown in RESEARCH and available on demand in PRODUCT	
The graph collects one record per ID from the snapshots. It combines provenance links and supplied edges before applying the mode filter. Both endpoints must be present. Measured links take their width from the magnitude of the pair's probe effect size, and proxy links use the target's influence proxy when available.
The inspector labels the selected record’s Attribution source as Measurement supplied when either delta is present, Proxy only when only influenceProxy is present, or Unscored when the supplied score object has none of these values. A missing score object is Not recorded. Record attribution displays supplied ablation and counterfactual deltas and Influence (proxy), including zero and negative deltas. These record-level values do not establish a measured link between two records or validate the experiment that supplied them.
Proxy-only records in snapshot counts distinct record IDs in the selected event’s snapshot. An empty snapshot is Not recorded, as in a raw kernel import; a snapshot with any missing score objects reports an incomplete count and the number identified. A fully supplied inventory with no proxy-only records reports zero. This is a snapshot count, not a whole-run count or a claim that every current record was exported. See proxy-only reporting for the Python store summary and the same field-presence rule.
MEASURED_ONLY, PROBE_STATUS and PRODUCT show only pairs with supplied direct probe evidence. A measured edge means the pair was assessed. The probe may support or weaken the proposed relationship. RESEARCH with INCLUDE_UNMEASURED also shows supplied inferences and provenance proxies. PROBE_STATUS additionally shows any supplied pending-probe queue and its estimated cost; selecting it does not run a probe. The legend counts the visible edges, and changing the mode closes the drawer if its edge becomes hidden.
The application’s drawer reports that probe execution is unavailable because it has no probe or inference stream. Supply handlers to the reusable drawer only if your embedding can run the probes and record their results.
Cost and outcome
(C) Budget vs Performance Frontier
Plot a measured outcome against a resource cost to compare two runs. The replay-budget task supplies final classification accuracy and slot allowances. Use the task result for accuracy and the operation log for write counts.
The reusable ParetoFrontier component accepts precomputed points, which bypass event extraction. Supply finite coordinates with xMetric and yMetric names on every point and matching axes descriptions. Supplied axes display raw numbers by default; percentage formatting is an explicit choice and scales uncertainty with the coordinates. Extra current-run and selection markers must use the same quantities. Its frontier calculation treats lower x as better and higher y as better, so orient other metrics accordingly.
The application currently passes events to the component. Its default x value is final bytes divided by a positive byte allowance. The default y value is writes divided by writes plus prunes, labelled as an operation proxy. This counts operations, not task success. The net-writes ratio is likewise labelled as a proxy. The selectors name these quantities: byteBudgetFraction and writeShare, with netWritesPerWrite for the alternate y ratio. Counts use byteCount, tokenCount, slotCount or writeCount. Missing inputs remain unavailable; task outcomes and probe costs require supplied measurements. Use the task result for accuracy or reward and the component reference to supply measured points.
Budget overruns retain their size and expand the plotted range beyond 100%. Frontier membership compares equal-cost points together and preserves exact duplicate candidates. A point is dominated only if another is at least as good on both axes and strictly better on one. The plot copies inputs before marking membership and refuses non-finite supplied coordinates. Repeated-trial aggregation and uncertainty remain the caller’s responsibility.
Add a view to an embedding
The graph view also mounts the compute ledger and transitivity panel below. Their store inputs start at null, and the application has no diagnostic-report or compute-accounting stream to fill them. They show unavailable messages until an integration supplies those inputs. A custom embedding can use the same components with its own measurements.
(D) Compute Ledger (HUD)
The reusable ComputeLedger component displays caller-supplied compute accounting. Its compact form sits below the debugger graph. A missing ledger leaves costs unavailable; it does not establish zero probe cost. An embedding supplies:
Metric	Description	
Base episodes	Episodes spent on task execution	
Probe episodes	Episodes spent on causal evaluation	
Overhead ratio	probe / (base + probe)	
Reward per total episode	Reward accounting for all compute	
Pending verification cost	Estimated cost to verify inferred edges	
Total compute includes both task episodes and probe episodes.
See Evaluation Metrics for details.
(E) Violations Panel
The reusable ViolationsPanel sits beside the debugger graph. A missing report displays an unavailable message. A supplied report with zero violations instead shows zero alongside the number of triples checked; that result applies only to the supplied report.
The panel renders the report it receives for detected A→B and B→C paths with an unconfirmed A→C edge. Its input can distinguish an untested pair from one that was measured below threshold. The Python diagnostic reports both under the same detection flag, with a null value for the missing pair. Richer fields in the debugger's report type are inputs to the view:
Edge status (tested/untested, holds/fails)
Statistical details (p, q, effect size, n)
Category (measured_failure, untested, borderline, power_issue)
Suggested action (verify edge, increase n)
(F) Representation Drift Panel (optional)
This panel remains a proposed extension; it is not a current application view. A future embedding could:
track chosen spectral stats over time/layers
flag collapse/drift correlated with failure
link drift events to memory decisions

Diagnose a task failure
Trace a suspected failure from the write to the read at the decision point, then check the task outcome. The timeline and provenance graph can tell you what to test. Run a properly timed intervention to measure the record’s contribution.
The retained key-door demonstration provides a small example. Import its run directory, select it and use Next event to inspect all eleven operations, starting with event ID zero. For the first blue cue, write event 4 at step 24 and read event 5 at step 26 name the same record; event 6 at step 29 changes its utility from 0 to 0.1. Event 7 removes it at step 33. Source operation exposes each complete original log entry. The two operations at step 24 and the two at step 33 remain separately selectable in sequence order.
The imported result shows 3 episodes | 67% success. The inspector reports wall time and snapshot attribution as Not recorded because the export supplies logical steps and no record snapshots. The two successful episodes establish this run’s outcome; the write/read sequence alone does not establish the cue’s causal contribution or rank retention policies.
Representation drift needs separately measured representation data. The proposed drift panel does not yet provide that diagnosis.
3. Output Artifacts
Callers preserve the task configuration, result and event log together. The replay comparison shows one complete layout. A notebook may separately save figures or a summary. The debugger application does not automatically export an HTML report or paper screenshots; the presence of those outputs is a property of the particular producer, not the import operation.
Implementation
Component	README	
FastAPI server	viz/README.md	
React debugger	viz-ui/README.md	
Timeline component	viz-ui/packages/components/	
Causal graph component	viz-ui/packages/components/	
Event data source	memory/README.md: EventLogger

It exposes retrieved IDs, prune reasons and score changes when supplied, and keeps the original operation under kernelEvent. It leaves snapshots empty. Logged slot/byte fields are retained in that source record rather than promoted to a complete usage measurement: the Python logger does not supply full usage for every operation. The graph and frontier need their own recorded inputs. Unsupported root fields and malformed input cause an explicit import error with a line number.
Relationship graph

(B) Relationship graph
The graph draws directed provenance links between records present in its snapshots. The projection also accepts cycles in provenance or additional edges. Read a cycle as a description of the supplied relationships. Measuring mutual influence would require evidence for the corresponding pairs.
Edge Types:
Type	Source	Visual	Description	
MEASURED	Supplied probe evidence bound to the edge ID, source and target	Solid green	A direct probe assessed the pair. Read its result in the drawer.	
INFERRED	Supplied by the caller	Dashed orange	Candidate reachability under a closure assumption, pending direct evidence	
PROXY	Target record's influence_proxy, or zero if absent	Dotted blue	Provenance link with a heuristic display weight	
UI Controls:
Control	Purpose	Default	
EdgeDisplayControl	Choose measured pairs, all supplied edges or measured pairs with probe-queue details	MEASURED_ONLY (direct probe evidence only)	
TruthModeSwitch	Change the debugger's presentation	PRODUCT	
EdgeLegend	Explains edge visual encoding	Shown in RESEARCH and available on demand in PRODUCT	
The graph collects one record per ID from the snapshots. It combines provenance links and supplied edges before applying the mode filter. Both endpoints must be present. Measured links take their width from the magnitude of the pair's probe effect size, and proxy links use the target's influence proxy when available.
The inspector labels the selected record’s Attribution source as Measurement supplied when either delta is present, Proxy only when only influenceProxy is present, or Unscored when the supplied score object has none of these values. A missing score object is Not recorded. Record attribution displays supplied ablation and counterfactual deltas and Influence (proxy), including zero and negative deltas. These record-level values do not establish a measured link between two records or validate the experiment that supplied them.
Proxy-only records in snapshot counts distinct record IDs in the selected event’s snapshot. An empty snapshot is Not recorded, as in a raw kernel import; a snapshot with any missing score objects reports an incomplete count and the number identified. A fully supplied inventory with no proxy-only records reports zero. This is a snapshot count, not a whole-run count or a claim that every current record was exported. See proxy-only reporting for the Python store summary and the same field-presence rule.
MEASURED_ONLY, PROBE_STATUS and PRODUCT show only pairs with supplied direct probe evidence. A measured edge means the pair was assessed. The probe may support or weaken the proposed relationship. RESEARCH with INCLUDE_UNMEASURED also shows supplied inferences and provenance proxies. PROBE_STATUS additionally shows any supplied pending-probe queue and its estimated cost; selecting it does not run a probe. The legend counts the visible edges, and changing the mode closes the drawer if its edge becomes hidden.
The application’s drawer reports that probe execution is unavailable because it has no probe or inference stream. Supply handlers to the reusable drawer only if your embedding can run the probes and record their results.
Cost and outcome
(C) Budget vs Performance Frontier
Plot a measured outcome against a resource cost to compare two runs. The replay-budget task supplies final classification accuracy and slot allowances. Use the task result for accuracy and the operation log for write counts.
The reusable ParetoFrontier component accepts precomputed points, which bypass event extraction. Supply finite coordinates with xMetric and yMetric names on every point and matching axes descriptions. Supplied axes display raw numbers by default; percentage formatting is an explicit choice and scales uncertainty with the coordinates. Extra current-run and selection markers must use the same quantities. Its frontier calculation treats lower x as better and higher y as better, so orient other metrics accordingly.
The application currently passes events to the component. Its default x value is final bytes divided by a positive byte allowance. The default y value is writes divided by writes plus prunes, labelled as an operation proxy. This counts operations, not task success. The net-writes ratio is likewise labelled as a proxy. The selectors name these quantities: byteBudgetFraction and writeShare, with netWritesPerWrite for the alternate y ratio. Counts use byteCount, tokenCount, slotCount or writeCount. Missing inputs remain unavailable; task outcomes and probe costs require supplied measurements. Use the task result for accuracy or reward and the component reference to supply measured points.
Budget overruns retain their size and expand the plotted range beyond 100%. Frontier membership compares equal-cost points together and preserves exact duplicate candidates. A point is dominated only if another is at least as good on both axes and strictly better on one. The plot copies inputs before marking membership and refuses non-finite supplied coordinates. Repeated-trial aggregation and uncertainty remain the caller’s responsibility.
Add a view to an embedding
The graph view also mounts the compute ledger and transitivity panel below. Their store inputs start at null, and the application has no diagnostic-report or compute-accounting stream to fill them. They show unavailable messages until an integration supplies those inputs. A custom embedding can use the same components with its own measurements.
(D) Compute Ledger (HUD)
The reusable ComputeLedger component displays caller-supplied compute accounting. Its compact form sits below the debugger graph. A missing ledger leaves costs unavailable; it does not establish zero probe cost. An embedding supplies:
Metric	Description	
Base episodes	Episodes spent on task execution	
Probe episodes	Episodes spent on causal evaluation	
Overhead ratio	probe / (base + probe)	
Reward per total episode	Reward accounting for all compute	
Pending verification cost	Estimated cost to verify inferred edges	
Total compute includes both task episodes and probe episodes.
See Evaluation Metrics for details.
(E) Violations Panel
The reusable ViolationsPanel sits beside the debugger graph. A missing report displays an unavailable message. A supplied report with zero violations instead shows zero alongside the number of triples checked; that result applies only to the supplied report.
The panel renders the report it receives for detected A→B and B→C paths with an unconfirmed A→C edge. Its input can distinguish an untested pair from one that was measured below threshold. The Python diagnostic reports both under the same detection flag, with a null value for the missing pair. Richer fields in the debugger's report type are inputs to the view:
Edge status (tested/untested, holds/fails)
Statistical details (p, q, effect size, n)
Category (measured_failure, untested, borderline, power_issue)
Suggested action (verify edge, increase n)
(F) Representation Drift Panel (optional)
This panel remains a proposed extension; it is not a current application view. A future embedding could:
track chosen spectral stats over time/layers
flag collapse/drift correlated with failure
link drift events to memory decisions

Diagnose a task failure
Trace a suspected failure from the write to the read at the decision point, then check the task outcome. The timeline and provenance graph can tell you what to test. Run a properly timed intervention to measure the record’s contribution.
The retained key-door demonstration provides a small example. Import its run directory, select it and use Next event to inspect all eleven operations, starting with event ID zero. For the first blue cue, write event 4 at step 24 and read event 5 at step 26 name the same record; event 6 at step 29 changes its utility from 0 to 0.1. Event 7 removes it at step 33. Source operation exposes each complete original log entry. The two operations at step 24 and the two at step 33 remain separately selectable in sequence order.
The imported result shows 3 episodes | 67% success. The inspector reports wall time and snapshot attribution as Not recorded because the export supplies logical steps and no record snapshots. The two successful episodes establish this run’s outcome; the write/read sequence alone does not establish the cue’s causal contribution or rank retention policies.
Representation drift needs separately measured representation data. The proposed drift panel does not yet provide that diagnosis.
3. Output Artifacts
Callers preserve the task configuration, result and event log together. The replay comparison shows one complete layout. A notebook may separately save figures or a summary. The debugger application does not automatically export an HTML report or paper screenshots; the presence of those outputs is a property of the particular producer, not the import operation.
Implementation
Component	README	
FastAPI server	viz/README.md	
React debugger	viz-ui/README.md	
Timeline component	viz-ui/packages/components/	
Causal graph component	viz-ui/packages/components/	
Event data source	memory/README.md: EventLogger

body:
Reckon Debugger Application
The application turns imported run events into three coordinated views: a timeline, a relationship graph and a cost/outcome plot. Its Zustand store owns the selected run, events, records and interface state. Feature panels adapt that state to the reusable components; the WebSocket hook connects it to the Python server.
The Relationship graph tab shows record links. The inspector labels each record’s supplied attribution source, displays its ablation and counterfactual deltas and Influence (proxy), and counts proxy-only records in the selected snapshot. The data contract defines missing-data states and field-presence rules; these values do not establish a measured relationship between two records.
Use this guide to change a panel or diagnose a connection/state problem. Check the debugger data contract first when a view lacks records or measurements: successful transport does not supply data absent from the export.
Architecture
flowchart TB
    subgraph App["Debugger App"]
        Main["App.tsx"]
        Providers["providers.tsx"]
    end

    subgraph Features["Feature Modules"]
        TimelinePanel["timeline/\nTimelinePanel.tsx"]
        CausalPanel["causal-graph/\nCausalGraphPanel.tsx"]
        ParetoPanel["pareto-frontier/\nParetoFrontierPanel.tsx"]
        Inspector["event-inspector/\nEventInspector.tsx"]
    end

    subgraph Infrastructure["Infrastructure"]
        Store["store/\nZustand"]
        Hooks["hooks/\nuseWebSocket"]
    end

    subgraph Components["@rtepl/reckon-components"]
        Timeline["Timeline"]
        CausalGraph["CausalGraph"]
        Pareto["ParetoFrontier"]
    end

    Main --> Features
    Main --> Providers
    Providers --> Store

    TimelinePanel --> Timeline
    CausalPanel --> CausalGraph
    ParetoPanel --> Pareto

    Features --> Store
    Features --> Hooks

Directory Structure
For a new panel, start in src/features/ and connect it in App.tsx. For a state or connection issue, use the store (src/store/index.ts) or the WebSocket hook (src/hooks/useWebSocket.ts).
Components
App.tsx
Main application shell:
Header with view mode tabs
Connection status indicator
Main content area with view panels
Sidebar with event inspector
Features
Each feature wraps a component with store integration:
Feature	Component	Purpose	
TimelinePanel	Timeline	Memory event chronology	
CausalGraphPanel	CausalGraph	Directed record-dependency and evidence graph; cycles are not rejected	
ParetoFrontierPanel	ParetoFrontier	Budget/performance tradeoffs	
EventInspector	Custom	Selected event/record details	
Zustand Store
Global state management:
Slice	State	Actions	
Events	events[], selectedEventId	addEvents, selectEvent, clearEvents	
Connection	connectionStatus, lastError, wsUrl	setConnectionStatus, setWsUrl	
UI	viewMode, sidebarOpen	setViewMode, toggleSidebar	
Selectors:
selectConnectionInfo: Derived connection state
selectEventStats: Event counts by type
WebSocket Hook
The hook returns connect, disconnect, send and subscribeToRun. Connection state is read from the Zustand store, rather than returned by the hook:
Store state	Type	Purpose	
connectionStatus	'connecting' | 'connected' | 'disconnected' | 'error'	Connection state	
lastError	string | null	Last connection error	
Action	Purpose	
connect()	Establish WebSocket	
disconnect()	Close connection	
send(data)	Send a caller-supplied message on an open connection	
subscribeToRun(runId)	Select an imported run stream	
Features:
Automatic reconnection with exponential backoff
RAF batching for high-frequency updates
Run subscription
Data Flow
Connection Flow
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant App
    participant Hook as useWebSocket
    participant WS as WebSocket
    participant Server

    User->>App: Click Connect
    App->>Hook: connect()
    Hook->>WS: new WebSocket(url)
    WS->>Server: Connection
    Server->>WS: Connected
    WS->>Hook: onopen
    Hook->>App: status = 'connected'

Event Flow
sequenceDiagram
    participant Server
    participant WS as WebSocket
    participant Hook as useWebSocket
    participant Store as Zustand
    participant RAF
    participant Component

    Server->>WS: events message
    WS->>Hook: onmessage
    Hook->>Hook: buffer.push(events)
    RAF->>Hook: animation frame
    Hook->>Store: addEvents(buffer)
    Store->>Component: re-render

View Modes
Mode	Component	Description	
timeline	TimelinePanel	Chronological event view	
causal	CausalGraphPanel	Record dependency graph	
pareto	ParetoFrontierPanel	Budget tradeoff analysis	
Building
Development
Start with the workspace setup to install dependencies and build the shared components. Once they are built, run this from the debugger package for Vite with hot reload.
pnpm dev

Production
pnpm build

Output: dist/
From viz-ui/, pnpm test:record-scores exercises the actual inspector against the shared Python/TypeScript score cases. It uses Playwright’s installed Chromium by default; PLAYWRIGHT_CHANNEL=chrome pnpm test:record-scores uses an installed Chrome. The check covers proxy-only, measured zero and negative, unscored and missing-data cases without running an experiment.
Styling
Uses Tailwind CSS v4 with CSS custom properties:
Variable	Purpose	
--color-bg	Background	
--color-text	Text	
--color-primary	Primary accent	
--color-accent	Secondary accent	
Troubleshooting
Store Immutability: Zustand requires immutable updates. Use spread operators or immer.
RAF Batching Timing: Foreground events wait for an available animation frame; 16ms is not a latency guarantee. The hook flushes a full 1,000-event batch immediately. The hidden-document branch sends events directly to the store.
WebSocket Reconnection: Exponential backoff may delay reconnection. Reset on manual connect.
View Mode Sync: The URL does not record the selected view. Select the view again when reopening the application.
Large Event Sets: The store defaults to 50,000 events and 50,000 records and evicts older entries at those limits. The timeline reports how many earlier events are omitted from its window. The server retains the full history, available through paginated reads; preserve the original export too.
Sidebar State: The sidebar stays open or closed when you change views. Use its toggle to change that state.
Related guides
Parent: viz-ui
Components Package
Python Server
Debugger Visualization Spec
