body:
Reckon Visualization Components Embed these React components when an application needs a memory timeline, relationship graph or cost/outcome plot. Supply their events, measurements and selection callbacks through props. Components may keep local display state, but they do not manage the debugger's global run store, collect experiment results or execute intervention probes. The cost/outcome example supplies a complete small plot. Read each component's input contract before reusing it; an operation log alone does not contain the full records or measured outcomes required by every view. Architecture flowchart TB subgraph Package["@rtepl/reckon-components"] Timeline["timeline/\nTimeline.tsx"] CausalGraph["causal-graph/\nCausalGraph.tsx"] Pareto["pareto-frontier/\nParetoFrontier.tsx"] Shared["shared/\nUtilities"] end subgraph Libraries["Libraries"] Canvas["HTML5 Canvas"] ReactFlow["@xyflow/react"] Plotly["react-plotly.js"] end Timeline --> Canvas CausalGraph --> ReactFlow Pareto --> Plotly Timeline --> Shared CausalGraph --> Shared Pareto --> Shared Directory Structure Find public exports in src/index.ts and input types in src/types.ts. The component sections below show which props to pass to each view. Components Timeline High-performance timeline visualization using HTML5 Canvas. Feature Implementation Virtualized rendering Only draws visible events Zoom/pan Mouse wheel + drag Hit testing Spatial index for click detection Lane-based grouping Multiple event tracks Key Props: Prop Type Purpose events DebuggerEvent[] Events to display timeRange [number, number] Visible time window onEventClick (event) => void Click handler onTimeRangeChange (range) => void Zoom/pan callback lanes TimelineLane[] Lane configuration Performance: Draws only visible events Schedules pan/zoom drawing with RAF 100K+ events is a design target; actual frame rate depends on the data, viewport and host CausalGraph React Flow draws links from record inputs and any edges you supply. It can display cycles. If you see one, check where the edges came from before interpreting it as causal feedback. Feature Implementation Node layout Positions derived from event records; the current layout selector is not implemented Edge rendering React Flow edges Selection Node/edge highlighting Pan/zoom React Flow controls Key Props: Prop Type Purpose events DebuggerEvent[] Required events from which record nodes and provenance edges are derived additionalEdges CausalEdge[] Optional externally supplied candidate edges onNodeClick (record: MemoryRecord) => void Record selection callback selectedRecordId string | null Optional highlighted record identity ParetoFrontier Scatter plot of cost versus a supplied outcome using Plotly. An embedding can pass measured points; the current application instead uses its event-derived default, whose default y axis is explicitly labelled as an operation-count proxy. The frontier data contract distinguishes these paths. Feature Implementation Scatter plot Plotly scatter trace Frontier line Computed from data Tooltips Plotly hover Click selection Plotly click events Key Props: Prop Type Purpose events DebuggerEvent[] Required event input; use an empty array when supplying precomputed points points ParetoPoint[] Optional precomputed points, each with finite x/y and matching xMetric/yMetric names axes FrontierAxes Required with supplied points; each axis names its metric, optional label and number or percent format xLabel string X-axis label (e.g., "Memory Bytes") yLabel string Y-axis label (e.g., "Success Rate") onPointClick (point) => void Selection handler When supplying precomputed points, name each measurement in both the points and axes. Missing or inconsistent names are refused, including extra current-run or selected markers. Labels describe the chosen quantities; they do not select data or units. Supplied axes use raw numbers unless explicitly set to format: "percent", which multiplies coordinates and standard deviations by 100. A mean return of 7.5 therefore remains 7.5; it does not silently become 750%. Lower x and higher y are considered better; a loss or latency metric needs the appropriate transformation before using that convention. A point is dominated when another has no higher cost and no lower outcome, with at least one strict improvement. Equal-cost points are compared together, so (2, 0.60) is dominated by (2, 0.80) in either input order. Exact duplicate coordinates remain separate candidates and do not dominate each other; another point can dominate both. The component does not choose between their configurations. Inputs are copied before marking frontier membership. Missing or non-finite supplied coordinates are refused. Event extraction offers byteBudgetFraction, byteCount, tokenCount and slotCount on x, and writeShare, netWritesPerWrite and writeCount on y. The defaults are final bytes divided by the byte allowance and writes divided by writes plus prunes. Net writes per write is (writes - prunes) / writes. Both y ratios are labelled as operation proxies and displayed as percentages; they do not measure task success. Missing counts or denominators do not become zeros. Counts do not require a budget when no ratio is requested. Budget ratios above one and negative net-write ratios retain their values and expand the plot range. Other measurements, including task outcomes and probe costs, require supplied points with their own axes. The old performance/retention selectors and budget/performance coordinate aliases are removed. ViolationsPanel Panel for displaying supplied transitivity diagnostics (A->B and B->C detected, with A->C unconfirmed). The debugger mounts it beside the graph, but no application producer supplies its report. A null report displays an unavailable message; a supplied report with zero violations displays that count and the number of triples checked. These are different states. Feature Implementation Violation list Scrollable cards Filters measuredOnly, insufficientNOnly, borderlineOnly, untestedOnly Edge status Visual indicators for tested/untested edges Actions onVerifyEdge, onIncreaseN callbacks Key Props: Prop Type Purpose report TransitivityReport | null Violations to display onViolationSelect (v) => void Selection handler onVerifyEdge (src, tgt) => void Trigger edge verification ComputeLedger A compute-accounting panel for caller-supplied task and probe costs. The debugger mounts its compact form below the graph, but no application producer supplies the ledger. A null ledger displays an unavailable message, not zero cost. An embedding must supply its own accounting measurements; memory events alone do not provide them. Feature Implementation Episode split Base vs probe bar chart Overhead ratio Probe overhead percentage with color coding Efficiency Reward per episode/second metrics Pending Cost to verify unverified edges Key Props: Prop Type Purpose ledger ComputeLedgerData | null Compute metrics compact boolean HUD vs full panel mode onVerifyPending () => void Trigger pending verifications EdgeDrawer Side drawer showing detailed information about a causal edge. Feature Implementation Status badge Measured/Inferred/Proxy type Probe evidence p-value, q-value, effect size, n, CI Confidence sparkline Historical q-values Actions Rerun probe, verify edge Key Props: Prop Type Purpose edge EdgeStatus Edge to display isOpen boolean Drawer visibility onRerunProbe (edge, n) => void Rerun with sample size onVerifyEdge (edge) => void Verify inferred edge Probe and verification callbacks notify the consuming application. These components do not execute a record probe or turn a supplied edge label into independent evidence. EdgeDisplayControl Choose which supplied edges appear and inspect an optional pending-probe queue. Mode Description MEASURED_ONLY Show pairs with direct probe evidence (debugger default) INCLUDE_UNMEASURED Also allow supplied inferences and enabled provenance proxies PROBE_STATUS Show measured pairs and any caller-supplied probe queue and cost The control emits a mode choice to its parent; the graph applies the corresponding evidence filter. It neither computes transitive closure nor verifies an edge. The Product view still hides inferred and proxy links regardless of the requested edge display mode. An embedding may supply onVerifyAll with counts and cost estimates; both unmeasured-edge and pending-queue actions ask for confirmation before invoking it. Cancellation makes no callback. The standalone debugger supplies no execution handler. Probe evidence requirements are described in the debugger chapter. TruthModeSwitch Toggle between research and product modes. Mode Description RESEARCH Requests the research presentation PRODUCT Requests the product presentation EdgeLegend Legend explaining edge visual encoding. Edge Type Visual Description Measured Solid green Supplied probe evidence matched to the edge ID, source and target; the pair was assessed, not necessarily supported Inferred Dashed orange Supplied candidate reachability, pending direct evidence Proxy Dotted blue Provenance link weighted by the target's influence proxy, or zero when absent A target record's attribution delta does not make its incoming links measured. The graph needs pair-bound probe evidence for that label; see the graph evidence and filtering contract. Shared Types Defined in src/types.ts: Type Purpose TimeRange [start, end] tuple TimelineLane Lane configuration DebuggerEvent Memory event data CausalNode Graph node CausalEdge Graph edge ParetoPoint Frontier data point EdgeStatus Full edge status with probe evidence ProbeEvidence Statistical evidence (p, q, effect size, n, CI) TransitivityViolation Violation triple (A->B, B->C, A->C fails) TransitivityReport Full validation report ComputeLedgerData Compute accounting metrics Edge Semantics Enum Values Purpose EdgeType measured, inferred, proxy Causal edge classification EdgeDisplayMode measured_only, include_unmeasured, probe_status Supplied-edge display and queue view TruthMode research, product Information display mode ConfidenceLevel weak, medium, strong Edge confidence badge MultipleTestingMethod none, bonferroni, bh_fdr, holm Statistical correction Integration With Debugger App The debugger imports components and passes store data: import { Timeline, CausalGraph, ParetoFrontier, } from "@rtepl/reckon-components"; With Custom Applications For example, save this component as BudgetComparison.tsx in a browser-based React application with the components package linked. The three points are illustrative inputs, not laboratory measurements; replace them with results from your own fixed comparison. import { ParetoFrontier, type ParetoPoint } from "@rtepl/reckon-components"; const points: ParetoPoint[] = [ { x: 2, y: 0.6, xMetric: "budget_slots", yMetric: "final_accuracy", isPareto: false, label: "2 slots" }, { x: 8, y: 0.72, xMetric: "budget_slots", yMetric: "final_accuracy", isPareto: false, label: "8 slots" }, { x: 16, y: 0.68, xMetric: "budget_slots", yMetric: "final_accuracy", isPareto: false, label: "16 slots" }, ]; export function BudgetComparison() { return (
); } The plot places 2 and 8 slots on the frontier. The 16-slot point costs more than the 8-slot point and has lower accuracy, so the plot marks it as dominated. indexed.body:
Reckon Visualization Components Embed these React components when an application needs a memory timeline, relationship graph or cost/outcome plot. Supply their events, measurements and selection callbacks through props. Components may keep local display state, but they do not manage the debugger's global run store, collect experiment results or execute intervention probes. The cost/outcome example supplies a complete small plot. Read each component's input contract before reusing it; an operation log alone does not contain the full records or measured outcomes required by every view. Architecture flowchart TB subgraph Package["@rtepl/reckon-components"] Timeline["timeline/\nTimeline.tsx"] CausalGraph["causal-graph/\nCausalGraph.tsx"] Pareto["pareto-frontier/\nParetoFrontier.tsx"] Shared["shared/\nUtilities"] end subgraph Libraries["Libraries"] Canvas["HTML5 Canvas"] ReactFlow["@xyflow/react"] Plotly["react-plotly.js"] end Timeline --> Canvas CausalGraph --> ReactFlow Pareto --> Plotly Timeline --> Shared CausalGraph --> Shared Pareto --> Shared Directory Structure Find public exports in src/index.ts and input types in src/types.ts. The component sections below show which props to pass to each view. Components Timeline High-performance timeline visualization using HTML5 Canvas. Feature Implementation Virtualized rendering Only draws visible events Zoom/pan Mouse wheel + drag Hit testing Spatial index for click detection Lane-based grouping Multiple event tracks Key Props: Prop Type Purpose events DebuggerEvent[] Events to display timeRange [number, number] Visible time window onEventClick (event) => void Click handler onTimeRangeChange (range) => void Zoom/pan callback lanes TimelineLane[] Lane configuration Performance: Draws only visible events Schedules pan/zoom drawing with RAF 100K+ events is a design target; actual frame rate depends on the data, viewport and host CausalGraph React Flow draws links from record inputs and any edges you supply. It can display cycles. If you see one, check where the edges came from before interpreting it as causal feedback. Feature Implementation Node layout Positions derived from event records; the current layout selector is not implemented Edge rendering React Flow edges Selection Node/edge highlighting Pan/zoom React Flow controls Key Props: Prop Type Purpose events DebuggerEvent[] Required events from which record nodes and provenance edges are derived additionalEdges CausalEdge[] Optional externally supplied candidate edges onNodeClick (record: MemoryRecord) => void Record selection callback selectedRecordId string | null Optional highlighted record identity ParetoFrontier Scatter plot of cost versus a supplied outcome using Plotly. An embedding can pass measured points; the current application instead uses its event-derived default, whose default y axis is explicitly labelled as an operation-count proxy. The frontier data contract distinguishes these paths. Feature Implementation Scatter plot Plotly scatter trace Frontier line Computed from data Tooltips Plotly hover Click selection Plotly click events Key Props: Prop Type Purpose events DebuggerEvent[] Required event input; use an empty array when supplying precomputed points points ParetoPoint[] Optional precomputed points, each with finite x/y and matching xMetric/yMetric names axes FrontierAxes Required with supplied points; each axis names its metric, optional label and number or percent format xLabel string X-axis label (e.g., "Memory Bytes") yLabel string Y-axis label (e.g., "Success Rate") onPointClick (point) => void Selection handler When supplying precomputed points, name each measurement in both the points and axes. Missing or inconsistent names are refused, including extra current-run or selected markers. Labels describe the chosen quantities; they do not select data or units. Supplied axes use raw numbers unless explicitly set to format: "percent", which multiplies coordinates and standard deviations by 100. A mean return of 7.5 therefore remains 7.5; it does not silently become 750%. Lower x and higher y are considered better; a loss or latency metric needs the appropriate transformation before using that convention. A point is dominated when another has no higher cost and no lower outcome, with at least one strict improvement. Equal-cost points are compared together, so (2, 0.60) is dominated by (2, 0.80) in either input order. Exact duplicate coordinates remain separate candidates and do not dominate each other; another point can dominate both. The component does not choose between their configurations. Inputs are copied before marking frontier membership. Missing or non-finite supplied coordinates are refused. Event extraction offers byteBudgetFraction, byteCount, tokenCount and slotCount on x, and writeShare, netWritesPerWrite and writeCount on y. The defaults are final bytes divided by the byte allowance and writes divided by writes plus prunes. Net writes per write is (writes - prunes) / writes. Both y ratios are labelled as operation proxies and displayed as percentages; they do not measure task success. Missing counts or denominators do not become zeros. Counts do not require a budget when no ratio is requested. Budget ratios above one and negative net-write ratios retain their values and expand the plot range. Other measurements, including task outcomes and probe costs, require supplied points with their own axes. The old performance/retention selectors and budget/performance coordinate aliases are removed. ViolationsPanel Panel for displaying supplied transitivity diagnostics (A->B and B->C detected, with A->C unconfirmed). The debugger mounts it beside the graph, but no application producer supplies its report. A null report displays an unavailable message; a supplied report with zero violations displays that count and the number of triples checked. These are different states. Feature Implementation Violation list Scrollable cards Filters measuredOnly, insufficientNOnly, borderlineOnly, untestedOnly Edge status Visual indicators for tested/untested edges Actions onVerifyEdge, onIncreaseN callbacks Key Props: Prop Type Purpose report TransitivityReport | null Violations to display onViolationSelect (v) => void Selection handler onVerifyEdge (src, tgt) => void Trigger edge verification ComputeLedger A compute-accounting panel for caller-supplied task and probe costs. The debugger mounts its compact form below the graph, but no application producer supplies the ledger. A null ledger displays an unavailable message, not zero cost. An embedding must supply its own accounting measurements; memory events alone do not provide them. Feature Implementation Episode split Base vs probe bar chart Overhead ratio Probe overhead percentage with color coding Efficiency Reward per episode/second metrics Pending Cost to verify unverified edges Key Props: Prop Type Purpose ledger ComputeLedgerData | null Compute metrics compact boolean HUD vs full panel mode onVerifyPending () => void Trigger pending verifications EdgeDrawer Side drawer showing detailed information about a causal edge. Feature Implementation Status badge Measured/Inferred/Proxy type Probe evidence p-value, q-value, effect size, n, CI Confidence sparkline Historical q-values Actions Rerun probe, verify edge Key Props: Prop Type Purpose edge EdgeStatus Edge to display isOpen boolean Drawer visibility onRerunProbe (edge, n) => void Rerun with sample size onVerifyEdge (edge) => void Verify inferred edge Probe and verification callbacks notify the consuming application. These components do not execute a record probe or turn a supplied edge label into independent evidence. EdgeDisplayControl Choose which supplied edges appear and inspect an optional pending-probe queue. Mode Description MEASURED_ONLY Show pairs with direct probe evidence (debugger default) INCLUDE_UNMEASURED Also allow supplied inferences and enabled provenance proxies PROBE_STATUS Show measured pairs and any caller-supplied probe queue and cost The control emits a mode choice to its parent; the graph applies the corresponding evidence filter. The standalone debugger supplies no execution handler. Probe evidence requirements are described in the debugger chapter. TruthModeSwitch Toggle between research and product modes. ); } The plot places 2 and 8 slots on the frontier. The 16-slot point costs more than the 8-slot point and has lower accuracy, so the plot marks it as dominated. To compare real experiments, report variation across repeated runs beside the plot. The component requires browser APIs; it is not a server-rendered chart. Import at app entry point: import "@xyflow/react/dist/style.css"; The component imports this internally, but bundlers may externalize it. Always import in the consuming app. Plotly Type Definitions: Types from @types/react-plotly.js may lag behind library. Check compatibility. body:
Reckon Visualization UI
Build the browser interface here when changing the debugger or embedding one of its views. The workspace separates reusable view components from the application that selects runs, maintains state and receives events. The Python backend is a separate process; the server guide explains its import and streaming interfaces.
For ordinary inspection of a saved run, follow Inspect an exported run. The build and package boundaries below are for interface development.
Architecture
flowchart TB
    subgraph Workspace["pnpm Workspace"]
        Components["@rtepl/reckon-components\n(stateless)"]
        Debugger["@rtepl/reckon-debugger\n(stateful)"]
    end

    subgraph Backend["Python Backend"]
        Server["viz/server.py"]
        WS["WebSocket"]
        REST["REST API"]
    end

    subgraph Libraries["External Libraries"]
        Canvas["HTML5 Canvas"]
        ReactFlow["@xyflow/react"]
        Plotly["plotly.js"]
        Zustand["zustand"]
    end

    Debugger --> Components
    Debugger --> WS
    Debugger --> REST

    Components --> Canvas
    Components --> ReactFlow
    Components --> Plotly

    Debugger --> Zustand

Directory Structure
Run build commands from viz-ui/, where package.json defines the workspace scripts. Change the components for a reusable view or the debugger application to change how it receives and displays a run.
Packages
@rtepl/reckon-components
Stateless, reusable visualization components:
Component	Library	Purpose	
Timeline	Custom Canvas	Memory event timeline; 100K+ events is a design target	
CausalGraph	@xyflow/react	Directed graph of record dependencies and supplied evidence	
ParetoFrontier	plotly.js	Named cost/outcome comparison or operation-count proxies	
ViolationsPanel	React	Transitivity violation display and filtering	
ComputeLedger	React	HUD showing base/probe episodes, overhead	
EdgeDrawer	React	Side drawer with edge details (measured/inferred/proxy)	
EdgeDisplayControl	React	Choose visible edge evidence and show a supplied probe queue	
TruthModeSwitch	React	Switch between RESEARCH/PRODUCT modes	
EdgeLegend	React	Legend for edge visual encoding	
See: packages/components/README.md
@rtepl/reckon-debugger
Stateful debugger application:
Feature	Purpose	
Store (Zustand)	Global state management	
WebSocket Hook	Real-time event streaming	
Feature Modules	Timeline, CausalGraph, ParetoFrontier panels	
See: packages/debugger/README.md
Data Flow
flowchart LR
    subgraph Server["Python Server"]
        Stored["Imported or appended run events"]
    end

    subgraph Transport["Transport"]
        WS["WebSocket"]
    end

    subgraph Client["React App"]
        Hook["useWebSocket"]
        Store["Zustand Store"]
        RAF["RAF Batching"]
        Components["Components"]
    end

    Stored --> WS
    WS --> Hook
    Hook --> Store
    Store --> RAF
    RAF --> Components

RAF Batching
The WebSocket hook batches foreground updates with requestAnimationFrame:
Events arrive via WebSocket
Accumulated in pending buffer
RAF callback flushes to store
Components update on the available browser animation frame.
At 1,000 pending events the hook flushes the batch immediately. A hidden-document branch forwards events directly to the store. This reduces update frequency without dropping queued events; it does not guarantee a frame rate. The application guide describes the store’s separate limits.
The server converts native kernel operations once for imports, REST reads, snapshots and live messages. A manager registered in the server process supplies a live subscription; other processes export or append events. The browser consumes that shared format without another raw-event conversion. Server integration distinguishes this from process-local CMM registration.
Building
Development
From the Reckon root, install workspace dependencies, build the shared components and start Vite. The debugger imports the components package from dist/index.js, so a fresh checkout needs that build before the application can start.
cd viz-ui
pnpm install
pnpm build:components
pnpm dev

Production
cd viz-ui
pnpm build

Output goes to packages/debugger/dist/.
Deploy to Python Package
cp -r packages/debugger/dist/* ../src/reckon/viz/static/

Check the graph’s evidence rules
Install the test browser once, then run the component tests and the synthetic pair-evidence browser test:
pnpm exec playwright-core install chromium
pnpm test

The browser test starts its own loopback server and loads the current component source. It checks graph, drawer and legend agreement across edge display and product modes, mismatched probe pairs, missing endpoints, duplicate edges and explicit probe unavailability. It separately exercises the reusable control's optional probe callback, cost confirmation and cancellation. The fixture supplies evidence directly to the application store; it does not establish backend probe execution, admission or performance at scale. A separate frontier browser fixture checks raw return values, explicit accuracy percentages, uncertainty scaling, current-run markers and the event-count proxy axes. These inputs are illustrative. RECKON_CHROMIUM can select an existing Chromium executable for either browser test; the result reports its actual version. Use pnpm test:components, pnpm test:evidence or pnpm test:frontier to run a part separately.
Check a real manager in the browser
After the Python dev,viz environment and Rust extension are installed, build the interface and install the test browser:
pnpm build
pnpm exec playwright-core install chromium
pnpm test:browser

The test starts its own loopback servers, produces a real manager run, imports a second copy and inspects every operation in both runs. It uses temporary test storage under the repository's excluded experiments/runs/ directory and removes that storage on exit. Set RECKON_PYTHON if the environment is not at ../.venv/bin/python. This checks transport and inspection for a small actual run; the 100,000-event performance target needs a separate benchmark.
Check native record conversion
pnpm test:record-wire sends actual manager records through native storage, explicit byte encoding and the Rust-derived JSON/TypeScript model to the inspector. It also checks the historical Python/native/protobuf-ts wire round trip. Opaque bytes, ordered duplicate tags, supplied or absent origin, optional zero values and signed measurements survive. Unknown token counts display “Not recorded”; a declared zero displays zero. The adapters refuse int64 values outside the viewer's exact integer range while the exchange formats retain their decimal strings. Set RECKON_PYTHON for the rebuilt Python environment and RECKON_CHROMIUM for an existing browser. The Python environment needs the dev,rpc extras.
This is a small conversion fixture, separate from the live server test above. It does not change how existing run imports or WebSocket events arrive or exercise the daemon's different typed-tag record. Component builds generate record descriptions from kernel/src/record.rs; pnpm generate:records runs that step separately and requires the Rust toolchain. Generated descriptions stay outside Git.
TypeScript Configuration
Base Config
tsconfig.base.json provides shared settings:
ES2022 target
Strict mode
Path aliases
Package Configs
Each package extends the base and adds local paths.
Proto Integration
TypeScript types are generated from Protocol Buffers:
pnpm proto:gen

Run from viz-ui/; the script enters the repository’s protos/ directory. Output: modules under viz-ui/generated/reckon/. The reckon.ts and index.ts entry files re-export those modules; they contain no duplicate type definitions.

Troubleshooting
pnpm Workspace: Use pnpm commands from viz-ui/ root. Individual package commands may miss workspace dependencies.
Path Aliases: The @/ alias resolves differently per package. Check each package's tsconfig.json.
Canvas Performance: Timeline uses raw Canvas API for performance. Avoid React state for frequently updated visual elements.
React Flow Layout: CausalGraph uses manual positioning. Automatic layout (dagre) can be added but impacts performance.
Plotly Bundle Size: plotly.js-dist-min is used to reduce bundle size. Full features require the complete package.
WebSocket Reconnection: The hook implements exponential backoff. Test reconnection behavior after server restarts.

Related guides
Components Package
Debugger Package
Python Server
Debugger Visualization Spec

body:
Key-door export demonstration
Three episodes executed once on 16 November 2026 from Reckon source 06e01a1c75d6879cc604e0b53307af954da38c95, using the native KeyDoorTask, CausalMemoryManager and JSONL event exporter. Seed 42, FIFO, one slot and 50,000 bytes were chosen before execution. Memory and utility learning carry across episodes; no record probes or comparison arms run. The configuration, executed script, task result, import metadata, source and environment identities and kernel lockfile retain the inputs and outputs.
Episode	Cue read back	Correct door	Outcome	
keydoor_ep0	Green	Right, (3, 3)	Failure	
keydoor_ep1	Blue	Right, (3, 3)	Success	
keydoor_ep2	Blue	Right, (3, 3)	Success	
Each episode wrote and retrieved its own cue once. The controller chooses right for a retrieved blue cue and otherwise guesses left; it does not try the other door after a failed guess. Green leaves the door random, so remembering green did not identify the right door in the first episode. Two successes out of three describe these episodes only. One slot holds the current cue until its read; the two FIFO removals replace earlier episodes’ records. This demonstration supplies no retention-policy ranking or causal comparison.
Follow the saved events
The native log contains 11 events: three writes, three reads, three utility updates and two removals. Event IDs run from 0 through 10. For the first blue cue, write event 4 at logical step 24 names record b4b5c6bb-df57-4f6f-ac60-da08406783e8; read event 5 at step 26 returns that same ID, score-update event 6 records utility 0.1 after the successful episode, and removal event 7 replaces it during the next episode. The first removal and next write share step 24 with sequences 0 and 1; the following replacement uses step 33 in the same order. These are the logger’s logical steps, not wall-clock times.
The log records activity and partial counters, without full record payloads or a grid trajectory. Its zero slots_after fields do not measure an empty store. The separate final record retains the last surviving blue cue, ID 795ba66d-e0d1-44d8-868a-91e56b38011b; it does not add snapshots to earlier events. Read the episode result for the observed cue and outcome, and the native task source for the controller’s movement rule.
Environment
The run used Python 3.13.13, NumPy 2.4.2 and SciPy 1.17.0 with the existing importable Rust extension. Its binary and runtime source hashes match the preceding retained laboratory run. This is execution evidence for that environment, not qualification of every supported interpreter. wall_time_ms in the import metadata measures the task call only, excluding setup and file writes.

indexed.title: Key-door export demonstration
indexed.body:
Key-door export demonstration
Three episodes executed once on 16 November 2026 from Reckon source 06e01a1c75d6879cc604e0b53307af954da38c95, using the native KeyDoorTask, CausalMemoryManager and JSONL event exporter. Seed 42, FIFO, one slot and 50,000 bytes were chosen before execution. Memory and utility learning carry across episodes; no record probes or comparison arms run. The configuration, executed script, task result, import metadata, source and environment identities and kernel lockfile retain the inputs and outputs.
Episode	Cue read back	Correct door	Outcome	
keydoor_ep0	Green	Right, (3, 3)	Failure	
keydoor_ep1	Blue	Right, (3, 3)	Success	
keydoor_ep2	Blue	Right, (3, 3)	Success	
Each episode wrote and retrieved its own cue once. The controller chooses right for a retrieved blue cue and otherwise guesses left; it does not try the other door after a failed guess. Green leaves the door random, so remembering green did not identify the right door in the first episode. Two successes out of three describe these episodes only. One slot holds the current cue until its read; the two FIFO removals replace earlier episodes’ records. This demonstration supplies no retention-policy ranking or causal comparison.
Follow the saved events
The native log contains 11 events: three writes, three reads, three utility updates and two removals. Event IDs run from 0 through 10. For the first blue cue, write event 4 at logical step 24 names record b4b5c6bb-df57-4f6f-ac60-da08406783e8; read event 5 at step 26 returns that same ID, score-update event 6 records utility 0.1 after the successful episode, and removal event 7 replaces it during the next episode. The first removal and next write share step 24 with sequences 0 and 1; the following replacement uses step 33 in the same order. These are the logger’s logical steps, not wall-clock times.
The log records activity and partial counters, without full record payloads or a grid trajectory. Its zero slots_after fields do not measure an empty store. The separate final record retains the last surviving blue cue, ID 795ba66d-e0d1-44d8-868a-91e56b38011b; it does not add snapshots to earlier events. Read the episode result for the observed cue and outcome, and the native task source for the controller’s movement rule.
Environment
The run used Python 3.13.13, NumPy 2.4.2 and SciPy 1.17.0 with the existing importable Rust extension. Its binary and runtime source hashes match the preceding retained laboratory run. This is execution evidence for that environment, not qualification of every supported interpreter. wall_time_ms in the import metadata measures the task call only, excluding setup and file writes.

body:
Reckon Viz Module
The FastAPI backend imports saved runs, indexes their metadata and delivers their events to the browser over REST and WebSocket. It can also serve a React interface when that interface has been separately built and copied into the static directory. Importing a run copies its recorded data; it does not rerun the task or create missing observations.
Use this page to call an endpoint, embed run storage or build the interface bundle. For the ordinary startup/import procedure, follow Inspect an exported run.
Architecture
flowchart TB
    subgraph Server["FastAPI Server (port 8000)"]
        App["server.py"]
        subgraph Routes["Routes"]
            RunsAPI["runs.py\n(REST)"]
            WSRoute["ws.py\n(WebSocket)"]
            LegacyEvents["events.py\n(legacy REST)"]
        end
        Registry["Process-local CMM registry"]
        subgraph Storage["Storage"]
            SQLite["runs.db\n(SQLite index)"]
            Artifacts["run_artifacts/\n(JSONL, configs)"]
        end
        Static["static/\n(React bundle)"]
    end

    subgraph DataSources["Data Sources"]
        Notebooks["Notebook Runs\n(runs/ directory)"]
        Fixtures["Fixtures\n(runs/_fixtures/)"]
        CMM["CausalMemoryManager\n(buffered events)"]
    end

    subgraph Client["React Debugger (port 5173)"]
        Timeline["Timeline"]
        CausalGraph["CausalGraph"]
        Pareto["ParetoFrontier"]
    end

    Notebooks -->|"reckon viz import"| RunsAPI
    Fixtures -->|"RECKON_VIZ_LOAD_FIXTURES=1"| Storage
    CMM -->|"register_cmm() in server process"| Registry
    Registry -->|"live.py subscription"| Storage
    Registry --> LegacyEvents
    CMM -->|"explicit event export and import or append"| RunsAPI

    RunsAPI --> Storage
    Storage --> WSRoute
    WSRoute --> Client
    Static --> Client

Module Structure
Change projection.py for the shared kernel-to-viewer conversion, live.py for manager subscriptions, server.py for app setup or static assets, storage.py for the SQLite index and run files, and routes/runs.py or routes/ws.py for the HTTP and WebSocket interfaces.

Get started
Follow Inspect an exported run to start both servers, import a saved event log and read the views. A metrics table or figure alone cannot supply events.
Complete installation, including the extension import check, before working on the backend. The sections below cover its API, storage, embedding and interface build. The server imports recorded observations; it does not rerun tasks or probes.
REST API
Runs Management (routes/runs.py)
Endpoint	Method	Purpose	
/v1/runs	GET	List all runs with summaries	
/v1/runs/{id}	GET	Get run details	
/v1/runs/{id}/events	GET	Read a page of stored events	
/v1/runs/{id}/events	POST	Append events and notify subscribers	
/v1/runs/import	POST	Import run from JSON body	
/v1/runs/import-path	POST	Import run from filesystem path	
Read	Filters	Pagination	
GET /v1/runs	task_name, config_id	limit defaults to 50 and accepts 1–100. offset defaults to 0.	
GET /v1/runs/{id}/events	episode_id, event_type	limit defaults to 1,000 and accepts 1–10,000. offset defaults to 0.	
Imports validate every nonempty JSONL line before writing. The accepted event formats are native Rust operation records, the bundled legacy named-event export and the camelCase debugger format described in the data contract. Unknown root fields, malformed operations and conflicting content under one event ID are refused. Identical repeats are skipped by event identity; distinct events at tied steps remain distinct. HTTP imports refuse an existing run ID. There is no HTTP deletion endpoint; explicit local CLI deletion remains available.
WebSocket (routes/ws.py)
Real-time event streaming:
Message Type	Direction	Purpose	
subscribe	Client→Server	Subscribe to run: {"type": "subscribe", "run_id": "..."}	
snapshot	Server→Client	Initial events: {"type": "snapshot", "run_id": "...", "events": [...]}	
events	Server→Client	New events batch	
ping/pong	Both	Keepalive	
Connection URL: ws://localhost:8000/v1/stream?run_id=<run_id>
The server serializes snapshot subscription and appends within each run. A slow connection is closed after a ten-second send timeout; reconnecting obtains the persisted snapshot. Messages are not silently dropped. Run one server process per data directory: these locks do not coordinate separate workers or CLI imports.
Storage (storage.py)
RunIndex and RunStore
RunIndex stores and queries metadata in SQLite. RunStore reads and writes event bytes and optional summary files; it does not import a directory or list indexed metadata. The CLI coordinates those two owners when importing a run.
The store accepts a run directory only when its resolved parent is the store root, and an artifact only when its resolved parent is that run directory. Invalid run names, traversal and symlinks resolving outside those locations are refused. These path checks keep run files inside their selected store; they do not authenticate a caller.
Success rate is nullable in the index, HTTP responses and run snapshots. An observed zero remains a measurement and displays 0% success; a missing measurement displays Success unavailable. Live memory operations do not imply a task success rate. Snapshot summary retains the supplied source fields, while the separate success_rate field carries the index’s measurement presence.
Opening an older derived index upgrades its measurement handling once. The earlier default stored missing success as zero: a zero explicitly recorded in its retained summary stays zero, positive stored measurements stay measured, and an ambiguous old zero becomes unavailable. New explicit zeroes remain measured when the index reopens. This updates the index only; original summaries and saved run files are unchanged.
From the repository root with the project environment active, this integration example copies the example export into a new local data directory:
import json
from pathlib import Path
from reckon.viz.projection import parse_events_jsonl
from reckon.viz.storage import create_storage, parse_run_export

data = Path("storage-example-data")
data.mkdir()  # Choose a new directory; do not replace an earlier example.
index, store = create_storage(data)

export = json.loads(Path("runs/_fixtures/golden_run_export.json").read_text())
meta, events_bytes = parse_run_export(export)
parse_events_jsonl(events_bytes)  # Refuse data the viewer cannot interpret.
store.store_events(meta.run_id, events_bytes)
if meta.summary_json:
    store.store_summary(meta.run_id, meta.summary_json)
index.add_run(meta)

runs = index.list_runs(limit=10, task_name=meta.task_name)
assert any(run.run_id == meta.run_id for run in runs)

# The store returns the complete JSONL bytes, not a paginated event list.
events = store.get_events(meta.run_id)
assert events == events_bytes

The directory now contains runs.db and run_artifacts/<run_id>/events.jsonl, plus summary.json for the supplied summary. This copies the example's metadata and events without running its task. Replace the export path with your own file when embedding storage. To inspect a run through the application, use the import command in the product guide.
RunIndex.list_runs accepts limit, offset, config_id and task_name. RunStore.get_events returns all stored bytes for one run; the REST event endpoint owns event pagination. Neither operation reconstructs missing configuration, figures or event history from a summary.
CLI Commands (cli.py)
Set RECKON_VIZ_DATA_DIR to a directory you can write to. Use the same value for the import, server and listing commands so they use the same run index.
export RECKON_VIZ_DATA_DIR="$PWD/reckon-debugger-data"

# Import a run directory
reckon viz import "<run_path>"

# Import with custom run ID
reckon viz import "<run_path>" --run-id my_custom_id

# Start the server
reckon viz serve --port 8000

# List imported runs
reckon viz list

Integration
With Notebooks
Notebook artifacts default to notebooks/runs/ relative to the repository root. Use an actual exported event-log run with the quick start; the notebook guide owns modes and optional dependencies.
With CausalMemoryManager (Process-Local Registration)
register_cmm() exposes one manager to a server running in the same Python process. During its lifespan, the server subscribes to that manager, copies its retained kernel log, persists subsequent operations and broadcasts them through the v1 run stream. Each logger generation gets a live-<source-id> run; resetting memory starts a new source even though its event IDs restart at zero.
from reckon import CausalMemoryManager, MemoryBudget
from reckon.viz import register_cmm
from reckon.viz.server import create_app

cmm = CausalMemoryManager(MemoryBudget(max_slots=1000))
register_cmm(cmm)
app = create_app()  # Serve this app in this process while the task uses cmm.

Registration alone does not start the server. Starting reckon viz serve in another terminal creates a different process and registry. For that arrangement, save and import the log or append operations through the REST API. Refresh the run selector when a new live source appears.
The subscription copies each operation under the manager lock, before a caller can drain its log. It refuses attachment after known ring overflow and reports that error in /health as live_error. Events drained before attachment are unavailable to the subscription. Start the server before the task for a complete capture. Graceful server shutdown detaches the subscription and flushes its remaining queue; abrupt process loss is not a durability guarantee. The diagnostic queue is outside the task's memory budget and grows if production outruns persistence. This is a trusted local laboratory interface, without user authentication or a cross-process manager protocol.
With viz-ui
Build and deploy the React application:
# From the repository root, build without changing the calling terminal's directory
(cd viz-ui && pnpm install && pnpm build)

# Copy to static (for bundled deployment)
mkdir -p src/reckon/viz/static
cp -r viz-ui/packages/debugger/dist/* src/reckon/viz/static/

For development, follow the separate backend and interface terminals in the quick start; the interface proxies to the backend on port 8000.
Fixture Loading
To try the server with the example export after installing a wheel, import the file from the repository root:
reckon viz import runs/_fixtures/golden_run_export.json

When Python loads the server directly from the checkout, you can set RECKON_VIZ_LOAD_FIXTURES=1 on python -m reckon.viz.server. This looks for runs/_fixtures/ relative to the loaded module, so use the explicit import if you installed a wheel.

Troubleshooting
Two Servers: Development requires both Python (8000) and Vite (5173) servers running.
Storage Location: The default is $XDG_DATA_HOME/reckon/viz, or ~/.local/share/reckon/viz when unset. Existing source-tree data is left in place; select its directory explicitly or import its run files into the new store. Use RECKON_VIZ_DATA_DIR for CLI and server commands. For an embedded store, pass a base_path to RunStore.
CORS: Enabled for development (allows localhost:5173). Restrict in production.
WebSocket State: Connections track subscribed run_id. Re-subscribe after reconnection.
SQLite Locking: Single-writer model. Don't run multiple import commands simultaneously.
Fixture Schema: Fixtures must match MemoryRecord interface (payloadType, provenance.inputIds, etc.).

content.title: Entropy, Coarse-Graining, and the Conditional Emergence of Arrows

body:
Entropy, Coarse-Graining, and the Conditional Emergence of Arrows
An entropy computed from observations depends on what you group together. If a task records only which room contains a key, all positions within that room produce the same observation. Recording the exact position would make different distinctions. That choice of which detailed states share one observation is the coarse-graining. MONAD’s formal reference locates its entropy-conservation result and hypotheses. An entropy of macrostates depends on the coarse-graining, and any direction of increase needs the boundary conditions and typicality assumptions of the declared model.
What the laboratory needs, and no more
If you claim that entropy must increase, state the coarse-graining and boundary conditions that make the claim apply. Reckon also has a spectral-entropy helper, which measures a different object: the spectrum of a graph Laplacian. Its edge-list entry builds an undirected graph, computes the selected Laplacian and normalises eigenvalues above its numerical cutoff before taking their entropy. Report the graph, Laplacian choice, cutoff and logarithm base with the value. This graph statistic does not by itself show that physical entropy increased or that an arrow of time emerged.
Implementation
Core module README: the CoarseGraining abstract base class in channels.py

body:
Planned evaluation contract
This specification describes a future evaluator that runs an experiment against fixed, permitted inputs and returns an immutable signed result. It is separate from the implemented laboratory metrics.
Note

Proposed. Its manifest schema, wire identifier and signing implementation have not been published.
Inputs and permissions
An evaluation receives two immutable inputs: the experiment owner's manifest and one permitted dataset, corpus version with its use record, or owner-supplied export. It does not discover a wider database, store, model, route or purpose at runtime. Refuse inputs that are unknown, floating, widened, stale, expired, incompatible with the rights, over budget or of the wrong provenance before execution.
The profile must specify how a change in permission reaches a running evaluation and how affected work stops or is isolated. Frozen input bytes remain fixed. Before delivery, check current permission for the exact artifact and recipient. Retained evidence keeps its original limits; a new comparison or promotion needs its own current permission.
Experiment manifest
The manifest fixes:
The question and permitted operations.
Identities and hashes of experiment, candidates, baselines, code, model, runtime and any corpus version.
Sources and dataset splits; interventions or probes declared in advance.
Causal assumptions and falsifiers where a causal interpretation is sought.
Metrics, uncertainty, the margin that counts as a difference, resource and latency budgets, iteration limits and stopping rule.
Treatment of missing or failed evidence, redaction and output policy, result schema and signer.
The kind of artifact being changed and its full base: package and program dependencies, policy/content packs, model and runtime profile, application releases, compiled generation, the evidence available through the stated point, owner revisions and decision environment.
Separate permission to run on sources, retain context, evaluate, train or fine-tune, derive a model, generalise and publish.
Each evaluator's exact version, configuration and role, including whether it generated candidates, rewards or evidence for selection and promotion.
If an evaluator generated a candidate or its reward, its evidence alone cannot justify promotion. Keep generation, evaluation and the owner's decision distinct.
Result and signature
The result records profile and experiment references, input digest and corpus-use record, ordered candidates and baselines, actual operations, measurements and uncertainty, costs, violated assumptions, failed/unknown/omitted cases, reproduction requirements, limited diagnostic views, redaction summary and signer. Reckon must publish its identifier and manifest; consumers cannot invent equivalent wire definitions.
The signing contract must define canonical bytes, authorised signer, key lifecycle and exactly what the signature authenticates. Test a valid signed result as the control. A result without its runtime signature must fail even beside a valid release attestation. Changed result bytes under the original signature must also fail.

body:
Evaluation Metrics
Decide whether you are comparing policies, reporting memory activity or testing a record’s contribution. A policy comparison needs the task outcome and memory cost. For a record-removal test, also verify that the intervention ran during the task. Keep the producer and denominator with every metric because task counters, current-record summaries and intervention results answer different questions.
To run a complete comparison, follow Compare two replay budgets. That task records classification accuracy and memory cost; it does not measure a record’s causal contribution.
Task outcomes and diagnostics
Read the task runner before interpreting its metrics. Each built-in task constructs its own values. The helper formulas in the next sections apply only when your code calls those helpers.
Producer	Task outcome	Memory and contribution fields	
KeyDoorTask.run	Successful episodes divided by episodes; mean_return uses the same binary reward.	successful_key_episodes_per_write is useful writes divided by writes. successful_stored_key_episode_fraction is stored-key episodes with retrieval and success divided by stored-key episodes. Both use zero with an empty denominator.	
BanditTask.run	mean_regret is accumulated regret divided by steps; mean_return is reward divided by episodes.	first_mode_detections_per_successful_read is counted first detections divided by successful reads. first_mode_detections_per_write uses those detections divided by writes. Both use zero with an empty denominator.	
ContinualTask.run	Final accuracy averaged over subtasks and episodes; forgetting averages positive diagonal-to-final drops for earlier subtasks.	reads_per_write is reads divided by max(writes, 1). mean_episode_accuracy_per_write averages episode accuracy divided by max(episode writes, 1). one_minus_mean_forgetting is one minus mean forgetting.	
TutorTask.run	Mean fraction of initial misconceptions cleared; an episode with none initially uses one.	mean_episode_effective_hint_read_fraction averages each episode's successful effective-hint reads divided by successful reads, using zero with no reads. pooled_effective_hint_read_fraction uses those useful reads divided by max(total reads, 1) across episodes; mean_misconception_clearance is the mean improvement fraction.	
Task-specific fields above live in diagnostics; Bandit, Continual and Tutor also report memory.reads_per_write as successful reads divided by max(writes, 1). Key-Door instead reports diagnostics.key_retrievals_per_query: successful cue queries divided by all query attempts, including empty queries. These usage ratios and improvement measures are not record-ablation results. Tasks and benchmarks explains the schedules and exact definitions. Saved runs from earlier revisions retain their original causal and memory keys; interpret those through their captured source, never as aliases for new results.
Memory activity and cost
Caution

This helper drains the event buffer. MemoryEfficiencyMetrics.from_cmm combines retained events, current memory and caller-supplied totals. It drains get_event_log(): preserve required run artifacts before calling it, and report how much of the run the buffer covers.
Field	Calculation and scope	
reads_per_write	Read count divided by write count. This can exceed one and does not measure relevance.	
useful_reads_per_read	Caller-supplied useful reads divided by read count; an operation ratio, not a fraction of distinct records.	
peak_usage_bytes	Largest bytes_after write sample, or current stored bytes when no write samples remain.	
average_usage_bytes	Mean of those write samples, unavailable without samples; not a time-weighted average.	
total_reward_per_byte, total_reward_per_slot	Supplied total reward divided by sampled peak/current bytes or current occupied slots respectively.	
mean_return_per_byte, mean_return_per_slot	The same denominators with supplied mean return, only when total reward is absent.	
Read and write counts come from the native logger's op_type events, with task-supplied counts used when no events of that kind remain. A read event represents one retrieval call. The byte and slot denominators have different scopes; neither is automatically a whole-run peak. A supplied total reward of zero takes priority over mean return. Missing reward inputs or nonpositive denominators leave the affected ratios unavailable, omitted by to_dict().
Record usage and stored scores
RecordSummaryMetrics.from_cmm examines current records, caller-owned labels and already-stored deltas. It neither runs nor validates an intervention.
Field	Calculation	
used_record_fraction	Currently stored records with positive use_count, divided by stored records. No ground-truth labels are needed.	
necessary_cue_retention	Retained necessary-cue IDs divided by positive total_cues, whose default is the number of supplied necessary IDs.	
useful_retrieval_fraction	Supplied useful retrievals divided by retrievals, selected only when the necessary-cue denominator is nonpositive.	
max_abs_stored_ablation_delta	Largest absolute finite stored ablation_delta.	
mean_stored_ablation_delta	Signed mean of finite stored ablation_delta values.	
Missing positive denominators or finite scores leave the affected field unavailable. A retrieval fraction cannot stand in for cue retention, and a stored delta needs its original experiment before it can support a claim about contribution.
Distinguish proxy-only records
Reports must flag a record as proxy-only when influence_proxy is present and both ablation_delta and counterfactual_delta are absent. A stored zero or negative delta is still present; a record with all three fields absent has no supplied attribution score. Preserve those distinctions when reporting record counts or interpreting a retention decision. Field presence describes the supplied score, while the original experiment establishes whether it is a valid measurement.
CausalScore.is_proxy_only computes the flag from those supplied fields. RecordSummaryMetrics.from_cmm() reports sorted proxy_only_record_ids and proxy_only_record_count for the current store without draining its event log. An examined empty store reports an empty list and zero; a summary constructed without an inventory leaves both unavailable. The flag is computed, so record serialization keeps the original score fields and their missing values without adding a wire field.
The debugger inspector labels each selected record’s supplied attribution source and counts proxy-only records in the selected event’s snapshot. Missing snapshots or score objects remain explicitly unavailable or incomplete. The experiment runner’s retention_score_source describes a whole run, and the graph’s measured, inferred and proxy edge labels describe relationships; neither replaces this record-by-record inventory. None of these reporting fields changes retention or validates a measurement.
What a contribution measurement should establish
The proposed record-contribution protocol asks whether removing a record or replacing it with random or null content, under the same budget and policy, causes a statistically significant performance drop at least as large as a declared threshold. Define the outcome, intervention, trial seeds and minimum useful difference before running it. The targets are:
Target	Meaning	
Causal precision	Fraction of stored records meeting that positive-usefulness test.	
Causal recall	Fraction of ground-truth necessary records retained.	
Counterfactual sensitivity	Outcome difference under the specified replacement or removal.	
Useful memory rate	Fraction of stored items retrieved and shown to affect a decision. Access counts alone do not establish that effect.	
Only measured ablation_delta or counterfactual_delta values can supply intervention evidence; report influence_proxy separately. An identified causal effect also needs a declared estimand, identification assumptions, negative controls, repeated runs and an uncertainty interval. A metric name, the ABLATION credit policy, matched seeds or a p-value cannot supply those conditions.
The working evaluator below implements one removal test. Its aggregate denominators differ from these proposed whole-store targets, and replacement remains unsupported.
Evaluation Protocol
CausalRecordEvaluator in src/reckon/metrics/evaluator.py runs paired task invocations with one actual record removal. Its defaults are 10 trials, an absolute delta threshold of 0.05 in the outcome’s units and alpha 0.05; the delta is not divided by the baseline. Trial independence still depends on the experiment. The procedure is:
Setup: Fix the task configuration, policy, budget, seed set and episodes per arm. Factories must return fresh instances. The evaluator snapshots declared task configuration, every budget field and policy configuration, then checks each arm against that snapshot. Tasks must derive their randomness from the supplied seed.
Select the record: An exact ID is accepted when it exists in both runs. For task-created records with fresh UUIDs, pass record_selector and use record_id as a stable report label. At the first read whose candidates match, the selector must identify exactly one record; multiple matches or a target that never reaches a read fail the evaluation.
Apply the intervention: The baseline retains the candidate. The other arm calls prune before access, logging or credit assignment, checks its success and verifies that the record is absent. The read then resolves again, so a ranked query can return its next candidate. An explicit-ID read returns no match for the removed ID.
Verify the pair: Both arms must reach the same read ordinal with matching selected payload, creation step, episode, cost, tags, source operation, utility, measured scores and metadata. Their digest excludes generated UUIDs and provenance input IDs; the selector supplies logical identity. A mismatch raises instead of returning a result. The report retains seeds, episodes per arm, both actual IDs, the shared target digest, removal status and both outcomes.
Measure the difference: Delta is baseline mean minus intervention mean, using a finite outcome where higher is better. A paired two-sided permutation test enumerates sign patterns up to 10,000; larger sets use 10,000 seeded draws. is_significant requires both the configured absolute effect threshold and p < alpha. is_useful additionally requires a strictly positive delta at or above the threshold.
Only ABLATE executes. MASK and REPLACE raise before task execution; their enum values do not imply support. The intervention removes one record instance at its first eligible read. A later replacement record is allowed, so this does not measure permanent suppression of the same fact. All four built-in tasks support this read-boundary intervention. Tutor reuses successful hints across episodes, so its comparison needs at least two episodes per arm; a one-episode run with no eligible record fails explicitly.
For example, evaluate a task-created key without pretending its UUID survives a fresh run:
from reckon.core.resources import MemoryBudget
from reckon.memory.manager import CausalMemoryManager
from reckon.metrics import CausalRecordEvaluator
from reckon.tasks import KeyDoorTask

evaluator = CausalRecordEvaluator(
    KeyDoorTask,
    lambda: CausalMemoryManager(MemoryBudget(max_slots=16)),
    lambda result: result.performance.success_rate,
    n_trials=10,
)
result = evaluator.evaluate_record(
    "first key", record_selector=lambda record: "key" in record.tags
)

The report preserves per-record deltas, trial counts and permutation p-values. It does not compute per-record confidence intervals. contract_precision is the fraction of distinct evaluated target labels with is_useful=True, using zero when none are evaluated. With non-empty ground-truth labels, contract_recall is the useful overlap divided by that set’s size; absent or empty ground truth leaves recall unavailable. Harmful and zero effects remain in the signed results but enter neither numerator. These descriptive aggregates use unadjusted per-record tests and establish neither family-wise error nor false-discovery control.
Supply your own paired runner
The separate Prober calls run_fn(ablated_ids, seed) twice per trial: ([], seed) for the baseline and ([record_id], seed) for removal. Each arm must start from the same task state; the caller owns removing the requested record after setup and before its use. Both arms must execute; precomputed unmatched baselines are refused. Replacement and shuffle requests raise before the runner is called. probe_episodes counts both arms, probe_wall_time_s measures the entire probe including statistics, and the returned configuration includes the actual first seed when one was generated.
Tests and intervals use the paired differences. The permutation test swaps labels within pairs (paired permutation design); it enumerates all sign patterns when they fit the configured resample count and otherwise samples them. The t-test is a one-sample test of differences against zero, equivalent to the paired t-test. Bootstrap resamples differences and centers its null draws at zero. Intervals are normal approximations for permutation, Student-t for t-tests and percentile bootstrap for bootstrap. Their assumptions and finite-sample limits still apply; a matched seed alone does not identify causation.
Fixed sampling uses n_trials pairs. Adaptive sampling applies only when both adaptive_sampling and early_stopping are true; otherwise the run uses n_trials. Adaptive sampling checks at min_trials, successive doublings, n_trials clipped to the allowed range, and max_trials. It stops for a significant difference or an interval wholly within ±delta_threshold; otherwise it reaches the maximum. Before the across-record correction, p-values are multiplied by the number of scheduled looks and intervals use alpha / looks. This Bonferroni adjustment covers the planned repeated looks subject to each test’s assumptions; the approximate intervals are not exact confidence sequences. Evidence.p_value is therefore the look-adjusted value, while p_value_adjusted additionally applies the configured correction across records. Benjamini–Hochberg assumes independence or the appropriate positive dependence across tests; shared seeds do not establish that assumption. Choose Bonferroni when arbitrary dependence must be covered. Both significance flags are two-sided; usefulness still requires the signed outcome comparison. The debugger graph displays supplied evidence and does not execute these probes.
Measure outcomes; do not optimise against a judge
Use the task outcome to test whether a record helped. A model's opinion that a record looks useful can be a labelled input, but should not replace the measured outcome. Validate a changed policy on held-out evidence before using it.
Diagnostic goals
Time to diagnose a failure is a qualitative measure in early versions. A later diagnostic comparison should also count which failures it can detect automatically: a missing cue, wrong retrieval, budget waste or drift. These are evaluation goals, not fields computed by the helpers above.
Probe Cost Accounting
Report task and probe episodes together, with their full elapsed time. ProbeCostTracker measures the bracketed probe time; the caller supplies base costs and records calls, episode counts, environment steps and evaluated records. A tracking label does not execute an intervention or establish its benefit.
Probe Cost Metrics
Metric	Description	Unit	
probe_episodes_total	Total episodes used for probing	count	
probe_wall_time_total_ms	Total wall time for all probes	milliseconds	
probe_calls_total	Total task.run invocations for probing	count	
probe_env_steps_total	Total environment steps for probing	count	
probe_records_evaluated	Number of records evaluated	count	
probe_episodes_per_record	Average episodes per record	episodes/record	
probe_wall_time_per_record_ms	Average wall time per record	ms/record	
probe_overhead_ratio	probe_time / (base_time + probe_time)	ratio (0-1)	
ProbeCostSummary aggregates these measurements. Per-record averages use zero when no records were evaluated; the overhead ratio uses zero when total elapsed time is zero.
Efficiency Metrics
EfficiencyMetrics.compute combines supplied reward, utility improvement and the recorded costs. Missing positive denominators produce zero. These ratios help compare costs; the caller still has to measure any claimed improvement.
Metric	Formula	Interpretation	
reward_per_total_episode	reward / (base_episodes + probe_episodes)	Performance accounting for all compute	
reward_per_total_wall_time	reward / (base_time_ms + probe_time_ms)	Reward per millisecond, including probe overhead	
utility_gain_per_probe_episode	utility_improvement / probe_episodes	Return on probing investment	
Usage Example
Use this Key-Door example to check how the tracker reports invocations and their binary rewards. It runs two task invocations for accounting. To measure a contribution or utility improvement, supply a runner, intervention and comparison under the protocol above.
from time import perf_counter

from reckon import CausalMemoryManager, MemoryBudget
from reckon.metrics import ProbeCostTracker, EfficiencyMetrics
from reckon.tasks.task_a_keydoor import KeyDoorTask

task = KeyDoorTask()
tracker = ProbeCostTracker()
base_episodes = 100
started = perf_counter()
baseline = task.run(
    CausalMemoryManager(MemoryBudget(max_slots=100, max_bytes=50_000)),
    num_episodes=base_episodes,
    seed=41,
)
tracker.set_base_costs(
    episodes=base_episodes,
    wall_time_ms=(perf_counter() - started) * 1000,
)

# Account for a second task run; no record-removal runner is invoked here.
with tracker.track_probe(probe_type="accounting-demo", seed=42):
    tracker.record_call(episodes=10)
    result = task.run(
        CausalMemoryManager(MemoryBudget(max_slots=100, max_bytes=50_000)),
        num_episodes=10,
        seed=42,
    )

summary = tracker.summarize()
print(f"Probe overhead: {summary.probe_overhead_ratio:.1%}")

# Key-Door awards one for a successful episode and zero otherwise.
total_reward = sum(
    episode["success"]
    for run in (baseline, result)
    for episode in run.raw_data["episodes"]
)
efficiency = EfficiencyMetrics.compute(
    total_reward=total_reward,
    probe_costs=summary,
)
print(f"Reward per total episode: {efficiency.reward_per_total_episode:.3f}")

Proto Schema
Probe costs are defined in protos/reckon/events.proto:
ProbeCostEvent: Per-probe operation costs
ProbeCostSummary: Aggregated probe metrics
Choose what a frontier compares
A frontier compares declared costs and outcomes. Choose the outcome explicitly and keep its producer, units and direction with the comparison. The dictionary and notebook helpers retain the axis names and reject missing or nonfinite measurements. An observed zero stays zero; an absent accuracy value cannot become success rate or a measured zero. This prevents an incomplete row from appearing artificially cheap or successful.
The notebook efficiency helper also requires a named outcome. Its overhead-weighted value is that outcome multiplied by one minus the fraction of episodes spent probing. That arithmetic does not establish a causal effect or decide whether the measurement cost is worthwhile.
For helper inputs, serialization and integration with tasks, use the metrics reference. The future service that returns signed evaluation artifacts has a separate planned contract.
