The timings are design targets. The listed data structures explain the implementation; they do not establish measured latency or attainment of those targets.
Measure the native store
Run cargo bench --manifest-path kernel/Cargo.toml --bench store_bench -- --noplot from the repository root. The benchmark measures three batches: inserting 1,000 prepared 100-byte records, reading 100 evenly spaced keys from 1,000 records, and selecting 100 records from a 10,000-record store. Selection identifies records totaling 10,000 bytes and leaves them stored. The read keys are fixed, not random.
Fixture construction is outside the timed operations. Insertion also excludes destruction of the resulting store; reads include cloning and dropping each returned record, and selection includes restoring the index and dropping the returned IDs. Criterion uses 30 samples with a one-second warmup and three-second measurement window per case. Its estimates and raw samples go under kernel/target/criterion/. Batch timings and per-record throughput are different quantities; neither establishes the Python API's latency or a memory-policy benefit.
The 15 November 2026 measurement retains the raw samples, estimates, source hashes and toolchain. It predates the direct-insert cost and overflow checks. On an Apple M4 Max with macOS ARM64 and Rust 1.94.0, while other development work was active, the estimated batch times were:
Batch	Estimate	95% confidence interval	
Insert 1,000 records	433.52 µs	345.83–521.70 µs	
Read 100 keys	32.92 µs	28.38–39.07 µs	
Select 100 of 10,000 records	34.32 µs	28.31–41.82 µs	
These are observations from one shared development host and one workload, not a latency guarantee. Re-run the command on the intended deployment workload before comparing it with the targets above.
Memory Layout
Records stored by value in HashMap
PriorityIndex stores lightweight RecordRef (ID + priority)
Lazy deletion avoids heap rebuild on updates
Future storage and performance choices
The current kernel keeps records and events in memory. The following choices are conditional design work; the native store measurements provide a baseline for deciding what needs to change.
Batch statistics. Consider faer for the probe's numerical batches only when profiling a measured experiment identifies those calculations as a material cost. Measure that cost separately from running the paired task episodes, copying memory and collecting results. A faster calculation must preserve the experiment's estimates and uncertainty; the reproducibility guide defines the comparison it serves. faer is not a current dependency.
Graph dependencies. The kernel has no runtime use of petgraph and no MONAD source dependency. The resolved build still includes petgraph through prost-build, the protocol compiler listed in Cargo.toml. That build dependency supplies no graph capability to Reckon's record store. Add a runtime graph representation only for an identified operation and its data requirements.
Durable records and replay. A future laboratory store must define what survives a restart and retain enough record state and ordered operations to reconstruct the run it promises to replay. The current event ring can overwrite entries and omits full record state; RecordStore.fork() makes an independent in-memory trial. The debugger's RunStore saves supplied event files and summaries for viewing. Those exports remain useful, but recovering the live manager requires a separate persistence and replay contract, including how an interrupted write is handled.
Arena allocation. Consider a generational slot arena only if measurements of the intended workload identify the map and heap as the store's bottleneck. The existing batch timings alone do not establish that cause. Share reusable arena and ring mechanics through rtepl-common when that work is justified. Reckon keeps the meaning of its records, budgets and retention policies; Pale keeps the meaning of its own graph and scheduling state. Shared storage mechanics must preserve those separate contracts.
Linux I/O. Consider an io_uring adapter only after a durable store and a Linux deployment exist. The adapter owns its pinned I/O buffers; the record arena has a separate lifetime. Its portable fallback must produce identical stored and replayed results for the same operations. Establish the store's correctness and recovery behavior before comparing I/O throughput.
Building
Follow installation for a new CPython 3.11 environment. The documented CPython range is 3.9–3.12. Pass the interpreter explicitly so the build and import check use the same environment. Run the commands below from the Reckon repository root.
Protocol Buffers compiler
The kernel and daemon build scripts use protoc-bin-vendored = 3.3.0, which supplies protoc 36.2 for the build host. Cargo fetches those packages with the other build dependencies; installing a system compiler is optional. Rust consumers such as HENA and Q-HENA inherit this build requirement through the kernel. An offline build needs the packaged compiler in Cargo's cache.
Set PROTOC to an executable path to select a compiler explicitly. PROTOC_INCLUDE can select its include directory. When choosing the packaged compiler, the build also uses its packaged includes unless PROTOC_INCLUDE is already set. Cargo reruns generation when either selection changes. Generated Rust stays in Cargo's build output directory.
Development
(cd kernel && cargo build)

This builds the Rust API without PyO3. The daemon and Rust re-export consumers use that default. The kernel has no sibling source dependency. MONAD remains the manual’s source of formal definitions; no implemented kernel path uses its types. Use cargo check --features python in kernel/ when checking the binding without extension-module linking.
Run cargo test --manifest-path kernel/Cargo.toml --test store_properties for the exhaustive small-state checks. They compare 32,768 length-five operation traces with an independent map, checking replacement, removal, utility/access updates, pruning, rebuilding, accounting and repeatable priority selection. A second property checks all 341 cost vectors of up to four records over zero, small and large costs, across 13 policy configurations and feasible or infeasible byte/slot pressures. These tests cover valid input domains; RecordStore leaves admission limits to its caller.
Python Extension
# With the supported project environment active, from the repository root
maturin build --interpreter "$VIRTUAL_ENV/bin/python" --out "$VIRTUAL_ENV/wheels"
python -m pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps "$VIRTUAL_ENV"/wheels/*.whl
python -c "from reckon._rust import EventLogger, RecordStore"

The installation guide installs the runtime dependencies before this rebuild. --force-reinstall --no-deps replaces the installed package with the new wheel while keeping those dependencies. cargo build alone does not refresh the Python extension. For editable Python development, maturin develop uses the active supported environment and writes its extension into the source package; do not use that route when preserving an existing source-tree extension.
Release
# From the repository root with the project environment active
maturin build --release --interpreter "$VIRTUAL_ENV/bin/python"

Proto Integration
Types are generated from Protocol Buffers via prost:
// build.rs
prost_build::compile_protos(&["../protos/reckon/record.proto"], &["../protos"])?;

// lib.rs
pub mod proto {
    include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/reckon.rs"));
}

Lock Ordering
To prevent deadlocks in RecordStore, always acquire locks in this order:
records (RwLock)
priority_index (RwLock)
current_bytes (RwLock)
current_tokens (RwLock)
Never hold priority_index while acquiring records.
Error Handling
The crate uses thiserror for error definitions. Common error patterns:
Record not found: Returns Option<Record> (None if missing)
Insert with duplicate ID: Returns Ok(Some(record)) containing the replaced record
Negative byte or token cost, or either overflowing total: Returns RecordStoreError without mutation; Python receives ValueError or OverflowError, respectively
Buffer overflow: Events are dropped (check dropped_count())
Tracing Instrumentation
Key operations are instrumented with tracing:
use tracing::{instrument, debug};

#[instrument(skip(self))]
pub fn insert(&self, record: Record) -> Option<Record> {
    debug!(id = %record.id, "inserting record");
    // ...
}

Enable tracing by configuring a subscriber in your Python code or Rust tests.
Source map and dependencies
Architecture
flowchart TB
    subgraph Crate["reckon"]
        Lib["lib.rs\n(PyO3 module)"]
        Store["store.rs\n(RecordStore)"]
        Policies["policies.rs\n(RetentionPolicy)"]
        Logging["logging.rs\n(EventLogger)"]
        Proto["generated/\n(prost types)"]
    end

    subgraph Python["Python Layer"]
        CMM["CausalMemoryManager"]
        PyStore["_rust.RecordStore"]
        PyLogger["_rust.EventLogger"]
    end

    subgraph External["External"]
        Protos["protos/*.proto"]
        Build["build.rs"]
    end

    Lib --> Store
    Lib --> Policies
    Lib --> Logging
    Store --> Proto
    Build --> Protos
    Protos --> Proto

    CMM --> PyStore
    CMM --> PyLogger
    PyStore --> Store
    PyLogger --> Logging

Module Structure
Start in store.rs to trace a lookup or change index maintenance, logging.rs for buffer behavior, and policies.rs for the Rust-side rankings.

Troubleshooting
Python version: PyO3 0.20.3 builds an abi3-py39 wheel. If the extension will not import, activate the documented environment, pass its interpreter to the build and verify that you installed the resulting wheel into that same environment.
Non-Local Definitions Warning: PyO3 generates code with non-local impl warnings. Suppressed with #![allow(non_local_definitions)].
Thread Safety: The store and logger protect shared state with parking_lot locks and atomic counters. Follow the store’s lock ordering above; a cloned Record is a value, not another synchronized store.
Lazy Deletion Overhead: PriorityIndex accumulates invalidated entries. Call rebuild() periodically for long-running processes.
Event Buffer Overflow: Ring buffer overwrites oldest events. Monitor dropped_count() to detect overflow. Ensure capacity matches expected event rate.
Prost Regeneration: build.rs declares each selected schema with cargo:rerun-if-changed. Cargo reruns that build step when those inputs change. Rebuild the extension with maturin to make the regenerated types available to Python.
NaN Handling: priority_score() returns NEG_INFINITY for NaN scores, ensuring such records are pruned first.
Testing
# From the repository root
(cd kernel && cargo test)

Key tests:
test_priority_index: Heap ordering correctness
test_record_store_insert_get: Basic CRUD
test_select_for_pruning: Priority-based selection
test_ring_buffer_overflow: Buffer wrap behavior

Related guides
Architecture Overview
Python Memory Module
Protocol definitions: records, budgets, influence relations and events.

body:
Learning as a special case

When two training runs end with similar parameters, those parameters alone can hide different histories. This chapter explains what to log for a reconstruction, what a budgeted learner can store and how to interpret a spectral diagnostic.
1. Training is an Open Reduction
Let the full microstate be z = (\theta, \xi):
\theta: model parameters
\xi: minibatch order, RNG state, data pipeline state, optimizer buffers, hardware nondeterminism, etc.
What we observe as "training on \theta" is a coarse-grained/open projection:
\Pi(\theta, \xi) = \theta

Thus, apparent irreversibility in training is expected: many-to-one projection merges histories.
2. Memory as Reliable Records in Learning Loops
A "record" may be:
a gradient summary
a training example kept for replay
a compressed representation snapshot
a reasoning trace
an environment cue
If you can keep only some records, compare how the task behaves when you change one of them under the same test conditions. A reliable record also needs to let you distinguish the alternatives within the allowed trials and error rates.
3. Representation Geometry as a Macro-Observable
Given embeddings h_\theta^{(\ell)}(x_i), construct a similarity graph and Laplacian L^{(\ell)}(\theta). Spectral statistics are coarse observables of representation geometry.
For an undirected graph with non-negative weights, form a symmetric adjacency matrix. Decide whether to use a normalized or unnormalized Laplacian. Define spectral entropy from the positive eigenvalues \lambda_i:
p_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_{j:\, \lambda_j > 0} \lambda_j}, \quad S_{\text{spec}} = -\sum_{i:\, \lambda_i > 0} p_i \log p_i

This is a deliberately chosen summary of the graph, a macro-functional, rather than a unique entropy of the representation. The similarity rule, edge weights and Laplacian choice determine which quantity it measures. It is separate from the fine-grained entropy conserved in MONAD’s formal profile; that conservation does not impose a direction of change on this statistic.
Notes:
The ideal formula excludes zero modes. The implementation uses eigenvalues greater than epsilon. The normalized Laplacian gives an isolated node a diagonal entry of 1. In the unnormalized Laplacian it contributes a zero mode.
Log base determines units (bits for \log_2, nats for \ln). Unless stated otherwise, we use natural log; implementations MAY use \log_2: comparisons are invariant up to a constant factor.
The implementation normalizes those retained eigenvalues, then computes the log of each probability plus epsilon. This is a numerical approximation to the displayed formula.
If you use the statistic to investigate collapse, drift or a phase transition, report how you built the graph and what you compared. The same change in spectral entropy can have several explanations.
Implementation: compute_spectral_entropy(adjacency, normalized=False, log_base="natural") accepts the supplied adjacency matrix and defaults to the unnormalized Laplacian. The caller must supply the symmetric graph required by this interpretation. spectral_entropy_from_edges() builds an unweighted undirected projection: each supplied edge fills both adjacency directions. It therefore discards direction in a record-influence graph. Neither function constructs an embedding similarity graph for the caller. Units are nats by default; use log_base="2" for bits.
Caution

Spectral entropy can be expensive. This is an opt-in metric (O(n³) eigenvalue decomposition). Compute only when explicitly requested; do not include in default metric collection for large graphs.
4. Retrodiction Lens on Training
To reconstruct early \theta_0 from late \theta_\tau, remember that \Pi maps several histories to the same parameters. Missing \xi acts as effective noise. Logging \xi can reduce uncertainty at a storage and compute cost. Apply the retrodiction estimate only if you can identify the target and describe how errors grow. A property of the parameters can be identifiable even when the full training state is not.
Implementation

Tasks Module README: Benchmark tasks that exercise memory under budget constraints

body:
Mathematical Core
Home | Prev: Overview | Next: Operational Causality
Use this chapter to interpret influence diagnostics, compare retention policies or design a test under resource limits. For method signatures and data types, see the core Python reference.
Where the foundations live
MONAD owns the state space and measure-preserving evolution, invariant fine-grained entropy, observer interface, reliable-record criterion, detectable influence and information bounds. Its formal reference locates the definitions and proofs; its kernel reference maps Rust types to those declarations or names a missing counterpart. Neither a resolved reference nor Reckon’s handwritten Python interfaces establishes implementation conformance. This chapter explains what a Reckon experiment must supply and what its diagnostics can report; the full paper remains private pending publication.
Test influence under resource limits
Declare the comparison
To investigate influence from A to B, declare the resources R, an allowed protocol and the two preparation operations that set A to zero or one. Record which outcome y you observe for B, its two induced probability laws P_0 and P_1, the divergence D (for example total variation, KL divergence or Hellinger distance) and the detection threshold \eta. The distributional comparison is:
D(P_1, P_0) \geq \eta

To interpret this comparison under MONAD’s influence relation, establish the protocol’s reliable-record conditions for A and B as well. Reliability means repeatable discrimination within the declared trial and error limits, not persistence. A laboratory experiment may instead measure another downstream observable; specify that target and its interpretation rather than assuming it satisfies the reliable-record criterion for B.
MONAD's intervention notation selects allowed preparation operations that set A to zero or one. Those operations can also change other properties, so a detected difference establishes influence of the chosen intervention pair; isolating A's contribution needs additional assumptions or interventions matched outside A. This is not automatically the mechanism-replacement intervention of a structural causal model. The formal profile owns that distinction; a laboratory comparison must declare which operations it actually runs.
The observation model matters too. MONAD’s profile uses deterministic measurable coarse-graining followed by a separate noisy record channel. A stochastic coarse-graining would need its own induced-distribution definitions for fibers and events; the laboratory’s abstract channel interfaces do not establish that generalization.
Code: See CausalRelation and DirectInfluenceRecords.
Current recorded-pair diagnostic
DirectInfluenceRecords stores supplied distinguishability values and thresholds. causes() compares each stored pair against its threshold; check_transitivity() scans the resulting decisions. It does not estimate the pair values or run significance tests.
Use the recorded thresholds to interpret the scan. The report echoes alpha and multiple_testing_correction as metadata. Passing either setting leaves the pair decisions unchanged.
Code: See DirectInfluenceRecords.check_transitivity() for the recorded-pair scan.
These illustrative values produce one eligible path whose endpoint falls below its threshold. They exercise the recorded-pair scan; they are not measurements from an experiment:
from reckon.core.causality import DirectInfluenceRecords
from reckon.core.resources import ResourceVector

pairs = DirectInfluenceRecords(ResourceVector(memory_slots=3))
pairs.add_relation("A", "B", distinguishability=0.5, threshold=0.1)
pairs.add_relation("B", "C", distinguishability=0.5, threshold=0.1)
pairs.add_relation("A", "C", distinguishability=0.08, threshold=0.1)
report = pairs.check_transitivity(alpha=0.05)
print(f"Violation rate: {report.violation_rate:.2%}")
print(f"Violations: {len(report.violations)}/{report.total_triples_tested}")

The report contains one tested path and one below-threshold endpoint:
{
  "violations": [
    {
      "triple": ["A", "B", "C"],
      "a_b_detected": true,
      "b_c_detected": true,
      "a_c_detected": false,
      "a_b_distinguishability": 0.5,
      "b_c_distinguishability": 0.5,
      "a_c_distinguishability": 0.08,
      "a_c_threshold": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "violation_rate": 1.0,
  "total_triples_tested": 1,
  "alpha": 0.05,
  "multiple_testing_correction": "none"
}

Read the diagnostic’s counts
The Python diagnostic scans recorded two-edge paths through three distinct events. When the endpoint pair is missing or has a recorded value below threshold, it reports the path as a diagnostic. A missing pair has a_c_distinguishability: null and inherits the first edge's threshold for display. A tested pair below threshold carries its own value and threshold. causes() returns false in both cases. Use get_relation() to tell them apart. Both count toward violation_rate, whose denominator counts the eligible recorded paths. A two-event cycle alone produces a zero rate with no eligible paths.
Interpret the recorded pairs
MONAD’s influence relation, written \preceq_R in this manual, is resource-monotone when larger budgets admit every smaller-budget protocol, but is neither reflexive nor transitive in general. The formal reference owns those results. When effects cancel along a path works through exact cancellation and a reliable channel whose total variation of 0.6 falls below a detection threshold of 0.9.
For Reckon, the consequences are concrete: DirectInfluenceRecords stores supplied pairs without assuming closure, and its current diagnostic does not test reflexivity. A missing A-to-C detection after detecting A-to-B and B-to-C need not be sampling error; the population relation itself can fail to compose. Finite samples add further uncertainty, and a larger resource budget need not produce more detected edges in the empirical graph, especially near the noise floor. Keep the population statement separate from that estimate.
Closure remains explicit
The library does not infer transitive closure from recorded pairs.
If downstream logic requires closure, it must be computed explicitly with an associated cost and uncertainty model. Closure computation is still planned. The relationship graph describes how the view filters snapshot edges and handles separately supplied edges.
Planned closure modes (not yet implemented in the library):
Mode	Description	Trade-off	
Optimistic	Assume transitivity holds	Dangerous, low compute	
Verified	Require direct evidence for implied edges	Expensive, high confidence	
Probabilistic	Propagate posterior confidence along paths	Medium compute, uncertainty-aware	
Code: See TransitivityReport for violation reports.
Proposed empirical estimator
The estimator described here is a research proposal for pairwise tests. Today, DirectInfluenceRecords takes pair values you have already measured and compares them with their thresholds. You run the interventions and calculate significance separately.
Theoretical relation and proposed estimator
The population relation describes detectability under the model. A finite experiment can only estimate it:
Relation	Notation	Meaning	
Theoretical	\preceq_R	Population/"true" detectability under resources R	
Empirical	\hat{\preceq}_{R,n,\alpha,M}	Estimated from data with parameters below	
The empirical estimator is indexed by:
n = samples/episodes per pairwise test
\alpha = per-test significance level (default: 0.05)
M = number of hypotheses tested (for multiple testing)
Plus implicit noise model and task stochasticity
Pairwise significance does not imply transitivity
The proposed empirical estimate \hat{\preceq}_{R,n,\alpha,M} adds noise and thresholds to the population relation. Detecting A→B and B→C at p < \alpha does not imply A→C is detectable at p < \alpha.
Why empirical pairs can fail to compose
Whether a finite test detects an effect depends on its size, the variance and the number of samples.
On top of the failures the relation itself allows, the empirical estimator can violate transitivity because of:
Stochasticity / finite n: Limited samples increase false negative rate
Type I errors (false edges): Some detected edges are spurious
Type II errors (missing edges): Some true edges fail detection
Effect size dilution: Causal effects often attenuate along paths (A \to B \to C weaker than A \to B or B \to C)
Selection bias: "We only tested some triples", so coverage is incomplete
Multiple testing inflation: Testing M hypotheses without correction inflates false positives
Multiple testing
The per-test \alpha = 0.05 is a per-comparison error rate.
When testing M hypotheses, options include:
Method	Control	Formula	Notes	
None	Per-test	\alpha	Fast, high false positive rate	
Bonferroni	FWER	\alpha / M	Conservative, low power	
Holm	FWER	Sequential adjustment	Less conservative than Bonferroni	
Benjamini-Hochberg	FDR	Ranks p-values	Controls expected false discovery rate	
q-values	Estimated FDR or positive FDR at rejection thresholds	Minimum estimated rate over thresholds including the test	A thresholded-set quantity, not the test's posterior null probability	
A q-value describes the estimated false-discovery rate associated with calling a test significant. Local FDR instead estimates the probability that the test's null hypothesis is true, conditional on its observed statistic under the selected model. The maintained qvalue package distinguishes these two outputs. Neither is a causal probability, and neither is computed by the recorded-pair diagnostic.
Planned options: FWER control (Bonferroni/Holm), FDR control (Benjamini-Hochberg), q-values.
Note

Correction does not establish transitivity. Correcting the error rate across tests does not make detected paths compose. The result is still a graph of pairwise decisions.
Save a reproducible report
The scan orders event identifiers by Unicode code point, so the resulting triples have the same order across insertion orders and Python hash seeds. to_json(indent=2) gives a readable report. For a saved identity, use to_canonical_json() and hash its UTF-8 bytes without adding a newline:
import hashlib

artifact = report.to_canonical_json().encode("utf-8")
digest = hashlib.sha256(artifact).hexdigest()

The canonical profile adds schema_version: "reckon.transitivity-report/v1" to the report. It sorts violations by the event triple, breaks repeated-triple ties by the complete encoded entry and retains duplicate entries. Object keys sort lexically; Python JSON uses compact separators, ASCII string escapes and its finite-number spelling. Event identifiers keep their exact Unicode sequences, and numeric representations such as 1 and 1.0 remain distinct. NaN and either infinity are refused. Serialization leaves the original report unchanged.
The digest covers the report's supplied fields, including significance and correction metadata. Those labels still do not change the pair decisions or perform statistical correction. Keep the source records, resource configuration and implementation revision with the artifact when another run must reproduce it. Missing endpoint values remain null, distinct from a measured zero or a value below threshold.
Use scores to choose what survives
Read the stored signals
Each record r carries:
utility.value: accumulated utility estimate (updated via update_score())
utility.last_used: timestep of last access
causal_score.ablation_delta: performance change when record removed (MEASURED)
causal_score.counterfactual_delta: change under hypothetical intervention (MEASURED)
causal_score.influence_proxy: heuristic proxy (e.g., gradient magnitude) (PROXY)
These labels describe the intended source of each score. A populated field alone does not establish that its intervention ran or was valid; keep the experiment with the value and follow the proxy-only reporting rule.
Policy Score for Retention
When the Python memory manager prunes, it calls its configured retention policy. EvidencePerBytePolicy prefers the non-negative part of an ablation result, then the non-negative part of a counterfactual result, then a separate proxy. Deltas use outcome with the record minus outcome without it: a negative value means removal helped, so that effect gives zero retention credit. The stored measurement keeps its sign:
C_m(r) = \begin{cases}
\max(\Delta_a, 0) & \text{if ablation measured} \\
\max(\Delta_c, 0) & \text{else if counterfactual measured} \\
\bot & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}

C_p(r) = |\phi|

Combined score:
S(r) = (1 - \alpha) \cdot U(r) + \alpha \cdot C(r)

where:
C_m(r) = beneficial part of the measured attribution (from ablation_delta or counterfactual_delta)
C_p(r) = proxy magnitude (from influence_proxy)
C(r) = C_m(r) if defined, else C_p(r) as fallback. If the record has neither a measured value nor a proxy, the causal term is zero.
A negative or zero measured result remains the selected measured branch; it does not fall through to a positive proxy. The proxy is separately labelled and is not evidence of benefit.
U(r) = utility estimate
\alpha = evidence weight (0-1)
To free bytes, slots and tokens, the Python policy removes the records with the lowest combined score divided by max(record.cost.bytes, 1) first.
Design note: The Python policy selects the kernel's EvidencePerByte rule above. The Rust WeightedEvidencePolicy wrapper selects WeightedEvidence, which adds non-negative ablation and counterfactual contributions and the absolute proxy with weights 1, 0.5 and 0.25, then mixes that sum with utility. It ranks the combined score without dividing by cost. Both rules live in the kernel, and they remain different policies; a comparison must name the rule and revision it uses.
The store’s priority index is a third ranking: utility plus 0.5[\max(\Delta_a, 0) + \max(\Delta_c, 0)], with missing measurements contributing zero. The daemon calls the same function for capacity pruning. It uses neither the proxy nor cost division. NaN measurements contribute zero; a NaN total has the lowest priority. Both stores break equal scores by record ID.
Code: Kernel retention rules implement the rankings and byte/slot selection; Python policy objects select the laboratory rules.
To interpret ablation_delta or counterfactual_delta, report what you changed, what you compared, how you identified the effect, the controls and the uncertainty. Keep proxy scores separate. See evaluation metrics for what each method tests.
Account for time since access
Define recency as \tau(r) := t_{now} - t_{last}, measuring steps since last access (not since creation).
A policy could weight utility by a decay function f(\tau), for example \exp(-\tau/T) with task-configurable T. The current FIFO policy sorts by creation time, and LRU sorts by last_used with creation time breaking ties. Neither applies this decay.
Keep every storage limit
Given budget B = (M_s, M_b, M_t) where M_s = max slots, M_b = max bytes, M_t = max tokens:
\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} 1 \leq M_s, \quad \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} |r|_b \leq M_b, \quad \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} |r|_t \leq M_t

Code: See MemoryBudget.
Choose which records to remove
Select records to prune by solving:
\arg\min_{S \subseteq \mathcal{R}} \sum_{r \in S} U(r) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{r \in S} |r|_b \geq \delta

where \delta = overflow amount to free.
This is a knapsack-style optimization and is NP-hard in general. The Python UtilityPolicy selects the kernel's greedy utility-per-cost heuristic. The Rust UtilityPolicy selects its raw-utility rule instead. Neither policy solves the general optimization problem, and sharing the kernel does not make those two rankings equivalent.
Code: See RetentionPolicy and Rust implementation in kernel/src/policies.rs.

The full foundational formalism is in MONAD’s “Information-theoretic bounds” section.

Resources	R = (M, B, \varepsilon)	ResourceVector

Record Channel	\mathcal{C}_R : \mathcal{M}_s \to \Delta(\mathcal{Y}_R)	RecordChannel	
Recorded influence pairs	Supplied values and thresholds, interpreted against \preceq_R	DirectInfluenceRecords	
Utility	U(r)	UtilityEstimate	
Budget	B = (M_s, M_b, M_t)	MemoryBudget

Mathematical Core
Home | Prev: Overview | Next: Operational Causality
Use this chapter to interpret influence diagnostics, compare retention policies or design a test under resource limits. For method signatures and data types, see the core Python reference.
Where the foundations live
MONAD owns the state space and measure-preserving evolution, invariant fine-grained entropy, observer interface, reliable-record criterion, detectable influence and information bounds. Its formal reference locates the definitions and proofs; its kernel reference maps Rust types to those declarations or names a missing counterpart. Neither a resolved reference nor Reckon’s handwritten Python interfaces establishes implementation conformance. This chapter explains what a Reckon experiment must supply and what its diagnostics can report; the full paper remains private pending publication.
Test influence under resource limits
Declare the comparison
To investigate influence from A to B, declare the resources R, an allowed protocol and the two preparation operations that set A to zero or one. Record which outcome y you observe for B, its two induced probability laws P_0 and P_1, the divergence D (for example total variation, KL divergence or Hellinger distance) and the detection threshold \eta. The distributional comparison is:
D(P_1, P_0) \geq \eta

To interpret this comparison under MONAD’s influence relation, establish the protocol’s reliable-record conditions for A and B as well. Reliability means repeatable discrimination within the declared trial and error limits, not persistence. A laboratory experiment may instead measure another downstream observable; specify that target and its interpretation rather than assuming it satisfies the reliable-record criterion for B.
MONAD's intervention notation selects allowed preparation operations that set A to zero or one. Those operations can also change other properties, so a detected difference establishes influence of the chosen intervention pair; isolating A's contribution needs additional assumptions or interventions matched outside A. This is not automatically the mechanism-replacement intervention of a structural causal model. The formal profile owns that distinction; a laboratory comparison must declare which operations it actually runs.
The observation model matters too. MONAD’s profile uses deterministic measurable coarse-graining followed by a separate noisy record channel. A stochastic coarse-graining would need its own induced-distribution definitions for fibers and events; the laboratory’s abstract channel interfaces do not establish that generalization.
Code: See CausalRelation and DirectInfluenceRecords.
Current recorded-pair diagnostic
DirectInfluenceRecords stores supplied distinguishability values and thresholds. causes() compares each stored pair against its threshold; check_transitivity() scans the resulting decisions. It does not estimate the pair values or run significance tests.
Use the recorded thresholds to interpret the scan. The report echoes alpha and multiple_testing_correction as metadata. Passing either setting leaves the pair decisions unchanged.
Code: See DirectInfluenceRecords.check_transitivity() for the recorded-pair scan.
These illustrative values produce one eligible path whose endpoint falls below its threshold. They exercise the recorded-pair scan; they are not measurements from an experiment:
from reckon.core.causality import DirectInfluenceRecords
from reckon.core.resources import ResourceVector

pairs = DirectInfluenceRecords(ResourceVector(memory_slots=3))
pairs.add_relation("A", "B", distinguishability=0.5, threshold=0.1)
pairs.add_relation("B", "C", distinguishability=0.5, threshold=0.1)
pairs.add_relation("A", "C", distinguishability=0.08, threshold=0.1)
report = pairs.check_transitivity(alpha=0.05)
print(f"Violation rate: {report.violation_rate:.2%}")
print(f"Violations: {len(report.violations)}/{report.total_triples_tested}")

The report contains one tested path and one below-threshold endpoint:
{
  "violations": [
    {
      "triple": ["A", "B", "C"],
      "a_b_detected": true,
      "b_c_detected": true,
      "a_c_detected": false,
      "a_b_distinguishability": 0.5,
      "b_c_distinguishability": 0.5,
      "a_c_distinguishability": 0.08,
      "a_c_threshold": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "violation_rate": 1.0,
  "total_triples_tested": 1,
  "alpha": 0.05,
  "multiple_testing_correction": "none"
}

Read the diagnostic’s counts
The Python diagnostic scans recorded two-edge paths through three distinct events. When the endpoint pair is missing or has a recorded value below threshold, it reports the path as a diagnostic. A missing pair has a_c_distinguishability: null and inherits the first edge's threshold for display. A tested pair below threshold carries its own value and threshold. causes() returns false in both cases. Use get_relation() to tell them apart. Both count toward violation_rate, whose denominator counts the eligible recorded paths. A two-event cycle alone produces a zero rate with no eligible paths.
Interpret the recorded pairs
MONAD’s influence relation, written \preceq_R in this manual, is resource-monotone when larger budgets admit every smaller-budget protocol, but is neither reflexive nor transitive in general. The formal reference owns those results. When effects cancel along a path works through exact cancellation and a reliable channel whose total variation of 0.6 falls below a detection threshold of 0.9.
For Reckon, the consequences are concrete: DirectInfluenceRecords stores supplied pairs without assuming closure, and its current diagnostic does not test reflexivity. A missing A-to-C detection after detecting A-to-B and B-to-C need not be sampling error; the population relation itself can fail to compose. Finite samples add further uncertainty, and a larger resource budget need not produce more detected edges in the empirical graph, especially near the noise floor. Keep the population statement separate from that estimate.
Closure remains explicit
The library does not infer transitive closure from recorded pairs.
If downstream logic requires closure, it must be computed explicitly with an associated cost and uncertainty model. Closure computation is still planned. The relationship graph describes how the view filters snapshot edges and handles separately supplied edges.
Planned closure modes (not yet implemented in the library):
Mode	Description	Trade-off	
Optimistic	Assume transitivity holds	Dangerous, low compute	
Verified	Require direct evidence for implied edges	Expensive, high confidence	
Probabilistic	Propagate posterior confidence along paths	Medium compute, uncertainty-aware	
Code: See TransitivityReport for violation reports.
Proposed empirical estimator
The estimator described here is a research proposal for pairwise tests. Today, DirectInfluenceRecords takes pair values you have already measured and compares them with their thresholds. You run the interventions and calculate significance separately.
Theoretical relation and proposed estimator
The population relation describes detectability under the model. A finite experiment can only estimate it:
Relation	Notation	Meaning	
Theoretical	\preceq_R	Population/"true" detectability under resources R	
Empirical	\hat{\preceq}_{R,n,\alpha,M}	Estimated from data with parameters below	
The empirical estimator is indexed by:
n = samples/episodes per pairwise test
\alpha = per-test significance level (default: 0.05)
M = number of hypotheses tested (for multiple testing)
Plus implicit noise model and task stochasticity
Pairwise significance does not imply transitivity
The proposed empirical estimate \hat{\preceq}_{R,n,\alpha,M} adds noise and thresholds to the population relation. Detecting A→B and B→C at p < \alpha does not imply A→C is detectable at p < \alpha.
Why empirical pairs can fail to compose
Whether a finite test detects an effect depends on its size, the variance and the number of samples.
On top of the failures the relation itself allows, the empirical estimator can violate transitivity because of:
Stochasticity / finite n: Limited samples increase false negative rate
Type I errors (false edges): Some detected edges are spurious
Type II errors (missing edges): Some true edges fail detection
Effect size dilution: Causal effects often attenuate along paths (A \to B \to C weaker than A \to B or B \to C)
Selection bias: "We only tested some triples", so coverage is incomplete
Multiple testing inflation: Testing M hypotheses without correction inflates false positives
Multiple testing
The per-test \alpha = 0.05 is a per-comparison error rate.
When testing M hypotheses, options include:
Method	Control	Formula	Notes	
None	Per-test	\alpha	Fast, high false positive rate	
Bonferroni	FWER	\alpha / M	Conservative, low power	
Holm	FWER	Sequential adjustment	Less conservative than Bonferroni	
Benjamini-Hochberg	FDR	Ranks p-values	Controls expected false discovery rate	
q-values	Estimated FDR or positive FDR at rejection thresholds	Minimum estimated rate over thresholds including the test	A thresholded-set quantity, not the test's posterior null probability	
A q-value describes the estimated false-discovery rate associated with calling a test significant. Local FDR instead estimates the probability that the test's null hypothesis is true, conditional on its observed statistic under the selected model. The maintained qvalue package distinguishes these two outputs. Neither is a causal probability, and neither is computed by the recorded-pair diagnostic.
Planned options: FWER control (Bonferroni/Holm), FDR control (Benjamini-Hochberg), q-values.
Note

Correction does not establish transitivity. Correcting the error rate across tests does not make detected paths compose. The result is still a graph of pairwise decisions.
Save a reproducible report
The scan orders event identifiers by Unicode code point, so the resulting triples have the same order across insertion orders and Python hash seeds. to_json(indent=2) gives a readable report. For a saved identity, use to_canonical_json() and hash its UTF-8 bytes without adding a newline:
import hashlib

artifact = report.to_canonical_json().encode("utf-8")
digest = hashlib.sha256(artifact).hexdigest()

The canonical profile adds schema_version: "reckon.transitivity-report/v1" to the report. It sorts violations by the event triple, breaks repeated-triple ties by the complete encoded entry and retains duplicate entries. Object keys sort lexically; Python JSON uses compact separators, ASCII string escapes and its finite-number spelling. Event identifiers keep their exact Unicode sequences, and numeric representations such as 1 and 1.0 remain distinct. NaN and either infinity are refused. Serialization leaves the original report unchanged.
The digest covers the report's supplied fields, including significance and correction metadata. Those labels still do not change the pair decisions or perform statistical correction. Keep the source records, resource configuration and implementation revision with the artifact when another run must reproduce it. Missing endpoint values remain null, distinct from a measured zero or a value below threshold.
Use scores to choose what survives
Read the stored signals
Each record r carries:
utility.value: accumulated utility estimate (updated via update_score())
utility.last_used: timestep of last access
causal_score.ablation_delta: performance change when record removed (MEASURED)
causal_score.counterfactual_delta: change under hypothetical intervention (MEASURED)
causal_score.influence_proxy: heuristic proxy (e.g., gradient magnitude) (PROXY)
These labels describe the intended source of each score. A populated field alone does not establish that its intervention ran or was valid; keep the experiment with the value and follow the proxy-only reporting rule.
Policy Score for Retention
When the Python memory manager prunes, it calls its configured retention policy. EvidencePerBytePolicy prefers the non-negative part of an ablation result, then the non-negative part of a counterfactual result, then a separate proxy. Deltas use outcome with the record minus outcome without it: a negative value means removal helped, so that effect gives zero retention credit. The stored measurement keeps its sign:
C_m(r) = \begin{cases}
\max(\Delta_a, 0) & \text{if ablation measured} \\
\max(\Delta_c, 0) & \text{else if counterfactual measured} \\
\bot & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}

C_p(r) = |\phi|

Combined score:
S(r) = (1 - \alpha) \cdot U(r) + \alpha \cdot C(r)

where:
C_m(r) = beneficial part of the measured attribution (from ablation_delta or counterfactual_delta)
C_p(r) = proxy magnitude (from influence_proxy)
C(r) = C_m(r) if defined, else C_p(r) as fallback. If the record has neither a measured value nor a proxy, the causal term is zero.
A negative or zero measured result remains the selected measured branch; it does not fall through to a positive proxy. The proxy is separately labelled and is not evidence of benefit.
U(r) = utility estimate
\alpha = evidence weight (0-1)
To free bytes, slots and tokens, the Python policy removes the records with the lowest combined score divided by max(record.cost.bytes, 1) first.
Design note: The Python policy selects the kernel's EvidencePerByte rule above. The Rust WeightedEvidencePolicy wrapper selects WeightedEvidence, which adds non-negative ablation and counterfactual contributions and the absolute proxy with weights 1, 0.5 and 0.25, then mixes that sum with utility. It ranks the combined score without dividing by cost. Both rules live in the kernel, and they remain different policies; a comparison must name the rule and revision it uses.
The store’s priority index is a third ranking: utility plus 0.5[\max(\Delta_a, 0) + \max(\Delta_c, 0)], with missing measurements contributing zero. The daemon calls the same function for capacity pruning. It uses neither the proxy nor cost division. NaN measurements contribute zero; a NaN total has the lowest priority. Both stores break equal scores by record ID.
Code: Kernel retention rules implement the rankings and byte/slot selection; Python policy objects select the laboratory rules.
To interpret ablation_delta or counterfactual_delta, report what you changed, what you compared, how you identified the effect, the controls and the uncertainty. Keep proxy scores separate. See evaluation metrics for what each method tests.

Its interpretation as a reliable coding rate requires a declared channel class, repeated-use model, block code, error criterion and block-cost constraint, with converse and achievability results under those assumptions. body:
How the memory manager works

Your task decides what to remember and when to use it. Reckon's memory manager keeps those records within an allowance and chooses which ones to remove when another write needs room. This guide follows those decisions, then explains the checks and storage details you need when integrating or extending the manager.

Follow a cue through memory
In the delayed-cue example, the task writes the location of a key, retrieves it later and reports an outcome. retrieve() remembers which records it returned in an episode context. observe() shares credit among those records and updates their utility through a moving average. The task supplies the outcome and the decisions that led to it.
Writing another record may force a choice. With room for two records, a third admissible write needs to remove at least one of the first two. FIFO removes the oldest; a utility policy removes records with the lowest utility per byte. The same task can therefore keep different memories under the same allowance. A score affects that choice only when the retention policy uses it.
The manager retains native record values through PyO3, with the caller’s payload and mutable containers kept by reference. Rust also keeps fixed admission costs, priorities and the event buffer. Writes and reads also have separate operation-rate allowances. Before a write removes anything, the manager checks those limits and whether the new record can fit at all. If you limit tokens, your task must supply its token count. The budget rules explain refusals and what remains unchanged.

What a record carries
MemoryRecord
The payload holds the observation itself, raw or compressed. Its ID lets you retrieve that particular record; its step and episode identify when it was written. Tags describe its role, such as a cue, reward, trace or representation. Origin fields keep the creating operation, input record IDs and content hash.
The record also carries its cost in bytes, tokens and slots, its utility estimate and uncertainty, and when it was last used. Optional fields hold later ablation, counterfactual or proxy scores. Those stored signals are inputs to a policy: the mathematical core explains how a policy turns them into a ranking.
MemoryBudget
Use max_slots to limit the number of records, max_bytes to limit their byte cost and max_tokens when your task counts tokens. The manager enforces all active storage limits together. Reads and writes can also have independent max_read_ops_per_window and max_write_ops_per_window allowances over logical steps. Even an empty read counts as a successful call. The rate-limit rules explain expiry, calls in progress, failures and setting changes; the token rules keep a missing count distinct from zero.
A record larger than its byte or token allowance is refused before existing records or logs change. For an admissible write, the selected policy frees enough bytes, slots and tokens before insertion. See the Python memory implementation.
Episode boundaries
set_episode(id, reset_memory=False) carries records, learned scores, retained events and operation windows into the next episode. set_step() remains relative to that episode; the manager offsets it beyond the previous episode’s last step so FIFO and LRU can compare old and new records correctly. With operation limits enabled, the timeline cannot move backwards. An explicit reset clears records, scores, the event buffer, operation windows and the time offset. The default API call still resets; callers choose carry explicitly. Task or environment state has its own lifetime.

Choose what to keep
Pass a RetentionPolicy when creating the manager; the default is FIFOPolicy. FIFO removes the oldest records, while LRU removes those least recently accessed. Other built-in choices use utility per byte, caller-supplied importance, measured effects, a seeded random order or diversity of payload types. Choose the comparison that answers your task's question rather than assuming the more elaborate rule will do better.
The kernel follows the chosen removal order until enough bytes, slots and tokens are freed. Python supplies the random policy's seeded order. Before removing anything, the manager checks that the selection contains distinct existing records and frees enough space. The diversity rule protects a minimum number of each payload type while capacity permits. The wider design also considers avoiding redundancy in replay; protecting type counts alone does not implement that behaviour.
Ask for a record
To retrieve a known cue, pass its record_ids. To search the retained records, filter by tags, payload_type or min_utility; matches are ordered by utility and capped by limit. The memory module leads to the current API.
The intended retrieval design is broader: symbolic keys, similarity search and reads triggered by uncertainty or prediction error. The manager currently supports explicit IDs and the filters above. Your task must supply similarity search or decide when uncertainty warrants a read.

Why compare utility with cost?
Suppose each candidate record at time t has an estimated value v_i and a resource cost c_i. We want a subset whose total value ∑ v_i is as large as possible while its total cost stays within C_max. This is the knapsack view of retention; value here estimates downstream utility or influence, and cost describes the resource being limited.
New observations arrive before all their consequences are known. An online approximation is to remove the lowest utility per unit of cost when the allowance fills. Python's utility policy uses bytes as that cost, even when a slot or token limit triggers removal. It is a greedy rule to compare against the alternatives, rather than a guarantee of the best possible retained set.

Use measured effects in a retention decision
An outcome update shares credit among retrieved records. To ask what difference a particular record made, you need another experiment. An ablation removes it and measures the change in performance; a counterfactual probe replaces it with an alternative. The manager can also accept an influence proxy, such as a gradient or TD-error signal, when no such measurement is available.
Keep the comparison, assumptions, controls and uncertainty with a measured delta before interpreting it causally. A proxy supplies a heuristic for retention. The manager stores these inputs and uses the selected rule; the experiment has to justify what each input means.
Python's EvidencePerBytePolicy mixes utility with an effect score and divides by byte cost, using the kernel's EvidencePerByte rule. For the effect score, it takes the positive part of an ablation measurement if present, otherwise the positive part of a counterfactual measurement, otherwise the proxy magnitude. A harmful or zero measurement gives zero effect credit; it does not fall through to the proxy. The mathematical core gives the formulas and distinguishes this rule from Rust's weighted aggregation and the store's priority index.

Why the policy uses the first available score
The fallback lets the policy work with a proxy alone. Choosing that fallback is a product choice, not a theoretical claim about causality. Downstream reports must flag proxy-only records so a heuristic cannot appear to be an intervention result. To decide whether a score supports a causal claim, check how the caller obtained it. Keep the measurement’s context with its evaluation or graph.
An alternative policy could combine scores or keep separate tiers. Changing that rule changes the retention algorithm and needs its own comparison.

Keep the history needed to explain a run
The current Python manager emits Rust logger events for these operations:
Successful writes: record ID and the current total stored bytes in bytes_after.
Reads: the returned hit IDs in details, not the original query predicates.
Prunes: record ID and the emitted reason label.
Supported score updates on an existing record: record ID, score type, old/new values and signal source.
Caution

Collect the run before events are lost. These minimal operation events do not preserve full record payloads, tags, utility snapshots or query context, and a score-update event is not pair-bound graph evidence. The manager's in-memory ring holds 10,000 events and can overwrite older entries; get_event_log() drains the retained buffer. Saving a complete run requires explicit collection and export, as described in Reproducibility.
The kernel's future storage and performance choices describe the conditions for a durable laboratory store and replay, batch numerics, shared arena mechanics and a Linux I/O adapter.
Integrate the Python manager
The Rust laboratory model owns record fields and their TypeScript and JSON Schema descriptions. The public Python adapters preserve mutable references, dataclass helpers, copying and pickling around native fields. Resource configuration remains a Python dataclass. Protocol declarations for records, budgets, influence and events define separate historical wire models; check their adapters when changing an interface.
A write encodes the payload for admission, checks the budget, selects and verifies removals, retains the native object with its admission costs, and logs the operation before returning its record ID. A query filters those live objects and sorts matches by utility; explicit IDs retain caller order. After applying the limit, a read updates access statistics through the native store, logs the operation and returns the records. Python filtering scans the retained objects, so a workload needing indexed queries requires its own implementation and measurements.
All policies implement select_for_pruning(records, overflow_bytes, overflow_slots=0, overflow_tokens=0). Custom policies must accept the trailing token pressure and satisfy all three dimensions; the manager rejects an insufficient selection before removal.
These Python objects select rules implemented in the Rust kernel. Ranking inputs cross the binding; payloads stay with the caller. The kernel handles byte, slot and token pressure, preserves input order for equal keys and rejects invalid ranking inputs before the manager prunes or logs. The random arm retains Python's seeded permutation and passes that order to the kernel.
The laboratory’s explicit measured arm obtains deltas through paired trials from independent copies of retained memory before pruning. Each pair starts fresh task episodes under a declared reference policy, removing the target in one arm. Its point estimate enters the existing measured-effect-per-byte ranking. The probe configuration and cost report distinguish this experiment from continuing the live task, and preserve signed estimates, uncertainty and the full probe cost rather than turning significance into a pass mark.
Ordinary reads follow the query path described above. During before_read(callback), the callback sees the limited candidate list before access counts, logging or context tracking. It may prune a candidate; the query then resolves again so the returned IDs and later credit describe the changed memory. The scope holds the manager lock, survives episode resets and removes its callback after success or failure. Nested scopes are refused, and callbacks must not initiate another read. The evaluator uses this boundary for verified ablation.
For shaped credit, observe() records observe:shaped:softplus:scale=1.0 as the signal source on each score update. A bare observe:shaped in an older trace needs the run's source revision to identify its formula.
Credit weights and the utility update come from the shared kernel implementation, also called by the daemon. The manager validates every proposed utility update before changing either store. ABLATION gives measured non-positive effects zero credit, including an all-non-positive set; equal fallback is reserved for a set with no measurements.
Utility updates synchronize the native priority index; attribution and proxy updates remain in the live native records. Writes and prunes must keep both representations aligned. Tasks own the decisions and outcomes that drive these operations, and compute their metrics from the relevant task state. The kernel guide explains storage mechanics, while the architecture guide owns performance targets; those targets are not measured guarantees.
Thread Safety
Manager operations use a reentrant RLock. retrieve() also updates a caller-supplied or current episode context outside the locked read() call. Returned MemoryRecord objects are mutable references, not isolated snapshots. A lock around storage does not make the whole context, caller mutation and observation sequence atomic.
Key points:
The lock is reentrant to support nested method calls (e.g., write() calling _enforce_budget_combined())
Internal state (_records, _store, _logger) should not be accessed directly without holding the lock
Callers coordinate context lifetime and mutation of returned records separately; copy a returned record if you need a stable snapshot
JSON Encoding
The ReckonJSONEncoder class handles serialization of complex types:
from reckon.memory.manager import ReckonJSONEncoder
import json

# Serialize payload with custom encoder
json.dumps(complex_payload, cls=ReckonJSONEncoder)

Supported types:
datetime: Converted to ISO format string
Dataclasses: Converted to dict via asdict()
Objects with __dict__: Converted to their __dict__
NumPy arrays: Converted to list via tolist()
Numeric Safety
The memory module includes several safeguards for numeric stability:
Safeguard	Location	Purpose	
MAX_DELTA = 1000.0	UtilityEstimate.update_utility()	Clamps that helper's additive delta	
NORMALIZATION_THRESHOLD = 1e6	UtilityEstimate.update_utility()	Returns a flag when the resulting magnitude exceeds the threshold; does not normalize it

indexed.body:
How the memory manager works

Your task decides what to remember and when to use it. Reckon's memory manager keeps those records within an allowance and chooses which ones to remove when another write needs room. This guide follows those decisions, then explains the checks and storage details you need when integrating or extending the manager.

Follow a cue through memory
In the delayed-cue example, the task writes the location of a key, retrieves it later and reports an outcome. retrieve() remembers which records it returned in an episode context. observe() shares credit among those records and updates their utility through a moving average. The task supplies the outcome and the decisions that led to it.
Writing another record may force a choice. With room for two records, a third admissible write needs to remove at least one of the first two. FIFO removes the oldest; a utility policy removes records with the lowest utility per byte. The same task can therefore keep different memories under the same allowance. A score affects that choice only when the retention policy uses it.
The manager retains native record values through PyO3, with the caller’s payload and mutable containers kept by reference. Rust also keeps fixed admission costs, priorities and the event buffer. Writes and reads also have separate operation-rate allowances. Before a write removes anything, the manager checks those limits and whether the new record can fit at all. If you limit tokens, your task must supply its token count. The budget rules explain refusals and what remains unchanged.

What a record carries
MemoryRecord
The payload holds the observation itself, raw or compressed. Its ID lets you retrieve that particular record; its step and episode identify when it was written. Tags describe its role, such as a cue, reward, trace or representation. Origin fields keep the creating operation, input record IDs and content hash.
The record also carries its cost in bytes, tokens and slots, its utility estimate and uncertainty, and when it was last used. Optional fields hold later ablation, counterfactual or proxy scores. Those stored signals are inputs to a policy: the mathematical core explains how a policy turns them into a ranking.
MemoryBudget
Use max_slots to limit the number of records, max_bytes to limit their byte cost and max_tokens when your task counts tokens. The manager enforces all active storage limits together. Reads and writes can also have independent max_read_ops_per_window and max_write_ops_per_window allowances over logical steps. Even an empty read counts as a successful call. The rate-limit rules explain expiry, calls in progress, failures and setting changes; the token rules keep a missing count distinct from zero.
A record larger than its byte or token allowance is refused before existing records or logs change. For an admissible write, the selected policy frees enough bytes, slots and tokens before insertion. See the Python memory implementation.
Episode boundaries
set_episode(id, reset_memory=False) carries records, learned scores, retained events and operation windows into the next episode. set_step() remains relative to that episode; the manager offsets it beyond the previous episode’s last step so FIFO and LRU can compare old and new records correctly. With operation limits enabled, the timeline cannot move backwards. An explicit reset clears records, scores, the event buffer, operation windows and the time offset. The default API call still resets; callers choose carry explicitly. Task or environment state has its own lifetime.

Choose what to keep
Pass a RetentionPolicy when creating the manager; the default is FIFOPolicy. FIFO removes the oldest records, while LRU removes those least recently accessed. Other built-in choices use utility per byte, caller-supplied importance, measured effects, a seeded random order or diversity of payload types. Choose the comparison that answers your task's question rather than assuming the more elaborate rule will do better.
The kernel follows the chosen removal order until enough bytes, slots and tokens are freed. Python supplies the random policy's seeded order. Before removing anything, the manager checks that the selection contains distinct existing records and frees enough space. The diversity rule protects a minimum number of each payload type while capacity permits. The wider design also considers avoiding redundancy in replay; protecting type counts alone does not implement that behaviour.
Ask for a record
To retrieve a known cue, pass its record_ids. To search the retained records, filter by tags, payload_type or min_utility; matches are ordered by utility and capped by limit. The memory module leads to the current API.
The intended retrieval design is broader: symbolic keys, similarity search and reads triggered by uncertainty or prediction error. The manager currently supports explicit IDs and the filters above. Your task must supply similarity search or decide when uncertainty warrants a read.

Why compare utility with cost?
Suppose each candidate record at time t has an estimated value v_i and a resource cost c_i. We want a subset whose total value ∑ v_i is as large as possible while its total cost stays within C_max. This is the knapsack view of retention; value here estimates downstream utility or influence, and cost describes the resource being limited.
New observations arrive before all their consequences are known. An online approximation is to remove the lowest utility per unit of cost when the allowance fills. Python's utility policy uses bytes as that cost, even when a slot or token limit triggers removal. It is a greedy rule to compare against the alternatives, rather than a guarantee of the best possible retained set.

Use measured effects in a retention decision
An outcome update shares credit among retrieved records. To ask what difference a particular record made, you need another experiment. An ablation removes it and measures the change in performance; a counterfactual probe replaces it with an alternative. The manager can also accept an influence proxy, such as a gradient or TD-error signal, when no such measurement is available.
Keep the comparison, assumptions, controls and uncertainty with a measured delta before interpreting it causally. A proxy supplies a heuristic for retention. The manager stores these inputs and uses the selected rule; the experiment has to justify what each input means.
Python's EvidencePerBytePolicy mixes utility with an effect score and divides by byte cost, using the kernel's EvidencePerByte rule. For the effect score, it takes the positive part of an ablation measurement if present, otherwise the positive part of a counterfactual measurement, otherwise the proxy magnitude. A harmful or zero measurement gives zero effect credit; it does not fall through to the proxy. The mathematical core gives the formulas and distinguishes this rule from Rust's weighted aggregation and the store's priority index.

Why the policy uses the first available score
The fallback lets the policy work with a proxy alone. Choosing that fallback is a product choice, not a theoretical claim about causality. Downstream reports must flag proxy-only records so a heuristic cannot appear to be an intervention result. To decide whether a score supports a causal claim, check how the caller obtained it. Keep the measurement’s context with its evaluation or graph.
An alternative policy could combine scores or keep separate tiers. Changing that rule changes the retention algorithm and needs its own comparison.

Keep the history needed to explain a run
The current Python manager emits Rust logger events for these operations:
Successful writes: record ID and the current total stored bytes in bytes_after.
Reads: the returned hit IDs in details, not the original query predicates.
Prunes: record ID and the emitted reason label.
Supported score updates on an existing record: record ID, score type, old/new values and signal source.
Caution

Collect the run before events are lost. These minimal operation events do not preserve full record payloads, tags, utility snapshots or query context, and a score-update event is not pair-bound graph evidence. The manager's in-memory ring holds 10,000 events and can overwrite older entries; get_event_log() drains the retained buffer. Saving a complete run requires explicit collection and export, as described in Reproducibility.
The kernel's future storage and performance choices describe the conditions for a durable laboratory store and replay, batch numerics, shared arena mechanics and a Linux I/O adapter.

Protocol declarations for records, budgets, influence and events define separate historical wire models; check their adapters when changing an interface.

A query filters those live objects and sorts matches by utility; explicit IDs retain caller order. It may prune a candidate; the query then resolves again so the returned IDs and later credit describe the changed memory. The evaluator uses this boundary for verified ablation.
For shaped credit, observe() records observe:shaped:softplus:scale=1.0 as the signal source on each score update. A bare observe:shaped in an older trace needs the run's source revision to identify its formula.
Credit weights and the utility update come from the shared kernel implementation, also called by the daemon. The manager validates every proposed utility update before changing either store. ABLATION gives measured non-positive effects zero credit, including an all-non-positive set; equal fallback is reserved for a set with no measurements.
Utility updates synchronize the native priority index; attribution and proxy updates remain in the live native records. Writes and prunes must keep both representations aligned. Tasks own the decisions and outcomes that drive these operations, and compute their metrics from the relevant task state. The kernel guide explains storage mechanics, while the architecture guide owns performance targets; those targets are not measured guarantees.
Thread Safety
Manager operations use a reentrant RLock. retrieve() also updates a caller-supplied or current episode context outside the locked read() call. Returned MemoryRecord objects are mutable references, not isolated snapshots. A lock around storage does not make the whole context, caller mutation and observation sequence atomic.
Key points:
The lock is reentrant to support nested method calls (e.g., write() calling _enforce_budget_combined())
Internal state (_records, _store, _logger) should not be accessed directly without holding the lock
Callers coordinate context lifetime and mutation of returned records separately; copy a returned record if you need a stable snapshot
JSON Encoding
The ReckonJSONEncoder class handles serialization of complex types:
from reckon.memory.manager import ReckonJSONEncoder
import json

# Serialize payload with custom encoder
json.dumps(complex_payload, cls=ReckonJSONEncoder)

Supported types:
datetime: Converted to ISO format string
Dataclasses: Converted to dict via asdict()
Objects with __dict__: Converted to their __dict__
NumPy arrays: Converted to list via tolist()
