body:
Core API¶



Resources¶


Resource vectors and memory budgets.


Defines the multi-dimensional resource constraints under which agents operate.




class reckon.core.resources.ResourceVector(memory_slots=None, memory_bytes=None, memory_tokens=None, bandwidth=None, compute=None, noise_floor=0.0)¶



A multi-dimensional resource constraint vector.



Variables:





memory_slots (int | None) – Maximum number of memory slots




memory_bytes (int | None) – Maximum memory in bytes




memory_tokens (int | None) – Maximum memory in tokens




bandwidth (float | None) – Maximum bandwidth (ops/step)




compute (float | None) – Maximum compute per step




noise_floor (float) – Irreducible noise level






Parameters:





memory_slots (int | None)




memory_bytes (int | None)




memory_tokens (int | None)




bandwidth (float | None)




compute (float | None)




noise_floor (float)









is_satisfied(usage)¶



Compare supplied slot, byte and token usage with the supplied limits.


A dimension is skipped when either value is None. Bandwidth, compute
and noise are not checked; this is not the full formal protocol order.



Parameters:



usage (ResourceVector)




Return type:



bool













class reckon.core.resources.MemoryBudget(max_slots=100, max_bytes=None, max_tokens=None, max_write_ops_per_window=None, max_read_ops_per_window=None, window_size=100)¶



Memory-specific budget configuration for the Causal Memory Manager.



Variables:





max_slots (int) – Maximum number of records to store




max_bytes (int | None) – Maximum total bytes




max_tokens (int | None) – Maximum total tokens




max_write_ops_per_window (int | None) – Write rate limit




max_read_ops_per_window (int | None) – Read rate limit




window_size (int) – Window size for rate limiting (in steps)






Parameters:





max_slots (int)




max_bytes (int | None)




max_tokens (int | None)




max_write_ops_per_window (int | None)




max_read_ops_per_window (int | None)




window_size (int)









to_resource_vector()¶



Copy slot, byte and token limits, without constructing a formal protocol budget.



Return type:



ResourceVector













Channels¶


Coarse-graining and record channels.


Defines the observer interface through which agents interact with microstates.




class reckon.core.channels.CoarseGraining¶



Abstract interface for projecting a microstate to a macrostate at scale s.


Implement project() and the corresponding fiber measure for the chosen
state spaces. MONAD’s model uses a deterministic measurable projection
followed by a separate noisy record channel; this interface does not
verify those mathematical assumptions.




abstract property scale: float¶



The scale parameter s for this coarse-graining.







abstractmethod project(microstate)¶



Project a microstate to a macrostate.



Parameters:



microstate (MicroState)




Return type:



MacroState










abstractmethod fiber_measure(macrostate)¶



Compute μ(Γ_m) - the measure of the fiber/preimage.


Used for Boltzmann entropy: S_B(m) = k log μ(Γ_m)



Parameters:



macrostate (MacroState)




Return type:



float













class reckon.core.channels.RecordChannel¶



Abstract record channel: M_s -> Δ(Y_R)


A noisy storage/measurement channel that maps observations
to stored records under resource constraints.




abstractmethod encode(observation)¶



Encode an observation into a record.



Parameters:



observation (MacroState)




Return type:



Record










abstractmethod decode(record)¶



Decode a record back to an observation (possibly lossy).



Parameters:



record (Record)




Return type:



MacroState










abstractmethod noise_level()¶



Return the effective noise level ε_noise of this channel.



Return type:



float










abstractmethod cost(record)¶



Return the resource cost (e.g., bytes) of storing this record.



Parameters:



record (Record)




Return type:



int













Recorded influence¶


Resource-indexed direct influence between event pairs.


The empirical relation records thresholded pairwise observations under
declared resource constraints. Detectable influence from A to B and
from B to C does not establish detectable influence from A to C.




class reckon.core.causality.DistinguishabilityMeasure(*values)¶



Measures for detecting causal influence.







class reckon.core.causality.CausalRelation(source, target, resources, distinguishability, measure=DistinguishabilityMeasure.TOTAL_VARIATION, threshold=0.1)¶



Caller-supplied distinguishability for an event pair under resources R.


The stored threshold classifies the supplied value; this object neither
runs an intervention nor validates causal identification assumptions.



Variables:





source (str) – The upstream event A




target (str) – The downstream event B




resources (reckon.core.resources.ResourceVector) – Resource constraints under which relation holds




distinguishability (float) – Measured distinguishability D(P(y|do(A=1)), P(y|do(A=0)))




measure (reckon.core.causality.DistinguishabilityMeasure) – The divergence measure used




threshold (float) – The threshold η for detectability






Parameters:





source (str)




target (str)




resources (ResourceVector)




distinguishability (float)




measure (DistinguishabilityMeasure)




threshold (float)









property is_causal: bool¶



Compare the supplied value with threshold minus EPSILON (1e-9).


Uses epsilon-based comparison to avoid floating-point precision issues.










class reckon.core.causality.DirectInfluenceRecords(resources)¶



Observed direct-influence pairs under a fixed resource vector.


Callers supply distinguishability values and thresholds. This collection
checks those recorded numbers; it does not run interventions or establish

Credit and utility¶


Credit Assignment Policies for observe().

to retrieved records. The credit is used to update utility estimates
which inform retention decisions.

Active weights sum to one within floating-point rounding




Measured non-positive effects can produce an all-zero vector

body:
Memory API¶



Manager¶


Store observations under byte, slot, token and operation-rate allowances.


Python holds full records and queries; the required Rust store maintains
compact records, priorities and a bounded event ring. Store/cache mutations
use a reentrant lock. Returned records remain mutable references, and callers
coordinate episode contexts and retrieval/observation sequences separately.
Storage locking does not make that complete sequence atomic.


Use retrieve() to track returned IDs for observe(), or read() for a query

indexed.body:
Memory API¶



Manager¶


Store observations under byte, slot, token and operation-rate allowances.


Python holds full records and queries; the required Rust store maintains
compact records, priorities and a bounded event ring. Store/cache mutations
use a reentrant lock. Returned records remain mutable references, and callers
coordinate episode contexts and retrieval/observation sequences separately.
Storage locking does not make that complete sequence atomic.


Use retrieve() to track returned IDs for observe(), or read() for a query
without context tracking. Preserve events before draining or resetting the
finite log; a saved operation alone does not preserve the full record payload.

body:
Reckon core module
Configure resources, implement a channel or inspect supplied influence pairs with these core types. The mathematical framework explains their interpretation. A type or stored threshold alone does not demonstrate record reliability or a causal effect.
The generated core API reads fields, signatures and method documentation from resources, channels, recorded influence, credit and episode-context code. Build it from the selected checkout; keep the explanations below beside the generated reference.
Credit assignment in Python
compute_credit attaches record IDs to weights calculated by the Rust kernel. The same kernel supplies the moving-average update to Python and the daemon. SHAPED normalizes stable softplus weights, with a laboratory default scale of 1.0 and utility 0.5 for a missing record. Empty retrieval and NONE yield no assignment. Non-finite outcomes or invalid weights fail before an observation changes utility; finite negative outcomes use the same weights.
ABLATION normalizes only positive measured ablation deltas. If no record has a measurement, it falls back to equal credit. If measurements exist but none is positive, every weight is zero; a harmful measured effect does not earn fallback credit. The signed measurements remain unchanged. Supply them as ablation_deltas to compute_credit. Python policy values and new observation tags use ablation; serialized assignments use that spelling too. The former CAUSAL member and causal string have no aliases. Existing saved records keep their original labels and source revision. The utility update requires finite inputs, credit in [0, 1], a learning rate in (0, 1] and ordered finite bounds, then clamps its result to those bounds.
Resource and channel boundaries
ResourceVector contains optional slot, byte, token, bandwidth and compute limits plus a noise floor. Its is_satisfied() method checks only slots, bytes and tokens, and only where both compared values are present. It does not enforce bandwidth, compute, noise or MONAD's full protocol order.
Implement CoarseGraining and RecordChannel for your observation and storage model. MONAD uses a deterministic measurable coarse-graining map followed by a noisy record channel. Your implementation must satisfy the assumptions needed by the result you use; the abstract interfaces do not check them.
MemoryBudget.to_resource_vector() copies the slot, byte and token configuration, not a complete formal protocol budget. The memory-manager guide owns write-time admission and operation limits. Resource and relation dataclasses are mutable; copy or serialize a configuration before changing it when a saved result needs its original settings.
Interpret recorded pairs
add_relation() stores the supplied pair values. causes() checks the stored distinguishability against its threshold with the implementation's floating-point tolerance. Run the intervention and check whether it can reliably distinguish the outcomes before passing your measurement to this type. The operational causality chapter owns the stronger protocol criterion; new evidence remains an intervention contrast unless its causal assumptions are established.
Influence can fail to be transitive even in the theoretical relation. MONAD gives a finite counterexample, and measurement noise can create further violations in recorded results. Run DirectInfluenceRecords.check_transitivity() to find eligible stored paths that violate the relation. See docs/03-Math-Core.md for details.
The scan orders triples consistently across insertion orders and Python hash seeds. Use TransitivityReport.to_canonical_json() for the versioned finite-value encoding to save or hash. The serialization contract defines its byte spelling, duplicate handling and preserved distinction between missing and measured endpoint values.
The default stored-pair threshold is 0.1, compared as distinguishability >= threshold - EPSILON with EPSILON = 1e-9. Changing it changes classifications, not the statistical detectability of the upstream experiment. An eligible path with a missing endpoint pair remains untested; the diagnostic never infers an A-to-C effect from A-to-B and B-to-C.
Change resources.py for budget types, channels.py for abstract observation/storage interfaces and causality.py for recorded-pair diagnostics. The kernel credit module owns weights and moving-average updates; Python’s credit.py attaches record IDs and translates policy names. The protocol sources declare separate resource, budget, relation and divergence wire types; those do not make the Python objects generated or enforce the formal model.
Part of the Python library.

body:
Reckon memory module
The memory manager retains full native records through PyO3, keeping the caller’s Python payload and mutable containers by reference. A separate admission projection keeps accounting independent of later edits to those values. It filters reads, tracks retrievals for later credit and chooses existing records to remove when a write overflows its byte, slot or token allowance. Tasks supply observations and outcomes; stored scores do not establish a causal effect.
Start with one cue from retrieval to an outcome. The authored memory-manager guide explains the write/read path, policy choices, intervention boundary, thread safety, numeric updates and diagnostic subscriptions. Its budget section preserves trial-copy semantics, admission validation, caller-supplied tokens and operation windows, including the token-budget example.
The generated memory API reads signatures, fields and method documentation from the code. Build the reference alongside the authored manual; generated files are not source files.
MemoryRecord.provenance holds a RecordOrigin: the creating operation, input record IDs and content hash. The manager accepts source_op and input_ids when writing; the record computes a missing hash. The stored JSON keeps its provenance object and snake-case keys. These origin fields describe how the record was made; the debugger draws their input links as proxies unless separate pair-bound probe evidence is supplied.
Change manager.py for write, retrieval and scoring, record.py for Python record behavior and kernel/src/record.rs for their field model and policies.py for the Python selection of native retention rules. The kernel owns native rankings, store accounting and logging. Python and Rust wrappers may choose different rankings with similar names; compare their actual rules and tie behavior before interpreting results.
Protocol sources define separate wire models: record.proto covers record values, budget.proto retention-policy declarations and events.proto event types. The Rust model owns live laboratory records and their generated TypeScript/JSON Schema; explicit adapters preserve the historical wire meanings. For event capture, use the server's process-local subscription or export/import path; a bounded event ring can lose history, and a saved operation does not contain the whole record.
Part of the Python library.

body:
Reckon Metrics Module
Use these helpers to summarize outcomes, memory costs and the results of record tests. Start with the function that produces your number. Current tasks expose their specific summaries through TaskResult.diagnostics; historical runs retain their original field names. Record summaries name access, caller-labelled retention and stored scores separately; none is an intervention test.
For the intervention design, method limits and cost-accounting example, use Evaluation metrics. For a complete task comparison with saved outputs, use Compare two replay budgets.
Components
PerformanceMetrics
The current PerformanceMetrics fields are:
Metric	Description	
success_rate	Fraction of episodes achieving goal	
mean_return	Average cumulative reward	
mean_regret	Mean supplied regret	
mean_accuracy	Mean supplied classification accuracy	
backward_transfer	Optional field supplied directly by a producer; from_episodes() does not compute it	
forgetting	Mean supplied forgetting value	
from_episodes() averages available fields; it does not reconstruct task histories or invent missing measurements. An empty input produces an empty metrics object. Task runners may construct the fields directly with their own definitions, as described in Tasks and Benchmarks.
MemoryEfficiencyMetrics
MemoryEfficiencyMetrics.from_cmm() uses the following quantities:
Metric	Description	
total_reward_per_byte / mean_return_per_byte	Supplied total reward or mean return, identified by its key, divided by peak recognized write-event bytes; otherwise current stored bytes	
total_reward_per_slot / mean_return_per_slot	The corresponding supplied numerator divided by current occupied slots	
reads_per_write	Recognized read-event count divided by write-event count, with supplied total_reads/total_writes fallbacks; this can exceed one	
useful_reads_per_read	Supplied useful_reads divided by the selected read count; it is not a fraction of distinct stored records	
peak_usage_bytes	Maximum bytes_after among recognized write events; current usage when none are recognized	
average_usage_bytes	Mean bytes_after among recognized write events, or None when none are recognized; not a time-weighted memory average	
The helper calls cmm.get_event_log(), which drains the native buffer. Preserve required events before that consumption. When total_reward is supplied, only the total-reward keys are emitted, including an observed zero. Otherwise supplied mean_return uses its own keys. Missing both inputs leaves all reward ratios absent. Total reward and mean return are not interchangeable.
The helper reads op_type and bytes_after directly from the native logger’s Python drain. The manager supplies total stored bytes after each write. Retained write samples determine the peak and mean; when there are no write samples, current usage supplies only the peak. Supplied task counts remain fallbacks when the retained buffer has no events of that kind. Keep the buffer’s coverage with the result: draining it early or exceeding its capacity can leave only part of a run.
RecordSummaryMetrics
RecordSummaryMetrics.from_cmm() computes usage/oracle quantities from current records and supplied labels or scores:
Metric	Description	
used_record_fraction	Currently stored records with utility.use_count > 0, divided by stored records; a usage proxy requiring no ground truth or ablation	
necessary_cue_retention	Retained IDs from necessary_cues, divided by positive total_cues (defaulting to the number of necessary IDs)	
useful_retrieval_fraction	Supplied useful retrievals divided by retrievals, only when the necessary-cue denominator is not positive	
max_abs_stored_ablation_delta	Largest absolute finite stored ablation_delta	
mean_stored_ablation_delta	Signed mean of finite stored ablation_delta values	
proxy_only_record_ids, proxy_only_record_count	Sorted IDs and count of current records with a proxy but neither delta; see field-presence rules	
The helper does not perform or validate an intervention. Cue retention and the alternative retrieval fraction keep the existing branch rule but emit different names; other fields can be present without either input. Missing denominators or finite scores yield None in the affected branch. Treat usage, labels and supplied deltas as different inputs; the helper does not turn them into a causal conclusion.
The separate CausalRecordEvaluator removes a selected record at the first read where the task would use it. A logical selector can match task-created records across fresh UUIDs. Each arm checks declared configuration; each pair checks the selected state and read position, and removal must succeed. Missing or ambiguous records and unsupported masking/replacement fail explicitly. Reports preserve the signed contrast and actual intervention evidence; aggregate usefulness counts only beneficial significant effects. Set num_episodes to include the reuse being studied, including a later episode for Tutor’s effective hints. See the evaluation protocol for the executable example, single-instance estimand, unadjusted aggregate limits and separate caller-supplied Prober path.
Prober
Prober(run_fn) calls the same seeded runner with and without each requested record. The runner accepts (ablated_ids, seed) and owns setup and intervention timing; a stored baseline list cannot replace the matched run. Permutation, t-test and bootstrap use paired differences. Fixed and adaptive sampling report both arms’ episode counts and measured elapsed time, and unsupported replacement or shuffle requests fail before execution. The evaluation protocol explains adaptive-look correction, the signed results and interval assumptions.
ProbeCostTracker
Probe cost accounting for causal evaluation:
Metric	Description	
probe_episodes_total	Total episodes used for probing	
probe_wall_time_total_ms	Total wall time for all probes	
probe_overhead_ratio	probe_time / (base_time + probe_time)	
probe_episodes_per_record	Average episodes per record evaluated	
Count task episodes and probe episodes together when comparing total compute.
The caller records task calls and episode counts with record_call() and supplies baseline costs. The tracker measures the bracketed time; it does not execute the intervention named by probe_type. Supply any claimed utility improvement separately rather than treating an accounting total as measured benefit.
See Evaluation metrics for details.
Data Flow
Metric Computation Timing
Helpers can be called after task completion, but they are not an automatic pipeline:
Task executes N episodes with CMM
Task accumulates raw results (rewards, successes)
The producer constructs performance fields directly or calls from_episodes()
A caller may invoke the memory helper with the required counts and compatible events; it drains the log
A caller may invoke the usage/oracle helper with its labels and existing record scores
The four current task runners construct their own metrics and combine them into TaskResult; they do not all call these helpers
Event Log Analysis
The memory helper counts native op_type read and write events and samples bytes_after on writes. A read event records one retrieval call, regardless of how many records it returns, so reads divided by writes is an operation ratio and can exceed one; it does not measure retrieval relevance.
Ground Truth Integration
The usage/oracle helper accepts a ground_truth dictionary. Its branches use these keys; the caller owns the labels and their meaning:
ground_truth = {
    "necessary_cues": ["record_id_1", "record_id_2"],
    "total_cues": 5,
    "useful_retrievals": 10,
    "total_retrievals": 15,
}

Integration
With Tasks
BaseTask.run(cmm, num_episodes, seed) returns a TaskResult containing performance (PerformanceMetrics), memory (MemoryEfficiencyMetrics) and diagnostics (a dictionary of named task summaries). Each runner fills these from its own counters; it does not run the record-summary helper or an intervention implicitly.
For example, Key-Door reports successful_stored_key_episode_fraction; Continual reports one_minus_mean_forgetting; Tutor distinguishes mean_episode_effective_hint_read_fraction from pooled_effective_hint_read_fraction. Keep the task producer with the value. The complete task-specific definitions are in Tasks and Benchmarks.
With CLI
Metrics are serialized to JSON via to_dict() methods for CLI output.
Selecting a frontier outcome
make_quality_vs_overhead_points requires the outcome key explicitly. Both that key and the selected cost key must supply finite numbers in every input row. Missing, nonnumeric or nonfinite values fail; an observed zero remains zero. The points retain both metric names. Choose comparable producers and units, with lower cost and higher outcome being better.
The notebook helpers generate_pareto_data(..., y_metric="success_rate") and compute_efficiency_metrics(result, "success_rate") likewise require an explicit outcome. success_rate reads the supplied field; another name reads quality_metrics. An omitted success rate remains absent. No helper silently switches to a different outcome or treats a missing measurement as zero. The efficiency helper's effective_quality multiplies the selected outcome by one minus the probe-episode fraction; that weighting is a calculation, not evidence that probing caused a benefit.
Source map and dependencies
Architecture
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs["Inputs"]
        CMM["CausalMemoryManager\n(state after task)"]
        GT["Ground Truth\n(task-specific)"]
        TaskData["Task Results\n(rewards, etc.)"]
    end

    subgraph Computation["Metric Computation"]
        Perf["PerformanceMetrics"]
        Mem["MemoryEfficiencyMetrics"]
        Summary["RecordSummaryMetrics: separate current-record summary"]
        Diagnostics["Named task diagnostics"]
    end

    subgraph Output["Output"]
        Result["TaskResult"]
    end

    CMM --> Mem
    CMM --> Summary
    GT --> Summary
    TaskData --> Perf
    TaskData --> Mem

    Perf --> Result
    Mem --> Result
    TaskData --> Diagnostics
    Diagnostics --> Result

Module Structure
Trace the byte and slot denominators in memory.py, usage and labelled outcomes in record_summary.py, the intervention loop in evaluator.py, and probe cost accounting in probe_costs.py.

Troubleshooting
Event Log Timing: The memory helper drains the buffer itself. Decide which consumer preserves the events before invoking it; a second drain cannot recover them.
Missing Inputs: Inspect each helper branch. Record usage needs no ground truth; the cue-retention and retrieval-fraction branches name their different inputs. Missing labels do not make every field unavailable.
Reward Interpretation: The selected total-reward or mean-return ratio assumes higher outcome is better. Name a cost transformation explicitly rather than silently changing its sign.
Episode Boundaries: set_episode() resets stores and the logger unless the caller selects reset_memory=False; the built-in runners select carry by default. A helper sees current records and retained events, while caller totals may span several episodes. Align those scopes before dividing them.
Memory Efficiency Denominator: The byte helper uses recognized sampled write-event bytes, or current bytes on fallback. Slot efficiency uses current slots. Neither is automatically a whole-run peak or time average.

Related guides
Parent: Main Module
Evaluation Metrics Spec
Tasks Module
Memory Module

The evaluation protocol explains adaptive-look correction, the signed results and interval assumptions.
ProbeCostTracker
Probe cost accounting for causal evaluation:
Metric	Description	
probe_episodes_total	Total episodes used for probing	
probe_wall_time_total_ms	Total wall time for all probes	
probe_overhead_ratio	probe_time / (base_time + probe_time)	
probe_episodes_per_record	Average episodes per record evaluated	
Count task episodes and probe episodes together when comparing total compute.
The caller records task calls and episode counts with record_call() and supplies baseline costs. The tracker measures the bracketed time; it does not execute the intervention named by probe_type. Supply any claimed utility improvement separately rather than treating an accounting total as measured benefit.
See Evaluation metrics for details.
Data Flow
Metric Computation Timing
Helpers can be called after task completion, but they are not an automatic pipeline:
Task executes N episodes with CMM
Task accumulates raw results (rewards, successes)
The producer constructs performance fields directly or calls from_episodes()
A caller may invoke the memory helper with the required counts and compatible events; it drains the log
A caller may invoke the usage/oracle helper with its labels and existing record scores
The four current task runners construct their own metrics and combine them into TaskResult; they do not all call these helpers
Event Log Analysis
The memory helper counts native op_type read and write events and samples bytes_after on writes. A read event records one retrieval call, regardless of how many records it returns, so reads divided by writes is an operation ratio and can exceed one; it does not measure retrieval relevance.
Ground Truth Integration
The usage/oracle helper accepts a ground_truth dictionary. Its branches use these keys; the caller owns the labels and their meaning:
ground_truth = {
    "necessary_cues": ["record_id_1", "record_id_2"],
    "total_cues": 5,
    "useful_retrievals": 10,
    "total_retrievals": 15,
}

Integration
With Tasks
BaseTask.run(cmm, num_episodes, seed) returns a TaskResult containing performance (PerformanceMetrics), memory (MemoryEfficiencyMetrics) and diagnostics (a dictionary of named task summaries). Each runner fills these from its own counters; it does not run the record-summary helper or an intervention implicitly.
For example, Key-Door reports successful_stored_key_episode_fraction; Continual reports one_minus_mean_forgetting; Tutor distinguishes mean_episode_effective_hint_read_fraction from pooled_effective_hint_read_fraction. Keep the task producer with the value. The complete task-specific definitions are in Tasks and Benchmarks.
With CLI
Metrics are serialized to JSON via to_dict() methods for CLI output.
Selecting a frontier outcome
make_quality_vs_overhead_points requires the outcome key explicitly. Both that key and the selected cost key must supply finite numbers in every input row. Missing, nonnumeric or nonfinite values fail; an observed zero remains zero. The points retain both metric names. Choose comparable producers and units, with lower cost and higher outcome being better.
The notebook helpers generate_pareto_data(..., y_metric="success_rate") and compute_efficiency_metrics(result, "success_rate") likewise require an explicit outcome. success_rate reads the supplied field; another name reads quality_metrics. An omitted success rate remains absent. No helper silently switches to a different outcome or treats a missing measurement as zero. The efficiency helper's effective_quality multiplies the selected outcome by one minus the probe-episode fraction; that weighting is a calculation, not evidence that probing caused a benefit.
Source map and dependencies

        TaskData["Task Results\n(rewards, etc.)"]

Module Structure
Trace the byte and slot denominators in memory.py, usage and labelled outcomes in record_summary.py, the intervention loop in evaluator.py, and probe cost accounting in probe_costs.py.

Troubleshooting
Event Log Timing: The memory helper drains the buffer itself. Decide which consumer preserves the events before invoking it; a second drain cannot recover them.
Missing Inputs: Inspect each helper branch. Record usage needs no ground truth; the cue-retention and retrieval-fraction branches name their different inputs. Missing labels do not make every field unavailable.
Reward Interpretation: The selected total-reward or mean-return ratio assumes higher outcome is better. Name a cost transformation explicitly rather than silently changing its sign.
Episode Boundaries: set_episode() resets stores and the logger unless the caller selects reset_memory=False; the built-in runners select carry by default. A helper sees current records and retained events, while caller totals may span several episodes. Align those scopes before dividing them.
Memory Efficiency Denominator: The byte helper uses recognized sampled write-event bytes, or current bytes on fallback. Slot efficiency uses current slots. Neither is automatically a whole-run peak or time average.

body:
Reckon Main Module
Use CausalMemoryManager to write observations, retrieve relevant records and update their utility after an outcome. Your task supplies the action policy and reward. The manager decides which records to keep under its memory allowance. The example follows one delayed cue.
The package also supplies benchmark tasks, measurement helpers and a debugger server. Stored utility, attribution and influence-proxy fields support experiments; interpreting a score as a causal effect needs the experiment and its assumptions.
Connect retrieval to an outcome
After building the extension, save this as memory_outcome.py and run it with python memory_outcome.py from the repository root. It stores a delayed cue, retrieves it later and assigns one supplied outcome to the retrieved record.
from reckon import CausalMemoryManager, MemoryBudget, PayloadType
from reckon.core.episode_context import EpisodeContext

memory = CausalMemoryManager(
    MemoryBudget(max_slots=2, max_bytes=1_000),
    episode_id="key-door",
)
memory.set_step(1)
record_id = memory.write(
    payload={"key_room": "A"},
    payload_type=PayloadType.OBSERVATION,
    tags=["key"],
    source_op="observe_key",
)

memory.set_step(5)
with EpisodeContext(episode_id="key-door", step=5):
    hits = memory.retrieve(query={"tags": ["key"]})
    print(hits[0].payload["key_room"])
    credits = memory.observe(outcome=1.0)

record = memory.get_record(record_id)
assert record is not None
print(f"Credits: {len(credits)}, utility: {record.utility.value:.3f}")
print(f"Retained records: {memory.current_usage_slots}")

Expected output:
A
Credits: 1, utility: 0.100
Retained records: 1

At step 1, the task saves the key's room. At step 5, the query finds that record by its key tag and prints A. retrieve() also adds the returned ID to the current EpisodeContext, so the later observe() call knows which record to credit.
There is one retrieved record, so it gets all the credit. Its utility starts at zero; the default moving average keeps 90% of the old value and adds 10% of the credited outcome, giving 0.100. This example supplies the outcome directly. To find out whether the cue helps an agent open a door, connect the calls to a task's observations, decisions and reward, then compare runs with and without the cue. Changing the supplied outcome here only changes the score update.
Keep a context around the retrievals associated with one outcome. Start a fresh context for the next decision, or clear its tracked IDs, so an earlier retrieval does not receive credit again. Memory has a separate lifetime: leaving the context keeps the record. set_episode() resets the stores and logger by default; pass reset_memory=False when the next episode should inherit records, learned scores and retained events. Collect needed events before a reset or before the finite buffer overwrites them.
In your own task, handle an empty retrieval before using hits[0]. Query tags match any requested tag, matches are ordered by utility and the default limit is ten. When the store fills, the retention policy decides which record to remove. Keeping the retrieval and outcome code fixed while changing that policy lets you compare the consequences of different memory choices.
      
Choose a module
If you need to	Use	
Store, query and retain observations	Memory	
Define resources, channels or influence diagnostics	Core	
Add a task or learner	Tasks	
Compute outcomes, probes and costs	Metrics	
Import or stream a saved run	Debugger server	
The architecture guide follows the Python/Rust boundary and the build pipeline.
Follow the implementation
The memory-manager guide owns the write/read paths and the Python/Rust boundary: Python filters queries while Rust retains the live record objects, fixed admission costs, priorities, retention selection and the event buffer. Live cost metadata can change without changing admitted accounting. The architecture guide follows the complete component and build relationships.
Use the generated core and memory API for exact current signatures and docstrings. The reference build uses the selected source and its real extension; authored examples and experiment explanations remain in these guides.
Integration
With Debugger UI
The logger buffers operations. Export and save the events, then import the run or append events through the visualization service. The React timeline reads what the service makes available over REST and WebSocket.
The visualization module owns the import, live registration and streaming interfaces. A displayed event is not proof that the complete source run was exported.
With CLI
reckon run --config reads a YAML or JSON experiment; explicit task, policy, budget and carry/learning flags override it. reckon compare runs a task/policy/budget/seed matrix and keeps individual outcomes beside their spread, peak storage and elapsed time. The reproducibility guide owns the commands, configuration fields and current comparison limits.

Troubleshooting
Dual Storage: Records are stored in both Python (_records dict) and Rust (RecordStore). Ensure both are updated on write/prune operations.
Event Logger Capacity: The ring buffer has fixed capacity (default 10,000). Events are overwritten when full.
Policy Selection: Built-in Python policies call the kernel's shared selector. Python and Rust wrappers can choose different named rankings, including raw utility versus utility per byte. Name the rule in comparisons; a shared policy name does not imply the same ranking. Custom Python policies still implement RetentionPolicy.
Episode Boundaries: Call cmm.set_episode() at episode start to reset state and update logger context.
Step Tracking: Call cmm.set_step() before operations to ensure correct timestamps.

body:
Reckon Python Package
The reckon package connects a task's observations and outcomes to a budgeted record store. Python owns full records, queries and retention decisions; the required Rust extension owns compact storage, indexing and the event buffer. Start with the retrieval/outcome example to wire the API into a decision, or jump to the module overview to find the code responsible for a behavior.
Package Structure
The command-line runner (reckon/cli.py) dispatches tasks. The extension stubs (reckon/_rust.pyi) describe the types Python can import. Examples and tests show how to run and check an integration.
Architecture
flowchart TB
    subgraph Package["reckon Package"]
        direction TB
        Core["core/\n(abstractions)"]
        Memory["memory/\n(CMM)"]
        Tasks["tasks/\n(benchmarks)"]
        Metrics["metrics/\n(evaluation)"]
        Viz["viz/\n(server)"]
        Generated["generated/\n(proto models)"]
    end

    subgraph External["Dependencies"]
        Rust["Rust Extension\n(_rust module)"]
        Protos["Protocol Buffers"]
    end

    Generated --> Protos
    Memory --> Rust
    Memory --> Core
    Tasks --> Memory
    Tasks --> Metrics
    Viz --> Memory

Module Overview
Module	Purpose	Key Classes	
core/	Mathematical abstractions	ResourceVector, MemoryBudget, DirectInfluenceRecords	
memory/	Memory management	CausalMemoryManager, MemoryRecord, RetentionPolicy	
tasks/	Benchmark tasks	BaseTask, KeyDoorTask, BanditTask	
metrics/	Evaluation	PerformanceMetrics, MemoryEfficiencyMetrics, RecordSummaryMetrics	
viz/	Debugger server	FastAPI application, WebSocket routes	
generated/	Proto-generated wire models	betterproto2 dataclasses from .proto files	
Integration Points
Rust Extension
The reckon._rust module provides high-performance implementations:
RecordStore: O(1) lookup, O(log n) pruning
EventLogger: Ring buffer for memory events
Type stubs in _rust.pyi enable IDE support.
Protocol Buffers
Generated betterproto2.Message dataclasses in generated/ come from the protocol sources for records, budgets, influence relations and events. These are wire models. The public memory and resource API uses handwritten dataclasses in record.py and resources.py. Regenerating bindings does not change those public classes or give them automatic Pydantic validation or JSON Schema export; their implemented checks determine validation.

Troubleshooting
Rust Extension Required: The package will not function without the compiled Rust extension. Rebuild after Rust changes using the kernel procedure.
Proto Regeneration: After modifying .proto files, regenerate wire models with python protos/generate_python.py using the optional Python 3.10+ protocol tools. Review any corresponding handwritten public types and conversions separately.
Type Stubs: Keep _rust.pyi synchronized with Rust exports when adding new Python-visible functions.
Circular Imports: The TYPE_CHECKING guard is used throughout to avoid circular import issues between modules.

Related guides
Main Module Guide - Detailed module documentation
Architecture Overview - System design and data flows
Examples - Usage examples
Tests - Test organization

body:
Reckon Tasks Module
Choose a task to study a particular memory challenge, or implement BaseTask to add your own. Each runner receives a memory manager and returns its task-specific results. When testing a retention policy, keep the task settings and seeds matched so you can interpret a difference.

Task Descriptions
Task A: Key-Door Navigation
A grid-navigation task with an early colored-key cue and a later door choice. A wall forces the controller through one of two doors. It reads that episode's cue once, goes right for blue and left otherwise; green does not identify which door opens. An absent cue therefore uses the same fixed left guess. Each query attempt counts as a read, including an empty result. Records can carry across episodes, but each choice asks for the current episode's key. One slot holds that cue through its decision, so this workload checks memory use without necessarily distinguishing retention rankings. The task manual explains the controller and the exploratory comparison's limits.
Property	Value	
Challenge	Retain and retrieve a cue within an episode	
Memory Need	Cue-outcome associations	
Success Metric	Episodes reaching the goal / episodes; mean_return uses the same binary reward	
Reference	docs/09-Tasks-Benchmarks.md	
Task B: Multi-Armed Bandit
A bandit task whose optimal arm depends on a changing hidden mode, with occasional mode indicators. The runner re-reads the retained indicator before choosing an arm. It still prunes stale indicators at tracked switches and when a newer one arrives; each episode reports these task-directed prunes separately from the retention policy. The seed creates separate environment and action streams, so missing memory can increase random exploration without changing modes, indicator arrivals or reward noise in the paired run.
Property	Value	
Challenge	Track mode changes and use the available indicators	
Memory Need	Retained mode indicators used at each arm choice	
Success Metric	mean_regret per step and mean_return per episode; detection lag is in raw_data	
Reference	docs/09-Tasks-Benchmarks.md	
Task C: Continual Learning
A sequence of classification subtasks with rotating decision boundaries. The runner trains a linear classifier, writes misclassified examples and retrieves retained examples for replay.
Property	Value	
Challenge	Catastrophic forgetting	
Memory Need	Examples retained for replay across subtasks within an episode	
Success Metric	Final accuracy averaged over subtasks, and the positive drop from earlier post-training accuracy to final accuracy	
Reference	docs/09-Tasks-Benchmarks.md	
Task D: Interactive Tutoring
A structured simulation of student misconceptions, questions and hints across sessions. It records which hints succeeded for each concept; it is not a dialogue-model evaluation. Each episode has an independently seeded starting student, concept choices and hint choices. Response randomness is assigned to the question index, so skipped hints cannot shift a later question’s draw. Student state and the eligible concepts may still diverge because the hints have different effects.
Property	Value	
Challenge	Reuse concept/hint associations across simulated sessions	
Memory Need	Records of effective hints; the environment maintains its own student state	
Success Metric	Fraction of initial misconceptions cleared, averaged over episodes; an episode with none initially uses one	
Reference	docs/09-Tasks-Benchmarks.md	
BaseTask Interface
All tasks inherit from BaseTask and implement:
Method/Property	Purpose	
name	Human-readable task identifier	
description	Brief explanation of the task	
run(cmm, num_episodes, seed, *, reset_memory=False, learn_utility=True)	Execute task and return TaskResult	
Execution Flow
This schematic shows possible memory operations. Each task owns its schedule; not every step writes, reads and updates a score. By default the four runners carry records, scores and retained events across episodes. reset_memory=True selects empty memory at each boundary. Each episode has an EpisodeContext; retrieval is tracked and the outcome reaches observe(), unless learn_utility=False selects the fixed-score comparison. Both settings appear in raw_data. Task and environment state have their own lifetimes.
flowchart LR
    subgraph Setup["Setup"]
        Init["Initialize task"]
        SetEp["cmm.set_episode()"]
    end

    subgraph Loop["Episode Loop"]
        Step["Execute step"]
        Write["cmm.write()"]
        Read["cmm.retrieve()"]
        Score["cmm.observe()"]
    end

    subgraph Finalize["Finalize"]
        Compute["Compute metrics"]
        Return["Return TaskResult"]
    end

    Init --> SetEp
    SetEp --> Step
    Step --> Write
    Write --> Read
    Read --> Score
    Score --> Step
    Step --> Compute
    Compute --> Return

Integration
Outcome credit
Key-Door reports its final binary reward; Continual reports final mean accuracy; Tutor reports the fraction of misconceptions cleared. Each divides that episode’s supplied outcome among records retrieved in its context. Bandit clears retrieval credit at each arm choice and reports the resulting reward immediately. These are learned utility signals, not measured record-ablation effects. Continual and Tutor label their hand-supplied initial importance in record metadata instead of assigning it as learned utility; Tutor no longer increments utility by a hand-set half point. The importance-only comparison can use that separate input.
With CLI
Tasks are invoked via CLI:
reckon run --task keydoor --episodes 100 --budget-slots 50

The TASKS registry in cli.py maps CLI names to task classes. tasks/__init__.py exports the classes. One CLI invocation runs the selected task; it does not arrange all baseline arms or run record probes.
With Metrics
The four runners construct PerformanceMetrics, MemoryEfficiencyMetrics and a diagnostics dictionary with task-specific names. They do not automatically call the memory or usage/oracle helpers or invoke contract evaluation. Key-Door reports successful_stored_key_episode_fraction; Continual reports one_minus_mean_forgetting; Tutor distinguishes mean episode and pooled effective-hint read fractions. The exact producers and denominators are in Tasks and Benchmarks. Historical runs keep their original keys and source identity.
Keep raw episode data and the producer with each value. A usage association, oracle label and measured intervention contrast establish different things; the metrics guide explains the helper and evaluator paths.

Add a task
Implement name, description and run(cmm, num_episodes, seed, *, reset_memory=False, learn_utility=True). Use the supplied seed to initialize the task's random state. Set the logical step before memory operations, and choose carry or reset explicitly when calling set_episode(). Retained events share the native finite buffer; drain them before they are overwritten.
Keep state outside the manager explicit: a classifier, local belief or environment history can retain information even after CMM pruning. Report the outcome and denominator your runner actually computes. Supply necessary-cue labels only where the task provides them, and use a separate intervention experiment to test a record's contribution.
Source map and dependencies
Architecture
flowchart TB
    subgraph TaskExecution["Task Execution"]
        BaseTask["BaseTask (ABC)"]
        TaskA["KeyDoorTask"]
        TaskB["BanditTask"]
        TaskC["ContinualTask"]
        TaskD["TutorTask"]
    end

    subgraph Dependencies["Dependencies"]
        CMM["CausalMemoryManager"]
        Metrics["Metrics Module"]
    end

    subgraph Output["Output"]
        Result["TaskResult"]
    end

    TaskA --> BaseTask
    TaskB --> BaseTask
    TaskC --> BaseTask
    TaskD --> BaseTask

    BaseTask --> CMM
    BaseTask --> Metrics
    BaseTask --> Result

Module Structure
Implement the BaseTask interface when adding a runner. For a concrete example, trace the cue handling in task_a_keydoor.py or the replay loop in task_c_continual.py.

Troubleshooting
Random Seeds: Always use the provided seed parameter for reproducibility. Initialize RNG at task start.
Episode Reset: The task’s reset_memory option controls CMM state independently of task or environment resets. Carried records keep their original episode identity, while new events use the current episode.
Testing necessity: A record may appear in a successful run without affecting its outcome. Keep counts and labels separate from tests that change the record.
Step Synchronization: Call cmm.set_step() before each memory operation for correct timestamps.
Metric Computation Order: The current runners construct metrics from their own counters. An optional MemoryEfficiencyMetrics.from_cmm() call drains the event log; preserve required events before that consumption and inspect the helper's expected event shape.

Task Descriptions
Task A: Key-Door Navigation
A grid-navigation task with an early colored-key cue and a later door choice. A wall forces the controller through one of two doors. It reads that episode's cue once, goes right for blue and left otherwise; green does not identify which door opens. An absent cue therefore uses the same fixed left guess. Each query attempt counts as a read, including an empty result. Records can carry across episodes, but each choice asks for the current episode's key. One slot holds that cue through its decision, so this workload checks memory use without necessarily distinguishing retention rankings. The task manual explains the controller and the exploratory comparison's limits.
Property	Value	
Challenge	Retain and retrieve a cue within an episode	
Memory Need	Cue-outcome associations	
Success Metric	Episodes reaching the goal / episodes; mean_return uses the same binary reward	
Reference	docs/09-Tasks-Benchmarks.md	
Task B: Multi-Armed Bandit
A bandit task whose optimal arm depends on a changing hidden mode, with occasional mode indicators. The runner re-reads the retained indicator before choosing an arm. It still prunes stale indicators at tracked switches and when a newer one arrives; each episode reports these task-directed prunes separately from the retention policy. The seed creates separate environment and action streams, so missing memory can increase random exploration without changing modes, indicator arrivals or reward noise in the paired run.
Property	Value	
Challenge	Track mode changes and use the available indicators	
Memory Need	Retained mode indicators used at each arm choice	
Success Metric	mean_regret per step and mean_return per episode; detection lag is in raw_data	
Reference	docs/09-Tasks-Benchmarks.md	
Task C: Continual Learning
A sequence of classification subtasks with rotating decision boundaries. The runner trains a linear classifier, writes misclassified examples and retrieves retained examples for replay.
Property	Value	
Challenge	Catastrophic forgetting	
Memory Need	Examples retained for replay across subtasks within an episode	
Success Metric	Final accuracy averaged over subtasks, and the positive drop from earlier post-training accuracy to final accuracy	
Reference	docs/09-Tasks-Benchmarks.md	
Task D: Interactive Tutoring
A structured simulation of student misconceptions, questions and hints across sessions. It records which hints succeeded for each concept; it is not a dialogue-model evaluation. Each episode has an independently seeded starting student, concept choices and hint choices. Response randomness is assigned to the question index, so skipped hints cannot shift a later question’s draw. Student state and the eligible concepts may still diverge because the hints have different effects.
Property	Value	
Challenge	Reuse concept/hint associations across simulated sessions	
Memory Need	Records of effective hints; the environment maintains its own student state	
Success Metric	Fraction of initial misconceptions cleared, averaged over episodes; an episode with none initially uses one	
Reference	docs/09-Tasks-Benchmarks.md	
BaseTask Interface
All tasks inherit from BaseTask and implement:
Method/Property	Purpose	
name	Human-readable task identifier	
description	Brief explanation of the task	
run(cmm, num_episodes, seed, *, reset_memory=False, learn_utility=True)	Execute task and return TaskResult	
Execution Flow
This schematic shows possible memory operations. Each task owns its schedule; not every step writes, reads and updates a score. By default the four runners carry records, scores and retained events across episodes. reset_memory=True selects empty memory at each boundary. Each episode has an EpisodeContext; retrieval is tracked and the outcome reaches observe(), unless learn_utility=False selects the fixed-score comparison. Both settings appear in raw_data. Task and environment state have their own lifetimes.
flowchart LR
    subgraph Setup["Setup"]
        Init["Initialize task"]
        SetEp["cmm.set_episode()"]
    end

    subgraph Loop["Episode Loop"]
        Step["Execute step"]
        Write["cmm.write()"]
        Read["cmm.retrieve()"]
        Score["cmm.observe()"]
    end

    subgraph Finalize["Finalize"]
        Compute["Compute metrics"]
        Return["Return TaskResult"]
    end

    Init --> SetEp
    SetEp --> Step
    Step --> Write
    Write --> Read
    Read --> Score
    Score --> Step
    Step --> Compute
    Compute --> Return

Integration
Outcome credit
Key-Door reports its final binary reward; Continual reports final mean accuracy; Tutor reports the fraction of misconceptions cleared. Each divides that episode’s supplied outcome among records retrieved in its context. Bandit clears retrieval credit at each arm choice and reports the resulting reward immediately. These are learned utility signals, not measured record-ablation effects. Continual and Tutor label their hand-supplied initial importance in record metadata instead of assigning it as learned utility; Tutor no longer increments utility by a hand-set half point. The importance-only comparison can use that separate input.
With CLI
Tasks are invoked via CLI:
reckon run --task keydoor --episodes 100 --budget-slots 50

The TASKS registry in cli.py maps CLI names to task classes. tasks/__init__.py exports the classes. One CLI invocation runs the selected task; it does not arrange all baseline arms or run record probes.
With Metrics
The four runners construct PerformanceMetrics, MemoryEfficiencyMetrics and a diagnostics dictionary with task-specific names. They do not automatically call the memory or usage/oracle helpers or invoke contract evaluation. Key-Door reports successful_stored_key_episode_fraction; Continual reports one_minus_mean_forgetting; Tutor distinguishes mean episode and pooled effective-hint read fractions. The exact producers and denominators are in Tasks and Benchmarks. Historical runs keep their original keys and source identity.
Keep raw episode data and the producer with each value. A usage association, oracle label and measured intervention contrast establish different things; the metrics guide explains the helper and evaluator paths.

Add a task
Implement name, description and run(cmm, num_episodes, seed, *, reset_memory=False, learn_utility=True). Use the supplied seed to initialize the task's random state. Set the logical step before memory operations, and choose carry or reset explicitly when calling set_episode(). Retained events share the native finite buffer; drain them before they are overwritten.
Keep state outside the manager explicit: a classifier, local belief or environment history can retain information even after CMM pruning. Report the outcome and denominator your runner actually computes. Supply necessary-cue labels only where the task provides them, and use a separate intervention experiment to test a record's contribution.
Source map and dependencies
Architecture
flowchart TB
    subgraph TaskExecution["Task Execution"]
        BaseTask["BaseTask (ABC)"]
        TaskA["KeyDoorTask"]
        TaskB["BanditTask"]
        TaskC["ContinualTask"]
        TaskD["TutorTask"]
    end

    subgraph Dependencies["Dependencies"]
        CMM["CausalMemoryManager"]
        Metrics["Metrics Module"]
    end

    subgraph Output["Output"]
        Result["TaskResult"]
    end

    TaskA --> BaseTask
    TaskB --> BaseTask
    TaskC --> BaseTask
    TaskD --> BaseTask

    BaseTask --> CMM
    BaseTask --> Metrics
    BaseTask --> Result

Module Structure
Implement the BaseTask interface when adding a runner. For a concrete example, trace the cue handling in task_a_keydoor.py or the replay loop in task_c_continual.py.

Troubleshooting
Random Seeds: Always use the provided seed parameter for reproducibility. Initialize RNG at task start.
Episode Reset: The task’s reset_memory option controls CMM state independently of task or environment resets. Carried records keep their original episode identity, while new events use the current episode.
Testing necessity: A record may appear in a successful run without affecting its outcome. Keep counts and labels separate from tests that change the record.
Step Synchronization: Call cmm.set_step() before each memory operation for correct timestamps.
Metric Computation Order: The current runners construct metrics from their own counters. An optional MemoryEfficiencyMetrics.from_cmm() call drains the event log; preserve required events before that consumption and inspect the helper's expected event shape.

Related guides
Parent: Main Module
Tasks and Benchmarks Spec
Metrics Module
Memory Module

body:
Python wire messages and RPC
The protocol sources define laboratory records, budgets and events in reckon, and the daemon's five-method API in reckon.core.v1. These historical wire messages are separate from the Rust-owned laboratory model, its PyO3 public-record adapters and the Python resource configuration. Changing a wire declaration does not migrate those adapters automatically. Laboratory scalar token counts retain their original numeric meaning: new nullable counts use the Rust JSON snapshot model, and exporting an unknown count to the historical wire is refused.
The reference build compiles these schemas into a field and RPC reference for documentation assembly. Change the protocol source and its comments; generated reference stays outside Git.
Record origin
RecordOrigin holds the operation that created a record, its input record IDs and its content hash. MemoryRecord.provenance remains field 10, with source_op, repeated input_ids and hash at nested fields 1–3. The field names, repeated-value order and embedded bytes are unchanged. The new type name has no Provenance alias: reflection and any Any type URLs must select reckon.RecordOrigin. A content hash and input list do not establish authorship, rights or a measured causal link.
Read historical summary metrics
reckon.core.v1.RunSummary.metrics uses HistoricalRunMetricsV1. This is the historical v1 summary shape: its field numbers, optional presence, JSON keys and values stay intact. In particular, causal_precision at field 4 and useful_memory_rate at field 5 keep their original labels. Their formulas depend on the producer and source revision; the decoder does not translate them into current task diagnostics or record summaries. Current task and helper metrics are documented in the metrics reference.
The former RunMetrics type has no alias. The qualified descriptor name is now reckon.core.v1.HistoricalRunMetricsV1, so reflection lookups and any external Any type URLs must select that name explicitly; unchanged embedded bytes do not imply type-name compatibility. The historical JSON keys remain camelCase or their original protobuf snake_case inputs. Saved run files are not rewritten. The daemon’s record-only export leaves historical summary metrics absent; it does not synthesize a producer for them.
Install the optional tools
The core library supports CPython 3.9–3.12. Python wire messages, RPC and generation require Python 3.10 or later. The rpc extra pins betterproto2[grpclib] 0.10.0; proto adds compiler 0.10.1, grpcio-tools 1.78.0 and Ruff 0.17.5, which the compiler uses to format its output. These dependencies are unconditional inside their extras: requesting either extra on Python 3.9 fails dependency resolution rather than installing incomplete RPC support. The full extra includes proto and also requires Python 3.10+. Importing the core library does not import these tools.
After building the required extension, use the same environment from the repository root:
python -m pip install ".[rpc]"
# For schema changes and the independent presence tests:
python -m pip install ".[dev,proto]"

Call the local daemon
Start the daemon as described in the repository guide. The generated asynchronous client uses gRPC directly:
import asyncio
from grpclib.client import Channel
from reckon.generated.reckon.core.v1 import (
    CausalMemoryServiceStub, CreditPolicy, IdQuery, ObserveRequest,
    RetrieveRequest, WriteRequest,
)

async def main():
    channel = Channel("127.0.0.1", 50051)
    try:
        client = CausalMemoryServiceStub(channel)
        written = await client.write(WriteRequest(payload=b"observation"))
        retrieved = await client.retrieve(
            RetrieveRequest(by_ids=IdQuery(ids=[written.record_id]))
        )
        observed = await client.observe(ObserveRequest(
            episode_context_id=retrieved.episode_context_id,
            outcome_value=1.0,
            credit_policy=CreditPolicy.SIMPLE,
        ))
        print(observed.credits)
    finally:
        channel.close()

asyncio.run(main())

Probe returns UNIMPLEMENTED until its runner exists. ExportRun returns scoped run observations; set the same run_id on writes and retrievals, then request an explicit scope. Events, metrics and archive flags remain unsupported. Its state is separate from a Python memory manager's state. Use only a trusted local machine; the daemon has no caller authentication.
Generate and check the Python files
With the proto extra installed, activate that environment so the compiler can find Ruff, then run from the repository root:
python protos/generate_python.py
python protos/generate_python.py --check

The script reads the Python plugin options from buf.gen.yaml, compiles all schemas together with the packaged compiler and writes src/reckon/generated/. It refuses to overwrite a layout containing obsolete Python files; review their retirement first. --check compares the complete generated Python file set and bytes without changing the source. Buf can also run the same plugin through (cd protos && buf generate) when both configured Python and TypeScript plugins are installed; that command also regenerates debugger TypeScript output.
The compiler uses packages named by the schemas: reckon.generated.reckon for laboratory messages and reckon.generated.reckon.core.v1 for the daemon API. It also generates a shared message pool. Do not edit generated types by hand.
The migration from the old betterproto output changes Python calls while preserving the protobuf field numbers and RPC paths:
Pass a request object, such as client.write(WriteRequest(payload=...)), instead of keyword fields directly to the method.
Use enum members such as CreditPolicy.SIMPLE and RecordScope.RETRIEVED, without repeating the enum name as a prefix.
Use class methods such as RunExport.parse(data) and RunExport.from_json(text) to construct decoded messages.
Optional fields use None for absence. Explicit 0, 0.0, "" and b"" remain present through binary and JSON serialization.
Run the protocol checks after regeneration:
python -m pytest src/tests/test_proto_conformance.py src/tests/test_proto_presence.py src/tests/test_proto_rpc.py
cargo build --manifest-path daemon/Cargo.toml
RECKON_DAEMON="$PWD/daemon/target/debug/reckon-daemon" python -m pytest src/tests/test_proto_rpc.py

The presence test walks every optional field in the actual compiled schemas and checks its wire presence with Google's independent protobuf runtime. The RPC suite exercises all five generated client/server methods over HTTP/2. The opt-in daemon case checks writes, retrieval, observation and scoped export, plus refused probes and unsupported export attachments over loopback TCP, then stops its own daemon. Without RECKON_DAEMON, that case is reported as skipped. Without the optional dependencies, the protocol modules are reported as skipped so the base-library suite remains usable on Python 3.9.
Retention-policy names
MemoryManagerConfig names the per-byte rule with EVIDENCE_PER_BYTE (enum number 4) and evidence_weight (field 3). The rule uses a supplied ablation effect, then a counterfactual effect, then a proxy only when neither measurement is present. The renamed enum and field preserve protobuf wire numbers and bytes; protobuf JSON now uses RETENTION_POLICY_TYPE_EVIDENCE_PER_BYTE and evidenceWeight. Earlier saved JSON retains its names and must be read with its source revision. The type and field names have no compatibility aliases.

References and Orientation Leads
Find background reading by topic. See the framework overview for the connection to the code.
Arrow of time / Boltzmann entropy / Past Hypothesis
Lebowitz, J. L. "Boltzmann's entropy and time's arrow." Physics Today 46(9):32–38 (1993).
Goldstein, S. Boltzmann's Approach to Statistical Mechanics. Preprint (2001).
Goldstein, S., Tumulka, R., & Zanghì, N. Is the Hypothesis About a Low Entropy Initial State of the Universe Necessary for Explaining the Arrow of Time? Physical Review D 94, 023520 (2016).
Information Theory & Hypothesis Testing
Cover, T. M. & Thomas, J. A. Elements of Information Theory. Wiley-Interscience, 2nd ed. (2006), Chapter 11.
Chernoff, H. "A measure of asymptotic efficiency for tests of a hypothesis based on the sum of observations." Annals of Mathematical Statistics 23(4):493–507 (1952). MONAD's testing exponent cites this work; the mathematical core explains when that result applies.
Inverse problems / well-posedness
Hadamard, J. Sur les problèmes aux dérivées partielles et leur signification physique. Princeton University Bulletin 13(4), 49–52 (1902). On existence, uniqueness and stability.
Open quantum systems / irreversibility as reduction
Lindblad, G. "On the generators of quantum dynamical semigroups." Commun. Math. Phys. (1976).
Records / decoherence / objectivity
Zurek, W. H. "Decoherence, einselection, and the quantum origins of the classical." Rev. Mod. Phys. (2003).
Zurek, W. H. Quantum Darwinism. Nature Physics 5, 181–188 (2009).
Reversibility and fidelity decay
Gorin, T., Prosen, T., Seligman, T. H., Žnidarič, M. "Dynamics of Loschmidt echoes and fidelity decay." Physics Reports (2006).
Learning as stochastic/open dynamics
Mandt, S., Hoffman, M. D., Blei, D. M. "Stochastic Gradient Descent as Approximate Bayesian Inference." (2017).
Representation geometry / graph Laplacians
Belkin, M. & Niyogi, P. Laplacian Eigenmaps for Dimensionality Reduction and Data Representation. Neural Computation 15(6), 1373–1396 (2003).
von Luxburg, U. "A tutorial on spectral clustering." Statistics and Computing (2007).
Delay embedding / observability intuition
Sauer, T., Yorke, J. A., Casdagli, M. "Embedology." J. Stat. Phys. (1991).
Information loss and irreversibility in computation
Landauer, R. "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process." IBM J. R&D (1961).
Bennett, C. H. "Logical Reversibility of Computation." IBM J. R&D (1973).
Lorentz violation constraints (optional branch)
Mattingly, D. "Modern Tests of Lorentz Invariance." Living Reviews in Relativity (2005).
Kostelecký, V. A., Russell, N. "Data Tables for Lorentz and CPT Violation." (arXiv:0801.0287; updated regularly).

body:
Reckon

Reckon, a laboratory for causal records under resource budgets, measures what an agent with limited memory should keep: what changes outcomes for what it costs, with the uncertainty shown. This repository holds its working laboratory: the Python package and command reckon, the Rust crate reckon-kernel, benchmark tasks and a debugger. Reckon belongs to Causality, a research programme of RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited, and Harsh Joshi is its author.
The laboratory is research software under Apache-2.0. It is not published to any package registry.
The problem
Agents have finite memory. What should they remember? Reckon's starting problem is that memory, measurement and intervention are resource-bounded, yet an agent design can leave those limits implicit. What the agent can reliably record and what it can change determine which causal relationships it can detect. The problem and context develops that argument.
The task writes an observation, retrieves records when it needs them and reports an outcome. Reckon tracks which records were returned, assigns them credit and updates their utility through a moving average. When memory fills, the selected retention policy chooses what to discard under byte and slot limits. Learned utility per byte is one policy; oldest first and least recently used supply simple comparisons. The memory manager design explains the choices and the other resource limits still to enforce.
But finding out what caused a difference is not free. A probe runs matched trials with and without a record, reports the difference and its uncertainty, and counts both arms’ episodes and elapsed time. Ablation attribution and influence proxies do not by themselves identify causal effects; every causal interpretation needs its stated intervention, assumptions and controls. The benchmark account keeps the completed comparisons, including a small Tutor gain over learned utility at substantial probing cost. Whether the measurement earns its cost remains a question to test.
A quick example
from reckon import CausalMemoryManager, MemoryBudget, PayloadType, UtilityPolicy
from reckon.core.episode_context import EpisodeContext

# Configure byte and slot allowances
memory = CausalMemoryManager(
    MemoryBudget(max_slots=100, max_bytes=50_000),
    retention_policy=UtilityPolicy(),
)

# Store an observation
record_id = memory.write(
    payload={"observation": "key is in room A"},
    payload_type=PayloadType.OBSERVATION,
    tags=["key", "location"],
)

# Connect these retrieved records to one supplied outcome
with EpisodeContext(episode_id="key-door"):
    hits = memory.retrieve(query={"tags": ["key"]})
    print(hits[0].payload["observation"])
    memory.observe(outcome=1.0)

print(f"Utility: {memory.get_record(record_id).utility.value:.3f}")
# The selected policy removes the lowest utility per byte when space runs out.

This prints key is in room A and Utility: 0.100: one returned record receives all the credit, and the default update blends 10% of its credited outcome with 90% of its previous utility. The outcome is supplied here; the example demonstrates the update, not an agent opening a door or proof that the record helped. A real task supplies its observed outcome. The complete integration guide explains context lifetime, empty retrievals and carrying memory between episodes. Direct update_score() calls can still supply a score explicitly; compare those separately from learned utility. See budget enforcement for write validation and resource limits.
The core idea
The framework studies resource-relative detectable influence: which allowed interventions produce a detectable outcome difference under a memory budget, compute limit and noise floor. A scorer's label or observed difference alone does not establish that relation. This connects information theory (channel capacity) with engineering (memory budgets).
What you get
Component	Description	
Causal Memory Manager	Write, read, score and prune records under budget constraints	
Four benchmark tasks	Key and door, a hidden-mode bandit, continual classification and a tutoring loop	
Debugger	Event timeline, attribution graph and budget-versus-performance frontier	
Framework	The ideas and the design, in docs/	
reckon compare runs declared tasks, policies, budgets and seeds and saves outcomes, spread, storage and elapsed time. The reproducibility guide owns its configuration and the eight notebooks provide worked experiments. The debugger shows saved or live laboratory events; it does not decide which policy to adopt.
Beyond the laboratory
The laboratory runs today for Causality’s research; the problem in front is making Reckon the shared instrument for RTEPL’s agent tools: a way to turn a correction from ordinary work, with permission for that use, into a fixed case, compare a proposed model, skill or policy change against it, and show the outcome, cost and uncertainty to the person who decides. This repository holds the local laboratory and its memory experiments; the services for shared cases, evaluations and decisions are not part of this code. Cases, evaluations and decisions explains them, and the evaluation contract specifies the evaluator.
In the design that path is a learning loop, and in it Reckon has nothing to add without Pale's genealogy, the git history of context: an append-only map of references that shows where work came from, what it relied on and what followed, while each record stays with its owner. Scope writes back to it a pointer to the context it gave each agent, so the chain runs from what an agent was given to what it did and what followed. From that chain Reckon builds interventional and counterfactual traces for Counsel's and SkillOpt's training, each an intervention contrast and not an identified causal effect. None of that path is in this repository, whose memory laboratory runs without genealogy.
Getting started
The library and daemon build from this checkout. MONAD supplies the theoretical definitions described in the manual; the implemented kernel does not call its types or require its source. The commands below assume access to the Reckon repository. Reproducible builds require the selected Reckon revision and dependency lockfiles. The installation guide selects CPython 3.11 explicitly, builds the wheel and checks the extension. The documented CPython range is 3.9–3.12. The PyO3 build targets the abi3-py39 ABI. If you build with a newer interpreter, run the extension import check before relying on it.
git clone https://github.com/getHarshOnline/reckon.git
cd reckon

After completing that installation with its environment active:
# Run a benchmark task
reckon run --task keydoor --episodes 10

Run these commands from the repository root with the supported environment active. For contributor dependencies and pytest, follow Run and extend the tests. Notebook use additionally needs the packages in the notebook guide. For the debugger's separate server and interface terminals, follow Open the debugger. The memory manager chapter explains budgets and retention policies.
The gRPC daemon is a local tool
The daemon/ folder holds a Rust gRPC service, with a TypeScript client in sdks/. It keeps its state in memory and uses plaintext without caller authentication. It defaults to 127.0.0.1 and accepts only loopback addresses. Probe returns UNIMPLEMENTED until an episode runner can measure baseline and intervention trials; ExportRun returns scoped observations from named runs, with explicit refusals for unsupported attachments. Run it on a trusted machine:
(cd daemon && cargo run --release -- --host 127.0.0.1)

--max-slots must be positive. Writes serialize capacity admission and byte accounting; replacing an existing record in the state store uses its existing slot and subtracts its old byte cost. The public Write operation creates a fresh record ID each time. These controls limit the in-memory record count; they do not supply a daemon byte budget or persistence.
--max-contexts also must be positive and defaults to 10,000. A context expires five minutes after creation; reuse does not extend it. Retrieval reclaims expired contexts before admission and returns RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED when every context slot is still live, without touching records or evicting active attribution. Retrievals sharing a live context merge their returned IDs once. Missing or expired retrieval IDs start a fresh context, whose ID is returned to the caller. Observation refuses expired contexts with FAILED_PRECONDITION, or NOT_FOUND if cleanup already removed them. An observation admitted before expiry keeps its attribution snapshot. The daemon also sweeps expired contexts every 30 seconds while the server runs. These limits bound context count, not total attribution bytes.
Never expose it to a network. See SECURITY.md.
The Python wire guide shows the optional asynchronous gRPC client and its generated request types. That path requires Python 3.10+; the core library keeps its documented Python 3.9 support.
Repository structure
To change a memory rule, start in the Python library at src/reckon/. The Rust kernel/ builds through PyO3 and maturin, and protos/ defines the messages shared by those layers.
To inspect a run, open the React debugger in viz-ui/ or use the examples in notebooks/. For local daemon clients, use sdks/ with the gRPC service in daemon/.
For setup, use the installation guide or the optional setup.sh helper. docs/ contains the developer manual, ARCHITECTURE.md explains how the parts connect, and paper/ contains the LaTeX source.
Design goals
Make memory decisions explicit and measurable.
Provide tasks where selective retention is necessary.
Make failures debuggable: what was stored, what mattered, what broke.
Stay laptop-scale: no cloud infrastructure required.
Documentation
Looking for	Read	
Where to start	The manual's front page	
An introduction and experiments to follow	Reckon's product guide	
System architecture	ARCHITECTURE.md	
The memory manager	docs/08-Causal-Memory-Manager-Design.md	
Benchmark tasks	docs/09-Tasks-Benchmarks.md	
Notebooks and demos	notebooks/README.md	
Glossary	docs/13-Glossary.md	
Citation
See CITATION.cff and docs/99-References.md.
Product version
The product version is set in kernel/Cargo.toml. Maturin reads it for Python package metadata, and the required native extension supplies Python's runtime version. The CLI and debugger reuse that runtime value; the daemon reads its own projected Cargo package version.
From a complete checkout, after changing the kernel version, run python tools/sync_version.py --write with Python 3.11 or newer to update the daemon and npm manifests. Run python tools/sync_version.py before building to refuse version drift without changing files. Rebuild the extension when checking the new runtime version. Schema versions and saved runs keep their own identities.
Licence
Reckon is licensed under Apache-2.0: the kernel, the daemon, the Python package, the SDKs and the debugger. Third-party material keeps its own licence and notices.
Related repositories
Repository	Relationship	
MONAD	The formal definitions used by the laboratory manual	
HENA	The swarm; its kernel depends on this one, and its store may speak this laboratory's record protocol	
Q-HENA	The quantum swarm; its kernel depends on this one
